The researchers who studied the remains here called the people buried here the ancestors, and their bones told stories that no written record kept.
Start with the children.
About four in ten of the people found here were children, many of them infants, a sign of how hard life was for enslaved families in the colonial city.
Among the adults, the skeletons showed the marks of brutal labor: enlarged and torn muscle attachments, spines compressed by heavy loads, and joints worn far beyond their years.
Many showed signs of malnutrition and disease.
Some graves hold individual stories.
One young woman, known by the number of her grave as Burial 25, had a musket ball lodged in her rib cage, and her face had been struck with great force.
She seems to have died violently.
Another woman, Burial 340, had front teeth filed into points, a custom in parts of Africa, which suggests she was born there and survived the Middle Passage.
She was buried wearing a strand of glass beads and cowrie shells around her waist.
Most of the dead were wrapped in shrouds held with pins and laid in wooden coffins with their heads to the west.
Some were buried with coins over their eyes or with shells, as offerings.
And on the lid of one coffin, Burial 101, someone had hammered iron tacks into the heart-shaped design that many see as the Sankofa symbol.

Chemical tests of teeth helped show who had been born in Africa and who in New York, and the answer was both: a community of Africans and their New York born children and grandchildren, burying their dead together, outside the town that depended on their work, for about a hundred years.
Long before this was a burial ground, the land north of the Dutch town was farmed by Africans who had won a limited kind of freedom, and their story is one of the most surprising in early New York.
In 1644, eleven enslaved men owned by the Dutch West India Company petitioned for their freedom.
They had worked for the company for close to twenty years, building its fort and clearing its land.
The director, Willem Kieft, granted what historians call half-freedom.

They could live as free people, marry, own land and work for themselves, but they owed the company a yearly payment of grain and a hog, and labor whenever it was demanded, and the grant said their children would remain enslaved.
The company gave these men and others farms on the land north of town, roughly from where you are standing up toward Washington Square, along the road that became the Bowery.
The area became known as the Land of the Blacks.

Their names survive in the records: Paulo Angola, Simon Congo, Anthony Portuguese, Big Manuel and Little Manuel, names that point to Angola, the Congo, and the Portuguese Atlantic world those men had been taken from.
Some historians think the Dutch placed them there on purpose, as a buffer between the town and the Lenape after the bloody wars of the 1640s.
Under English rule, things got worse.
After the revolt of 1712, a new law barred free Black people from owning land, and by then most of the farms had already passed into white hands.
Slavery in the city grew harsher, and this ground, just outside the town, became the place where its Africans, free and enslaved, buried their dead.
Everything around you stands on a lost lake, and the ground still remembers it.
The Collect Pond was fed by underground springs, and next to it rose a hill later called Bunker Hill.
The Dutch called the pond the Kalck Hoek, probably for the heaps of oyster shells on its shore, and the English turned that into the Collect.
By the 1790s, tanneries, breweries and slaughterhouses lined its banks and drained into it.
One plan would have cleaned it up and made it the centerpiece of a park.
Instead, starting around 1811, the city cut down Bunker Hill, dumped the earth into the pond, and filled it in.
The new land was cheap, but it didn't stay put.
Buried springs and rotting fill made cellars flood and buildings sag, and anyone who could afford to leave did.
That's how Five Points began.
The city built its new jail on the filled pond in 1838, a massive building in the style of an Egyptian temple.
New Yorkers called it the Tombs, for its look, and people joked that it was sinking into the old pond, which it was.
Its successor, a few steps north on Centre Street, still goes by the same nickname.
Now a legend.
Across Centre Street is Collect Pond Park, rebuilt in 2014 with a shallow pool to recall the water that was here.
Its history includes a famous story: that in 1796 the inventor John Fitch tested a steamboat on the Collect, years before Robert Fulton's success on the Hudson, while a young Fulton watched.
It's a wonderful story, but it seems to have been published decades later by Fitch's admirers, and no evidence from the time has been found to back it up.
Even the park's own sign says so.
Five Points' reputation comes largely from one book, Herbert Asbury's The Gangs of New York, published in 1928 and later the basis of Martin Scorsese's film.
Asbury was a gifted storyteller.
How well do his stories hold up?
Take the Old Brewery, a former brewery on the edge of the filled pond that had become a crumbling tenement.
Asbury wrote that for fifteen years it averaged a murder a night.
The building was real and wretched, but there's no record of anything like that many murders.
In 1852, a group of Methodist women bought it, tore it down while crowds watched, and built a mission on the site.
The gangs were real too, but not quite the armies Asbury described.
The Plug Uglies were mostly a Baltimore gang.
The Dead Rabbits seem to have been as much a newspaper label as a club.
What is well documented is the Dead Rabbits Riot of July 4th, 1857, when gangs tied to rival political factions fought for two days around Bayard Street, leaving several people dead.
Gangs like these were the street muscle of politics.
They guarded polling places, scared off rival voters, and fought for their patrons, often in the service of Tammany Hall.
The historian Tyler Anbinder, digging through census records, court files and savings bank ledgers, found a different Five Points.
Most residents worked hard at legal jobs, as laborers, seamstresses, shoemakers and peddlers, and Irish immigrants here saved and sent remarkable sums home to their families in Ireland.
Crime and misery were real, but so was a community.
Even Abraham Lincoln came to see it.

In 1860, on the trip to New York that included his famous speech at Cooper Union, he visited the Sunday school at the Five Points House of Industry, a reform mission, and gave a short talk to the children.
In the 1840s, Five Points had a nightlife that drew sailors, slummers and famous visitors, and in one of its dance halls, American dance was being invented.
The best known hall was Almack's, run by a Black proprietor named Pete Williams on Orange Street, now Baxter Street.
It was named, as a joke, after a very exclusive ballroom in London.

In 1842, Charles Dickens was taken there on his tour of the slum, and in his book American Notes he described a young Black dancer whose feet seemed to be everywhere at once, spinning, leaping, shuffling and finishing with a flourish to roars from the crowd.
Most historians believe that dancer was William Henry Lane, known as Master Juba.
Juba was then a teenager, probably born free around 1825.

In 1844 he met John Diamond, a celebrated white dancer from the minstrel stage, in a series of challenge matches billed as contests for the championship, and Juba came away with a reputation as the best dancer of his time.
He is believed to have blended Irish jigs and reels with African American step dancing, and that mix of fast, percussive footwork is counted among the roots of tap dance.
He was also one of the first Black performers to tour with a white minstrel company and get top billing.
In 1848 he went to London, where critics raved.
He died there, still young, around 1852.
The dance halls were rough places, but they were also among the few spaces in the city where Black and Irish New Yorkers, sailors and laborers, drank and danced together.
Respectable New York was horrified, and fascinated, and kept coming downtown to look.
Look around Foley Square and let it tell you a few more stories.
The square is named for Thomas Foley, known as Big Tom, a saloon keeper and Tammany Hall district leader in the early 1900s.
He was the political mentor of Al Smith, the Lower East Side boy who became governor of New York and, in 1928, the first Catholic nominated for president by a major party.
The little park in the middle of the square is named for a very different figure, Thomas Paine.
The courthouse with the gilded pyramid, now named for Thurgood Marshall, has seen some of the most famous trials of the twentieth century.
In 1949, eleven leaders of the American Communist Party were tried here in a trial that lasted most of the year.
Alger Hiss, the State Department official accused of spying for the Soviet Union, was convicted of perjury here in 1950.
And in 1951, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were tried here for passing atomic secrets to the Soviets, convicted, and sentenced to death.
Historians still argue over the case, especially over how much Ethel knew.
Now find the tall black granite sculpture in the middle of the square.
It's called Triumph of the Human Spirit, by the artist Lorenzo Pace, unveiled in 2000.
Its shape comes from a traditional antelope headdress of the Bamana people of Mali, a symbol of farming and work, and it rises from a base that suggests the hull of a ship.
It honors the Africans buried at the African Burial Ground, a block away, and the millions carried across the Atlantic.
Pace has said it was inspired by a family heirloom: a lock and key that had been used on his great-great-grandfather, enslaved in Alabama.
You're now in the heart of old Chinatown, the triangle formed by Mott, Pell, and Doyers Streets.

Chinese immigrants began settling here in significant numbers in the 1870s and 1880s, many coming east after working on the railroads and in the mines of the American West, where violent anti-Chinese movements had made life dangerous.
Then, in 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, the first major federal law to bar immigration by a specific national group.
It wasn't repealed until 1943.
Because of exclusion and related laws, the community remained small and overwhelmingly male for decades.
Most men worked in laundries, restaurants, and small shops, often sending money home to families in southern China, especially from the Guangdong province region around Taishan.
To navigate a hostile country, residents relied on family associations, district associations, and merchant organizations.
The most prominent umbrella group was the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, which acted almost like a local government.

There were also tongs, secret fraternal societies like the On Leong and Hip Sing, which could function as mutual aid societies but also controlled gambling and other rackets, and fought violent wars with each other in the early twentieth century.
Walk down Doyers Street, the short street with the sharp bend in it.
That curve gave it the nickname the Bloody Angle.
During the tong wars of the early 1900s, the curve made it a notorious ambush spot, because you couldn't see who was waiting around the corner.
Today it's quiet, lined with restaurants and barbershops.
One of them, Nom Wah Tea Parlor, has been serving dim sum and pastries on this street since 1920, making it one of the oldest restaurants in Chinatown.
On Mott Street, look for the Church of the Transfiguration, at the corner of Mott and Mosco Streets.
The building dates to 1801.

It was built for an English-speaking Lutheran congregation, which soon became Episcopal, and in 1853 it became a Catholic church that served, in succession, Irish immigrants, then Italians, then Chinese.
In that sense, this one building tells the whole immigrant history of the neighborhood.
After the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 eliminated national-origin quotas, Chinatown grew rapidly, with newcomers from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Guangdong, and later Fujian province.
The garment industry became the neighborhood's economic engine through the 1980s and 1990s, with hundreds of small factories employing tens of thousands of women.
That industry has largely faded, but the neighborhood's restaurants, groceries, and markets remain.

At Chatham Square, where many streets converge, look for the Kimlau Memorial Arch, honoring Chinese Americans who died in World War Two, and the statue of Lin Zexu, the Qing dynasty official famous for trying to stop the British opium trade in the 1830s.
To understand old Chinatown, you have to understand the law that shaped it for sixty years.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred Chinese laborers from entering the country, and later laws tightened it.
Chinese immigrants already here couldn't become citizens.
Only a few groups were exempt, including merchants, students and diplomats, so the community stayed small and overwhelmingly male.
Many men lived for decades with their wives and children on the other side of the Pacific.
People found ways around it.
In 1906, the San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed that city's birth records.
Many Chinese men then claimed to have been born in San Francisco, which made them citizens, and citizens could bring in their children.

Some reported the births of sons who didn't exist, then sold those places to young men in China, who memorized thick coaching books about their new families before facing interrogation by immigration officers.
They were called paper sons.
Many Chinese American families today carry surnames that were bought on paper.
Shut out of most trades, Chinese New Yorkers built businesses where they could, above all hand laundries, thousands of them across the city.
In 1933, the city proposed licensing rules that would have required laundry owners to be citizens, which the law barred most Chinese from becoming, and to post a large bond.
Laundry workers formed their own group, the Chinese Hand Laundry Alliance, hired lawyers, and got the rules softened, an early act of Chinese American civil rights organizing.
Exclusion ended in 1943, when China was an ally in the war, but the new quota allowed only a hundred and five Chinese immigrants a year.
The real change came with the immigration reform of 1965.
Doyers Street's nickname, the Bloody Angle, comes from real violence.
But tong war stories have grown in the telling, so let's sort them out.
The tongs were sworn brotherhoods.
In New York the two biggest were the On Leong, whose stronghold was Mott Street, and the Hip Sing, on Pell Street.
The On Leong boss, Tom Lee, a merchant who had been made a deputy sheriff, was called the Mayor of Chinatown in the newspapers.
His great rival was a young Hip Sing leader known as Mock Duck.
They fought over the neighborhood's gambling halls and other rackets, and over who would collect the payments to protect them.
The worst single attack is well documented.
On August 7th, 1905, during a crowded performance at the Chinese Theatre on Doyers Street, a burst of firecrackers distracted the audience, and gunmen among them opened fire on On Leong men.
At least three people were killed.
A few years later, the theater was turned into a rescue mission.
Now the legends.
Mock Duck was said to wear a shirt of chain mail, and to fight by crouching in the street, shutting his eyes, and firing two pistols in every direction.
Those stories come from reporters and later writers who loved a colorful villain, and they may be partly true.
Then there are the secret tunnels.
You may hear that tong gunmen escaped through tunnels under Doyers Street.
There is a real underground passage at the bend of the street, now a corridor of small shops that leads toward Chatham Square.
But no one has shown that it was a gangsters' escape route.
Truces were signed in the early 1900s, the violence faded by the 1930s, and the tongs settled into life as merchant associations.
Their buildings still stand on Mott and Pell Streets.
Chinatown has been feeding outsiders for well over a century, and its menus are a history of the neighborhood.
The first Chinese food in New York was Cantonese, because nearly all the early immigrants came from the Taishan area of Guangdong.
Around 1900, New Yorkers went wild for chop suey, a stir-fry of meat and vegetables.
A popular legend says it was invented in New York for the Chinese statesman Li Hongzhang, who visited in 1896.
It wasn't.
A similar dish of odds and ends already existed in the Taishan region, and Chinese American cooks were serving it before Li arrived.
But his much-publicized visit helped set off a craze, and chop suey houses spread across the city.
Nom Wah, at the bend of Doyers Street, opened in 1920 as a bakery and tea parlor known for its mooncakes and almond cookies.
It still serves dim sum, the Cantonese meal of small plates eaten with tea.
After 1965, newcomers arrived from Hong Kong, Taiwan, and later Fujian and other provinces, and the menus exploded.

In the 1970s, New Yorkers discovered the fiery cooking of Hunan and Sichuan, and menus filled with General Tso's chicken, a dish created in Taiwan by a Hunanese chef named Peng Chang-kuei and reinvented, much sweeter, in New York.
Fujianese immigrants opened restaurants and markets along East Broadway, and later waves brought hand-pulled noodles and soup dumplings.
As you walk, read the windows.
Roast ducks and strips of red-glazed char siu pork hang in rows.
Tanks hold live fish and crabs.
Bakeries sell egg tarts and pineapple buns, which contain no pineapple at all.
They're named for their crackly sugar crust, which looks like a pineapple's skin.
Every generation that settled here is still on the menu.
Three landmarks around here bookend Chinatown's history.
Look for them as you walk toward the Bowery.
First, at the corner of the Bowery and Pell Street, find the narrow brick house with dormer windows at 18 Bowery.
It's the Edward Mooney House, built in the 1780s by a meat merchant, just after the British left New York.
It is the oldest surviving townhouse in Manhattan, and it has been a store, a hotel, a saloon, a pool hall and a bank.
When it was built, the land around it was still mostly farms.
Second, at Chatham Square, look at the Kimlau Memorial Arch.
Its architect, Poy Gum Lee, was born in New York, spent years working in China, and helped complete the great mausoleum of Sun Yat-sen, the founder of the Chinese republic, in Nanjing.
Back home, he became Chinatown's architect, and the arch, finished in the early 1960s, is his modern take on a traditional Chinese gateway.
It honors Benjamin Ralph Kimlau, a Chinese American bomber pilot killed in the Pacific in 1944, and all the Chinese Americans who died in the war.
Third, the statue of Lin Zexu, the Qing official who tried to stop the British opium trade.
It was put up in 1997 by the Fujianese community, because Lin was from Fujian, and its base reads, in English and Chinese, Pioneer in the war against drugs.
It went up the same year Britain handed Hong Kong back to China, the territory Britain had taken in the Opium War that Lin's crackdown set off.
On the way, notice the red and green balconies and the pagoda-style roofs added to ordinary tenements in the twentieth century.
Some were built with pride, and some to give tourists the Chinatown they expected to see.
End your walk at the corner of Canal Street and the Bowery, at the entrance to the Manhattan Bridge.
Canal Street really was a canal, or at least a drainage ditch.
Around 1805, the city dug a channel to drain the polluted Collect Pond westward to the Hudson River.
It quickly became a stinking, stagnant mess, and by the 1820s it was covered over and turned into a broad street.

Today, Canal Street is one of Manhattan's busiest and most chaotic commercial streets, long famous for its street vendors, jewelry shops, and, notoriously, counterfeit handbags and watches sold out of storefront back rooms.
The Bowery, the street running north from here, is one of the oldest roads in Manhattan, following the path of a Lenape trail.
Its name comes from the Dutch word bouwerij, meaning farm.
Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director of New Amsterdam, had his farm along this road.
We'll talk more about the Bowery on the Lower East Side and East Village tours.
Now look at the monumental arch and the curving colonnades in front of you.
This is the Manhattan entrance to the Manhattan Bridge, which opened in 1909.
The arch and colonnade were designed by the firm Carrère and Hastings, which also designed the New York Public Library.
They were completed in 1915 as part of the City Beautiful movement, which held that grand public architecture could ennoble a city and its citizens.
The arch was modeled on the Porte Saint-Denis in Paris, and the curving colonnades were inspired by Bernini's colonnade at St. Peter's Square in Rome.
Above the arch runs a frieze of a buffalo hunt by Charles Cary Rumsey, and the two pylons carry figures by Carl Augustus Heber representing the Spirit of Commerce and the Spirit of Industry.
The point was to give working-class commuters crossing to Brooklyn a gateway as grand as anything in Europe.
The Manhattan Bridge itself was a technical milestone.
It was among the first suspension bridges designed using deflection theory, a mathematical method that allowed for a lighter, more flexible deck.
That theory later influenced bridges like the Golden Gate.
It also carries subway trains, which is why you may hear a rumble overhead.
If you have energy left, you can walk across the bridge's pedestrian path, which offers great views of the Brooklyn Bridge, and lands in DUMBO, where another tour in this app begins.
Right here at the foot of the Manhattan Bridge, two protests changed how Chinatown saw itself.
Look for the tall brick apartment tower and the statue of Confucius at the corner of the Bowery and Division Street.
That's Confucius Plaza, a big housing complex finished in the mid 1970s.
When it was going up, in 1974, almost none of the construction workers were Asian American, on a project built in the middle of Chinatown.
Young activists formed a group called Asian Americans for Equal Employment and picketed the site for weeks, and some were arrested.
In the end, the contractor agreed to hire Asian American workers.
The group grew into Asian Americans for Equality, still an important organization in the neighborhood.
The statue of Confucius, a gift from the community, came a couple of years later.
The second protest was much bigger.
In 1982, Chinatown had hundreds of garment shops employing around twenty thousand workers, nearly all of them immigrant women, sewing clothes for the fashion industry uptown.
When the shop owners refused to sign the union's new contract, the workers of the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, Local 23-25, took to the streets.
On June 24th, 1982, as many as twenty thousand of them rallied in Columbus Park and marched through Chinatown.
It was one of the largest protests in the neighborhood's history, by women who had often been dismissed as too timid to organize.
Within weeks, the holdout shops signed.
Both protests mark the moment when a neighborhood that had long let old merchant associations speak for it began to speak for itself, in English and Chinese, out in the street.
The Manhattan Bridge looks like a sturdy workhorse, but its design launched a line of ideas that ended in one of the most famous engineering failures in history.
The engineer behind its final design was Leon Moisseiff, an immigrant from Riga who had come to New York as a young man.
Moisseiff championed deflection theory, a mathematical way of working out how a suspension bridge's cables and deck share the load.
It showed that a long, heavy deck didn't need to be as stiff as engineers had assumed, so bridges could be lighter, slimmer and cheaper.
The Manhattan Bridge, opened in 1909, was among the first designed this way, and the approach spread around the country.
Each new bridge pushed it further.
In 1940, a bridge across the Tacoma Narrows in Washington State, built to Moisseiff's design, opened with an extraordinarily thin deck.
In the wind it rose and fell so much that people called it Galloping Gertie.
Four months after it opened, in a wind of about forty miles an hour, it twisted itself apart and fell into the water, all caught on film.
Engineers learned to take aerodynamics seriously, and Moisseiff's reputation never recovered.
The Manhattan Bridge had a problem of its own.
Its subway tracks run along the outer edges of the deck, so when a train crosses, that side dips.
Decades of trains twisted the deck and cracked the steel.
Starting in 1982, the city spent more than twenty years and hundreds of millions of dollars rebuilding it, closing subway tracks for years at a time.
Ride across on the train and you may still feel the deck lean.
Canal Street has been a street of bargains for as long as anyone can remember, and its merchandise tells the story of the city's economy.
For much of the twentieth century, the stretch of Canal west of here was a famous jumble of surplus and hardware shops.
You could buy war surplus, plastic sheeting, electronics, tools, and odd lots of almost anything.
Artists from nearby SoHo shopped here, and the art supply store Pearl Paint, at 308 Canal Street, served generations of painters and students from the 1930s until it closed in 2014.
Closer to the Bowery, Canal became a jewelry district, with rows of small shops glittering with gold.

And by the 1990s, Canal Street was the city's best-known market for counterfeits: fake designer handbags, watches and sunglasses, sold from folding tables and from back rooms behind ordinary storefronts.
Brands sued sellers and even landlords, the police staged raids, and much of the trade moved out of sight and online.
You may still be offered a handbag in a whisper.
Now look at the corner of the Bowery and Canal for the bank building with the dome, at 58 Bowery.

It was built in 1924 for the Citizens Savings Bank, a bank for working people, designed by Clarence Brazer in a style borrowed from the Italian Renaissance, with a dome you can see from far down the street.
It became a city landmark in 2011 and is still a bank.
Buildings like this were meant to promise permanence and safety to small savers, many of them immigrants, who might otherwise have kept their money sewn into a mattress.
Many of the Italians who crowded these streets never meant to stay, and that shaped Little Italy in ways that are easy to miss.
Most came from the poor rural south, where land was scarce and wages were miserable.
Young men crossed the Atlantic to earn money for a few years, often in seasonal work, then went home to buy land or pay off debts.
Italians called them ritornati, the returned.
Americans called them birds of passage.
In some years, nearly as many Italians sailed home from New York as arrived, and something like half of all the Italians who came in those decades eventually went back.
Many of the men who stayed found work through a padrone, a labor broker, usually a fellow countryman who spoke English.
The padrone met new arrivals, found them beds, and sent them out in gangs to dig railroad cuts, lay track, and build tunnels and reservoirs, taking a cut of their pay along the way.
Some were honest, and many were not.
Italian laborers did much of the heavy digging for New York's first subway, and for the aqueducts that bring the city its water.
The village loyalties you heard about went deep.
Immigrants from the same town lived on the same block, married within it, formed mutual aid societies under the name of their hometown saint, and held their own feast days.
Italian had dozens of dialects, and a Sicilian and a Genoese could barely understand each other.
In a real sense, many of these people became Italians in America, by being treated as one group by everyone else.
By the 1920s, families had put down roots, children were born here, and the birds of passage had become Italian Americans.
Around 1900, Little Italy lived in fear of letters marked with a black hand, and the man who fought them became a legend on both sides of the Atlantic.
The Black Hand was a method more than an organization.
A shopkeeper, a banker or a successful family would receive a letter demanding money, signed with a drawing of a black hand, a dagger or a skull.
Those who didn't pay might see their shop bombed or a child kidnapped.
Most of the extortionists were small independent gangs, preying on their own countrymen, and most victims were too frightened to go to the police.
Even the great tenor Enrico Caruso reportedly received a Black Hand letter.
Joseph Petrosino was born near Salerno and came to New York as a boy.
He joined the police in 1883, at a time when there were almost no Italian speaking officers, and rose to detective.

In 1905 he was put in charge of a new Italian Squad, a handful of Italian American detectives who went undercover, worked their own neighborhoods, and sent hundreds of criminals to prison or back to Italy.
In 1909, Petrosino sailed secretly to Sicily to collect criminal records that would let the United States deport Italian criminals who had lied about their pasts.
The secret leaked to the press.
On the evening of March 12th, 1909, he was shot dead in a square in Palermo.
His killers were never convicted.
His funeral back in New York drew a crowd estimated at a quarter of a million people.
Just a few blocks northwest of here, at the corner of Lafayette and Kenmare Streets, a small triangular plaza carries his name: Petrosino Square.
Just north of here, on Spring Street, Lombardi's proudly calls itself America's first pizzeria, licensed in 1905.
It's one of the best-loved origin stories in American food.
How well does it hold up?

The standard version says that Gennaro Lombardi, an immigrant from Naples, got a license to sell pizza in 1905 at 53 Spring Street, and that his shop trained a whole generation of pizza makers, including the founders of famous pizzerias like Totonno's in Coney Island and John's on Bleecker Street.
The training part seems to be true.
The license is the problem.

In 2019, a pizza historian named Peter Regas, after digging through old city records and Italian language newspapers, reported that he couldn't find any such license, and that Lombardi had only arrived in the country in 1904.

He also found ads showing that other Neapolitans were already selling pizza in New York, including a pizzaiolo named Filippo Milone, who appears to have run pizzerias in the neighborhood a few years earlier, possibly including the one at 53 Spring Street that Lombardi later took over.
And there are hints of pizza being sold in New York as far back as the 1890s.
None of that makes Lombardi's pizza any worse.
Its coal oven still turns out the classic New York pie: thin, blistered, and big enough to fold.
But the honest version is that pizza arrived in New York with Neapolitan immigrants, probably in more than one shop, before anyone thought to write down who was first.
The rest of the Italian American table took shape here too.
In southern Italy, meat was a luxury.
In New York, with steady wages, it became everyday food, and dishes like spaghetti with meatballs and veal parmigiana grew out of that new abundance.
The brick wall around this churchyard is wrapped in a story about the most formidable Catholic leader New York ever had.
In the 1840s, Irish Catholic immigrants were pouring into the city, and many native-born Protestants feared them as poor, drunk, and loyal to the Pope rather than to America.
Nativist politicians campaigned against them.
In the spring of 1844, nativist mobs in Philadelphia burned two Catholic churches, and people were killed in the rioting.
New York's nativists, who had just won the mayor's office, planned a large rally, and many expected the churches here to be next.
New York's bishop, John Hughes, was an Irish immigrant who had worked as a gardener before becoming a priest.
People called him Dagger John, partly for the cross he drew before his signature, and partly for his temperament.
Hughes let it be known that if a single Catholic church were burned in New York, the city would become a second Moscow, a reference to the fire that consumed Moscow when Napoleon invaded.
Armed parishioners, by many accounts in the thousands, guarded the churches.
The rally fizzled, and no church burned.
The story usually told here is that men stood guard behind this very wall, with muskets ready.
Hughes's warning is well documented.
Whether the wall was really built as a fortification is less certain, but it certainly served as one.
Hughes went on to become New York's first archbishop.

He founded the college that became Fordham University, built a network of Catholic schools, and in 1858 laid the cornerstone of the new St. Patrick's Cathedral on Fifth Avenue, far uptown in what many people called Hughes's folly.
The city grew right up to it.
Pierre Toussaint, whom you heard about, may one day be New York's first saint, and his life is worth knowing in full.
He was born into slavery in 1766 in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, now Haiti.
In 1787, as revolution brewed on the island, his owner, Jean Bérard, brought him to New York along with a few other enslaved people.
Toussaint was apprenticed to a hairdresser, and he became one of the most fashionable hairdressers in the city, going from house to house to dress the elaborate hair of wealthy women.
Then Bérard's fortune collapsed, and Bérard died on a trip back to the island.
Toussaint, still legally enslaved, used his own earnings to support Bérard's widow for years, paying her bills and keeping up appearances.
Before she died, she freed him, in 1807.
As a free man, Toussaint bought the freedom of his sister and of Juliette Noël, whom he married.
They took in his orphaned niece, and they took in other orphans and young men who needed work.
He gave money to Catholic charities and orphanages, and helped fund the building of this cathedral.
During epidemics of yellow fever, when many who could fled the city, he is said to have nursed the sick in their homes.
He went to Mass every day for some sixty years, at St. Peter's Church on Barclay Street, near today's World Trade Center.
He died in 1853 and was buried here, in the churchyard, next to his wife.
In 1990 his remains were moved to the crypt under the high altar of the Fifth Avenue cathedral, a place usually reserved for archbishops.
In 1996, Pope John Paul the Second declared him Venerable, a step on the road to sainthood.
Beneath this church is something almost nobody expects to find in Manhattan: catacombs.
When the cathedral was built, its basement was laid out with burial vaults, and its churchyard with graves.
For decades, prominent Catholic families bought vaults here: merchants, politicians, and some of the church's early bishops.
The most famous family down there is the Delmonicos, whose restaurant invented fine dining in New York; about twenty members of the family are buried in their vault.
The burial rooms run in narrow brick corridors lined with marble plaques, lit, on the candlelight tours that the parish began offering in recent years, by flickering lamps.
Then there's the bishop under the door.
John Dubois, New York's third Catholic bishop, was French-born, and he never won over his largely Irish flock.
The story goes that he asked to be buried beneath the entrance, so that the people who had walked all over him in life could keep doing it after his death.
It's a good story, and the bishop is indeed said to lie near the front door, but the famous line about being walked over may be a later embellishment.
The churchyard outside the wall is one of the oldest Catholic burial grounds in the city.
Its graves stopped taking new burials in the 1800s, as the city banned burials in lower Manhattan for health reasons and moved the dead to big new cemeteries in Brooklyn and Queens.
That's why the Catholic dead of later generations lie in Calvary Cemetery, in Queens, and why this patch of old trees and leaning stones feels like a time capsule.
If you take one of the catacomb tours, look closely at the names on the vault doors.
They are a who's who of early Catholic New York.
In the 1840s, the Bowery gave American popular culture its first great urban hero, and twenty years later it took one of its greatest songwriters.
The hero was Mose.

He was a Bowery B'hoy, as they said it, a working class young man in a red flannel shirt and a tall hat, with his hair slicked into curls called soaplocks, a volunteer fireman who loved a fight and loved his girl, Lize.
Mose first appeared on stage in 1848, in a play called A Glance at New York, and audiences went wild.
The actor Frank Chanfrau played him in sequel after sequel.
Mose was brash, funny, loyal and proud, and the real Bowery boys in the audience saw themselves.
He was the ancestor of every streetwise New York character since, from the Dead End Kids to sitcom cab drivers.
The songwriter was Stephen Foster, the author of Oh!
Susanna, Camptown Races, and Beautiful Dreamer, the most famous American composer of his time.
Foster sold his songs outright for small sums and earned little from their success.
By the early 1860s, he was living alone in New York, drinking heavily and selling songs for a few dollars each.
In January 1864, in a cheap hotel on the Bowery, he fell in his room and was badly hurt.
He died a few days later at Bellevue Hospital, at the age of thirty seven.
In his pocket was a worn purse with thirty eight cents and a scrap of paper on which he had written five words: dear friends and gentle hearts.
It may have been the start of a song.

The Bowery's reputation was summed up by a hit song of 1891, called simply The Bowery, which warned that they say such things and they do strange things on the Bowery, and ended, I'll never go there anymore.
For nearly eighty years, an elevated railway ran above the Bowery, and when it came down, it took a promise with it.
The Third Avenue El was finished over the Bowery in 1878.
Its tracks covered almost the whole width of the street, dropping ash, oil and noise on the sidewalks below.
Rents fell, and the Bowery filled with the businesses that cheap rents attract: pawnshops, saloons, and lodging houses.
By the early twentieth century, the Bowery had dozens of flophouses that could sleep thousands of men a night.
The cheapest spaces were cubicles a few feet wide, with walls that stopped short of the ceiling and chicken wire stretched over the top, rented for a few cents a night.
The men who lived here were not all drunks.
Many were laborers between jobs, seamen ashore, old men on tiny pensions, and veterans.
During the Depression, the Bowery's missions served huge breadlines, and after World War Two, the street became the national symbol of men who had fallen through the cracks.
In 1955, the El was torn down, and light fell on the Bowery for the first time in generations.
The city had promised a replacement: a new subway under Second Avenue, first planned back in 1929.
Money for it was raised in a bond issue in 1951, and then spent on other projects.
Construction finally started in the 1970s, and stopped during the city's fiscal crisis, leaving sealed tunnel sections buried in East Harlem and downtown.
Only in 2017 did the first piece of the Second Avenue subway open, on the Upper East Side.
Down here, the promise is still waiting.
Walk a few blocks north along the Bowery, and two buildings tell the story of how the street went from skid row to art destination.
At the northwest corner of the Bowery and Houston Street, look for the big painted wall.
In 1982, the young artist Keith Haring painted a mural there, a riot of his dancing cartoon figures.
It was soon painted over.
In 2008, a developer who owned the wall had Haring's mural recreated, and since then the wall has been repainted every few months by street artists from around the world.
Whatever is on it today is a temporary exhibition, and you're seeing it for a limited run.
A little farther north, at 190 Bowery, at the corner of Spring Street, stands a heavy granite bank building from 1898, built for the Germania Bank.
For decades it looked abandoned, its doors and walls thick with graffiti.
In fact, it was a home.

In 1966, the photographer Jay Maisel bought the whole building, six floors and about seventy rooms, for around a hundred thousand dollars, and lived and worked there with his family for nearly fifty years, letting the graffiti accumulate outside.
In 2015, he sold it for about fifty five million dollars, which says everything about what happened to the Bowery and to New York real estate in between.
On the way, notice how many restaurant supply stores still line the street, with stacks of pots and steel tables on the sidewalk.
And look up at the facades.
Above the storefronts, many buildings still carry the cornices and window decorations of the 1800s, from the years before the El darkened the street.
The Tenement Museum doesn't tell history through famous people.
It tells it through the families who actually lived in this building, and a few of their stories are worth knowing before you go in.
In 1869, an Irish couple, Joseph and Bridget Moore, lived here with their children.
That year, their infant daughter Agnes died of malnutrition.
The Moores had come from a country devastated by famine and found poverty here too, and anti-Irish prejudice everywhere.
In 1874, during the depression that followed the Panic of 1873, a German Jewish shoemaker named Julius Gumpertz walked out one morning and never came back.
His wife, Nathalie, raised their children alone, working as a dressmaker in the apartment, and years later, she won an inheritance from her husband's family in Germany and moved her family uptown.
In the 1890s, Harris and Jennie Levine ran a small garment shop in their apartment, with several workers sewing in the same rooms where the family ate and slept.
It was a sweatshop in the literal sense: home and work in one hot, crowded space.
In 1918, a Lithuanian Jewish family, the Rogarshevskys, lost the father, Abraham, to tuberculosis, the great killer of the tenements.
And in the 1930s, during the Great Depression, a Sicilian Catholic family, the Baldizzis, lived here until the landlord evicted everyone in 1935.
Their daughter Josephine, who grew up in the apartment, came back decades later to help the museum recreate it, remembering where the furniture stood and how her mother cooked.
Together, these families tell the American story in one stairwell: different languages, the same narrow rooms, and the same hope of moving out and up.
Look up at the buildings on Orchard Street, and with a little knowledge you can read how they were built and lived in.
Almost every tenement here sits on a standard city lot, twenty five feet wide and a hundred feet deep.
Builders covered as much of it as the law allowed.
A typical building of the 1860s like number 97 had four apartments on each floor, two in front and two in back, with a narrow staircase up the middle.
In each apartment, only the front room had windows to the outside.
The bedrooms in the middle were dark.
Water at first came from a pump in the backyard, and the toilets were outhouses back there too.
Over the decades, laws forced upgrades: a cold water tap in each hallway, then, in the early 1900s, toilets in the hallways, shared by two families.
Bathtubs were rare.
People went to the public baths that the city built after 1900, some of which still stand around here.
Look at the fronts of the buildings.
The iron fire escapes were required by law after the 1860s, and families used them as balconies, places to sleep on hot summer nights, and shelves for laundry and food.
Up at the top, the decorative cornices of pressed metal were bought from catalogs and bolted on to make cheap buildings look prosperous.
Many facades also have stone or cast decorations around the windows, chosen from builders' pattern books.
The ground floors were usually shops or saloons, often a few steps down from the street, and the cellars held workshops, storerooms, and sometimes more people.
At number 97, a German family named Schneider ran a beer saloon in the basement for years in the 1860s and 1870s, and the museum has rebuilt it.
It was a place to drink, eat, cash a paycheck, and hear the news from home.
In May 1902, the women of the Lower East Side went to war over the price of meat, and they wrote a new chapter in American protest.
The trigger was a sudden jump in the price of kosher beef, from about twelve cents a pound to eighteen, blamed on the big meat packers.
For families who already lived on the edge, it meant no meat at all on the Sabbath table.

On May 14th, a group of neighborhood women, led by two housewives named Fanny Levy and Sarah Edelson, met near Pike and Monroe Streets and agreed: nobody would buy kosher meat until the price came down.
The next morning they took to the streets.
Women organized door to door, patrolled the butcher shops, and stopped other women from buying, sometimes by pulling meat out of their hands and throwing it into the street.
Some shop windows were broken.
Newspapers reported crowds in the thousands, and police arrested dozens of women.
The boycott spread to Brooklyn, Harlem, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia.
The women formed a committee, held mass meetings in synagogues, and pressed rabbis to back them.
By early June, prices had come down somewhat, and the boycott ended.

Historians see it as a dress rehearsal for what came next on these streets: the rent strikes of the early 1900s, the great garment strikes, and the idea that immigrant women, without votes or money, could organize and win.
The tactics they invented, from picket lines at shop doors to neighborhood committees, would be used again and again.
If the museum is open, go inside and climb to the main sanctuary.
Here is what to look for.
At the far end, on the east wall facing Jerusalem, is the ark, the great carved cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept, with a lamp burning before it.
In the middle of the room is the bimah, the raised platform where the Torah was read aloud, so that the reading happened in the midst of the congregation rather than at the front.
Look up and around.
On three sides runs the women's balcony.
In Orthodox practice, men and women prayed separately, and the women's gallery let them see and hear everything from above.
The walls and ceilings are painted with stenciled patterns, and in places, painted marble and painted woodwork imitate costlier materials that the congregation couldn't afford.
The brass chandeliers were built to burn gas and were later wired for electricity.
Then look down.
Near the old wooden pews, the floorboards are worn into shallow hollows.
Guides here will tell you they were worn by the feet of generations of men swaying as they prayed, the traditional motion called shuckling.
Whether every hollow came from prayer, or some from simple foot traffic, it's hard to stand there and not imagine the crowds of 1900.
Finally, turn around and face the rose window above the entrance.
When light comes through Kiki Smith's window of stars, it fills the back of the sanctuary with blue.
The restorers decided to leave some of the old damage visible, a patch of original paint here, a worn surface there, so that the building shows its age honestly.
It's not a replica of 1887.
It's a survivor.
One of the surprises of the Eldridge Street Synagogue is who designed it: two Catholic brothers from Germany.
Peter and Francis William Herter were young immigrant architects who had designed only a few buildings in the city when the congregation hired them in 1886.
They had never designed a synagogue.
They went on to a long career, mostly designing the very kind of building that surrounds this one: tenements, many of them still standing on the Lower East Side.

For the synagogue, they drew on a style that was hugely popular for synagogues in Germany and Central Europe in the nineteenth century: the Moorish Revival, with horseshoe arches, stripes and geometric ornament borrowed from the Islamic architecture of Spain.

Great synagogues in Berlin, Vienna and Budapest had been built in this style, and so had New York's Central Synagogue on Lexington Avenue, finished in 1872 for a congregation of established German Jews.
For a Jewish congregation, the style did several things at once.
It set the building apart from Christian churches, it recalled Jewish life in medieval Spain, and it announced, with all its towers and finials, that this congregation was here to stay.
But look closely at the facade and you'll see the Herters mixed their sources freely.
The rose window is Gothic, the arches Moorish, and the round-arched windows Romanesque.
Architects of the time weren't worried about purity.
They wanted a building that would stand out on a street of plain brick tenements and make a statement.
They succeeded: more than a century later, this building still stops people on the sidewalk.
The world that built this synagogue was proud, pious and divided, and one day in 1902 shows all three.
In 1888, a group of Orthodox congregations on the Lower East Side brought a famous scholar from Vilna, Rabbi Jacob Joseph, to be the chief rabbi of New York's Orthodox Jews.
They hoped he would bring order to a chaotic religious scene, especially in the supervision of kosher meat.
It went badly.
When the rabbi's backers tried to pay for supervision with a small fee on kosher meat, many immigrants resented it, other rabbis refused to accept his authority, and the effort fell apart.
Rabbi Joseph spent his last years ill and poor.
When he died, in July 1902, the neighborhood gave him one of the largest funerals New York had ever seen.
Tens of thousands of mourners followed his coffin through the streets.
As the procession passed a big printing press factory on Grand Street, workers there threw scrap metal and other objects from the windows and sprayed the crowd with water.
When mourners fought back, the police waded in, and many officers beat the mourners instead of the attackers.
Around two hundred people were hurt.
The Jewish community was outraged, and for once it was united.
Mass meetings demanded justice.
The mayor appointed an investigating committee, which criticized the police harshly.
Historians see the riot as a turning point.
It showed the Lower East Side's Jews that they needed to organize politically to protect themselves, and they did, with organizations, voting blocs and leaders who could stand up to City Hall.
You're at Seward Park, at the corner of Essex Street and East Broadway.
Opened in 1903, it's often cited as the first permanent, municipally built public playground in the United States.
Reformers argued that children of the tenements had nowhere to play but the street, and that parks with organized play would make them healthier and keep them out of trouble.
On opening day, crowds of children reportedly swarmed the playground.
Now look at the tall building across the street at 175 East Broadway, with ornate carvings and the name FORWARD across the top.
This was the headquarters of the Jewish Daily Forward, known in Yiddish as the Forverts.
It was founded in 1897, and under its legendary editor, Abraham Cahan, it became the most widely read Yiddish newspaper in the world.
At its peak in the 1920s, it had a circulation of around a quarter million copies.
The Forward was socialist, pro-union, and passionately engaged in teaching immigrants how to become Americans.
It ran English lessons, advice on etiquette and hygiene, and serialized fiction by writers including Isaac Bashevis Singer, who later won the Nobel Prize.

Its most famous feature was the Bintel Brief, meaning a bundle of letters, an advice column where readers wrote in with their problems: husbands who had abandoned them, children who refused to keep kosher, dilemmas of love, work, and faith in a new country.
It's one of the great primary sources of immigrant life.
Look closely at the facade.
Above the entrance, there are relief portraits of socialist figures, including Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels.
Today the building has been converted into luxury condominiums, which says something about how far the neighborhood has traveled.
Nearby on East Broadway is the Educational Alliance, a settlement house founded by established German Jews to help the newer Eastern European arrivals assimilate.
It offered classes, libraries, art lessons, and a gym.
Among the young people who passed through it were artists and performers who went on to shape American culture.
The garment unions also had deep roots here.
The International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, founded in 1900, drew much of its strength from Jewish and Italian women working in shops on these streets.
In 1909, tens of thousands of shirtwaist makers went on strike in what became known as the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand.
Two years later, the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, which you'll hear about on the Greenwich Village tour, killed one hundred forty six workers, many of them young women from this neighborhood.
The Forward was the voice of the Lower East Side, and for nearly half a century it was the voice of one man, Abraham Cahan.
Cahan was born in 1860 near Vilna, in the Russian Empire, and fled to America in 1882 as a young radical with the police on his trail.
He learned English fast, taught it to other immigrants, and began writing in both languages.
His novella Yekl, a story of a Jewish immigrant couple pulled apart by Americanization, was turned many decades later into the film Hester Street.
His novel The Rise of David Levinsky, about a poor immigrant who becomes a rich garment manufacturer and finds himself empty inside, is still read as one of the great immigrant novels.
As editor of the Forward from the early 1900s, Cahan made a radical choice: he wrote in plain, everyday Yiddish, the language people actually spoke, rather than the formal Yiddish of intellectuals.
He mixed socialism with practical advice, gossip with literature, and he understood that an immigrant newspaper's job was to help readers live in America.
He also gave the paper its home.
The ten-story Forward Building went up in 1912, towering over the tenements of East Broadway.
Its facade carries four portraits of socialist thinkers: Marx and Engels, whom you heard about, and the German labor leaders Ferdinand Lassalle and Wilhelm Liebknecht.
Cahan ran the paper into the 1940s and died in 1951.
The Forward moved uptown in 1974.
A Chinese church owned the building for years, and then it became apartments.
The newspaper itself survived, shrinking, and today it publishes online in English and Yiddish.
The garment strike of 1909 began with a young woman pushing her way to a stage, and it changed the American labor movement.

Clara Lemlich was a Ukrainian Jewish immigrant in her early twenties who worked in the shirtwaist shops, where young women sewed the fashionable blouses of the era for long hours and low pay, often paying for their own needles and thread and being fined for mistakes.
She had already been beaten on a picket line by thugs hired by her employer.
On November 22nd, 1909, the union held a mass meeting at Cooper Union.
Speaker after speaker, many of them men, urged caution.
Then Lemlich climbed onto the platform and spoke in Yiddish.
She said she was a working girl, one of those on strike against intolerable conditions, that she was tired of talk, and that she moved for a general strike.
The hall erupted.
The next day, thousands of workers walked out, and within days, the strike had grown to some twenty thousand, maybe more, mostly young Jewish and Italian women.
They picketed through a freezing winter.
Hundreds were arrested.
Wealthy women, including the banker's daughter Anne Morgan and the suffragist Alva Belmont, joined them, raising money and showing up at night court.
Newspapers called these supporters the mink brigade.
By February 1910, most shops had settled, with shorter hours and better pay, and the union's membership soared.
But some of the biggest shops, including the Triangle Waist Company, refused the demand for safer conditions.
A year later, the Triangle fire killed one hundred forty six workers.
Clara Lemlich spent the rest of her life organizing, for suffrage, against high rents, and for the cause of working people.
A few blocks south of here, on Henry Street, a young nurse from Rochester changed the way America takes care of its poor and its children.
In 1893, Lillian Wald was teaching a home nursing class on the Lower East Side when a little girl led her to a tenement where the girl's mother lay sick in a filthy room.
Wald later said that this was her baptism of fire.
She and a fellow nurse, Mary Brewster, moved into the neighborhood to live among their patients.
With money from the banker Jacob Schiff, she opened a house at 265 Henry Street, which became the Henry Street Settlement.
Wald's nurses went into tenements to care for the sick at home, charging little or nothing.
To save time and avoid endless stairs, they often traveled from building to building across the rooftops.
Wald coined the term public health nurse for what they did.
She pushed the city to put nurses in the public schools, and the experiment worked so well that school nursing spread across the country.
She had an eye for causes.
She campaigned against child labor and was among those who first proposed a federal Children's Bureau, created in 1912.
She championed playgrounds like Seward Park, supported unions and women's suffrage, and opposed America's entry into the First World War.
The settlement started a theater, the Neighborhood Playhouse, and music classes that grew into a music school.
The Henry Street Settlement still operates today, out of the same row of houses, and the Visiting Nurse Service that grew out of Wald's rooftop nurses is still caring for New Yorkers at home.
The foods that made this neighborhood famous each have a story, and a few have a legend attached.
Pastrami came from Romania and Moldova, where pastrama was a way of preserving meat, often goose or mutton, by salting, seasoning and drying it.
In New York, cheap beef took over.
Brisket or navel is cured in brine for weeks, rubbed with pepper and coriander, smoked, then steamed until tender.
A popular story says a butcher named Sussman Volk introduced pastrami to New York in 1888, after a Romanian friend gave him the recipe in exchange for storing his luggage.
It's a nice tale, and impossible to confirm.
Pickles were everywhere.
Barrels of sour and half-sour cucumbers sat on the sidewalks of Essex and Orchard Streets, and pickle men sold them from the brine with their bare hands.
A few pickle sellers still carry on, and every fall the neighborhood holds a pickle festival.
Bagels came with the Jews of Poland.
For much of the twentieth century, New York's bagels were made by hand by a small union of Jewish bakers, who guarded their trade fiercely and often passed their jobs down from father to son.
Machines eventually broke their hold.
And then there's the egg cream, a fizzy drink of milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup, containing neither egg nor cream.
Nobody knows where the name came from.

A candy store owner on Second Avenue named Louis Auster is often credited with inventing it in the 1890s, but there are rival claims and rival theories, including one that the name is a garbled Yiddish phrase.
Pick one of each, and you have a Lower East Side lunch that has barely changed in a century.
The street names around here are a map of history, if you know how to read them.
Before the Revolution, much of this land was the farm of the De Lancey family, wealthy merchants and politicians.
James De Lancey sided with the British, and after the war, New York State confiscated his estate and sold it off in lots.
His name survives anyway, on Delancey Street, and so does his orchard, on Orchard Street.
Rivington Street is named for James Rivington, who printed the leading Loyalist newspaper in British-occupied New York.
There's a twist.

Historians have long suspected that Rivington was secretly passing information to George Washington's spies, and after the war, he stayed in New York unharmed, which suggests that someone was protecting him.
Then look at the streets between the Bowery and Allen Street: Chrystie, Forsyth, Eldridge and Allen.
They were named in 1817 for young American officers who died in the War of 1812, a war now mostly forgotten, which once mattered enough to rename a neighborhood.
Houston Street, as you heard, honors William Houstoun, and New Yorkers still pronounce it his way.
Kenmare Street, a few blocks west, was named for the Irish hometown of the mother of Big Tim Sullivan, the Tammany boss of the Bowery.
Even the neighborhoods have invented names.
SoHo, south of Houston, was coined by a city planner in the 1960s.
Nolita, north of Little Italy, came from real estate agents in the 1990s.
And Loisaida, the Puerto Rican name for the Lower East Side, was spread by the poet Bimbo Rivas in the 1970s.
Ludlow Street, the narrow street beside Katz's, has had more lives than most streets in the city.
At its southern end, near Broome Street, stood the Ludlow Street Jail, a county jail for debtors and civil prisoners.
Its most famous inmate was Boss Tweed, who died there in 1878.
The jail closed in the 1920s, and a high school was built on the site.
In the tenement years, Ludlow Street was as crowded as any in the neighborhood, lined with shops on the ground floors and sweatshops above.
In the 1960s, its cheap, run-down apartments drew a different kind of immigrant: young artists and musicians.

In 1965, the Welsh viola player John Cale shared an apartment at 56 Ludlow Street, and that's where he and a young songwriter named Lou Reed rehearsed with friends and began forming the Velvet Underground, one of the most influential rock bands ever.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, Ludlow Street became one of the centers of a downtown scene of small bars, galleries and music clubs, with names like Max Fish and Pianos, where bands played to a few dozen people and sometimes went on to fame.
Today, the street's mix is typical of the new Lower East Side.
A hundred-year-old tenement may hold a cocktail bar on the ground floor and expensive apartments above, next to a new glass hotel, across from a shop that has sold the same goods for decades.
Walk its length, and you pass through a century and a half of the neighborhood's history in about five minutes.
The man who built this market was the most popular mayor in New York history, and almost nothing about him was typical.
Fiorello La Guardia, whose first name means little flower, was born in Greenwich Village in 1882, but grew up mostly in Arizona, where his father was an army bandmaster.
As a young man, he worked at American consulates in Hungary and in the port city of Fiume, then came back to New York and worked as an interpreter at Ellis Island while studying law at night.
He spoke Italian, Yiddish, German and Croatian, and he campaigned in all of them.
He was short, loud and tireless, a Republican who backed Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal and fought Tammany Hall.
Elected mayor in 1933, he served three terms.
He smashed slot machines with a sledgehammer for the newsreels, chased gangsters out of the city's markets, rebuilt parks and bridges with federal money, and gave his name eventually to an airport.
During a newspaper delivery strike in 1945, he read the Sunday comics aloud on the city's radio station, doing the voices himself, so the children wouldn't miss them.
The pushcarts were one of his targets.
He thought they were unsanitary, chaotic and a traffic hazard, and he also wanted to give vendors a better life.

His answer was a string of enclosed public markets, with stalls, running water and refrigeration: this one on Essex Street, opened in 1940, La Marqueta in East Harlem under the railroad viaduct, and the market on Arthur Avenue in the Bronx, which is still the heart of the Bronx's Little Italy.
Some vendors hated leaving the streets.
But the markets lasted, and several of them still operate.
The Williamsburg Bridge was built fast and cheap, nearly burned before it opened, and nearly fell apart eighty years later.

Its chief engineer, Leffert Buck, had built bridges across canyons in South America, and he designed this one for heavy traffic: two tracks for elevated trains, two for trolleys, roadways and walkways.
To save money and time, he used steel towers instead of masonry ones, and a stiff, boxy truss to carry the deck.
Critics hated how it looked.
But it opened in 1903 as the longest suspension bridge in the world.
In November 1902, with the cables in place, a fire broke out in the wooden scaffolding at the top of the Manhattan tower.
Crowds watched it burn from the streets below, and engineers feared that the heat would ruin the cables.
The fire burned itself out, the damaged wires were checked and repaired, and the bridge opened a year later.
The bridge's real problem came later and more slowly.
The cables had been made of wire that wasn't galvanized, without a protective coating of zinc, and over the decades, water and salt went to work.
By the 1980s, inspectors found cables badly rusted and steel beams rotted through.
In April 1988, the city closed the bridge to cars and trains, at a moment's notice, fearing it could not safely carry them.
Some engineers argued it should be torn down and replaced.
Instead, the city rebuilt it, piece by piece, over many years, while keeping it partly open.
Today the bridge carries the J, M and Z trains, cars, and some of the busiest bike lanes in the country.
Walk or bike up its long ramp and you'll understand why: the view of Manhattan from the top is worth every step.
In 1959, one of the greatest jazz musicians in the world disappeared from the scene, and he could be found, if you knew where to look, on the walkway of the Williamsburg Bridge.
Sonny Rollins was already a star of the tenor saxophone, with acclaimed albums behind him, when he decided he wasn't good enough.
He stepped away from performing and recording to work on his playing.
He lived in an apartment on Grand Street, near here, and he worried that practicing for hours a day would disturb his neighbors, including a woman who was expecting a baby.
So he took his horn up onto the bridge.
For about two years, day and night, in all kinds of weather, Rollins practiced on the walkway, high above the East River, with the subway trains rumbling past.
He said later that the bridge was the perfect place: he could play as loud as he wanted, and the noise of the trains and boats pushed him to play bigger.
Passersby occasionally stopped to listen.
Most had no idea who he was.
When he came back, in 1962, he named his comeback album The Bridge.
It's considered one of the great records of its era.
Rollins played into his eighties and became one of the last living giants of his generation of jazz.
So as you walk up the bridge's ramp, imagine the sound of a tenor saxophone floating over the rumble of the trains.
You're near the corner of West Houston Street and West Street, beside the long, massive building that stretches south along the river.
This is St. John's Terminal, and if you work at Google New York, you may know it well from the inside.
The name goes back to St. John's Park, which once existed a few blocks south of here.
In the early 1800s, Trinity Church built a grand chapel, St. John's Chapel, and laid out a private, fenced square around it, modeled on London's elegant residential squares.
It became one of the most fashionable addresses in the city.
But in 1867, Trinity sold the park to Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt, who paved it over and built a giant freight terminal for his Hudson River Railroad.
The chapel was demolished in 1918.
The fashionable families had already fled uptown.
Trains used to run down the middle of the West Side streets, at street level.
Tenth Avenue, in Chelsea, was nicknamed Death Avenue because of the number of people killed by freight trains.
In the 1930s, the New York Central Railroad built the West Side Improvement Project, which lifted the trains onto an elevated viaduct.
That viaduct is what we now know as the High Line.
Its southern end was right here: freight trains rolled directly into the second floor of this building, which opened in 1934, so that goods could be unloaded straight into storage.
As trucking took over, the rail line was cut back.
The southern portion, including the connection to this building, was demolished in the early 1990s.
If you look at the building's north end, you may notice where the old rail tracks once entered.
In recent years, Google acquired and rebuilt the terminal as a major office, adding new floors above the old freight structure.
It's part of a broader reinvention of Hudson Square.
The neighborhood, much of which is still owned by Trinity Church's real estate arm, was the printing district for most of the twentieth century.
The big industrial buildings with heavy floors, built to hold the weight of printing presses, now hold offices for media and tech companies.
The Walt Disney Company has also built its New York headquarters a few blocks south.
As you head south, you'll pass the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, which opened in 1927 under the Hudson River to Jersey City.
It was the first mechanically ventilated underwater vehicle tunnel in the world.
Its chief engineer, Clifford Holland, died during construction, possibly from the stress and exhaustion of the job, and the tunnel was named after him.
Huge ventilation buildings on both sides of the river exchange the air inside the tunnel every ninety seconds.
You heard how Trinity Church sold St. John's Park to Cornelius Vanderbilt in 1867.
Here's what became of the pieces.
Start with the chapel.
St. John's Chapel was finished in 1807, designed by the brothers John and Isaac McComb, with a columned portico and a tall steeple rising over the park.
It stayed even after the park became a freight yard, though its congregation dwindled.
In 1892, Trinity's leaders announced plans to tear it down, and the remaining parishioners rebelled, joined by New Yorkers who simply loved the building.
Their pastor, Philip Brown, led the holdouts until his death in 1909.
It was one of the city's earliest fights to save a historic building.
In the end, the street won.
When the city widened Varick Street for the new subway, the chapel's portico stood in the way, and the whole building came down in 1918.
If you ride the 1 train, look for the mosaics in the Canal Street station that remember it.
Then the depot.

Vanderbilt's freight depot went up in 1868, and the next year he unveiled a monument New Yorkers never forgot: an enormous bronze sculpture across the front of the building, crowded with steamships, locomotives and scenes from his career, with a statue of the Commodore himself standing in the middle.
It was designed by Albert De Groot, who had once captained one of Vanderbilt's steamships, and sculpted by Ernst Plassmann.
Critics found it ridiculous: a monument a man had raised to himself, on top of a freight shed.
The statue outlived the depot.
In 1929, it was moved to Grand Central Terminal, the family's grandest monument, where it still stands on the south side of the building, above Park Avenue.
The depot was later torn down, and its land became the exit plaza of the Holland Tunnel.
When you see cars pouring out of the tunnel and around the traffic circle a few blocks south of here, you're looking at the ground where the city's most exclusive park once stood.
Much of the ground around you belongs to a church, and that church is one of the great landlords of New York.
Trinity's fortune began in 1705, when Queen Anne granted the parish a large farm on Manhattan's west side, land that had passed from the Dutch to the English crown.
Over the next two centuries, the city grew over it.

Trinity sold some of the land, gave some away for other churches and for King's College, which became Columbia University, and leased much of the rest on long leases, collecting ground rent while others built.
In the early twentieth century, the city cut through the neighborhood.
Seventh Avenue was pushed south, Varick Street was widened, and the subway was dug underneath.
Trinity and its neighbors put up big, heavy loft buildings, and printers filled them.
For decades, the presses here turned out magazines, books, catalogs, stock certificates and phone books, and typesetters, binders and paper merchants clustered around them.
When printing moved away, the area was rebranded in the 1990s as Hudson Square, after the old park.
Trinity pushed for a rezoning, approved by the city in 2013, that allowed apartments alongside offices.
Then, in 2015, the church went into partnership with an unexpected investor: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, which invests that country's oil money.
The fund paid about one and a half billion dollars for a stake of nearly half in eleven of Trinity's office buildings here.
So as you walk south, you're crossing land granted by an English queen to a church, now shared with a Norwegian oil fund and filled with tech companies.
Look at the buildings as you go.
Many still have their freight elevators, loading docks and huge steel-framed windows, built to light the press rooms.
The rents pay for Trinity's churches, programs and charitable grants, as the land has done for more than three hundred years.
The Holland Tunnel was one of the great engineering feats of its time, and it cost the lives of the two men who first led it.
When construction began, in 1920, no one had ever built a long underwater tunnel for cars.
The hard part wasn't the digging.
It was the air.
Car exhaust carries carbon monoxide, and in a tube more than a mile and a half long, with thousands of cars passing every hour, drivers could be poisoned.
The engineers worked with the United States Bureau of Mines and with scientists from Yale University, who tested the gas on volunteers to learn how much people could safely breathe.
Their answer was a new kind of ventilation: fresh air blown in through ducts beneath the roadway, and foul air drawn out through the ceiling, around the clock.

The digging itself was done by sandhogs, who pushed huge steel shields through the mud beneath the river, working in compressed air to hold back the water, and lined the tunnel behind them with rings of cast iron.
The chief engineer, Clifford Holland, was thirty six when he took the job, and he drove himself without rest.
In 1924, worn out, he went to a sanatorium in Michigan to recover, and died there of a heart attack at forty one, just before the two halves of the tunnel were due to meet under the river.
His successor, Milton Freeman, died of pneumonia a few months later.
A third engineer, Ole Singstad, finished the job, and went on to build the Queens Midtown and Brooklyn Battery Tunnels.
The tunnel opened in November 1927.
Before any cars were let in, about twenty thousand people walked through it, for the thrill of strolling under the Hudson.
It was named for the man who didn't live to see it, and the ventilation system his team designed became a model for road tunnels around the world.
This firehouse looks perfectly proportioned, but you're looking at only half of the building that opened here in 1903.
When Ladder 8 moved in, the firehouse was twice as wide, with two big doors, and the rigs were pulled by horses.
In the firehouses of that era, the horses lived in stalls on the ground floor, behind the apparatus, and the firefighters slept upstairs, ready to slide down a brass pole.
When the alarm bell rang, the horses were trained to step out of their stalls and take their places in front of the rig, where harnesses hanging from the ceiling dropped onto their backs.
A good company could be rolling in moments.
Then came the subway.
Around 1913, the city widened Varick Street for the new line being dug beneath it, and the firehouse was in the way.
Rather than move the company, the fire department cut the building down to fit.
The half nearest Varick Street was taken down, a new wall went up along the new sidewalk, and the front you see on North Moore Street, with its single big door, is the half that survived.
The same street widening doomed St. John's Chapel, a few blocks north.
The horses didn't last much longer.
The department replaced them with motor rigs through the 1910s, and in 1922, the last horse-drawn engine in the city made its final run, in Brooklyn, with a ceremony to mark the end of an era.
The firehouse itself has been well looked after.
In the late 2010s it was renovated for about six million dollars, while Ladder 8 spent about three years in a firehouse in SoHo.
Then the company moved back home, and its rig still squeezes out of that single door onto North Moore Street, to answer calls all over lower Manhattan.
In 1984, a comedy about three scientists who lose their university jobs and go into business catching ghosts made this firehouse one of the most famous buildings in the world.
In the film, the three buy a run-down old firehouse for their headquarters.
Dan Aykroyd's character, Ray, falls in love with it and slides down the pole, and the team parks their converted 1959 Cadillac ambulance, the Ecto One, in the bay.
Here's a movie secret.
Only the outside was filmed here.
Most of the interior scenes were shot in Los Angeles, in an old downtown firehouse that had been taken out of service, Fire Station 23, which fans still visit on the West Coast.
The movie also caught a real moment in New York.

In the 1970s, during the city's fiscal crisis, the fire department shut down companies across the city, and lower Manhattan was full of empty industrial lofts that a team of oddballs could rent for very little.
Under the jokes, Ghostbusters is a movie about downtown real estate.
The firefighters here have made peace with their fame.
Inside, they display half of an actual sign used in the sequel, Ghostbusters Two, from 1989.
When Harold Ramis, who played Egon, died in 2014, they hung a Ghostbusters sign outside in his memory.
And in 2021, a fan group from Buffalo raised money for a new, weatherproof copy of the famous logo, a ghost inside a red circle with a slash through it, and gave it to the firehouse.

If you'd like more of the movie's New York, it opens at the main library on Fifth Avenue at Forty Second Street, with its stone lions, and Sigourney Weaver's character lives in the grand apartment building at 55 Central Park West, where the film's final battle takes place on the roof.
You heard that Tribeca is short for Triangle Below Canal.
The story behind the name is odder than it sounds.

In the early 1970s, during a fight over zoning, the residents of one small, triangle-shaped block just south of Canal Street, between Church Street and Broadway, formed a group they called the Triangle Below Canal Block Association.
They soon shortened that to the Tribeca Block Association.
Other accounts credit city planners with the name.
Either way, by the mid 1970s it was in print, and it had spread to the whole district, west to the river and south to Chambers Street.
That area isn't a triangle at all.
It's a lopsided four-sided shape.
The name stuck anyway.
The artists who moved into Tribeca's empty warehouses mostly lived there illegally, in buildings zoned for manufacturing.
