In 1982, the state passed the Loft Law, which protected tenants who had moved into commercial lofts and required landlords to bring the buildings up to the code for homes.
It let many of the pioneers stay, but it couldn't stop the neighborhood from changing around them.
Preservationists, meanwhile, went to work on the buildings themselves.
In 1991 and 1992, the city created four historic districts here, Tribeca West, East, North and South, protecting hundreds of the warehouses and stores you're walking past.
That's why these streets still look much as they did a century ago, even as lofts with eighteen foot ceilings sell for tens of millions of dollars.
Real estate agents have been trying to repeat the trick ever since, inventing names for every corner of the city.
A few, like Nolita, for North of Little Italy, have caught on.
Most fade away.
Tribeca lasted, partly because it sounds good, and partly because the people who lived here embraced it.
Picture this neighborhood at four in the morning around 1900.
You'd hardly be able to move, and you'd smell the market before you saw it.
Wagons, and later trucks, jammed every street.
Dealers sold by the crate and the barrel to grocers, hotel chefs, restaurant owners and pushcart peddlers, who loaded up before dawn and fanned out across the city.
There were mountains of oysters and clams, barrels of apples, crates of oranges and bananas off the ships, butter and cheese from upstate farms, and live chickens by the thousands.
In the nineteenth century there was also an enormous trade in wild game.

A butcher named Thomas De Voe, who kept a stall at the Jefferson Market in Greenwich Village, published a book in 1867 called The Market Assistant, describing everything sold in the markets of New York and other eastern cities.
It lists venison and bear meat, wild turkeys, ducks and geese, and a long list of small birds, robins among them, sold by the dozen.
It's a picture of a time before game laws, when almost anything that ran, flew or swam could end up on a New York table.
Some dealers specialized in a single thing: eggs, or poultry, or turtles and terrapin for the rich soups that fancy restaurants served.
Many of these businesses were family firms, handed down for generations.
The market was also a mess.
Food spoiled in the gutters, carts and trucks blocked the streets for hours, and each middleman along the way added to the price.
For decades, reformers argued that New Yorkers paid more for their food because of it, which is part of why the city finally moved the trade to the Bronx.

Look around for the clues that remain: metal canopies over the sidewalks, where crates were stacked out of the rain, loading platforms at the height of a wagon bed, and the names of old food companies, still carved or painted on the buildings.
Walk to the corner of Harrison and Hudson Streets and look for the red brick building with the tower over its entrance.
It was the home of a market that grew from butter and eggs into oil.
In 1872, dairy merchants in this district founded the Butter and Cheese Exchange of New York, so they could trade under agreed rules, grades and prices.
Eggs were soon added, and in 1882 the exchange took a grander name: the New York Mercantile Exchange.
In the mid 1880s it moved into this building, designed by Thomas Jackson in a style called Queen Anne, and traders shouted their bids on the floor inside for about ninety years.
For much of the twentieth century, the exchange's biggest business was potato futures: contracts to buy or sell Maine potatoes at a set price on a set date.
Then, in 1976, traders who had sold contracts for May potatoes failed to deliver them, the largest default the futures markets had ever seen.
The scandal nearly ruined the exchange.
It survived by reinventing itself.
It left this building for the new World Trade Center, and began trading contracts on heating oil, and then, in 1983, on crude oil.
That crude oil contract became one of the most closely watched prices on earth.
When you hear on the news that the price of oil rose or fell, it's often the price set by a market that began with butter, a few steps from where you're standing.
In 2008, the exchange was bought by its great rival, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
Its old home here has been converted to new uses, but look up at the tower over the Harrison Street entrance, recently restored with a new copper spire.
It's a monument to the butter and egg men.
You heard that Duane Park was once part of a farm owned by a Dutch woman named Annetje Jans.
For nearly two centuries, people claiming to be her heirs tried to take that farm back.
Annetje Jans came to New Netherland around 1630 with her first husband, Roelof Jansen.

In 1636, the Dutch governor granted them a farm of about sixty two acres, just outside the little town of New Amsterdam, along the shore of the Hudson, beginning near today's Warren Street and running north toward Canal Street.
After Roelof died, Annetje married the minister of the Dutch church, Everardus Bogardus, and the land became known as the Domine's farm, the minister's farm.
She died in 1663.
In 1671, her heirs sold the farm to the English governor, Francis Lovelace.
All of them signed the deed, except the family of one son, Cornelius Bogardus, who had died a few years before.
That missing signature was the seed of the legend.
The farm passed to the English crown, and in 1705 Queen Anne granted it to Trinity Church.
As the city grew over it, the land became some of the most valuable on earth, and Annetje's descendants multiplied into thousands of families across America.
Many grew up hearing that they were the rightful owners of lower Manhattan, cheated out of their inheritance by a church.
They went to court again and again.
In 1749, one descendant simply moved onto part of the old farm, and lost when Trinity took him to court.
Another case, begun in 1830, dragged on until 1847 before it was dismissed.
Trinity won every time, in part because the church had held the land openly for so long.
Still the legend lived on, and through the nineteenth century, promoters collected money from hopeful descendants to pay for new lawsuits.
So the legend is checked: no court ever accepted the heirs' claim.
But the story is true in another way.
Annetje Jans's farm really is under your feet, and Trinity's fortune really did grow from it.
Western Union was the most powerful communications company in America for half a century, and the most famous story about it is almost certainly made up.
The company grew in the 1850s by buying up and merging small telegraph lines.
In 1861 it completed the first telegraph line across the continent, and two days later, the Pony Express, which had carried mail on horseback across the West, announced it was shutting down.
Western Union carried news for the papers, orders for the railroads, and stock prices for brokers.
A young Thomas Edison worked as a telegraph operator, and later invented machines for the company.
Now the story.
In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell's backers are said to have offered his telephone patent to Western Union for a hundred thousand dollars, and to have been turned down.
A memo is often quoted, supposedly from a Western Union committee, saying that the telephone had too many shortcomings to be seriously considered as a means of communication.
That memo is almost certainly a fake.
It surfaced decades later, and no one has ever found an original.
There may have been an informal offer, and Western Union certainly didn't buy the patent.
But the company wasn't blind to telephones.

It quickly hired Edison and others to build telephones of its own and went into the business, until 1879, when it settled a patent lawsuit with Bell's company and agreed to leave telephones to Bell, in return for a share of the rental fees.
Western Union carried on with telegrams for another century.
It introduced the singing telegram in the 1930s, and grew into a business that sends money around the world.
It sent its last telegram in 2006.
Its old headquarters at 60 Hudson Street still hums with wires, but the messages passing through them now belong to the internet.
Look up as you walk around here and notice what you don't see: telephone poles and overhead wires.
Their absence has a story.
By the 1880s, the streets of lower Manhattan were a tangle of wires.

Telegraph companies, telephone companies, stock ticker services, fire alarm systems and the new electric light companies each strung their own lines on their own poles, some of them as tall as ninety feet and carrying dozens of crossbars.
On some streets the wires were so thick they darkened the sky.
The most dangerous were the high voltage lines for the new electric arc lights.
The state ordered the wires buried in the 1880s, but the companies dragged their feet.
Then the Blizzard of 1888 brought down poles and wires all over the city.
And in October 1889, a Western Union lineman named John Feeks was electrocuted while working high on a pole at Centre and Chambers Streets, near City Hall.
His body hung in the tangle of wires above a horrified crowd.
That was the end of the poles.
Mayor Hugh Grant sent crews with axes to chop down the poles of companies that wouldn't comply.
The wires went into underground conduits, which New Yorkers called subways years before the trains took that name.
One of the companies formed to build and run them, the Empire City Subway Company, founded in 1891, still manages the conduits for telephone and internet cables under Manhattan's streets.
When fiber optic cables arrived a century later, many of them were pulled through those same old ducts.
That's part of why buildings like 60 Hudson Street became internet hubs.
The paths under these streets lead to them, as they once led to the telegraph headquarters.
So every manhole cover you pass is a door into another city below, full of copper, glass fiber and history.
Three of the finest Art Deco buildings in lower Manhattan were built for the companies that carried words and voices, and one architect designed all three.
Ralph Walker was a young designer at the firm of McKenzie, Voorhees and Gmelin when the New York Telephone Company asked for a new headquarters in the early 1920s.

His Barclay Vesey Building, finished in 1926 beside today's World Trade Center, was the first skyscraper to treat the city's new zoning rules, which made tall buildings step back as they rose, as a chance for drama instead of a burden.
It's often called one of the first Art Deco skyscrapers.
Then came 60 Hudson Street for Western Union, finished in 1930, with the brickwork you heard about, shading from dark to light as it rises.
And a few blocks north of here, at 32 Avenue of the Americas, Walker enlarged an older building and gave it new fronts for AT&T's long distance service, finished in 1932.
If you have a few minutes, walk up and look into its lobby, which is an official city interior landmark.
One wall holds a tiled map of the world, its continents separated by oceans but tied together by lines of wire, under the words: Telephone wires and radio unite to make neighbors of nations.

Overhead is a glittering ceiling of glass mosaic by Hildreth Meière, the artist who covered the banking hall at One Wall Street in red and gold, with figures of the continents and messengers linked by golden lines.
It's an office building, so you may only be able to look in from the door.
Walker was proud and opinionated.
Frank Lloyd Wright, who admired very few architects, reportedly called him the only other honest architect in America.
In 1957, when the American Institute of Architects turned one hundred, it created a special award for him, and The New York Times called him the Architect of the Century.
Today he's half forgotten, but his telephone palaces are still here, still full of wires.
You heard that Robert Moses wanted to run an expressway along Broome Street, a few blocks south of here.
Here's how close it came.
The Lower Manhattan Expressway was first proposed in the early 1940s, and for years it was official city policy.
As planned in the 1960s, it would have been ten lanes wide, much of it raised above the streets, slicing across the island.
Estimates at the time said it would displace about two thousand families and some eight hundred businesses, many of them small manufacturers employing thousands of workers.
The buildings on this street would have stood in its shadow, if they survived at all.

The opposition was a patchwork: families in Little Italy and on the Lower East Side, small business owners, churches, preservationists, artists quietly living in lofts, and the writer Jane Jacobs, who had already fought Moses in Greenwich Village.
In April 1968, at a state hearing on the plan, Jacobs and other protesters rushed the stage, and the stenographer's tape was torn up and scattered.
Jacobs was arrested and charged with inciting a riot, among other things.
The charges were later reduced.
In 1969, Mayor John Lindsay, who had once supported the road, withdrew his backing, and a couple of years later the expressway was finally wiped off the city's plans.
Without the highway hanging over it, the neighborhood could finally plan a future.
The city legalized artists' lofts in 1971, and in 1973 the cast iron district was protected.
If Moses had won, you might be standing beside a wall of concrete pillars, in the roar of trucks.
Instead you're on one of the most beautiful streets in America.
You heard that firefighters called this district Hell's Hundred Acres.
Here's why, and how that reputation nearly doomed it.
The cast iron fronts made the buildings look solid, but behind them most had wooden floors and joists, and they were packed with bales of cloth, paper and rags.
When a fire took hold, iron columns could crack when cold water from the hoses hit them, and whole fronts could come down.
Firefighters learned to keep their distance.
The deadliest fire came on March 19th, 1958, at 623 Broadway, a few blocks east of here.
Flames trapped workers at the Monarch Underwear Company on the upper floors.
The building had no sprinklers, and twenty four people died, a short walk from the site of the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, nearly half a century later.
Mayor Robert Wagner called for laws requiring sprinklers in loft buildings, and the city tightened its rules.
Fires like that gave the district's critics ammunition.
In 1962, a civic group, the City Club of New York, published a report called The Wastelands of New York City, which described this area as a commercial slum, ready to be cleared.

But when the city asked a planner named Chester Rapkin to study the district, he found something else: hundreds of small businesses employing thousands of workers, in jobs that depended on cheap space near the center of the city.
His 1963 report helped make the case against tearing it all down.
Rapkin is also credited with the district's nickname: SoHo, for South of Houston.
So the district survived its reputation.
Today almost every building on this street has sprinklers and fire escapes, and the hundred acres are among the most valuable in the world.
Stand on Greene Street and look for the details most shoppers walk right past.
Start at your feet.
The street is paved with Belgian blocks, rectangular granite paving stones laid to stand up to iron wagon wheels and heavy loads.
People call them cobblestones, but true cobblestones are rounded stones from riverbeds.
Look at the vault lights in the sidewalk, the small round glass lenses set in iron plates.
Many have turned a pale purple.
That's because the glass contained manganese, which slowly turns violet after decades in the sun.
Now look at the bottoms of the iron columns on the building fronts, just above the sidewalk.
Many carry small raised plates with the names and addresses of the foundries that cast them, names like Cornell, or Badger's Architectural Iron Works, cast right into the building like a signature.
Then walk to the corner of Prince Street and look at the wall of 112 Prince Street that faces Greene Street.
Count its windows, columns and cornices.
Almost all of them are paint.
In the mid 1970s, the artist Richard Haas painted that blank brick wall to match the building's real cast iron front around the corner, with more than fifty painted windows.
Look for the painted cat in one of them.
The architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable called the mural a triumph.
It was Haas's first outdoor mural, and after four decades of weather it was carefully repainted, and rededicated in 2024.
That wall sums up SoHo: artists making something beautiful out of a blank industrial wall, in tribute to the buildings they had come to love.
The man who made skyscrapers possible was a tinkerer who never lived to see one.
Elisha Graves Otis was born on a farm in Vermont in 1811 and drifted through many trades: wagon driver, mill builder, wagon and carriage maker, and inventor of small machines.
In 1852 he was working as a master mechanic at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, just north of the city, when he had to work out how to move heavy equipment to the upper floors.
Hoisting platforms were common, but workers feared them, because when the rope broke, the platform and everything on it fell.
His answer was simple and brilliant.
He fixed a wagon spring to the top of the platform, attached to the hoisting rope.
As long as the rope pulled taut, the spring stayed bent.
If the rope snapped, the spring straightened and pushed two catches outward into toothed rails on either side of the shaft, locking the platform in place.
He started a small business making safety hoists, and in 1854 he took one to the Crystal Palace exhibition, on the site of today's Bryant Park, for the famous demonstration you heard about.
Otis died in 1861, at forty nine, only four years after the Haughwout elevator went in.
His sons, Charles and Norton, built up the company.
Otis elevators went into hotels, stores and office towers across the country.

In 1889 the company built elevators that climb the curving legs of the Eiffel Tower, and in the twentieth century, Otis elevators carried people up the Empire State Building and the original World Trade Center.
The safety elevator changed how buildings were valued, too.
Before elevators, the best rooms were on the lower floors, and the top floors went to servants and the poor, who had to climb.
After elevators, the top floors became the most desirable of all.
The penthouse is, in a sense, an Otis invention.
In the 1850s, this stretch of Broadway was the most fashionable shopping street in America, and the stores along it helped invent the way we still shop.

It began a little south of here, at Broadway and Chambers Street, where an Irish immigrant named Alexander Turney Stewart opened his Marble Palace in 1846: a huge store faced in white marble, often called the first department store in America.
Stewart sold an enormous range of goods under one roof, at fixed prices, with no haggling, behind big plate glass windows.
It was a place where respectable women could spend a day shopping on their own.
Stewart became one of the richest men in the country.
Rivals soon lined Broadway north into SoHo.
Lord and Taylor and Brooks Brothers both had stores at Broadway and Grand Street, a block south of here.
Tiffany and Company was a couple of blocks north, at 550 Broadway, with a carved wooden figure of Atlas holding up a clock over its entrance.
That Atlas clock moved uptown with the company, and it still stands over the door of its flagship on Fifth Avenue.
Just across Broadway and up the block stood the St. Nicholas Hotel, opened in 1853, one of the most luxurious hotels in the world, with hundreds of rooms and marble and gilding everywhere.
And Haughwout's sold fine china, silver and glass.

In May 1861, the new first lady, Mary Todd Lincoln, came to New York on a shopping trip to refurnish the White House, and ordered a state dinner service of French porcelain, decorated by Haughwout's with a wide border in a fashionable purplish pink called solferino, around the arms of the United States.
Pieces of it survive in the White House collection and in museums.
The shopping district kept moving north.
By the 1870s, the big stores had moved up to Ladies' Mile, near Union Square, and SoHo became a district of wholesalers and warehouses.
It took a century for the shoppers to come back.
Stand across Broadway from the Haughwout Building and give it a slow look.
It repays the time.
The architect was John Gaynor, and most historians credit the iron to Daniel Badger's Architectural Iron Works.

Notice how one unit, an arched window framed by small columns and set between larger columns, repeats across the Broadway front and down the long Broome Street side, dozens of times, floor after floor.
That repetition was the whole point of cast iron.
Once the molds were made, every additional window was cheap.
In Venice, the library it imitates was carved from stone.
Here, the iron was painted to look like stone, so that shoppers would see a palace, not a factory product.
Now find the big clock on the Broadway side.
Stores of the time liked to put clocks on their buildings, as a public service and an advertisement at once.
Look closely at how it writes the number four.
Most clocks with Roman numerals use four strokes, I I I I. This one uses the proper Roman form, I V.
Then look at the windows themselves.
The iron could carry the building's weight on slender supports, so most of the front is glass, letting daylight deep inside.
That mattered in a store whose customers were examining fine china and crystal, decades before electric light.
The building had a hard twentieth century.
The store moved out, the iron rusted, and some of the ornament was lost.
It was one of the first buildings the city protected under its new landmarks law, in 1965, and in the early 1990s, its iron fronts were carefully restored.
And remember what's inside: the place where the first safe passenger elevator went into service, in 1857, the first step toward the skyscrapers uptown.
The Singer sewing machine was a model of reliability.
The life of the man behind it was anything but.
Isaac Merritt Singer was born in upstate New York in 1811, left home as a boy, and spent years as a touring actor and a part-time machinist.
In 1850, in a Boston machine shop, he was asked to look at a sewing machine that didn't work well.
In about eleven days, he redesigned it, with a needle that moved straight up and down, an arm that held the needle over the cloth, and a foot to hold the fabric in place.
He patented it in 1851.
The sewing machine business quickly became a war of patents, with Singer, Elias Howe and others suing each other.
In 1856, they settled it in a new way: they pooled their patents and shared the fees, so that all of them could keep making machines.
It's often called the first patent pool in American business.
Singer's private life was a scandal even by the standards of the time.
He kept several families at once, with different women, sometimes under different names, and fathered about two dozen children.
When the scandals became public, his partner Edward Clark, a proper lawyer, insisted that Singer step back from the company, and Singer moved to Europe.
He built a mansion in Paignton, on the English coast, and died there in 1875, very rich.
Now a legend.
Singer's young widow, Isabella Boyer, a striking Frenchwoman, is often said to have been the model for the face of the Statue of Liberty.
The sculptor, Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, never said who posed for it, and many historians think the face is closer to his own mother, Charlotte.
So the Isabella story is a nice one, but unproven.
SoHo's great gallery era is mostly over, but two works of art from it are still here, and they're among the strangest and most wonderful things in New York.
The first gallery in SoHo was Paula Cooper's, which opened on Prince Street in 1968 with an exhibition that raised money for the movement against the Vietnam War.
Leo Castelli followed in 1971, as you heard, and through the 1970s and 1980s, SoHo was where artists showed new work, from minimalism and conceptual art to the big paintings of the 1980s boom.
On Saturday afternoons, West Broadway was crowded with collectors.
Now the survivors.
At 141 Wooster Street, a short walk from here, climb to the second floor and look through the doorway at the New York Earth Room, a work by the artist Walter De Maria, installed in 1977.
It's a large loft filled with dirt, twenty two inches deep, about two hundred fifty cubic yards of earth, and nothing else.
The room smells like a forest after rain.
The Dia Art Foundation has kept it for decades, raking and watering it, and lets visitors see it for free for much of the year.

At 393 West Broadway, you can see another De Maria work, The Broken Kilometer, from 1979: five hundred polished brass rods, laid in five rows across a gallery floor, which together would stretch for one kilometer.
There's something perfect about these works surviving in SoHo.
They take up a great deal of very expensive space and do nothing but sit there, being beautiful.
In one of the most valuable neighborhoods in the world, a room full of dirt is the ultimate luxury.
The Little Singer Building looks decades ahead of its time, and its architect, Ernest Flagg, was a man of strong ideas.

Flagg trained in Paris at the École des Beaux-Arts, the great school of classical architecture, and designed grand buildings in that style, like the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington and much of the Naval Academy in Annapolis.
His brother-in-law was the publisher Charles Scribner, and Flagg designed the Scribner company's buildings on Fifth Avenue.
But he was an engineer at heart, interested in fireproofing, ventilation and how to make cities healthier.
The Little Singer Building shows the engineer.
Its front is a light frame of iron and steel, painted green, filled with sheets of glass, with delicate balconies and panels of terracotta.
Instead of hiding the frame behind stone, Flagg made it the design.
He also thought about the city as a whole.
As skyscrapers rose, he worried they were turning streets into dark canyons.
He proposed that tall buildings be allowed to rise without limit only if their towers covered a small part of their lots, leaving light and air around them.
His slender Singer Tower downtown, finished in 1908, was meant to show how.

The city's first zoning law, in 1916, adopted a version of the idea, letting towers rise without limit over a quarter of the lot, and that rule helped shape the tower-topped skyscrapers of the 1920s and 1930s.
Flagg also designed small, fireproof stone houses for ordinary families, and built himself an estate on Todt Hill, on Staten Island.
He died in 1947.
Twenty one years later, his Singer Tower was torn down, and he was spared the sight.
Walk over to the arch and look closely.
You heard that the marble arch replaced a much loved wooden one.
Its cornerstone was laid in 1890, and it was formally dedicated in 1895.
Look up at the winged figures carved into the spaces above the curve of the arch.
They're by the sculptor Frederick MacMonnies.
Then look along the top for an inscription, words attributed to Washington: Let us raise a standard to which the wise and the honest can repair.
The event is in the hand of God.
Now walk around to the north side, the side facing Fifth Avenue, to see the two statues of Washington.
As you face the arch from Fifth Avenue, on the left, on the eastern pier, is Washington as commander in chief, by Hermon MacNeil, from 1916, with figures of Fame and Valor at his back.
On the right is Washington as president, from 1918, with figures of Wisdom and Justice, by Alexander Stirling Calder.
New Yorkers often call them Washington at War and Washington at Peace.
That second sculptor comes from a remarkable family.
His father, Alexander Milne Calder, made the giant statue of William Penn on top of Philadelphia's City Hall.
His son, Alexander Calder, became one of the most famous artists of the twentieth century, known for his hanging mobiles.
Three generations of sculptors, and the middle one is right here.
Notice, too, how late the statues came.
Stanford White's plans had called for sculpture on the piers, but for about twenty years after the dedication the piers stood bare, until these two groups were finally carved.
Finally, go back into the park, stand south of the arch, and look north through it.
The arch frames the start of Fifth Avenue, for generations the city's grandest street, so that the avenue begins with a ceremonial gateway at the edge of a village.
You heard that historians doubt anyone was hanged from the old elm in the northwest corner of the park.
Walk over and look at it anyway.
It's an English elm, and the city's parks department estimates it's more than three hundred years old, which would make it one of the oldest trees in Manhattan.
The stories attached to it come in several versions.
In one, traitors were hanged from its branches during the Revolution.
In another, it served as the gallows when this was a potter's field.
The trouble is the map.
Until 1827, the ground where the tree stands was private farmland, outside the burial ground, and the city added it to the square only after the cemetery had closed.
No record shows anyone hanged from it.
There was, though, an execution in the potter's field itself, and it's well documented.
Rose Butler, an enslaved teenager, was convicted of setting a fire in the house of the family who held her.
The fire did little damage and hurt no one, but she was sentenced to death, and the courts upheld the sentence.
She was hanged on a gallows built in the field, in front of a huge crowd, and buried in the ground nearby.
Her story is far less famous than the tree's, and far more certain.
The burial ground itself is no legend either.
Some estimates put the number of people buried here as high as twenty thousand.
When workers dug the foundation for the arch's eastern pier in 1890, about ten feet down they found human bones, a coffin, and a gravestone dated 1803.
So if you sit on a bench here, you may be sitting above some of those forgotten New Yorkers, near a tree that is famous for something it almost certainly never did.
For more than half a century, one of America's greatest painters climbed four flights of stairs on the north side of this square to get to work.
Edward Hopper moved into the top floor of number 3, Washington Square North, in 1913, and lived and painted there until his death in 1967.
His wife, the painter Josephine Nivison Hopper, joined him after they married in 1924.
The building was a walk-up heated with coal, and the coal had to be hauled up four flights of stairs.
Hopper painted the city as a place of quiet and solitude: empty streets in early morning light, lit windows at night, people alone in rooms.
You can feel this neighborhood in much of it.
Hopper's first one-man show opened in January 1920 at the Whitney Studio Club, a block from the square on West Fourth Street.
It sold nothing.
The club was founded by the sculptor and heiress Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, who bought and showed the work of living American artists when most museums wouldn't.
In 1931 she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in a row of houses on West Eighth Street, a block north of the square.
The museum later moved uptown, and now stands at the foot of the High Line, but its first home is still there, now an art school, the New York Studio School.
And the Whitney today holds the largest collection of Hopper's work anywhere.
Hopper was far from the first artist drawn here.
In 1857, a few blocks north on West Tenth Street, the architect Richard Morris Hunt built the Tenth Street Studio Building, one of the first buildings in America designed especially for artists.
Winslow Homer, Frederic Church and John La Farge all worked there.
It was torn down in 1956.
So when you look at the dignified houses of the Row, imagine a tall, silent painter climbing the stairs with a load of coal, to a room where he painted the loneliness of the modern city.
You heard that the owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried and acquitted.
In the trade they were known as the Shirtwaist Kings, and their story shows how the garment business worked.
The shirtwaist was the fashion of the age: a tailored blouse worn with a long skirt, made popular around 1900 by the confident Gibson Girl of magazine illustrations.
Millions were sold, and New York was the center of the trade.
Blanck and Harris were immigrants who had started small and built Triangle into one of the biggest blouse makers in the city, with hundreds of workers.
In 1909, Triangle was one of the shops where the great shirtwaist strike began, the walkout that grew into the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand.
Many shops settled and recognized the union.
Triangle's owners never did.

At the manslaughter trial, their lawyer, Max Steuer, one of the best trial lawyers in the city, had a key survivor, Kate Alterman, repeat her vivid testimony again and again, then suggested to the jury that her words sounded rehearsed.
The jury acquitted both men in less than two hours.
The civil cases ended even worse for the families.
In 1914, twenty three lawsuits brought by victims' families were settled for seventy five dollars per life lost.
Meanwhile, the owners' insurance had paid them about sixty thousand dollars more than their reported losses, roughly four hundred dollars for every worker who died.
And in 1913, Max Blanck was in court again, this time for locking a door during working hours at his new factory.
He was fined twenty dollars.

It's a story about two men, but also about a whole system: an industry with almost no rules, laws that barely punished anything, and workers with little power, until the fire changed the politics of the state.
In the chaos of the Triangle fire, two men kept going back into it.
Joseph Zito and Gaspar Mortillalo ran the passenger elevators in the building.

When the fire broke out, they began running their small cars up toward the burning floors, cramming in as many workers as they could and bringing them down to the street, again and again, as smoke filled the shafts.
Some workers, desperate, jumped down the elevator shaft itself.
Finally, the rails of one elevator buckled in the heat, and the cars could no longer climb.
No one knows exactly how many people they saved.
Estimates for Zito alone run from about a hundred to a hundred and fifty.
Their courage was reported in the newspapers at the time, but their names are far less known than the owners'.
Others helped too.
On the tenth floor, where the owners had their offices, people fled up to the roof.
In a taller building next door, used by New York University, a law professor and his students found ladders and helped the workers climb from the factory roof up to safety.
And there were the firefighters, who arrived within minutes, and found that the nets they held out could not hold people falling from so high.
When you stand at the corner, look at the building's entrance and imagine those two small cars rising into the smoke.
The names on the memorial are the people who were lost.
Many of the people who lived owed their lives to two elevator men who wouldn't stop.
In the hours after the fire, the bodies were carried to a pier on the East River at Twenty Sixth Street, where a temporary morgue was set up, and laid out in rows of coffins.
Through the night and the days that followed, long lines of people filed past, searching for daughters, sisters, sons and friends.
Some victims could be recognized only by a ring, a shoe, or a detail of their clothing.
The youngest of the dead were fourteen years old.
A handful of bodies could not be identified at all.

On April 5th, 1911, unions and community groups organized a funeral procession for them, and in a cold, driving rain, hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers turned out, marching or standing silently along the route.
The unidentified victims were buried together at the Evergreens Cemetery in Brooklyn.
For nearly a century, six of them stayed nameless.

Then a researcher named Michael Hirsch spent years combing through old newspapers, records and family histories, and in 2011, just before the hundredth anniversary of the fire, he announced their names: Max Florin, Fannie Rosen, Dora Evans, Josephine Cammarata, Maria Lauletti and Concetta Prestifilippo.
A new marker with their names was unveiled at the cemetery on April 5th, 2011, a hundred years to the day after the march in the rain.
Today every one of the hundred and forty six has a name.
You heard that people chalk those names on the sidewalk here each year.

A project called Chalk also sends volunteers to the sidewalks in front of the buildings where the victims lived, scattered across the city, so that each name returns, for a day, to the place that person called home.
So the memorial on this corner isn't only about how they died.
It's also about a long, stubborn effort, lasting a century, to remember exactly who they were.
If the folk revival had a center of gravity on these blocks, it was a big, bearded, gravel-voiced singer named Dave Van Ronk.
Van Ronk grew up in Brooklyn and Queens, played in traditional jazz bands, shipped out as a merchant seaman, and by the late 1950s was singing old blues and folk songs in the coffeehouses here.
He was a teacher as much as a performer.
Younger musicians came to him to learn guitar parts and old songs, and to argue about music and politics.
When Bob Dylan arrived in 1961, Van Ronk took him under his wing, let him sleep on his couch, and helped him get work at the Gaslight.
Dylan later called him the king of the street.
Van Ronk told one story about their friendship many times.
He had worked out his own arrangement of an old song, The House of the Rising Sun, and planned to record it.
Dylan learned it and put it on his own first album before Van Ronk got the chance.

Then, in 1964, a British band, the Animals, had a worldwide hit with a version that followed the same arrangement, and Dylan stopped playing the song, because audiences assumed he was copying the Animals.
Van Ronk loved telling that story.
Van Ronk never became a star, and he didn't seem to mind.
He kept playing the Village for decades, until his death in 2002.

His memoir, The Mayor of MacDougal Street, was finished after his death by the writer Elijah Wald, and it inspired the Coen brothers' 2013 film, Inside Llewyn Davis, set in the Village folk world of the early 1960s.
In 2004, the city named a corner of Sheridan Square, where Barrow Street meets Washington Place, Dave Van Ronk Street.
If you're heading west toward Christopher Street, look for the sign.
Before this was an Italian neighborhood, and long before it was a bohemian one, the streets around Minetta Lane were a center of Black New York.
The roots go back to the 1600s, when the Dutch granted farmland in this area to formerly enslaved Africans.
Later, the path along Minetta Brook was known as the Negroes' Causeway.

In the nineteenth century, after slavery finally ended in New York State in 1827, a Black community grew up here, on Minetta Lane and Minetta Street, and along Bleecker, Thompson and Sullivan Streets.
It was crowded and poor, but it was a real community, home to waiters, laborers, laundresses, sailors and musicians.
New Yorkers called it Little Africa.
In 1890, the reformer Jacob Riis described it in his book How the Other Half Lives, mostly as a slum, with the condescension of his time.
The community was pushed and pulled away.
After the Draft Riots of 1863, when white mobs attacked Black New Yorkers across the city, many families left Manhattan.
Later, rising rents and new waves of immigrants pressed on those who stayed.
By the turn of the century, Black New Yorkers were moving north, first to the Tenderloin, in the West Twenties and Thirties, and to San Juan Hill, near today's Lincoln Center, and then to Harlem.
Italian immigrants filled the tenements they left behind, and within a generation, Little Africa was almost forgotten.
There's little to mark it now.
But as you walk along Minetta Lane, remember that the Village's long history of outsiders making a home here didn't begin with the bohemians.
It began with people who had far fewer choices about where they could live.
Walk a block or two south and west of here, onto Bleecker Street, and you'll find what remains of the South Village's Italian past, much of it in the form of food.
By 1900, the blocks south of Washington Square had become one of the largest Italian neighborhoods in the city.
Life centered on the church of Our Lady of Pompeii, on Carmine Street, whose parish was founded in 1892 to serve Italian immigrants.

Its pastor for more than three decades, Father Antonio Demo, helped newcomers find their footing in a new country, and the little square beside the church, where Bleecker, Carmine and Sixth Avenue meet, is named Father Demo Square.
The food shops followed the people.
Along Bleecker Street, you can still find a pork store, Faicco's, that has been making sausage for more than a century, and a cheese shop, Murray's, open since 1940 and now known across the country.
Bakeries sell cannoli and pignoli cookies, and pizza by the slice gets folded and eaten on the sidewalk.
The Italian cafés on these streets were serving espresso long before the Beat poets and folk singers made coffeehouses the center of Village life.
When the folk clubs of the 1960s needed cheap basements and storefronts, many of them found space in these Italian blocks, and the landlords, the neighbors and the musicians didn't always get along.
Some older residents complained about the noise and the crowds, and those complaints were part of the background to the 1961 fight over folk singing in Washington Square.
Today the Italian population has thinned, and many of the old social clubs are gone.
But stop in for a sandwich or a pastry, and you're tasting the neighborhood that sat between Little Africa and the folk revival, and outlasted both.
You heard that neighbors saved this building from demolition.
Their campaign began with something small: a clock that didn't work.
By the late 1950s, the clock in the tower had stopped, a sad sign over an empty building.
A Village resident named Margot Gayle decided to start there.
With a group of neighbors, she formed a committee with a gloriously long name: the Committee of Neighbors to Get the Clock on Jefferson Market Courthouse Started.
One Christmas, they sent Mayor Robert Wagner a telegram that played on the song All I Want for Christmas Is My Two Front Teeth.
What they wanted was their clock.
It worked.
In October 1960, the clock started again.
The clock was a symbol, and once the neighbors had won it, they set their sights on the whole building.
In 1961, a new group formed, the Committee for a Library in the Courthouse, and it persuaded the city to turn the courthouse into the library you see today.
Margot Gayle went on to become one of the city's great preservationists.

She was a leader in the fight to protect SoHo's cast iron buildings, and she founded a group called the Friends of Cast Iron Architecture to champion them, at a time when many people saw those buildings as old factories ready for the wrecking ball.
Her method is worth remembering.
Instead of starting with a huge demand, she started with something everyone could agree on, a stopped clock on a neighborhood landmark, and built from there.
Each small win made the next, bigger one possible.
Look up at the tower.
If the clock is keeping time, it's partly because a neighbor thought a stopped clock was a bad sign for a neighborhood.
The garden next door stands on the site of the Women's House of Detention, which everyone called the House of D. You heard that Angela Davis and Dorothy Day were held there.
Many others passed through too.
The jail held women awaiting trial or serving short sentences, and it was famously overcrowded.
Ethel Rosenberg was held here after her arrest in 1950, during the espionage case in which she and her husband, Julius, were convicted and later executed.

Afeni Shakur, a member of the Black Panther Party, was held here as one of the Panther 21, accused of plotting bombings, and spent part of her time here pregnant with her son, the future rapper Tupac Shakur.
She defended herself at trial, and she and her codefendants were acquitted in 1971.

Historians have also recovered another side of the House of D. Many of the women held here were lesbians, or didn't fit the gender rules of their time, and were arrested for it, or for sex work, or simply for being poor.
The writer Hugh Ryan, in a history of the jail published in 2022, argues that it was a central place in queer New York, just a few blocks from the Stonewall Inn.
The shouted conversations between the windows and the sidewalk that you heard about included lovers, and the street outside became a meeting place in its own right.
Conditions were harsh, and complaints mounted.
In 1965, a college student named Andrea Dworkin, arrested at a protest against the Vietnam War, spoke out about brutal treatment by the jail's doctors.
Her account made the newspapers and added to the pressure to close the jail, which finally happened in the early 1970s.
Today, roses grow where the jail once stood, in a garden tended by volunteers.
Why is a library called Jefferson Market?
Because for nearly a century, this block was a market, named for Thomas Jefferson.
In 1833, the city opened a public market here, one of the neighborhood markets where New Yorkers bought meat, fish, vegetables and butter from licensed stall keepers.
Over the market rose a tall wooden fire lookout tower with a big bell.
Watchmen scanned the rooftops of the growing village, and when they spotted smoke, they rang the bell in patterns that told firefighters which part of town to run to.
One of the butchers who took a stall here when the market opened, Thomas De Voe, stayed for nearly forty years and became the great historian of the city's markets.
In 1862 he published The Market Book, a history of New York's public markets, and a few years later The Market Assistant, a guide to every kind of food sold in them, from game birds to oysters.
He went on to become the city's superintendent of markets.
In the 1870s, the city replaced the old wooden sheds with a whole civic complex in the same colorful Victorian style: the courthouse you see, a jail behind it, and a new market hall.
The courthouse tower took over the old lookout's job.

The market carried on into the twentieth century, but neighborhood markets were giving way to grocery stores, and in the late 1920s the market and the old jail were cleared to make way for the Women's House of Detention.
So the name over the library door remembers a place where Villagers once haggled over chickens and cabbages, under a watchtower keeping an eye out for fire.
You heard that bars could be punished for serving gay customers.
Three years before Stonewall, a few blocks from here, activists challenged that rule with a quieter kind of protest, and it worked.
The State Liquor Authority treated gay customers as a sign of a disorderly bar, so bartenders routinely refused to serve anyone they suspected of being gay.

In April 1966, three members of the Mattachine Society, one of the country's early gay rights groups, Dick Leitsch, Craig Rodwell and John Timmons, decided to challenge the rule the way civil rights activists in the South had challenged segregated lunch counters.
They called it a sip-in, and they brought reporters.
The men went from bar to bar, announcing that they were homosexual and asking to be served.
At Julius', at the corner of West Tenth Street and Waverly Place, the bartender set out glasses, heard their declaration, and put his hand over the top of a glass.
A photographer caught the moment, and the picture of that hand became famous.
The protest made the New York Times.

The city's Commission on Human Rights said that gay people had the right to be served in bars, and court decisions over the next few years made it harder for the state to punish a bar just because its customers were gay.
It didn't end police harassment, as the Stonewall raid would show.
But it was an early step toward gay bars that could operate openly and legally.
Julius' is still pouring drinks, and it's one of the oldest gay bars in the city.
In 2022, the city made it an official landmark, for what happened at its bar.
Craig Rodwell, one of the three, opened the Oscar Wilde Memorial Bookshop in 1967, one of the first bookstores devoted to gay and lesbian writers.
After Stonewall, he helped propose the march you heard about, the one that became the first pride parade.
Ask who started the Stonewall uprising, and you'll get many answers.
You heard that the details are still debated.
Here's what the debate is about.
The most famous story says that Marsha P. Johnson, the Black drag queen and activist, threw the first brick, or a shot glass, at the police.
But in an interview years later, Johnson herself said that by the time she got there, the uprising had already started.
Sylvia Rivera, her friend and fellow activist, also told dramatic stories about that night, but her accounts changed from one telling to the next, and historians still argue about what she saw.
Another account centers on a woman dressed in men's clothes, who fought back as police pushed her toward a patrol wagon, and called out to the crowd to do something.
Many people believe that woman was Stormé DeLarverie, a performer who later worked as a bouncer and was known around the Village as a protector of lesbian bars and the women in them.
DeLarverie said in interviews that it was her, but it's never been confirmed.
You heard that the crowd threw coins.
Many accounts say those coins carried a message: they mocked the payoffs the police took from the bar's owners.
Johnson and Rivera's greatest importance came afterward.

In 1970 they founded a group called STAR, Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries, which sheltered homeless young people, and for decades they fought to keep transgender people, especially transgender people of color, at the center of the movement.
Whoever threw the first brick, the uprising belonged to the whole crowd on the street that night: young, poor, many of them homeless or gender nonconforming, and out of patience.
The building across the street has been a pair of stables, a bakery, a restaurant, a Mafia bar, and the heart of a national monument.
It's actually two buildings, numbers 51 and 53 Christopher Street, built in the 1840s as stables.
In 1930 they were joined at the ground floor and housed a bakery, and a few years later a restaurant opened here called Bonnie's Stonewall Inn.
By the mid 1960s, the restaurant had closed, and men connected to the Genovese crime family took over the space.
In 1967, Tony Lauria, known as Fat Tony, reopened it as a gay bar.
You heard it had no liquor license.
To get around that, it called itself a private bottle club, and patrons signed a book at the door, often with made-up names.
There was no running water behind the bar, so glasses were rinsed in tubs and used again, and the police usually tipped off the owners before a raid.
After the uprising, the bar didn't last long.
It closed within months, and for years the space was rented to a string of other businesses, while the uprising itself grew into legend.
A new bar took the old name in the 1990s.
Recognition came slowly, then all at once.
In 1999, the building and the streets around it were listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the next year they became a National Historic Landmark.
In 2015, the city made the Stonewall Inn an official landmark, the first in New York designated mainly for its place in gay history.
The national monument followed the next year.
Look at the front of the building and notice how modest it is: two plain old stables, joined and painted, with a sign over the door.
History doesn't always choose grand buildings.
Sometimes it chooses the place where people finally refused to leave.
A few blocks north of here, at Seventh Avenue and Twelfth Street, stood a hospital that was woven into the life of the Village for a century and a half.
St. Vincent's Hospital was founded in 1849 by the Sisters of Charity, and it cared for the city in some of its worst moments.
In 1912, survivors of the Titanic were brought here.
On September 11th, 2001, its doctors and nurses lined up stretchers on the sidewalk, waiting for the wounded from the World Trade Center, most of whom never came.
In the 1980s, the hospital was at the center of another crisis.

As AIDS spread through the city, and hit gay men in neighborhoods like this one especially hard, St. Vincent's opened what is often described as the first and largest AIDS ward on the East Coast, in 1984.
Many of the Village's young men died there.
The nurses and doctors who cared for them, at a time when much of the country looked away, are remembered with deep gratitude.
The hospital closed in 2010, deep in debt, and its buildings were turned into apartments.
Across the street, on a triangle of land at Seventh Avenue, Twelfth Street and Greenwich Avenue, the New York City AIDS Memorial was dedicated on World AIDS Day, December 1st, 2016.
A white steel canopy rises over a fountain, and the granite paving around it is engraved with lines from Walt Whitman's poem Song of Myself, arranged by the artist Jenny Holzer.
If you have a few minutes, walk up and stand under it.
It's a quiet place in the middle of a busy intersection, for remembering a generation the Village lost.
You heard that the poet Edna St. Vincent Millay lived in the narrowest house on this street.
In her day she was one of the most famous poets in America, and a symbol of a new kind of freedom.
Millay grew up poor in Maine, raised by her mother, a nurse, and she became famous young: she was twenty when her long poem Renascence was published, in 1912.
She got her unusual middle name from St. Vincent's Hospital in New York, which had saved her uncle's life just before she was born.
Her friends called her Vincent.

After college, she moved to Greenwich Village in 1917, acted with the Provincetown Players, and wrote poems that captured the mood of young women in the years after the First World War: independent, witty, and a little reckless.
Her most famous lines, from a short poem called First Fig, are about a candle that burns at both ends.
It will not last the night, she wrote, but it gives a lovely light.
In 1923, the year of her Pulitzer Prize, she married Eugen Boissevain, a Dutch businessman who was devoted to her career, and the two lived for a time in the tiny house here.
In 1924, she joined a group of theater friends in founding the Cherry Lane Theatre, around the corner.
Millay and Boissevain soon moved to a farm in upstate New York called Steepletop, where she lived for the rest of her life.
She died there in 1950.

But the image of her in this little house, a famous poet in a home barely wider than a hallway, sums up the Village of the 1920s: talented, poor or pretending to be, and determined to live differently.
These few blocks hold some of the oddest and oldest houses in Manhattan.
Here's what to look for.
Start at 77 Bedford Street, at the corner of Commerce Street, right next to the narrow house, a plain little house with a brick front.
It was built in 1799, and it's often called the oldest house in the Village.
Its early owners included Harmon Hendricks, a copper merchant who served as Paul Revere's agent in New York.
The brick is only skin deep: it was added in 1836 to the older wooden house underneath.
Walk up Bedford to number 102, and you'll see something out of a fairy tale: a half-timbered house with two steep peaks, known as Twin Peaks.
It began as a plain house around 1830.
In 1925, a designer named Clifford Reed Daily, with money from the banker Otto Kahn, rebuilt it as a whimsical home and studios for artists, a little Alpine fantasy dropped onto a Village street.
Then walk to 39 and 41 Commerce Street, two matching houses with mansard roofs, standing apart with a garden between them.
Legend says a sea captain built them for two daughters who couldn't stand each other.
It's a good story, with no evidence behind it.
They were built in the early 1830s for a milkman, and the mansard roofs were added decades later.
Finally, walk to the corner of Bedford and Grove Streets and look up at the apartment building at number 90.
You may recognize it.
It's the building shown as the characters' home in the television comedy Friends.
As you go, notice the details that survive on the older houses: low doorways, small windows under the roofline, and iron railings worn smooth by two centuries of hands.
A short walk from here, at 59 Grove Street, a plaque marks the place where one of the most important writers of the American Revolution died, nearly forgotten.
Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in 1776, persuaded thousands of Americans to support independence.
His series The American Crisis, which begins These are the times that try men's souls, was read aloud to Washington's troops.
But his later book, The Age of Reason, which attacked organized religion, made him one of the most despised men in America.
When he came back from France in 1802, many old friends shunned him.
He spent his last months in Greenwich Village, poor and ill, and died on June 8th, 1809, in a small wooden house where 59 Grove Street now stands.
Only a handful of people came to his funeral.
The house is long gone.
The bar in the building there now is a piano bar called Marie's Crisis, named in honor of his pamphlets.
The Village didn't entirely forget him.
A nearby street was named Reason Street, after his book.
New Yorkers slurred it into Raisin Street, and it was later renamed Barrow Street.
Now the legend, and it's mostly true.
Paine was buried on his farm in New Rochelle, north of the city.
In 1819, an English admirer, the radical journalist William Cobbett, dug up the bones and shipped them to England, planning to build a grand memorial.
The memorial was never built.
After Cobbett died, the bones passed through other hands, and then they vanished.
Over the years, people have claimed to own pieces of him, a skull here, a jawbone there, a lock of hair.
None of the claims has been proven.
So one of the men who argued America into existence has no known resting place.
He has a plaque on a quiet Village street, beside a bar where people gather around the piano and sing show tunes late into the night.
Long before Bell Labs got its name, this building was full of engineers working on one enormous problem: how to make a voice travel across a continent.
The building belonged to Western Electric, and in 1907 the engineering staffs of Western Electric and its parent company, AT&T, were brought together here, at what was then 463 West Street.
Their task was to stretch the reach of the telephone.
Over long distances, the electrical signal of a voice grew weaker and weaker, until nothing was left.
The answer came from a strange new device, the vacuum tube.
An inventor named Lee de Forest had built a tube he called the Audion, and AT&T bought the rights to use it.
A young physicist here, Harold Arnold, turned it into a reliable amplifier, and engineers placed these amplifiers at stations along the line, boosting the voice as it traveled.
On January 25th, 1915, the transcontinental line opened.
In New York, Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, picked up the receiver and repeated the words from his first call, nearly forty years earlier: Mister Watson, come here, I want you.
In San Francisco, his old assistant, Thomas Watson, is said to have answered that it would take him five days to get there now.
That October, engineers from this building tried something bolder.
From a navy radio station in Arlington, Virginia, they sent a human voice across the Atlantic.
Listeners at the Eiffel Tower in Paris heard it, faintly.
They had no way to talk back, so they answered by telegraph.
The vacuum tube amplifier became the heart of radio, sound movies and long distance calling for half a century.
And when Bell Labs was founded in 1925, it grew out of this same engineering department, in this same building.
Some of the most important ideas of the twentieth century were worked out in this building, by people most of us have never heard of.
In 1927, two physicists here, Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, fired a beam of electrons at a crystal of nickel and found that the electrons scattered in patterns, the way waves do.
It was proof that particles of matter can behave like waves, one of the strange central ideas of quantum physics.
Davisson shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1937, the first of the many Nobel Prizes for work at Bell Labs.
That same year, an engineer named Harold Black was riding the ferry across the Hudson to work here when an idea came to him for making amplifiers far more stable and faithful.
He sketched it on the only paper he had, a blank space in his copy of the New York Times.
That idea, the negative feedback amplifier, became a foundation of modern electronics.

Around the same time, John Johnson discovered that every electrical circuit hums with a faint, unavoidable noise, caused by the jiggling of electrons in the warmth of the wire itself, and his colleague Harry Nyquist explained it with an equation.
Nyquist's name is also attached to a rule at the root of digital sound: how often a signal has to be measured to capture it completely.
During the Second World War, the British codebreaker Alan Turing came here in 1943 to study the secret system for scrambling the voices of Allied leaders.
While he was here, he often ate lunch in the cafeteria with a young Bell Labs mathematician named Claude Shannon, and the two talked about machines, minds and information.
Five years later, Shannon published the paper that founded information theory, the mathematics behind every text, photo and video you send.
Look up at these plain industrial walls and imagine the conversations behind them.
You heard that Jane Jacobs helped defeat the plan to designate the West Village for urban renewal.
Here's how that fight went.
In early 1961, the people of this neighborhood learned that the city wanted to study it for urban renewal.
To planners at the time, that meant declaring an area blighted and clearing it for new housing projects.
Blocks like these, with old houses, small factories and corner bars, were exactly what planners considered obsolete.
Neighbors formed the Committee to Save the West Village, and Jacobs became one of its leaders.
They knew that once an area was officially labeled a slum, demolition was hard to stop, so they fought the label itself.
They gathered evidence that the neighborhood was healthy, busy and loved.
They packed public hearings.
They pointed out that the people who would be displaced had never been asked.
The fight was fierce.
In October 1961, at a stormy hearing, the City Planning Commission voted its approval anyway, while furious residents shouted their protests.
But the pressure kept building, and within a few months the city dropped the plan.
The neighbors then went further.
They drew up their own plan for new housing that would fit the neighborhood: modest walk-up buildings on vacant lots and old industrial sites, without tearing down homes.
It took more than a decade.
The result, the West Village Houses, forty two small brick apartment buildings near the river, finished in the 1970s, had a rocky start, squeezed by budget cuts and delays.
But it was a rare thing: housing designed with a neighborhood rather than imposed on it.
The episode became a model for neighborhood fights across the country.
And today, the blocks that were nearly cleared are among the most sought-after places to live in America.
The woman who changed how the world thinks about cities had no degree in planning, and no college degree at all.
Jane Butzner was born in 1916 in Scranton, Pennsylvania.
She moved to New York in the mid 1930s, in the depths of the Depression, and took whatever work she could find, as a stenographer and freelance writer.
She wrote articles about the city's working districts, the fur district, the flower district, the leather district, learning how neighborhoods actually made a living.
She took classes at Columbia for a couple of years, but never finished a degree.
She married an architect, Robert Jacobs, in 1944, and a few years later they bought the modest building here on Hudson Street and fixed it up themselves.
In 1952 she joined the magazine Architectural Forum, where she wrote about the great housing projects and urban renewal schemes of the time.
The more of them she saw, the less she believed in them.
She noticed that the new projects were often empty and unsafe, while old, messy streets like her own were full of life.
In 1958, she wrote an article for Fortune magazine called Downtown Is for People, attacking the planners' visions for city centers.
It caught the attention of the Rockefeller Foundation, which gave her a grant to write a book.
That book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, came out in 1961 and opened with a line that announced a fight: This book is an attack on current city planning and rebuilding.
In the late 1960s, opposed to the Vietnam War and determined that her sons would not be drafted, she moved her family to Toronto.
She became a Canadian citizen, and she helped stop a highway there too.
Walk a block north to the little triangle where Hudson Street meets Eighth Avenue, called Abingdon Square, and you'll find a clue to who owned this land before it was a neighborhood.
In the 1740s, much of what's now the West Village belonged to Sir Peter Warren, an Irish-born officer in the British navy who had grown rich on prize money from capturing enemy ships.
He married into a prominent New York family, the De Lanceys, and put together a country estate here of around three hundred acres, with a mansion near the river.
Greenwich was then quiet countryside, a few miles north of the city.
Warren went back to Britain, became an admiral and a member of Parliament, and died in 1752, leaving his American lands to his daughters.
One of them, Charlotte, married an English nobleman, Willoughby Bertie, the Earl of Abingdon, and that's where Abingdon Square got its name.
Warren himself is remembered in Warren Street, far downtown in Tribeca.
Over the following decades, the estate was divided and sold off in lots, and some of its old boundaries and lanes live on in the angled streets you've been walking.
There's a nice twist to the name.
The Earl of Abingdon was no friend of the British government's war against the colonies.
During the Revolution, he spoke and wrote in defense of the Americans' rights.
So this little square, in a neighborhood that has always welcomed dissenters, is named for an English lord who took the rebels' side.
You heard that Herman Melville, the author of Moby-Dick, spent nearly twenty years as a customs inspector on these docks.
Here's how one of America's great novelists ended up checking cargo.
Melville was born in New York in 1819, the grandson of two heroes of the Revolution.
When he was a boy, his father's business failed and his father died, and the family fell on hard times.
As a young man, Herman went to sea.
He sailed on a whaling ship to the South Pacific, deserted it, and lived for a time among the islanders of the Marquesas.
His first book, Typee, based on those adventures, was a hit in 1846, and for a few years he was a celebrity.
Then his books grew stranger and more ambitious, and readers drifted away.
Moby-Dick, published in 1851, sold poorly and puzzled many reviewers.
By the 1860s, Melville was in debt and needed a steady income.
In December 1866, he was appointed an inspector of customs for the port of New York, at four dollars a day.
For the next nineteen years, he walked the wharves along the Hudson, checking cargo and paperwork, through summer heat and winter wind.
He never stopped writing.
In his off hours he wrote poetry, including a book-length poem called Clarel, about a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.
After he retired, he began a short novel about a young sailor, Billy Budd.
When he died in 1891, he was nearly forgotten.
Billy Budd sat unpublished among his papers until 1924, when a new generation of critics rediscovered him, and his reputation soared.

So as you walk toward the river, picture a gray-bearded inspector with a notebook, checking crates on a pier at the end of a street named for his own grandfather, with no idea that his whale book would one day be called the great American novel.
Gansevoort Street is one of the oldest names on this part of the waterfront, and it began with a fort.
In 1812, as war with Britain loomed again, a small fort was finished on the riverbank here, between what are now Gansevoort and West Twelfth Streets.
It was built of red sandstone, with openings for twenty two cannon, but its walls were whitewashed, so New Yorkers called it the White Fort.
Officially, it was named Fort Gansevoort, after Peter Gansevoort, a hero of the Revolution, who died that same year.
Gansevoort's fame came from the summer of 1777.
As a young colonel, he commanded Fort Stanwix, in the Mohawk Valley of upstate New York, when a British force and its Native American allies laid siege to it.
Gansevoort refused to surrender.
After about three weeks, the British gave up and withdrew, a blow to the British campaign that ended in defeat at Saratoga that fall.

A legend grew up around the siege: that the defenders stitched together an American flag from scraps, including soldiers' shirts and a woman's red petticoat, and that it was the first Stars and Stripes ever flown in battle.
The story is told with pride in upstate New York, but historians can't confirm what that flag looked like, or whether it was the Stars and Stripes at all.
The White Fort here never fired a shot in anger.
The British never attacked Manhattan during the War of 1812, and by the 1850s the fort was gone, swallowed by the growing waterfront.
All that remains is the name: on the street, on the old market, and on the whole district, which for a long time was simply called Gansevoort.
And through Peter Gansevoort's grandson, Herman Melville, the name reaches into American literature too.
For more than twenty years, the most famous place to eat on these cobblestones was a diner that never closed.
In 1985, a Frenchman named Florent Morellet took over an old luncheonette on Gansevoort Street called the R and L, which had been feeding meat workers since 1943.
He kept the counter and the booths, renamed it Florent, and stayed open twenty four hours a day.
Its menu, designed by the graphic designer Tibor Kalman and his studio, is now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.
At the time, the neighborhood was rough.
By day, butchers in bloody white coats pushed carcasses along the overhead rails.
By night, the streets belonged to clubgoers, drag queens, sex workers, artists and night owls.
Florent fed all of them, often at the same time.
Meat workers on the early shift sat beside people coming home from the clubs.
The diner became a gathering place for gay New York, especially in the worst years of the AIDS crisis.
Morellet learned in 1987 that he was HIV positive, and he did something remarkable.
On the board where the restaurant listed its daily specials, in little plastic letters, he posted his own T-cell count, the number doctors used to track the disease, along with jokes and puns.
For many customers facing the same diagnosis, that board said that they weren't alone, and that there was nothing to hide.
Morellet also became an activist for the neighborhood.
He helped found the group whose campaign led the city, in 2003, to protect the old market buildings as the Gansevoort Market Historic District.
But the popularity he helped create drove rents sky-high, and in 2008, when his landlord demanded far more, Florent closed.
The space became a clothing store.
So as you walk past the boutiques, imagine a lit diner window at four in the morning, a butcher and a drag queen sharing the counter, and a menu board that told the truth.
You heard about Death Avenue, and the West Side Cowboys who rode ahead of the trains.
Here's how that strange job came to an end.
For most of a century, freight trains rolled through the streets of the West Side, down Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, among wagons, pushcarts and children.
The toll was terrible.
By one count, the trains had killed more than four hundred people by the early 1900s, and newspapers and neighborhood groups campaigned for years to get the tracks off the street.
For a long time, the railroad's answer was the cowboys.
A rider on horseback went ahead of each train, waving a red flag by day and a red lantern by night, to warn people out of the way.
It was a slow, old-fashioned fix in one of the most modern cities on earth.
The real fix took decades of argument, and money from the city, the state and the New York Central Railroad.
You heard that the elevated line opened in 1934.
But a stretch of street-level track lingered on Eleventh Avenue, and so did the cowboys.
The last ride came in March 1941.
A twenty one year old rider named George Hayde, on a horse called Cyclone, led a train of fourteen cars loaded with oranges up the avenue.
After that, the job was gone for good.
Today, the High Line's old tracks are planted with wildflowers, and people stroll above the traffic.
But the viaduct was built because so many people died on the streets below it.
For a while, the only thing standing between the trains and the crowds was a young man on a horse with a red flag.
Look at the Whitney's building, and you might not guess that it's built like a ship ready for a storm.
Renzo Piano, the Italian architect who also designed the New York Times Building, shaped the museum to fit this odd corner of the city.
On the east side, it steps down toward the High Line in a series of outdoor terraces, where you can stand among sculptures with the city behind you.
On the west side, facing the river, it's heavier and more industrial, clad in steel panels, like the warehouses that once surrounded it.
And at the entrance, the building lifts up and hangs over the plaza, so the street seems to flow right under it.
The museum was still under construction in October 2012, when Hurricane Sandy pushed the Hudson River into these streets.
Millions of gallons of river water poured into the building's basement.
The museum and its engineers went back to work and added a whole system of flood defenses.
The most remarkable piece is a door.

On the building's west side, facing the river, is a flood door fourteen feet tall and twenty seven feet wide, built like a watertight door on a ship, and designed so that a single person can close it in an emergency.
When a big storm is coming, crews can also put up a temporary aluminum flood wall around the building.
Piano wanted all of it to stay out of sight, so most visitors never notice it.
It's a sign of the times.
This waterfront was built to bring cargo in from the river.
Now its newest buildings are designed to keep the river out.
Look at the plants along the High Line.
They look wild, as if they'd seeded themselves.
That's the idea.
When the trains stopped in 1980, the viaduct became an accidental meadow.
Seeds blew in on the wind or arrived with birds, and tough plants took root in the gravel between the rails: grasses, wildflowers, even small trees.
You heard that photographs of that wild landscape helped win support for saving the line.
When the park was designed, the Dutch garden designer Piet Oudolf set out to capture that feeling, not by copying it, but by composing it.

He is a leader of a style sometimes called the New Perennial movement, which uses grasses and long-lived flowering plants arranged as if in a natural meadow, and values how plants look in every season, not just when they bloom.
On the High Line, he used hundreds of kinds of plants, many of them native to North America, in a series of zones suited to the changing sun, shade and wind along the line.
Watch how the gardens change through the year.
In spring come bulbs and fresh green shoots.
In summer, the flowers and grasses are at their height, buzzing with bees.
In fall, the grasses turn gold and copper.
And in winter, instead of cutting everything down, the gardeners leave the dried stems and seed heads standing, where they catch the frost and feed the birds.
Then, each year in late March, gardeners and volunteers do what's called the spring cutback, clearing away the old growth so the new season can come through.
Even then, they leave some stems standing, because native bees and other pollinators nest inside them.
So the High Line's gardens are a kind of performance: a designed wilderness, tended every day to look as if no one tends it at all.
You heard that the Carpathia brought the Titanic's survivors here.
Its part in the story began with a lucky moment.
Late on the night of April 14th, 1912, the Carpathia's wireless operator, a young man named Harold Cottam, had been up on the bridge and missed the Titanic's first calls for help.
Back in his cabin, getting ready for bed, he listened in one more time, and heard them.
He ran to wake his captain, Arthur Rostron.
The Carpathia was about fifty eight miles away.
Rostron turned the ship around and drove it at top speed through waters full of ice, with extra lookouts posted, while the crew prepared blankets, hot drinks and the dining rooms for survivors.
The Carpathia reached the scene in the dark before dawn, after the Titanic had gone down, and spent hours picking up survivors from the lifeboats.
Then came the slow trip back to New York, with the world desperate for news.
On the evening of April 18th, in a cold rain, the Carpathia steamed up the Hudson.
It didn't go straight to its own pier.
First it went to the White Star Line's pier, a little to the north, to leave behind the Titanic's empty lifeboats.
Then it came back here, to Cunard's Pier 54, and tied up at about half past nine.
Survivors came down the gangways into a crush of relatives and reporters.
Some were met by family.
Many had become widows that week.
Relief groups were waiting to help the many who had lost everything.
Captain Rostron became a hero.
Congress awarded him a gold medal, and a group of survivors, led by Margaret Brown, the woman later remembered as the Unsinkable Molly Brown, presented him with a silver cup.
So the arch here also remembers a ship that turned toward the ice when another was in trouble.
You heard that the Lusitania sailed from this pier in May 1915, and was sunk by a German submarine.
The warning came in the morning newspapers.
On Saturday, May 1st, the day the ship was to sail, a notice from the German Embassy appeared in New York papers.
It reminded travelers that Germany and Britain were at war, that the waters around the British Isles were a war zone, and that anyone sailing there on British ships did so at their own risk.
In some papers, it was printed right next to Cunard's advertisement for the Lusitania's sailing.
Some passengers were alarmed, and a few canceled.
But most shrugged it off.
The Lusitania was one of the fastest ships on the ocean, and many people believed no submarine could catch her.
The ship left the pier a little after noon, delayed by the transfer of passengers from another ship.
