Six days later, on May 7th, off the southern coast of Ireland, a single torpedo struck.
The great liner sank in about eighteen minutes.
The sinking caused fury in the United States, but not war, at least not yet.
Three days later, President Woodrow Wilson gave a speech in Philadelphia in which he said that there is such a thing as a man being too proud to fight.
Critics mocked the line.
Wilson sent Germany a series of stern protests, and his Secretary of State, William Jennings Bryan, resigned rather than sign one of them, fearing it would drag the country into war.
The United States didn't enter the war until April 1917, nearly two years later, after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare.
But the Lusitania became a rallying cry, used on recruiting posters and in speeches for the rest of the war.
So this pier saw off one of the turning points of the century, on a spring day, with a warning in the newspaper that almost everyone ignored.
The park you're standing in exists partly because of a fish.
By the 1970s, the old elevated West Side Highway along the river was falling apart.
In 1973, a section of it collapsed near Gansevoort Street under the weight of a truck.
The piers along the shore were rotting.
Planners proposed a grand replacement called Westway: a highway buried in a tunnel inside new land, made by filling in the Hudson along this shore, with parks, apartments and offices built on top.
Westway had powerful supporters, and well over a billion dollars of federal highway money behind it.
But opponents argued that the money would be better spent on subways and buses, and environmental groups went to court.
Their unlikely champion was the striped bass.
Young striped bass spend the winter in the sheltered water among the old piers, and filling in the river would destroy that refuge.
In 1982, a federal judge, Thomas Griesa, blocked the project, ruling that government agencies had played down the harm to the fish.
The agencies tried again, and in August 1985 Griesa ruled against them a second time, finding that testimony they had given was tainted.
The next month, facing a deadline, New York gave up on Westway and traded the federal highway money for transit and local roads.
Instead of a buried highway, the West Side eventually got a surface boulevard, and the river's edge got a park.

In 1998, the state created Hudson River Park, which runs along the shore from Battery Park City up to Fifty Ninth Street, and includes the water around the old piers, where fish and other river life are protected.
So when you see the rows of old wooden pilings sticking out of the water, don't think of them only as ruins.
For the young striped bass, they're shelter, and they helped save this shoreline.
You heard that the National Biscuit Company sold its Uneeda Biscuit in a sealed package, backed by one of the first big national ad campaigns.
The man behind that strategy was a Chicago lawyer named Adolphus Green.
In the 1890s, the cracker business was a war.
Regional bakeries fought over territory, cutting prices until nobody made money.
Bankers and bakers merged them into larger and larger groups, and in 1898, the biggest of those groups combined into the National Biscuit Company.
Green became its first president.
Green decided that instead of fighting over price, the company would build a brand.
He wanted a cracker that was exactly the same everywhere, sold under one name, in a package that kept it fresh.
The company called its package the In-Er-Seal, a cardboard box with a waxed paper lining.
The name came from the company's advertising agency, N. W. Ayer and Son, which registered Uneeda at the end of 1898.
Early in 1899, ads began appearing that simply asked, Do you know Uneeda Biscuit?
Then came the mascot: a little boy in a rain slicker, carrying a box of crackers through a downpour.
The message was that the crackers inside stayed dry, whatever the weather.
It worked spectacularly.
Uneeda Biscuits sold in enormous numbers, and the cracker barrel began to disappear from American stores.
The idea that a company could sell the same packaged food, under the same name, in every store in the country, now seems obvious.
In 1899, it was new, and much of it was worked out in these buildings.
The boy in the raincoat became one of the most familiar faces in American advertising.
Look carefully at old brick walls, here and in other cities, and you can still sometimes find faded painted signs for Uneeda Biscuit.
The Oreo became the best-selling cookie in the world, and almost everything about its beginnings comes with a question mark.
Start with the fact that it wasn't first.
In 1908, four years earlier, a rival company, Sunshine Biscuits, had introduced Hydrox: two chocolate cookies with a cream filling.
When the Oreo arrived in 1912, it was, in effect, an imitation.
But Nabisco had bigger bakeries and a bigger advertising budget, and over the decades the Oreo buried its rival.
Today, many people assume Hydrox was the copy.
The first Oreos were sold on March 6th, 1912, to a grocer in Hoboken, New Jersey, just across the river.
Then there's the name.
You heard that nobody knows where it came from.
The theories are fun.
One says it comes from or, the French word for gold, because the early packages were gold colored.
Another points to a Greek word for mountain, because an early test version was shaped like a little hill.
Another notices the letters r and e, from the word cream, sandwiched between two O's, like the filling between two cookies.
Nabisco has never settled the question.
And then there's the design.
The pattern stamped on today's Oreo dates to 1952, and is generally credited to a Nabisco employee named William Turnier, who is said to have started in the company mailroom.
Over the years, people have read secret meanings into the little crosses and circles, linking them to the medieval Knights Templar or to secret societies.
There's no evidence that anyone at Nabisco meant any of that, and the company has never explained the design.
So the next time you twist one open, remember that you're holding a small mystery that started on this block.
Step back outside and look at Chelsea Market from the street.
It isn't one building but a patchwork, built in stages over about half a century, by several different architects, as the bakery kept growing.
The oldest parts date from the late nineteenth century, sturdy brick buildings with rows of arched windows.
As the business boomed, the company kept adding buildings until the complex filled the whole block.
In 1904, a railroad spur was routed right through the complex, so freight cars could pull up inside.
Now walk toward Tenth Avenue.

When the elevated freight line was built in the early 1930s, Nabisco rebuilt its whole Tenth Avenue side, designed by its own architect, Louis Wirsching Junior, so that the new tracks could pass straight through the building.
That's why the High Line seems to tunnel through Chelsea Market today.
Freight cars could stop inside to deliver flour and sugar, and leave with boxes of crackers and cookies.
Look up, too, for the bridge over Tenth Avenue.
The bakery reached across the avenue to the building on the other side, and a walkway bridge crosses high above the traffic.
As you look, notice how different the pieces are: different bricks, different windows, different heights.
Each one marks a moment when the company needed more room, and the whole block records the growth of one of America's first giant food companies.
You heard that this building was built by the Port Authority as a freight terminal.
To understand why, it helps to know what the Port Authority was for.
New York's harbor is shared by two states, and for decades New York and New Jersey squabbled over it while freight piled up.
Most of the railroads from the west ended on the New Jersey side of the Hudson, so goods had to cross the river on barges and ferries, an expensive, slow and chaotic system.
In 1921, the two states signed a compact creating the Port of New York Authority, an independent agency to run the region's port and transportation as one system.
It was one of the first agencies of its kind in the country.
The Port Authority's early projects changed the region: two bridges to Staten Island, then the George Washington Bridge in 1931, and control of the new Holland Tunnel, which had opened in 1927.
Trucks could now drive under the river.

So the Port Authority imagined a new kind of freight hub: a terminal in the middle of Manhattan, where trucks would carry goods to and from the railroad lines and the shipping piers on the Hudson, instead of every shipper making its own trips to the waterfront.
This building was the result.
Its ground floor and basement were the terminal, Union Inland Terminal Number One, and the floors above were rented out as warehouses and workshops.
Trucks drove into giant elevators, said to be the largest truck elevators ever built at the time, able to lift forty thousand pounds, and rode up to the tenants' doors.
The name, Number One, shows the planners were thinking big.
As trucks took over from trains, the freight terminal faded, and the Port Authority eventually sold the building.
But its strength and size kept it useful, first for manufacturers, then for the telephone and internet companies, and now for Google.
So this massive block is a monument to a big idea about freight, and to a building so well made that it kept finding new lives.
Somewhere in this building is a room where the internet shakes hands.
You heard that 111 Eighth Avenue became a hub for telecommunications and data.
Here's what that means.
The internet isn't one network.
It's thousands of networks, run by phone companies, cable companies, internet providers, banks and tech firms.
For data to pass from one network to another, their cables have to physically meet somewhere.
Buildings where many networks come together are called carrier hotels, and the room inside where they connect is called a meet-me room.
There, in long rows of locked cabinets, a technician can link two networks with a single cable, called a cross connect.

This building had what the carriers wanted: huge, strong floors to hold heavy equipment, plenty of electric power, and a central location near the fiber-optic cables that run under the city's streets.
Around the turn of the century, its owners turned much of it into telecom space, and its meet-me room was once said to be the largest in the city.
When Google bought the building in 2010, many people assumed it wanted the network connections.
In fact, it was mainly after the office space, and the telecom tenants stayed on, with long leases.
So today, software engineers work on some floors, while on others, racks of humming equipment pass data from one network to the next.

The next time a message from your phone reaches a friend across town, there's a fair chance it passed through a room like this one, maybe this very one, where cables from rival companies are plugged in side by side.
You heard that the Chelsea was built as one of the city's first cooperative apartment buildings.
The idea behind it came from its architect, Philip Hubert.
In the 1880s, respectable middle class New Yorkers lived in private houses if they could afford them.
Apartments were associated with crowded tenements, and many people thought living in one was not quite proper.
Hubert and his partner, James Pirsson, set out to change that.
They designed a series of buildings they called Home Clubs.
Instead of renting from a landlord, a group of members would pool their money to build a fine apartment house together, each owning a share.
The Chelsea was the grandest of them.
Look at its red brick front, its rows of iron balconies, and its steep roofline with gables and tall chimneys.
Inside, a famous staircase winds up through the full height of the building.
For about twenty years, the cooperative worked.
But the neighborhood changed as the theaters moved uptown, money grew tight, and the cooperative went bankrupt in the early 1900s.
By 1905, the building had become a hotel, with many long-term residents, which is how it came to house so many artists and writers.
Hubert's idea outlived his building's cooperative.
Today, cooperative ownership is the most common way people own apartments in Manhattan.
So when you see a movie scene of nervous buyers being grilled by a co-op board, you're watching the descendants of Philip Hubert's Home Clubs.
You heard that West Twenty-Third Street was once the center of the American theater.
In the years after the Civil War, this was the place to see a show.
The great actor Edwin Booth, the most famous Hamlet of his time, built his own theater at the corner of Twenty-Third Street and Sixth Avenue, and opened it in February 1869.
It was meant to give serious drama a worthy home.
Booth's name carried a heavy shadow.
His younger brother, John Wilkes Booth, had assassinated President Lincoln four years earlier, and Edwin had left the stage for months afterward.
His new theater was admired, but it was a financial disaster.
Booth went bankrupt, and the theater closed in 1883.
Two blocks west, at the corner of Eighth Avenue, a businessman named Samuel Pike opened Pike's Opera House in 1868.
Within a year, it belonged to Jim Fisk and Jay Gould, who renamed it the Grand Opera House, the theater you heard about where Fisk kept the offices of the Erie Railroad.
Later came vaudeville.

In 1889, the showman F. F. Proctor opened a theater on this street, between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, offering a mix of singers, comedians, acrobats and animal acts that ran one after another from late morning until night, so you could walk in at almost any hour.
Then, as the theaters moved north toward Herald Square and Times Square, the street's glory faded.
Some of the old theaters became movie houses, and the young film business found space in the neighborhood's lofts.
So as you walk along Twenty-Third Street, past the drugstores and apartment buildings, imagine carriages lined up outside the theaters on a winter night, a century and a half ago.
You heard that Jim Fisk owned the Grand Opera House on Eighth Avenue, and was shot by a rival.
His life was even wilder than that.
Fisk grew up in Vermont and started out as a peddler, selling goods from a wagon, and made money in the cotton trade during the Civil War.
He was loud, stout, flamboyant and funny, with a waxed mustache and a diamond on his shirt front, and he loved an audience.
In 1868, Fisk teamed up with the quiet, calculating Jay Gould and the old speculator Daniel Drew to fight Cornelius Vanderbilt for control of the Erie Railroad.
Vanderbilt kept buying Erie stock, and the Erie men kept issuing more of it.
When a judge friendly to Vanderbilt ordered their arrest, they fled across the Hudson to Jersey City, taking the company's books and millions of dollars in cash.
The battle, known as the Erie War, ended with Gould and Fisk in control of the railroad.
Fisk and Gould then bought the opera house, and Fisk ran the railroad from offices inside, while producing shows on the stage below.
In 1869, the two men tried to corner the market in gold.
When the government sold gold to break the scheme, prices collapsed on September 24th, a day remembered as Black Friday, and many investors were ruined.
Fisk and Gould came through largely unharmed, and Fisk barricaded himself inside the opera house.
His downfall was personal.
Fisk kept a mistress, an actress named Josie Mansfield, and she took up with his business partner, Edward Stokes.
The quarrel turned into lawsuits, and then into violence.
On January 6th, 1872, Stokes shot Fisk on a staircase at the Grand Central Hotel on lower Broadway.
Fisk died the next day, and his body lay in state at his opera house, where crowds lined up to see him.
He was thirty six years old.
You heard that some scholars doubt Clement Clarke Moore wrote A Visit from St. Nicholas.
Here's the case, and the case against it.
The poem first appeared on December 23rd, 1823, in a small newspaper in Troy, New York, with no author's name.
How it got there is unclear.
One story says a family friend who had heard it at the Moores' sent it in.
It was reprinted year after year, still anonymous.
Moore's name was attached to it in a collection of poems in 1837, and in 1844 he included it in a book of his own poetry.

But the family of another New Yorker, Henry Livingston Junior, a farmer, surveyor and occasional poet from the Hudson Valley, insisted that he had written it, and had recited it to his own children years before it was published.
Livingston had died in 1828, and his family's claim came years later, with no manuscript to back it up.
In 2000, a professor named Don Foster, famous for identifying anonymous authors from their writing style, took up the Livingston case.
He argued that the poem's bouncy, cheerful rhythm matched Livingston's other light verse, and didn't sound like Moore, a serious scholar.
He also pointed to the reindeer.
In the first printing, two of them were named Dunder and Blixem, Dutch words for thunder and lightning.
Livingston, who had Dutch roots, knew the language.
Moore did not.
Later versions changed the names to Donder and Blitzen.
Moore's defenders answered back.

They pointed out that Moore wrote playful verse too, that he claimed the poem openly while people who could have contradicted him were still alive, and that parts of the Livingston family story had been shown to be wrong.
No one can prove it either way.
The poem that helped create the American Santa Claus has an author on the plaque, and a question mark in the footnotes.
Why is this neighborhood named after a district of London?
Because of an old soldier, and the place where old soldiers retired.
In the middle of the 1700s, a retired British officer named Thomas Clarke bought farmland here, on the Hudson, a few miles north of the little city.
He named his estate Chelsea, after the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, the grand home for retired and wounded soldiers founded in the late 1600s, where veterans in scarlet coats still live today.
Clarke's daughter, Charity, married a young clergyman named Benjamin Moore, and their son, born in 1779, was Clement Clarke Moore.
Clement inherited the estate from his mother in 1813, and he's the one who later divided it into the house lots you see around you.
Clement's father had his own place in history.
Benjamin Moore became the Episcopal bishop of New York, and president of Columbia College.
In July 1804, he was called to the bedside of Alexander Hamilton, who had been mortally wounded in his duel with Aaron Burr.
Hamilton asked for holy communion.
Moore hesitated, because the church condemned dueling.
Only after Hamilton assured him that he repented of his part in the duel, and bore no ill will toward Burr, did the bishop give him the sacrament.
Hamilton died on the afternoon of July 12th, the day after the duel.

So the name of this neighborhood carries a chain of stories: a veterans' home in London, an old soldier's farm, a bishop at a famous deathbed, and a scholar who may or may not have written the most famous Christmas poem in America.
Behind the fence and brick walls of the General Theological Seminary is one of the most peaceful spaces in Manhattan, a quadrangle of lawns and trees that the seminary calls the Close.
The oldest building here is the West Building, a plain stone building from 1836, one of the earliest Gothic Revival buildings in the city.
It had a twin, the East Building, from the 1820s, which was later torn down.
These modest stone buildings were the seminary's first home on Clement Clarke Moore's land.
Most of what you see came later.

Beginning in the 1880s, under an ambitious dean, Eugene Augustus Hoffman, the seminary hired the architect Charles Coolidge Haight to build a whole campus in the English collegiate Gothic style, with red brick, stone trim, pointed windows and a chapel with a tall tower.
The idea was to give New York a little piece of Oxford, a college built around a green.
Look for the Chapel of the Good Shepherd, with its tower rising over the middle of the block.
Notice, too, how the buildings turn inward, toward the lawn, rather than out toward the street.
That's deliberate.
A seminary was meant to be a retreat from the world, even in the middle of a city.
In recent decades, the seminary has struggled with money, like many religious schools, and has sold or leased some of its property.
But the Close remains.
Peek through the gates, and you'll see Chelsea as Moore's generation imagined it: quiet, green and dignified, a few blocks from the freight yards.
You heard that the galleries came here from SoHo.
One dealer's story shows how that happened.
In October 1968, Paula Cooper opened a gallery in a loft on Prince Street, the first gallery in what would become SoHo.
Her first show was a benefit for a student group protesting the Vietnam War.
Over the next decades she championed Minimalist and conceptual artists, and SoHo grew into the center of the contemporary art world.
By the 1990s, SoHo had become a shopping district.
Rents had soared, and the big open lofts that artists and dealers loved were turning into boutiques.
Cooper looked west, to Chelsea's garages and warehouses, which were cheap, enormous, and a long walk from anywhere.
In 1995 she bought a building on West Twenty-First Street, and in 1996 she opened there, in a soaring space that people compared to a cathedral.
Other major dealers made the same move around the same time, and within a few years, Chelsea had replaced SoHo.
The galleries here are free and open to anyone, usually Tuesday through Saturday.
Don't be shy about walking in.
The people at the front desk may look forbidding, but you're welcome to look, and many will gladly tell you about the work.
Try walking one of the gallery blocks, between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues in the low Twenties, and ducking into whatever catches your eye.
You might find a single huge sculpture filling a former garage, a quiet room of drawings, or something you can't quite explain.
The art world keeps moving.
As rents here have climbed, some galleries have moved again, to the Lower East Side or to Tribeca.
But for now, these blocks remain one of the greatest free art museums in the world, spread across hundreds of storefronts.
The name Starrett-Lehigh joins a family of builders and a railroad, and the building tells the story of a partnership that didn't last.
The Lehigh Valley Railroad, which carried coal and freight from Pennsylvania, had no tracks into Manhattan.
Like other railroads, it stopped at the New Jersey shore.

So freight cars from its yard in Jersey City were loaded onto car floats, long barges with rails on their decks, and towed across the Hudson to its freight terminal here, where they were rolled ashore.

In 1930, the railroad joined with the Starrett family's real estate company to replace that old terminal with something new: a building where trains could pull in on the ground floor, and trucks could ride elevators to any of the nineteen floors above.
The builders were Starrett Brothers and Eken, the same firm that was putting up the Empire State Building at the very same time.
The designers were two brothers, Russell and Walter Cory, engineers who had studied at night at Cooper Union, working with the architect Yasuo Matsui.
The timing was terrible.
The building opened in the depths of the Depression, when few businesses could afford to expand.
William Starrett, one of the family's leading builders, died in 1932, and the railroad bought out the building, but by 1933 it was losing money.
In 1944 the railroad gave up on it, and in 1966 the tracks were taken out.
The truck elevators, though, kept running, and in recent years they have even carried food trucks up into the building, like their freight-hauling ancestors.
So look up at those ribbons of windows and imagine freight cars floating across the river, rolling off the barges and into the ground floor of a skyscraper.
Walk over to West Twenty-Second Street, between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, and look at the sidewalk.
Beside many of the street trees stands a tall, narrow column of dark stone, like a small standing stone from some ancient site.
It's a work of art, and part of a much bigger one.
The German artist Joseph Beuys began a project called 7000 Oaks in 1982, at a great art exhibition in the city of Kassel.
He had seven thousand basalt stones dumped in a huge pile in front of the museum there, and announced that each stone would be moved only when a tree was planted beside it.
Over the next five years, as the trees went in around the city, the pile shrank.
The project was finished in 1987, the year after Beuys died.
He saw it as social sculpture: an artwork made by a whole community, and a way of greening a city.
In 1988, the Dia Art Foundation, whose building on this street you heard about, brought the idea to New York, planting five trees with basalt stones outside its doors.
In 1996, Dia added more, along this block.
Today there are dozens of pairs here, though construction has sometimes forced a few of the stones to be taken away for a while.
Look at how the trees and stones change together over time.
The stones stay the same.
The trees keep growing, until one day they'll tower over their stone companions.
That contrast was the point.
There's one more connection worth knowing.
In 2003, Dia opened a huge museum up the Hudson, in the town of Beacon, in a former factory where the National Biscuit Company once printed its boxes.
So a trail of art and crackers runs from these blocks all the way up the river.
You heard that the city once planned a football stadium on this site.
The fight over it was one of the fiercest in modern New York politics.
In the early 2000s, Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his deputy mayor, Dan Doctoroff, wanted to bring the Olympic Games to New York in 2012.
The centerpiece was to be a stadium over the rail yards, built for the New York Jets, who played their home games in New Jersey.
It would host the Olympics first, and then the Jets, with hundreds of millions of dollars of public money for the platform and the roof, including three hundred million dollars from the state.
The opposition was fierce.
Many West Side residents didn't want a stadium in their neighborhood, and many critics thought the money should go elsewhere.
The most determined opponent was Cablevision, the company that owned Madison Square Garden, a few blocks east, which feared the competition.
It fought the stadium hard, and even made its own bid for the rail yards.
In March 2005, the transit authority, which owned the yards, chose the Jets' bid.

The last hurdle was an obscure state board, the Public Authorities Control Board, where three officials each held a veto: the governor, the leader of the State Senate, and the speaker of the Assembly.
On June 6th, 2005, the representatives of the Senate leader, Joseph Bruno, and the Assembly speaker, Sheldon Silver, declined to vote yes, and the stadium was dead.
A month later, the International Olympic Committee chose London for 2012.
The Jets eventually built a new stadium in New Jersey, together with the Giants.
And the city turned to a different plan for the yards: rezone the area, extend the subway, and let developers build the towers you see now.
Some people still wonder what this place would be like with a stadium in it.
Others are glad it never happened.
Either way, the land where it would have stood is now some of the most expensive real estate in the country.
You heard that the city extended the 7 train to a new station here.
That station is one of the deepest in the subway system, and its story says a lot about how Hudson Yards was built.
Before the extension, the far West Side was a long walk from the nearest subway.
Developers wouldn't build big towers here without one.
So the city made an unusual bet.

Instead of waiting for state and federal money, it paid for the extension itself, about two and a half billion dollars, by selling bonds through a new agency, the Hudson Yards Infrastructure Corporation.
The bonds were to be paid back with future tax revenue from the buildings the subway would attract.
In other words, the city borrowed against a neighborhood that didn't exist yet.
Tunnel boring machines dug a mile and a half of new tunnel from Times Square.
The new station opened in September 2015, the first completely new station in the subway system since 1989, about a hundred and twenty five feet below the street.
To get people up and down from that depth, the station was given something new to the New York subway: two inclined elevators, which ride up and down at an angle alongside the escalators.
They also caused trouble.
Problems with the inclined elevators and the fire safety systems helped delay the station's opening by almost two years.
When you ride the long escalators down, notice the curved ceiling and the mosaics and the sheer depth of the place.
Then remember what it represents: a subway built before the neighborhood, on the promise that a neighborhood would come.
This time, it did.
Look at the building next to the Vessel, the one with the quilted, puffy outer shell.
That's The Shed, and part of it moves.
The Shed was designed by Diller Scofidio and Renfro, one of the firms behind the High Line, working with the Rockwell Group.
It opened in 2019 as an arts center for every kind of performance and exhibition.
Its fixed base building holds galleries and theaters.
But its outer shell, a steel framework more than a hundred feet tall, sits on giant wheels, each six feet across, running on rails.
When the shell rolls out over the plaza next door, it creates a huge enclosed hall, about seventeen thousand square feet, for concerts and big events.
When it rolls back, the plaza becomes open public space again.
The shell weighs about eight million pounds, yet it travels the length of the plaza in about five minutes, moving at a quarter of a mile an hour.
The engineers borrowed the technology from the giant gantry cranes that load and unload ships at container ports, a fitting choice on a waterfront where freight once ruled.
The shell's skin is made of a tough, clear plastic called ETFE, puffed into cushions like a quilt.
It's far lighter than glass and lets daylight in.
The building is named for Michael Bloomberg, whose philanthropy helped pay for it.
It's the Bloomberg Building.
Next door, the honeycomb of stairs called the Vessel took the opposite approach: less a building than a giant sculpture you can climb.

Together, they say something about this whole neighborhood: built on top of a working rail yard, borrowing tools from the docks and the railroads, and still, at heart, a piece of the industrial West Side.
You heard that Lincoln's speech in the Great Hall helped make him president.
Here is how it happened.
The invitation was to speak at Henry Ward Beecher's church in Brooklyn.
Only when Lincoln reached New York did he learn that a club of young Republicans had taken charge of the evening and moved it here, to Peter Cooper's brand new hall.
His fee was two hundred dollars.
Lincoln knew that eastern audiences thought of him as a western stump speaker, a rail splitter with funny stories.
So he told no stories at all.

He had spent weeks in the state library in Springfield reading old congressional records, and he built the speech on one question: what did the men who wrote the Constitution believe about slavery in the western territories?

Of the thirty-nine who signed it, he showed, twenty-three had later acted on that very question, in Congress or elsewhere, and twenty-one of them, a majority of all thirty-nine, had acted as if Congress had every right to keep slavery out.
The founders, he argued, had treated slavery as an evil to be contained, and Republicans stood exactly where the founders stood.
About fifteen hundred people came.
Some remembered the tall, awkward man in a badly wrinkled new suit, and a high voice that put them off at first, until the argument took hold.
He ended with a line people still quote: let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.
The next morning, New York papers printed the whole speech.
Lincoln went on to speak across New England, partly so he could visit his son Robert at school in New Hampshire.
Less than three months later, the Republican Party nominated him for president.
Lincoln was only the beginning.
Before they were elected, Ulysses Grant, Grover Cleveland, William Howard Taft, Theodore Roosevelt and Barack Obama all spoke from this stage.
So did Frederick Douglass, and the suffrage leaders Susan B. Anthony and Victoria Woodhull.
In 1867, a young humorist from the West named Mark Twain gave his first New York lecture here, about the Sandwich Islands, as Hawaii was then called.
He wrote afterward that the night was a failure and a success at once.
In 1870, the hall filled for Red Cloud, the Lakota leader who had forced the army to abandon its forts along the Bozeman Trail.
Through an interpreter, he told New Yorkers that his people had been handed papers to sign that no one honestly explained, and asked the East to help them get fair treatment.
And on the night of November twenty-second, 1909, the hall was packed with young garment workers, most of them immigrant women from the tenements to the south.
For hours they listened to union leaders, Samuel Gompers among them, debate whether to call a general strike of the shirtwaist makers.
Then a twenty-three-year-old worker named Clara Lemlich, who had recently been beaten on a picket line, asked for the floor.
Speaking in Yiddish, she said she had no more patience for talk, and moved that a general strike be declared now.
The hall erupted.
The chairman asked the crowd to raise their right hands and swear an old oath: if I turn traitor to the cause I now pledge, may this hand wither from the arm I now raise.
Within days, some twenty thousand workers walked out, in what became known as the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand.
By February, nearly every shop had signed a union contract.
One that held out was the Triangle Waist Company, on Washington Place.
A year later, it burned.
You heard that the Astor Place Riot began as a feud between two actors.
It had been simmering for years.
When the American star Edwin Forrest toured Britain in the 1840s, he was hissed in London and blamed his English rival, William Charles Macready.
Soon after, Forrest stood up in a theater in Edinburgh and loudly hissed Macready's Hamlet.
To his fans back home, Forrest was the voice of a rough young democracy, and Macready was the darling of the snobs.
The Astor Opera House, just west of here, was built for those snobs.
It even had a dress code.
So when Macready came to play Macbeth there in May 1849, the Bowery's working men took it personally.
On the first night, the gallery pelted him with eggs and even chairs, and the play had to stop.
Macready meant to sail home.
But forty-seven prominent New Yorkers, Washington Irving and the young Herman Melville among them, signed an open letter begging him to stay, and promising that order would be kept.
The letter only made things worse.
Handbills went up around the city asking: working men, shall Americans or English rule in this city?
On May tenth, while Macready finished Macbeth under police guard, thousands outside hurled paving stones at the building.
The Seventh Regiment was called out, and when the stones kept coming, the soldiers fired into the crowd.
At least twenty-two people died.
Macready slipped out in disguise and left the city.
One of the men convicted of stirring up the mob was a writer named Edward Judson, better known as Ned Buntline.
He served a year on Blackwell's Island.
Twenty years later he found a better use for his gift for spectacle: he made a young army scout named William Cody the hero of his dime novels, and turned him into Buffalo Bill.
Two details nearby are easy to walk past.
First, find the row of tall marble columns on the west side of Lafayette Street, facing the Public Theater.
This is Colonnade Row, four survivors of a terrace of nine grand houses finished around 1833 and named La Grange Terrace, after the Marquis de Lafayette's country estate in France.
Behind one continuous screen of Corinthian columns, each family had its own house, so the whole row read as a single palace.
Members of the Astor family lived here, and so did Warren Delano, grandfather of Franklin Delano Roosevelt.
The marble is said to have been cut by prisoners at Sing Sing.
The other five houses were torn down long ago, and the survivors are grimy and patched, but squint and you can see one of the grandest addresses in the New York of Andrew Jackson's day.
Second, go down into the Astor Place subway station and look along the platform walls.
Every so often you'll find a glazed terra cotta plaque of a beaver.
The station opened in 1904 on the city's first subway line, and its designers chose the beaver as a nod to the fur trade that made John Jacob Astor rich.
More than a century later, the beavers are still there.
When you come back up, look at the little cast iron and glass pavilion over the uptown entrance.
It looks like 1904, but it's a replica, built in 1985 from old photographs of the kiosks that once stood over subway stairs all over the city.
The full name on Hilly Kristal's awning was longer than CBGB.
It read C B G B and O M F U G, for Country, Bluegrass, Blues and Other Music For Uplifting Gormandizers, a gormandizer being someone with a large appetite.
The other music arrived in the spring of 1974.
A young band called Television, with the guitarists Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd, needed somewhere to play, and their manager, Terry Ork, kept pushing Kristal to let them in.
Kristal finally gave them Sunday nights, his slowest of the week.
By the band's own account, their first Sunday was March thirty-first, 1974.
They brought their friends, the friends brought theirs, and the narrow room found its purpose.
That August, four young men from Queens in leather jackets and torn jeans, all calling themselves Ramone, played there for the first time.
Kristal ran the club for more than thirty years, through punk and the hardcore years that followed, until a long fight with the landlord closed it.
The last show, on October fifteenth, 2006, belonged to Patti Smith.
She played for more than three hours and ended with her song Elegie, reading out the names of musicians and friends who had died.
Kristal himself died the next summer.
Before you leave, walk a few steps north to the corner of East Second Street and look up, way up.
The street sign there reads Joey Ramone Place, named in 2003 for the band's singer, who had died two years earlier.
It became the most stolen street sign in New York, so in 2010 the city raised it to about twenty feet above the sidewalk.
Marky Ramone, the band's drummer, joked that now you'd have to be a basketball player to see it.
Before punk, the Bowery had jazz.
Just to the north, at number 5 Cooper Square, stood a plain workingman's bar called the Five Spot Café, run by the Termini brothers, Joe and Iggy.
In the mid-1950s they started booking jazz, and painters and poets from the cheap lofts nearby made it their hangout.
In the summer of 1957, Thelonious Monk began a run there that lasted about six months.
Monk had spent years barely able to work in New York, after the police took away the cabaret card that nightclub performers then needed.
Now he had a steady stage, and a new tenor saxophonist, John Coltrane, who had just kicked heroin.
Night after night, Coltrane worked his way through Monk's strange, angular tunes, and other musicians came to listen.
Coltrane said later that if you lost track of where Monk was going, you'd feel as if you'd stepped into an empty elevator shaft.
In November 1959, the Five Spot introduced New York to Ornette Coleman, whose quartet played without any set pattern of chords.
Critics and musicians packed the room to argue over whether it was genius or noise.
That same year, the poet Frank O'Hara wrote The Day Lady Died on the day Billie Holiday died.
The poem ends here, with the memory of a night at the Five Spot when she whispered a song along the keyboard to her pianist, Mal Waldron, and everyone, O'Hara included, stopped breathing.
In the early 1960s the club moved a few blocks north to St. Mark's Place, and it closed later that decade.
The original building is gone, but for a few years this was one of the most important rooms in jazz.
The Tredwells were not alone in their house on Fourth Street.
Climb to the top floor of the museum and you reach two small rooms under the roof where the family's servants slept.
The state census of 1855 lists four of them, all women, all born in Ireland.
They had come in the years of the Great Famine, when about a million Irish people died and more than a million left.

By the 1850s, roughly one New Yorker in four had been born in Ireland, and for young Irish women the most common work was domestic service: cooking, carrying coal and water up and down the stairs, scrubbing, washing and sewing.
A bell at the top of the stairs could summon them at any hour.
The museum considers these rooms the oldest intact place in New York City where Irish immigrants are known to have lived.
The house itself survived on a string of near misses.
By the 1960s it was crumbling, and the blocks around it had filled with factories and warehouses.

When New York passed its landmarks law in 1965, after the outcry over the demolition of the old Pennsylvania Station, this house was among the first buildings protected, and the very first in Manhattan.
In 1981 its interior became a landmark too, one of a small number of interiors in the city with that protection.
In recent years, its defenders have fought construction next door that they fear could crack its old walls.
You're on East Seventh Street, between Second and Third Avenues.
Look for McSorley's Old Ale House, at number 15, with its sawdust floor and dark wood interior.
McSorley's claims to date from 1854, which would make it one of the oldest continuously operating bars in New York, though some historians think it opened a bit later.
Its motto is: Be good or be gone.
McSorley's serves only two kinds of beer, light and dark, and you order them two mugs at a time.
The walls are covered with a dense layer of old photographs, newspaper clippings, and memorabilia, much of it untouched for over a century.
Above the bar hang wishbones, said to have been left by young men going off to fight in World War One, intended to be collected when they returned.
The ones still hanging belonged to those who didn't come back.
For most of its history, McSorley's banned women.
It finally admitted them in 1970, after two lawyers from the National Organization for Women sued and won, and New York City passed a law banning sex discrimination in public places.
Even then, it didn't have a women's restroom until 1986.
Now look east along Seventh Street, toward Second Avenue.
This stretch is the heart of Little Ukraine.
Ukrainians settled here starting in the late nineteenth century, and a larger wave arrived after World War Two, many of them people displaced by the war and fleeing Soviet rule.
Look for St. George Ukrainian Catholic Church, with its large dome, on Seventh Street.
Every year, its parish holds a Ukrainian festival.
At the corner of Second Avenue and Ninth Street, look for Veselka, a Ukrainian restaurant open since 1954, famous for its pierogi, borscht, and blintzes, and open nearly around the clock.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Veselka became a gathering place for the community and raised money for relief efforts.
The Ukrainian Museum, on East Sixth Street, holds a fine collection of folk art, including painted Easter eggs called pysanky.
Next door to Veselka, just south on Second Avenue, is the Ukrainian National Home, for decades a gathering place for the community.
Watch, too, for the occasional blue and yellow flag in windows.
The community has been shrinking for decades, but it remains visible here.
McSorley's founder, John McSorley, was an Irish immigrant remembered as Old John.
After he died, his son Bill kept the saloon almost exactly as his father had left it, which is one reason the walls look the way they do.
The painter John Sloan drank here and painted the bar several times, starting in 1912.
The poet E. E. Cummings wrote a poem that opens with him sitting in McSorley's while it snows outside.
And in 1940, Joseph Mitchell wrote a long, loving portrait of the place for The New Yorker, called The Old House at Home, after the name the saloon carried in its early days.
In 1936, Bill McSorley sold the bar to one of his regulars, a retired policeman named Daniel O'Connell.
Within a few years O'Connell died and left it to his daughter, Dorothy O'Connell Kirwan.
So for decades, the most famous men-only bar in New York belonged to a woman.

She had promised her father that she would not disturb the customers, and as the story is told, she kept her word, coming in only on Sundays, when the bar was closed, or stopping at the door to raise a glass when a round was on the house.
The bartenders ran the place, the old rules held, and the sawdust stayed on the floor.
When women were finally let in, in 1970, the walls did not change, and neither did the beer.
But remember, as you look around, that for decades the keeper of New York's most famous men's bar was a woman, honoring a promise to stay outside it.
A bar this old collects legends the way its walls collect dust, and McSorley's is happy to share them.
The biggest is that Abraham Lincoln stopped in for an ale after his speech at Cooper Union, a few blocks away, in February 1860.
It makes a good story, but there is no record that he ever set foot inside, and Lincoln barely drank at all.
Then there are the handcuffs.
Look for a pair fastened to the bar, and another hanging higher up.
Harry Houdini, the story goes, was a regular around the turn of the twentieth century, and left a pair of his cuffs behind.
Which pair, if either, is a matter of barroom debate, since one has been found to carry a serial number from after Houdini's death.
Some regulars add that if you see a cat sitting in the window, it is Houdini, back for a visit.
You heard that the wishbones over the bar were hung by young men leaving for the First World War.
That too is the bar's own story, passed down rather than written down.
What is certain is that each generation of owners has left them where they hung.
Legends like these do a job.
They tie a working man's saloon to the great names of the city, and they give every regular something to tell a newcomer.
Listen at the bar long enough and someone will tell you one of them as gospel.
Look for the short lane beside St. George's church, running between Sixth and Seventh Streets.
Its sign reads Taras Shevchenko Place.
Until 1978 it was Hall Place, a forgettable alley.
That spring, as the parish dedicated its new domed church, Mayor Ed Koch signed a law renaming the lane for the man Ukrainians consider their national poet.
Taras Shevchenko was born in 1814 a serf, the property of a landowner in central Ukraine.
He had a gift for drawing, and his owner took him to Saint Petersburg, where artists noticed him.
In 1838 they bought his freedom, raising the money by raffling off a portrait painted by Karl Bryullov.
Two years later Shevchenko published a book of poems called Kobzar, named for the wandering minstrels of the Ukrainian countryside.
Writing in the language of peasants, which the Russian Empire treated as a mere dialect, he helped turn it into a literary language.
His poems mourned his country's bondage, and the czar's government punished him for them.
In 1847 he was sent into exile as a common soldier on the edge of the Kazakh steppe, and forbidden to write or paint.
He kept writing anyway, in tiny notebooks he hid in the tops of his boots.
He was freed after ten years, and died in 1861, just as the czar was proclaiming the end of serfdom.
Ukrainian exiles, including the ones who rebuilt this neighborhood after the Second World War, carried his portrait and his poems with them.
Look for his face in Ukrainian shops and churches.
You'll also find him on monuments from Kyiv to Washington.
Walk east toward Avenue A and look for number 77.
Two very different men passed through its doors.
In the winter of 1917, its basement held the offices of Novy Mir, The New World, a Russian-language socialist paper for the city's immigrant radicals.
One of its editors was Nikolai Bukharin, later a leader of Soviet Russia.
That January a new writer joined them, just deported from France and Spain: Leon Trotsky.
Trotsky lived with his family in the Bronx, but he spent his days here, writing fierce articles against the First World War and speaking in halls around the neighborhood.
In March came the news that the czar had fallen.
Within weeks Trotsky sailed for Russia, and by the end of the year he and Bukharin were helping lead a revolution.
Thirty-six years later, the poet W. H. Auden moved into an apartment upstairs.
A plaque by the door says he lived here from 1953 to 1972.

By then Auden was one of the most celebrated poets in the English language, and friends remembered his apartment as cold, cluttered and run down, with books and papers everywhere and pipes that froze in winter.
He kept a famously strict schedule, working through the morning and serving cocktails at a set hour.
He stayed through the arrival of the hippies, and watched the street change around him for almost twenty years.
He left New York in 1972, and died the following year.
So the same doorway saw a revolutionary planning to overturn an empire, and a poet who wrote some of the century's most famous lines about love, grief and the city.
St. Mark's Place has always had room for both.
Two buildings on this street hold its whole history in their walls.
First, between Second and Third Avenues, find number 12, with its ornate front.
High on the facade, in raised letters, is its original German name, which translates as the German-American Shooting Society.
It was built in 1888 and 1889 as the clubhouse of a marksmanship club of about fourteen hundred members, organized into two dozen companies, who met here between their shooting contests.
Look for the society's emblem and its German motto, which means unity makes strength.
The members sold the building in 1920, as Little Germany emptied out, and the city made it a landmark in 2001.
It is one of the few buildings left that still announces Kleindeutschland in its own language.
Then go back to number 4, the Hamilton-Holly House you heard about, built in 1831 for an age of carriages and calling cards.
For about forty years, until 2016, it was the home of Trash and Vaudeville, the punk and rock clothing store whose racks of leather and studs dressed musicians from all over the neighborhood.
Picture Alexander Hamilton's son climbing that stoop, and then the crowd that climbed it a hundred and forty years later.
As you walk the rest of the street, read it the same way.
Look above the shop signs, at the cornices, the window frames and the old carved names, and you'll see a nineteenth-century street still standing behind the twenty-first.
You heard that an egg cream contains neither egg nor cream.
So where did the name come from?
Nobody knows, and New Yorkers have argued about it for generations.

The most famous story involves a candy store owner named Louis Auster, who sold egg creams at his shop near Second Avenue and Seventh Street, a block from here, around the turn of the twentieth century.
His family says he invented the drink, made his own chocolate syrup in secret, and turned down a fortune from a big ice cream chain that wanted the formula.
The last batch of that syrup, they say, was made in the 1970s.
The sociologist Daniel Bell credited someone else, a candy store man known as Uncle Hymie, on Second Avenue near Eighth Street.
Brooklyn has its own claimants.
As for the name, take your pick.
Some say egg comes from the Yiddish word echt, meaning genuine, so an egg cream was the real thing.
Some say customers asked for a chocolate A cream, made with grade A milk, and the A became egg.
Others think the name simply made a cheap drink sound rich.
The dullest explanation may be the right one.
Dictionary researchers have found nineteenth-century drinks called egg creams that really did contain eggs and cream, and the name may have stuck after the ingredients changed.
What is not in dispute is the method: a tall glass, a little cold milk, a hard blast of seltzer to raise a foam, and chocolate syrup stirred in.
The classic syrup is Fox's U-bet, made in Brooklyn.
Order one, and you are drinking an argument that is more than a century old.
In the spring of 1876, one of the richest men in America, Alexander Turney Stewart, was laid in his family's vault in this churchyard.

Stewart was an Irish immigrant who had built a dry goods shop into the first great American department store, first the Marble Palace on Broadway at Chambers Street, then the even bigger Iron Palace, a few blocks west of here on Broadway at Tenth Street.
On the morning of November seventh, 1878, the church's sexton noticed fresh earth over the Stewart vault.
Someone had dug down in the night, broken open the coffin and carried off the body.
The theft was real, and it made headlines around the world.
Letters arrived demanding a ransom, at one point reported as a quarter of a million dollars, and the executor of the estate, Judge Henry Hilton, refused to pay.
Detectives chased false leads for years.
What came next is the part that has never been proved.

According to the story told ever since, Stewart's widow, Cornelia, quietly made her own deal and paid about twenty thousand dollars, and one night, on a lonely country road, a bag of bones was handed over.
The remains were said to have been placed in the Cathedral of the Incarnation in Garden City, on Long Island, the planned town Stewart had founded, where his widow built the cathedral in his memory.
No one has ever shown that the bones were really his, or even that the exchange took place.
No one was convicted of the theft.
Somewhere, perhaps, Alexander Stewart is still missing.
Walk over to Third Avenue and up to Thirteenth Street, and look for a small tablet on the northeast corner.
It marks the spot where, for more than two centuries, a single pear tree grew.
According to tradition, Peter Stuyvesant brought the tree from Holland in 1647, the year he arrived to take charge of New Amsterdam, and planted it on his farm.
The farm became the city, but the tree stayed.
As the street grid crept north and Third Avenue was cut through, the old pear tree survived at the corner, and New Yorkers came to see it as a living link to the Dutch colony.
It was said to bear fruit almost to the end.
The end came in 1867.
A section of its trunk was saved, and it is now in the collection of the New-York Historical Society.
In 1890, the Holland Society, whose members descend from the colony's early Dutch settlers, put up a bronze tablet that reads: On this corner grew Petrus Stuyvesant's pear tree.
The tablet later went missing from the corner for decades, and was put back in 2005.
A couple of years before that, a new pear tree was planted at the corner in memory of the old one.
It is a small thing to look for, but think of what it means.
A tree planted by the last Dutch governor of New Amsterdam was still putting out blossoms every spring while horse cars rolled down Third Avenue and soldiers came home from the Civil War.
For more than half of New York's history, you could have picked a pear from Peter Stuyvesant's garden.
Before you leave, take a slow walk around the churchyard and the street beside it.
Look for the bronze bust of Peter Stuyvesant.

It was a gift in 1915 from Queen Wilhelmina and the government of the Netherlands, made by the Dutch sculptor Toon Dupuis, and given, its inscription says, to the people of New York in trust of this church.
Stuyvesant has company.
Daniel Tompkins, governor of New York and vice president under James Monroe, is buried here, a good reason to remember him before you reach the park that carries his name.
Commodore Matthew Perry, who forced Japan to open its ports to American ships in the 1850s, was laid in a vault here too, though his body was later moved to Rhode Island.
At the front gate, on either side, stands a sculpture of a Native American man, one called Inspiration and the other Aspiration.
They are by Solon Borglum, who grew up on the western frontier and spent his career portraying cowboys and Native Americans.
His brother Gutzon led the carving of Mount Rushmore.

Finally, cross to Stuyvesant Street, the diagonal street beside the church, and find number 21, a Federal-style brick house built around 1804 for Peter Stuyvesant's great-great-granddaughter Elizabeth and her husband, Nicholas Fish.
Their son, born here in 1808, was named Hamilton, after his father's friend Alexander Hamilton.
Hamilton Fish grew up to be governor of New York, a senator, and secretary of state under Ulysses Grant.
Today the house belongs to Cooper Union, and the college's president lives in it.
The Yiddish stage made its own royalty, and the greatest of them was Jacob Adler.
Born in Odessa, he reached New York after years of touring, tall and commanding, and his fans called him the Great Eagle, since adler means eagle.
In 1892, a Russian-born writer named Jacob Gordin wrote a play for him called The Jewish King Lear.

Gordin moved Shakespeare's story to a prosperous Jewish family in nineteenth-century Russia, borrowing too from Turgenev's King Lear of the Steppes: a proud father divides his fortune among his daughters and is cast out by those he trusted.
Adler's performance was a sensation, and the play became his signature, revived again and again.
It also marked a turning point.
Yiddish theater had leaned on improvised clowning and melodrama, and Gordin insisted that actors speak the lines as written and play real people.
Some historians date the golden age of Yiddish theater in New York from that production.

Stars like Adler and his rival Boris Thomashefsky, whose grandson is the conductor Michael Tilson Thomas, had fans so devoted that they formed clubs, called patriots, to cheer their favorite and jeer the competition.
A stroke ended Adler's career in 1920, and he died in 1926.
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that fifty thousand people attended his funeral.
His children carried the name on.

Luther Adler acted on Broadway and in Hollywood, and Jacob's daughter Stella became the acting teacher you heard about, who passed the passion of the Yiddish stage on to generations of American actors.
In 1932, the composer Sholom Secunda and the lyricist Jacob Jacobs wrote a love song for a Yiddish musical comedy called I Would If I Could.
The show is long forgotten, but one song from it is not: Bei Mir Bistu Shein, which means, roughly, to me you're beautiful.
Secunda, a trained composer who wrote for the Second Avenue stage for decades, sold the rights to a small Brooklyn publisher of Yiddish music for thirty dollars, and split the money with Jacobs.
For a song from a Yiddish operetta, it seemed a fair price.
Then the song escaped from Second Avenue.
The songwriter Sammy Cahn told the story that he first heard it at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, sung in Yiddish by two Black performers, Johnnie and George, to an audience that went wild for it.
Others claimed they had found it first.
Either way, Cahn and Saul Chaplin wrote English lyrics, and in November 1937 three young sisters from Minnesota, the Andrews Sisters, recorded it, with the title spelled the German way.
It became the most popular song in America the following year, and launched their career.
The money went to the publishers and the record companies, not to the men who wrote it.
In 1961 the copyright ran out and the rights came back to Secunda and Jacobs, who at last earned something from their song.
By then, millions of people who had never heard of the Yiddish Rialto had sung along to a tune born a few blocks from here.
After the curtain came down on Second Avenue, the actors went out to eat, and for more than forty years the place to go was the Café Royal, at the corner of Second Avenue and Twelfth Street.
From 1908 until 1952, the Royal was the living room of the Yiddish world.
Actors, playwrights, poets, critics and producers argued over coffee and cookies, made deals, settled feuds and started new ones.
The journalist and poet Judd Teller called it the Yiddish writers' Algonquin and the Yiddish actors' Sardi's.
The playwright Hy Kraft based a 1942 Broadway comedy, Café Crown, on it.
Two years after the Royal closed, the Second Avenue Deli opened a couple of blocks south, at Tenth Street, and took up its role.
Its founder, Abe Lebewohl, an immigrant who arrived after the Second World War, built it into an institution famous for pastrami, chopped liver and matzo ball soup.
He loved the Yiddish theater, and in the 1980s he set the stars of the Yiddish Walk of Fame into the sidewalk outside his door.
On March fourth, 1996, Lebewohl was shot and killed while taking the day's receipts to the bank.
The crime has never been solved.
His family kept the deli going, and when it lost its lease, they moved it uptown.
The stars stayed behind in the Second Avenue sidewalk, worn down by the shoes of everyone who has walked over them since.
You heard that the General Slocum's captain kept steaming forward instead of turning for shore.
He was heading for North Brother Island, a small island in the East River off the Bronx.
The island held Riverside Hospital, the city's hospital for contagious diseases, and as the burning boat bore down on it, the hospital's staff ran to the water.
Nurses, doctors, orderlies and even patients waded in and formed human chains, pulling the living and the dead from the river.
The boat finally grounded about twenty-five feet from the island's shore.
A few years later, the island received its most famous patient.
Mary Mallon was an Irish-born cook and a healthy carrier of typhoid fever, who had passed the disease to the families she cooked for.
In 1907 she was taken to North Brother Island and held there against her will.
She was released in 1910 on the promise that she would never cook again, broke it, and in 1915 was sent back.
She spent the rest of her life on the island, and died there in 1938.
The newspapers called her Typhoid Mary.
The hospital closed in the 1940s.
The island later housed veterans and then a drug treatment program for teenagers, and by the 1960s it was abandoned.
Its buildings are slowly collapsing into the trees, and the public is not allowed to land.
Today it is a bird sanctuary, and for some years it held one of the largest colonies of nesting herons in the city.
After the General Slocum burned, New York wanted someone to blame, and there was plenty of blame to go around.
The boat had passed a federal inspection only weeks before.

Investigators found its cork life preservers so old that they crumbled to dust, and they found that the company making new ones had hidden iron bars inside some of them to bring them up to the legal weight.
The cork company's managers were indicted, and so were the steamboat company's officers and the inspectors.
None of them was convicted.
In the end, only one man went to prison: the captain, William Van Schaick.
In 1906 a federal jury found him guilty of criminal negligence, for failing to train his crew and keep the boat ready for fire.
The judge told him, you are no ordinary criminal, I must make an example of you, and gave him the maximum sentence, ten years.
He served about three and a half years in Sing Sing.
President Theodore Roosevelt refused to pardon him, but in December 1912, President William Howard Taft did.
The disaster did change the rules.
A federal commission blamed careless inspection as well as the owners, and the government tightened its requirements for life preservers, lifeboats and fire drills on passenger steamboats.
Many of the victims were buried together at the Lutheran cemetery in Middle Village, in Queens, where a monument honors the dead who were never identified.
And the fountain here, with its two children gazing out to sea, was put up two years after the fire, a place for a neighborhood that had lost so many to remember them.
Look for a little temple of four columns sheltering a drinking fountain.
Above the columns, read the four words carved on its sides: Faith, Hope, Charity and Temperance.
This is the Temperance Fountain, put up in 1888, and it was meant to save souls one sip at a time.
It was the gift of Henry Cogswell, a San Francisco dentist who made his fortune in the Gold Rush years and spent it on drinking fountains.
His idea was simple: if a man could get a free drink of cold water on the street, he might walk past the saloon.
He once pledged to build one fountain for every hundred saloons in San Francisco.
Here, he worked with a local group called the Moderation Society, formed to fight drunkenness on the Lower East Side.
On top stands Hebe, the cupbearer of the Greek gods, modeled on a famous marble by the Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen.
The original figure was zinc.
By the 1980s the fountain was covered in graffiti and someone had sawed off Hebe's hands, and in 1992 she was replaced with the bronze you see now.
Not everyone loved Cogswell's gifts.
Brooklyn tore out the fountain he gave it.
In San Francisco, on New Year's 1894, a band of young men who considered his statue of himself an eyesore threw a rope around it and pulled it down.
One of them was Gelett Burgess, soon to be famous for a little poem that begins, I never saw a purple cow.
The park is named for Daniel D. Tompkins, and he deserves to be better remembered.
Tompkins was elected governor of New York in 1807, while still in his early thirties.
During the War of 1812, when the federal government was slow to pay, he borrowed money on his own name to raise and pay the militia that defended New York harbor.
After the war, neither the state legislature nor Congress would fully repay him, and he spent years fighting accusations over his accounts.
He is also the governor who finished off slavery in New York.
A law passed in 1799 had promised freedom only to children born after that year, and only once they were grown.
In 1817, at Tompkins's urging, the legislature set a final date: on July fourth, 1827, slavery in New York would end.
When the day came, many Black New Yorkers held their celebrations on July fifth instead, to avoid trouble from white crowds on the holiday.
That same year, 1817, Tompkins became vice president under James Monroe, and served two terms.
By the end his health and his fortune were both ruined.
He died in 1825, three months after leaving office, in the Staten Island village he had founded and named Tompkinsville.
He was fifty years old.
He is buried in the churchyard of St. Mark's in-the-Bowery, a few blocks from here.
The square was named for him in the decade after his death, and it has spent nearly two centuries living up to his restless, embattled name.
Start with the map.

Manhattan bulges out to the east here, so when the planners laid out the street grid in 1811, they added four avenues east of First Avenue and gave them letters, A, B, C and D. That is where the nickname Alphabet City comes from.
The name Loisaida came later, and it came from a poet.
Bittman Rivas, known to everyone as Bimbo, came to New York from Puerto Rico and made his life here as a poet, playwright, actor, teacher and community organizer.
In 1974 he wrote a poem called Loisaida, in a mix of English and Spanish, about the neighborhood he loved.
The word took the English name, Lower East Side, and spelled it the way his Puerto Rican neighbors said it.
Some people give a share of the credit to his friend and fellow organizer, Chino Garcia.
The word spread because it named something real.

In the 1970s, as landlords abandoned buildings and the city cut services, residents began rebuilding the neighborhood themselves, with sweat equity, community gardens and cultural centers, and Loisaida became their banner.
It went up on murals and posters, and into the names of community groups.
Eventually it reached the street signs, when Avenue C was given the second name Loisaida Avenue.
Bimbo Rivas died in 1992.
Every year, the Loisaida Festival fills the avenue with music, food and dancing, and the word he wrote down in a poem is still how many people here name their home.
Miguel Piñero, one of the founders of the Nuyorican Poets Cafe, lived the life he wrote about.
He was born in Puerto Rico in 1946 and brought to the Lower East Side as a small child.
He grew up poor, ran with gangs, used heroin, and was in and out of jail.

In the early 1970s, serving time at Sing Sing for armed robbery, he joined a prison theater workshop, and there he wrote Short Eyes, a raw drama set in a house of detention, about what happens when a man accused of molesting a child is thrown in among the other inmates.
The play opened in a church, moved to the Public Theater with Joseph Papp's help, and then to Lincoln Center.
In 1974 it won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award for best American play.
Piñero was suddenly famous.
He wrote for television, acted in films and in shows like Miami Vice, usually as a criminal, and kept writing poems.
He never escaped his addictions.
In one poem he asked for one last thing: after he had climbed up on a tenement sky, as he put it, he wanted his ashes scattered through the Lower East Side.
He died in June 1988, at forty-one.
His friend Miguel Algarín led a procession through the neighborhood, and they did as he had asked, scattering his ashes along the streets he had written about.
Another poet of the Cafe's early days, Pedro Pietri, wrote Puerto Rican Obituary, a long poem about workers who spent their lives chasing a dream that never arrived.
In 2001, Benjamin Bratt played Piñero in a film about his life.
But the Cafe itself, still filling up on poetry nights, may be the memorial Piñero would have liked best.
You heard that the first Labor Day parade marched to Union Square on September fifth, 1882.
Notice the day of the week: it was a Tuesday, an ordinary working day.
The ten thousand or so workers who marched up Broadway from City Hall had to take the day off on their own, and many of them gave up a day's pay to do it.
The parade was organized by the Central Labor Union, an alliance of the city's unions.
Who first thought of it is still argued about, and the argument has a comic twist: the two leading candidates had almost the same name.
One was Matthew Maguire, a machinist who was the union's secretary.
The other was Peter McGuire, a carpenter who helped found the national carpenters' union and later the American Federation of Labor.
The federal Department of Labor lays out both claims, and notes that more recent research seems to favor the machinist.
The idea spread.
Other cities held parades, states made the day a legal holiday, and in 1894 Congress made the first Monday in September a national one.
Most of the rest of the world honors workers on the first of May instead, a date tied to the strikes for an eight-hour day, and the Haymarket affair, in Chicago in 1886.
Union Square kept its role.
On March sixth, 1930, in the first winter of the Great Depression, tens of thousands of people filled the square for a Communist-led rally of the unemployed.
When part of the crowd set off to march on City Hall without a permit, police on foot and on horseback charged into it with nightsticks.
When you see a protest here today, you are watching one of the oldest traditions in the city.
You heard that Tiffany had its flagship on the west side of the square from 1870.
Charles Lewis Tiffany had a gift for publicity as sharp as his eye for jewels.
In 1858, when the first telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic, New York went wild with celebration.
Tiffany bought up leftover cable, cut it into short lengths, bound the pieces with brass bands, and sold them as souvenirs, each with a certificate.
The cable itself stopped working within weeks, but the souvenirs helped make Tiffany a household name.
During the Civil War, the store supplied the Union Army, including handsome presentation swords for its officers.
In 1878, Tiffany bought one of the largest yellow diamonds ever found, from the new mines at Kimberley in South Africa.
It weighed two hundred and eighty-seven carats in the rough, and was cut down to about a hundred and twenty-eight.
The Tiffany Diamond has been the company's showpiece ever since, and Audrey Hepburn wore it in publicity photographs for Breakfast at Tiffany's.
The famous color goes back even further.
Since 1845, Tiffany has published a catalog called the Blue Book, and its robin's egg blue, on covers, boxes and bags, became one of the most recognizable colors in commerce.
A New York newspaper reported in 1906 that there was one thing Tiffany would not sell you at any price: an empty box.
You could only get one with something inside.
You heard that Tammany Hall ended its days in the building on the east side of the square.
It began in the 1780s as a social and patriotic club, the Society of Saint Tammany, named for Tamanend, a Lenape chief remembered for his wisdom and for making peace with William Penn.
Its members borrowed Native American titles: their leaders were sachems, and their meeting hall was the Wigwam.
The tiger came later, and it came from an enemy.
William Tweed got his start as foreman of a volunteer fire company, Americus Engine Company Number Six, known as Big Six, whose emblem was a snarling tiger.
In 1871, the cartoonist Thomas Nast turned that tiger against him, drawing Tammany as a beast loose in a Roman arena, mauling the Republic, while Boss Tweed watched from the emperor's box.
Tammany, unashamed, made the tiger its symbol.
No one explained the system better than George Washington Plunkitt, a Tammany district leader who held court at a shoeshine stand in the county courthouse.
A reporter, William Riordon, wrote down his talks and published them in 1905.

Plunkitt drew a line between dishonest graft, like shaking down gamblers and saloon keepers, and what he called honest graft: learning ahead of time where the city planned a new park or bridge, buying the land cheap, and selling it to the city at a profit.
He summed up his career in a line that has never been forgotten: I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.
By the time Tammany moved here in 1929, its days were numbered.

Fiorello La Guardia, mayor from 1934 to 1945, cut the machine off from city jobs, and in 1963 a young Greenwich Village lawyer named Ed Koch beat the last great Tammany boss, Carmine DeSapio, in a race for district leader.
You heard about George Washington, on horseback at the south end.
His sculptor, Henry Kirke Brown, also made the Abraham Lincoln at the north end, put up a few years after Lincoln's assassination.
Lincoln didn't start there.
He first stood at the southwest corner of the square, and was moved when the park was rebuilt.
His old corner now belongs to Mahatma Gandhi, striding along with his staff.
The statue was dedicated on October second, 1986, Gandhi's birthday, and its sponsors chose Union Square for its long history of nonviolent protest.
Look for the Marquis de Lafayette, the young French nobleman who crossed the Atlantic to fight beside Washington, shown offering his heart and his sword to the American cause.
He is the work of Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, who designed the Statue of Liberty.
France gave him to New York to thank the city for its help to Paris during the siege of 1870 and 1871, and he was unveiled in 1876, in the very years Bartholdi was at work on Liberty.
Then find the tall flagpole rising from a massive bronze base.
It was made for the hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, in 1926, and its base carries the Declaration's entire text.
The Tammany Society paid for it, as a memorial to Charles Francis Murphy, the boss who had led the machine for more than twenty years.
Washington is the oldest of them all.
He has watched nearly every rally, march and protest this square has seen.
You heard that Macy's started out on Sixth Avenue at Fourteenth Street, at the southern edge of Ladies' Mile.
You can hear about Rowland Macy himself, the Nantucket whaler, on the Midtown walk.
This is the story of the person who ran his store.
Margaret Getchell was a distant cousin of Macy's, also from Nantucket.
Around 1860, not yet twenty, she came to work at his new store in New York, keeping the books and handling the cash.

She was quick with figures and even quicker at running things, and in 1866 Macy made her superintendent of the whole business, in charge of nearly two hundred employees and the store's daily operations.
That freed him to sail to Europe on buying trips.
Macy's has called her the first woman promoted to an executive position in American retailing.
She is credited with starting an early mail-order business, so customers could shop from home.
In 1869 she married a Macy's colleague, Abiel LaForge, and the next year she stepped down to raise a family.
She died in 1880, at only thirty-eight.
The Fourteenth Street store kept growing until it filled much of its block.
Macy's says it was the first department store to decorate its windows for Christmas, in 1874, with porcelain dolls posed in scenes from Uncle Tom's Cabin.
Macy died in 1877, and the store later passed to the Straus family, who carried the red star north to Herald Square in 1902.
Behind the counters of Ladies' Mile was a world the shoppers rarely saw.
Saleswomen stood on their feet for long days, often in hot, stuffy rooms.

And running between the counters were the cash girls and cash boys, children as young as ten, who carried each customer's money to the cashier's desk and brought back the change, whenever a clerk called out, Cash!

In 1890, the reformer Jacob Riis wrote that cash girls in New York stores earned about a dollar seventy-five a week, for days that in the busy season stretched to sixteen hours, and that girls fainted on the job.
A group of New York women decided to use the one power they had over the stores: their own shopping.

At the start of the 1890s, with the reformer Josephine Shaw Lowell as president, they founded the Consumers' League of New York, and drew up a White List, a published list of stores that paid fair wages, kept reasonable hours, and provided decent, sanitary working conditions.
Shoppers were urged to buy only from stores on the list, and in time about forty stores made it.
It was an early version of an idea that is still with us: that where you shop is a political act.
Wire carriers and pneumatic tubes eventually replaced the cash children, and state laws began to limit how long women and children could work in stores.
In 1910, the league hired a young social worker named Frances Perkins to run its New York office.
She went on to become secretary of labor under Franklin Roosevelt, the first woman in a president's cabinet.
In February 1886, a young ornithologist named Frank Chapman went bird watching in the uptown shopping district, which in those days meant streets like these.
He wasn't looking at the trees.
He was looking at women's hats.
