On two late afternoon walks, Chapman counted about seven hundred hats, and five hundred and forty-two of them were decorated with feathers, wings or whole stuffed birds.
Among them he identified about forty native species, many of them common songbirds.
He published his tally in the magazine Forest and Stream.
The milliners of Ladies' Mile were at the heart of the fashion.
Plume hunters were wiping out colonies of egrets and herons in Florida, shooting the adults in breeding season, when their plumes were finest, and leaving the chicks to starve.
Chapman's count became ammunition for a new movement.
In 1896, two Boston women, Harriet Hemenway and her cousin Minna Hall, held teas to persuade their friends to give up feathered hats, and founded the Massachusetts Audubon Society.
Other states followed.

In 1900 Congress passed the Lacey Act, which banned shipping illegally killed birds across state lines, and in 1903 Theodore Roosevelt, born just around the corner from here, created the first federal bird reservation, at Pelican Island in Florida.
Chapman spent more than half a century at the American Museum of Natural History, and in 1900 he proposed a new holiday tradition.
Instead of competing to shoot as many birds as possible on Christmas Day, as hunters then did, people should go out and count them.
The Christmas Bird Count still takes place every winter.
When Theodore was seven or eight, walking up Broadway, he passed a market and saw a dead seal laid out on a slab.
He was spellbound.
As long as the seal was there, he came back day after day to study it, and he measured it as best he could with a folding pocket ruler.
He never got the seal, but he did get its skull, and with two of his cousins he made it the first specimen of what the boys grandly called the Roosevelt Museum of Natural History.
The museum grew, specimen by specimen, with whatever a determined boy could collect and preserve.
For his fourteenth birthday, his father gave him lessons in taxidermy from John G. Bell, a taxidermist who had once traveled with John James Audubon.
That same year, Theodore got his first pair of glasses, and discovered how much of the world a nearsighted boy had been missing.
He later wrote that he had no idea how beautiful the world was until he got those spectacles.
That winter, on a family trip up the Nile, he spent the voyage shooting and preparing birds for his collection.
The boy naturalist became the president who protected more American land than any before him, in national forests, bird reservations and national monuments.
Some of the birds he collected as a teenager survive to this day in museum collections.
In 1895, at thirty-six, Roosevelt became president of the city's board of police commissioners, in charge of a department that a state investigation had just exposed as deeply corrupt.
He decided to see for himself what his patrolmen did at night.
With the journalist Jacob Riis as his guide, the commissioner walked the streets in the small hours, checking on the men on their beats.
They found officers asleep, chatting in saloons, or simply gone, and some were summoned to headquarters the next morning to face the commissioner himself.
The newspapers loved it, and cartoonists drew Roosevelt as little more than a pair of glasses and a mouthful of teeth.
Riis had his own reasons.

As a penniless young immigrant, he had once spent a night in one of the city's police station lodging houses, filthy rooms where the homeless were allowed to sleep, and there, he later wrote, a policeman killed the little stray dog that had been his only companion.
He showed Roosevelt the lodging houses, and soon afterward Roosevelt shut them down.
Not every crusade went so well.

Roosevelt insisted on enforcing the state law that closed saloons on Sundays, the one day most working men had free, and it made him enemies across the city, especially among German New Yorkers who loved their Sunday beer gardens.
He held the job for about two years before leaving for Washington as assistant secretary of the Navy.
In November 1902, President Roosevelt went bear hunting in Mississippi, at the invitation of the state's governor.
The other hunters found bears.
He didn't.
So his guide, Holt Collier, a renowned bear hunter who had been born into slavery, cornered a big black bear with his dogs, lassoed it, and tied it to a tree for the president to shoot.
Roosevelt refused.
It wasn't sporting.
The cuddly version stops there.
In most accounts, the bear had already been badly hurt, and Roosevelt had it put out of its misery.
A cartoonist at the Washington Post, Clifford Berryman, drew the scene on November sixteenth, under the title Drawing the Line in Mississippi: the president turning away from a frightened bear.
In later cartoons the bear got smaller and cuter, and became a regular companion of the cartoon president.
In Brooklyn, a shopkeeper named Morris Michtom saw the cartoon.
He and his wife, Rose, made stuffed toy bears and put them in their window with a sign that read Teddy's bears.
The family always said he wrote to the White House and got the president's permission to use his name.
The bears sold so well that the Michtoms went on to found the Ideal Novelty and Toy Company, one of the biggest toy makers in the country.
At almost the same moment, in Germany, Richard Steiff of the Steiff toy company designed a jointed stuffed bear of his own, and collectors still argue over who came first.
One more irony: Roosevelt is said to have disliked the nickname Teddy.
The bears made sure it stuck.
You heard that Edwin Booth was the brother of Lincoln's assassin.
There is a stranger story about him, and the witness was a Lincoln.
During the Civil War, the president's son Robert was traveling from New York to Washington.

On the crowded platform at the Jersey City station, passengers pressed toward the sleeping car as the train began to move, and Robert was twisted off his feet and slipped into the gap between the platform and the car.
A hand seized his coat collar and pulled him back to safety.
He turned to thank his rescuer, and knew him at once.
It was Edwin Booth, whose face was famous.
Robert told the story himself, many years later, in a letter published in The Century Magazine.
Booth learned whose life he had saved from his friend Adam Badeau, an officer on General Grant's staff, who wrote to tell him.
There is one more strange scene.

On November twenty-fifth, 1864, Edwin and his brothers Junius and John Wilkes appeared on stage together for the only time, in Julius Caesar at the Winter Garden Theatre on Broadway, a benefit to raise money for a statue of Shakespeare in Central Park, the one that stands on the Mall today.
Edwin played Brutus, the noble assassin.
John Wilkes played Mark Antony.
That same night, Confederate agents tried to set New York on fire, starting blazes in a string of hotels, one of them right next door to the theater.
When the fire bells rang, Edwin stepped to the footlights and calmed the audience, and the play went on.
Less than five months later, John Wilkes Booth shot Robert's father at Ford's Theatre.
You heard that Samuel Tilden won the popular vote for president in 1876 and lost the White House anyway.
He lost it by a single electoral vote.

He spent his last years among his books, here and at Greystone, his estate in Yonkers, and when he died in 1886, unmarried and childless, he left the bulk of his fortune to found a free library and reading room for the people of New York.
His relatives had other plans.
A nephew sued, other relatives joined in, and they attacked the clause of the will that created the library trust.
The case dragged on for years, and the courts largely sided with the family.
In the end, only part of the fortune, roughly two million dollars by most accounts, reached the library trust.
That wasn't enough to build a great library.
But New York had two other libraries that were struggling: the Astor Library, in the building on Lafayette Street that is now the Public Theater, and the Lenox Library on Fifth Avenue.
In 1895 the three joined forces as the New York Public Library, whose great marble building on Fifth Avenue you can visit on the Midtown walk.
So a disappointed candidate's last wish, half broken by his own family, helped create one of the great libraries of the world.
From 1903 to 1907, an apartment at 55 Irving Place, a short walk south of the park, was home to one of the most popular writers in America.
He signed his stories O. Henry.

His real name was William Sydney Porter, and he arrived in New York with a past: he had served three years in an Ohio prison for embezzling from a bank in Austin, Texas, where he had worked as a teller.
It was in prison that he began publishing stories under his new name.
In New York he wrote at a furious pace, for a time a story a week for the Sunday edition of the New York World, about shopgirls, clerks, waiters, swindlers and lonely people in rented rooms.
In 1906 he collected some of them in a book called The Four Million.

The title was a jab at Ward McAllister, the society arbiter who had declared that only about four hundred people in New York really mattered, the number, it was said, who could fit in Caroline Astor's ballroom.
O. Henry's answer was that all four million New Yorkers were worth a story.
The book included The Gift of the Magi, the tale of a poor young couple, Jim and Della, who each sell their most precious possession to buy the other a Christmas present.
She sells her long hair to buy a chain for his watch, and he sells his watch to buy combs for her hair.
As you heard, Pete's Tavern claims he wrote it there, and it points to its second booth.
O. Henry drank too much and spent faster than he earned, and he died in 1910, at forty-seven.
Walk around the park and look at the houses.
Several have stories on their doorsteps.
On the west side, numbers 3 and 4 share a lacy cast iron porch, usually credited to the architect Alexander Jackson Davis.
In front of number 4, look for a pair of tall lamps.
This was the home of James Harper, one of the brothers who founded the publishing house Harper and Brothers, and mayor of New York in the 1840s.
By an old custom, said to go back to Dutch New Amsterdam, a pair of lamps marked the mayor's home.
Harper's lamps are still here, though the custom faded after Gracie Mansion became the mayor's official residence in 1942.
On the east side, look at number 36, a white terra cotta apartment house in the Gothic style, finished around 1910 to a design by James Riely Gordon.
Two knights in armor stand guard at its door.
Next door, number 34, finished in 1883, is often described as the first cooperative apartment building in New York, where residents owned shares in the building instead of renting.
Its residents have included the actor James Cagney, and Margaret Hamilton, who played the Wicked Witch of the West in The Wizard of Oz.
Like the other buildings around the park, these come with the most coveted perk in the neighborhood: a key to the gate.
Walk to the north tip of the Flatiron and look at the bottom of the prow.
The building's sharp edge doesn't come all the way down to the sidewalk.
A low, one-story shop pokes out in front of it, like the cowcatcher on the front of a locomotive, and that is exactly what New Yorkers called it.
It wasn't part of the original design.
Harry Black, the head of the Fuller Company, wanted every square foot of rentable space he could get on his expensive lot, and he insisted on a storefront at the tip.
Burnham objected.
Black won, and the space was leased to United Cigar Stores.
You heard that the Flatiron is a steel-frame skyscraper.
On this lot, that frame was everything.
The building rises twenty-two stories, about two hundred and eighty-five feet, and the steel skeleton carries the weight, so the stone and terra cotta walls are a covering rather than a support.
A traditional masonry building this tall would have needed enormously thick walls at the bottom, and on a triangle that narrows to about six and a half feet, the tip would have been nearly solid.
Steel let the prow stay hollow, and full of offices.
Those offices at the prow are the most famous rooms in the building, narrow wedges with windows on both sides, looking out over Madison Square and up two of the most famous avenues in the world.
Once you notice the cowcatcher, though, you will never see the Flatiron quite the same way again.
You heard that Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen made famous photographs of the Flatiron.
Here is how.
In the winter of 1903, on a day of heavy snow, Stieglitz set up his camera in Madison Square, across the street, and framed the new building behind the forked trunk of a snow-covered tree.
Years later he recalled that the building had seemed to move toward him like the bow of a monster ocean steamer.
He published the photograph in his magazine, Camera Work.
Steichen's version came a year or so later, at twilight, with a horse-drawn cab and the dark branches of a tree in front of the building.
He printed the negative in layers of tinted gum over platinum, so each print came out a different color.
Three of them, each in a different tone, are now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a gift from Stieglitz in 1933.
The two men led a movement called the Photo-Secession, which argued that a photograph could be a work of art, as personal as a painting.
In 1905 they opened a small gallery a short walk up Fifth Avenue, at number 291, known simply as 291.
Besides photographs, it gave many Americans their first look at modern art from Europe: drawings by Rodin, work by Matisse, and in 1911, Picasso.
In 1916, Stieglitz showed the drawings of a young artist named Georgia O'Keeffe, whom he later married.
From the Flatiron's tip, look north across Twenty-third Street at the big building on the west side of Fifth Avenue, number 200.
For most of the twentieth century, this was the capital of the American toy business.
The site had been the Fifth Avenue Hotel, until it was torn down in 1908.

The office building that replaced it filled with toy companies, and it became the heart of the annual Toy Fair, which had begun in 1903 with fewer than ten companies showing their wares, Lionel electric trains among them.

Every winter, buyers from stores all over the country came to see what children would be asking for the following Christmas, in showrooms that spread into a second building on Broadway, joined to this one in 1967 by a bridge high above the street.
Some of the most famous toys in the world made their debuts at Toy Fair.
In 1959, a California toy company introduced a teenage fashion doll there.
Her name was Barbie.
In the 2000s the toy companies moved out, the building was sold and remade, and the fair moved to the Javits Center on the far West Side.
Today the old Toy Center holds Eataly, the Italian food hall, and the corporate offices of Tiffany and Company.
When you pass its doors, picture the buyers who once crowded in each winter to see what American children would want next.
You heard that the Statue of Liberty's arm and torch stood in this park.
They had already been on tour.
Bartholdi's workshop in Paris finished the arm first, and shipped it to Philadelphia for the Centennial Exhibition of 1876, the great fair for a hundred years of American independence.
It arrived months after the fair opened, but visitors still paid to climb up inside it to the balcony around the torch.
The arm alone is about forty-two feet long, and the index finger is eight feet.
After the fair, the arm came here, to the northwest corner of Madison Square, and stayed until 1882, to drum up money for the pedestal.
France was paying for the statue, but Americans were expected to pay for its base, and they were in no hurry.
In 1882 the arm went back to France, to be joined to the rest of the statue.
It took Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper campaign of 1885 to pay for the pedestal, and the statue was dedicated in October 1886.
The torch had a hard life after that.
In 1916, German saboteurs blew up a munitions depot on Black Tom Island, across the harbor in New Jersey, and flying debris damaged the arm.
The torch has been closed to visitors ever since.
That same year, the sculptor Gutzon Borglum, who later carved Mount Rushmore, cut windows into the torch's copper flame and fitted them with amber glass, so it could glow from within.
The windows leaked every time it rained, and for decades the water damaged the arm.
During the restoration for the statue's hundredth birthday, the old torch came down, and in 1986 a new one went up, its flame covered in gold leaf.
The original, the one that once rose out of this park, is now on display in the Statue of Liberty Museum on Liberty Island.
You heard that Harry Thaw shot Stanford White on the roof of Madison Square Garden in June 1906.
What followed filled the newspapers for years.
At the center of it was Evelyn Nesbit.
She had come to New York as a teenage model and chorus girl, and White, more than thirty years older, pursued her when she was sixteen.
In his apartment on Twenty-fourth Street there was a red velvet swing, and the girl on the red velvet swing became the most famous phrase of the scandal.
Thaw, the unstable heir to a Pittsburgh railroad fortune, married Nesbit in 1905, and his jealousy of White became an obsession.
At his first trial, in 1907, Nesbit testified that White had drugged and assaulted her when she was sixteen, and the whole country hung on her words.
The jury deadlocked.
At the second trial, in 1908, Thaw's lawyers argued that he was insane, and the jury agreed: not guilty by reason of insanity.
He was sent to the state hospital for the criminally insane at Matteawan.
His family's money kept working for him.
In 1913 he escaped from Matteawan and fled to Canada, and was brought back.
In 1915 a jury declared him sane, and he walked free.
Nesbit spent the rest of her long life trying to escape one night in 1906.
She danced in vaudeville, acted in silent films, and struggled with poverty and addiction.
In 1955 she served as an adviser on a Hollywood film about her own story, The Girl in the Red Velvet Swing, with Joan Collins playing her.
She died in 1967.
You heard that Met Life sold small policies to working-class families.
It was called industrial insurance.
For a few cents a week, collected door to door by an agent, a family could make sure there would be money for a funeral, and a little to live on, if the breadwinner died.
Millions of families signed up, and their nickels and dimes paid for the tower on the east side of the park.
For decades, the company used the tower as its symbol.
Its most remarkable idea came in 1909.
At the suggestion of Lillian Wald, the founder of the Henry Street Settlement on the Lower East Side, Met Life began sending visiting nurses into the homes of sick policyholders, free of charge.
It began with Henry Street nurses in Manhattan and grew into a service across the country that lasted more than forty years.
The company argued that it was good business, too: healthier policyholders lived longer and kept paying their premiums.
Now look across Twenty-fourth Street, at the massive limestone building just north of the tower.
It was meant to be the base of a skyscraper of up to a hundred stories.
The Great Depression stopped it at about thirty.
What you see is the stump of a tower that never was, and on its ground floor is the restaurant Eleven Madison Park.
Madison Square Park is full of statues, and three of them repay a closer look.
At the north end, find Admiral David Farragut, standing as if on the deck of his ship.
Farragut was the Union admiral who, in 1864, led his fleet through the mines, then called torpedoes, at the mouth of Mobile Bay, with an order remembered as: damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead.

The statue, unveiled in 1881, was the first major work of the young sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, and its curving stone base, with figures and lettering that seem to flow like water, was a collaboration with his friend Stanford White, then a young architect.
It made Saint-Gaudens famous, and began a partnership with White that lasted until White's death across the street.
At the southwest corner sits William Seward, Lincoln's secretary of state and the man who later bought Alaska.
For generations, New Yorkers have told a story that the sculptor saved money by putting Seward's head on a body made for a statue of Lincoln.
It is a good story, but no one has found evidence that it is true.
And at the southeast corner stands Roscoe Conkling, one of the most powerful senators of the Gilded Age.
In March 1888, during the great blizzard that buried New York, Conkling set out on foot from his law office on Wall Street, heading uptown.
The walk took about three hours, through deep drifts and a howling wind, and by most accounts he nearly collapsed in the snow around Union Square before he reached shelter.
He died a few weeks later.
His friends wanted his statue in Union Square, near where he fell.
The park commissioners said no, and he ended up here.
You heard that Irving Berlin came out of the Tin Pan Alley world.
He never learned to read music.
Israel Beilin was born in the Russian Empire in 1888 and came to New York with his family when he was five.
His father, a cantor, died when Israel was thirteen, and before long the boy left home to make his own way, singing for pennies on street corners and in saloons.
He found work as a singing waiter at the Pelham Café on Pell Street in Chinatown, making up parodies and new songs for the customers.
In 1907 he wrote the words for his first published song, Marie from Sunny Italy.
As the story is usually told, the printer got his name wrong, and the sheet music credited I. Berlin.
He kept it.
Berlin taught himself the piano, but he played almost entirely in one key, F sharp, which lies mostly on the black keys.
Once he was successful, he had special pianos built with a lever that shifted the whole keyboard, so he could keep playing on the black keys while the music came out in whatever key he chose.
Musical secretaries wrote down what he played and sang.
In 1911, Alexander's Ragtime Band made him a star.
He went on to write around fifteen hundred songs, among them Blue Skies, Puttin' On the Ritz, Cheek to Cheek, Easter Parade and There's No Business Like Show Business.
The composer Jerome Kern said that Irving Berlin had no place in American music.
He was American music.
Berlin lived to be a hundred and one.
You heard the legend that a journalist gave Tin Pan Alley its name.
The usual suspect is Monroe Rosenfeld, a songwriter and newspaperman who knew this block well.

As the story goes, around the turn of the twentieth century, Rosenfeld visited the office of the composer and publisher Harry Von Tilzer, who liked to weave strips of paper through his piano strings to give them a tinny, banjo-like sound.
Rosenfeld said it sounded like a tin pan, and when he wrote about the street, the name stuck.
That's the legend.

The article in which Rosenfeld supposedly coined the phrase has never been found, and others say tin pan was simply slang for a battered, tinny piano, a name that may have been around before anyone wrote it down.
Harry Von Tilzer deserves a story of his own.
He was born Aaron Gumbinsky, and as a teenager he took his mother's maiden name, Tilzer, and added a Von to make it sound grander.
He wrote hundreds of songs, including A Bird in a Gilded Cage and Wait Till the Sun Shines, Nellie.
His brother Albert wrote the music for Take Me Out to the Ball Game, though by most accounts neither Albert nor the lyricist, Jack Norworth, had ever been to a baseball game when they wrote it.
Whatever its origin, the name outlived the block.
By the 1920s, Tin Pan Alley meant the whole American popular song business, wherever it happened to be.
You heard that Al Smith had just lost the 1928 presidential election when he took on this building.
The two facts are connected.
Smith, the Lower East Side boy you may have heard about at Foley Square, had become a four-term governor of New York and, in 1928, the Democratic nominee for president.
His campaign chairman was John J. Raskob.
Smith was buried in a landslide by Herbert Hoover, after a campaign full of attacks on his religion, and he came home without a job.
Raskob and his longtime partner, Pierre du Pont, gave him one: president of the company building the tallest tower in the world.
Smith was its public face, the handshakes and the speeches.
On opening day, two of his grandchildren cut the ribbon, and it was Hoover, the man who had beaten him, who pressed the button in Washington to switch on the lights.
Now a story, told later and probably polished in the retelling.
Raskob is said to have pulled a thick pencil from a drawer, stood it on its end, and asked the architect, William Lamb, Bill, how high can you make it so that it won't fall down?
True or not, the building does look a little like a pencil.
Smith's politics took a turn in this tower's early years.
He had urged Franklin Roosevelt to run for governor in 1928, but he turned bitterly against the New Deal.
In 1934, Raskob and the du Pont family helped found the American Liberty League to fight it, and Smith became one of its loudest voices, attacking his old ally's program in a famous speech in 1936.
That fall, Roosevelt was reelected in one of the biggest landslides in American history.
Smith died in 1944.

His name lives on in the Al Smith Dinner, a Catholic charity dinner held each fall, where in many election years both presidential candidates have shown up in white tie to roast each other, and themselves.
You heard the steel went up at about four and a half stories a week.
Here are some of the men who put it there.
In 1930, the builders hired Lewis Hine to photograph the work.

Hine was a former schoolteacher who had spent years photographing children at work in mills, mines and factories for the National Child Labor Committee, pictures that helped build the case for child labor laws.
Now he turned his camera on the men building the tallest tower in the world, and he went up on the steel with them.
His best-known picture from the job, called Icarus, shows a young ironworker swinging from a cable with the city far below.
Hine later gathered many of these images in a book called Men at Work, a tribute to the skill and nerve of working people.
His pictures show how a riveting gang worked.
One man heated the rivets in a small coal forge until they glowed, then tossed them with tongs to a catcher, who caught them in a tin can.
Two more men set each rivet in its hole and hammered it home.
A sizable share of the ironworkers were Mohawk men from Kahnawake, near Montreal.

Their tradition in high steel went back to the 1880s, when a railroad bridge was built across the Saint Lawrence River onto their land, and the bridge company hired young Mohawk men, who proved superb on the beams.
Outsiders liked to say that Mohawks had no fear of heights.
The ironworkers themselves have always said that's a myth: they feel it like anyone else, and work anyway.
Generations of them commuted to New York for the big jobs, and their sons and grandsons later helped raise the World Trade Center.
The building came in ahead of schedule and under budget, helped by the Depression, which had pushed down the cost of labor and materials.
Officially, five workers died during construction.
Rumors at the time put the toll much higher, but the official count remains five.
You heard about the Waldorf-Astoria, the grand hotel that stood here before the skyscraper.
Its most famous employee wasn't a chef.
Oscar Tschirky was a Swiss immigrant who started working in New York restaurants as a teenager, and when the Waldorf opened in 1893, he became its maître d'hôtel, the man who ran the dining rooms.
He knew every regular's name, table and tastes, and the whole city came to know him simply as Oscar of the Waldorf.
He stayed with the hotel for about half a century, and moved with it to Park Avenue in 1931.
His most famous creation is a salad.
According to the usual story, Oscar introduced it at a grand charity ball at the hotel in 1896, and it appeared in a cookbook he published that same year.
The original Waldorf salad was very simple: diced apples and celery, bound with good mayonnaise.
The walnuts came later, added by other cooks, and stuck.
The Waldorf turns up in another food story you may have heard at Delmonico's, in the Financial District.

In one version of the origin of eggs Benedict, a stockbroker with a hangover ordered toast, poached eggs, bacon and hollandaise at the Waldorf in 1894, and Oscar liked the idea enough to put a version of it on the menu.
Like most famous food stories, it was told decades after the fact.
Oscar's real art was hospitality, and the hotel was built for it.
A long corridor joined the two halves of the Waldorf-Astoria, and well-dressed New Yorkers paraded up and down it to see and be seen.
It's said to have been nicknamed Peacock Alley, and the new Waldorf on Park Avenue named a restaurant after it.

So as you look up at the Empire State Building, picture the dining rooms that stood here first, where a waiter from Switzerland decided what society ate, and gave America a salad that's still on menus a hundred and thirty years later.
You heard that James Gordon Bennett Junior sent Henry Morton Stanley to find Livingstone.
Here's the man himself.
Bennett inherited the Herald from his father, who had founded it and made it one of the best-selling papers in the country.
The son was rich, reckless and impossible.
In 1877, he was engaged to a young woman from a prominent New York family.
On New Year's Day, he turned up at her family's party drunk and behaved so badly that the engagement was off.
The story told for a century is that he relieved himself in the fireplace, but that part may be legend.
Her brother, Frederick May, went after Bennett, and within days, the two men met for a duel at a remote spot in Delaware called Slaughter Gap.
Shots were fired, nobody was hurt, and Bennett soon left for Europe.
He spent most of the rest of his life in France, running the Herald by cable, and in 1887 he founded a Paris edition, which lived on for more than a century as the International Herald Tribune.
He paid for adventures as well as news.
Besides Stanley's expedition, he backed an attempt to reach the North Pole aboard a ship called the Jeannette, which was crushed by the Arctic ice in 1881.
Its captain and many of its crew died.
He also put up trophies for races in cars, balloons and airplanes, and the Gordon Bennett balloon race is still flown today.
And he loved owls.
He kept live ones, and when Stanford White designed the Herald building here, Bennett had a row of bronze owls set along its roof, with electric eyes that flashed at night.
Look at the monument: two of those owls are still perched on it.
Bennett even planned a tomb in the shape of a giant owl, about a hundred and twenty-five feet tall, to be designed by White.
It was never built.
White was shot dead in 1906, as you may have heard at Madison Square, and Bennett died in France in 1918.
Stand in front of Macy's and picture a music hall.
Before the store was built, part of this block held Koster and Bial's Music Hall, a popular variety house, with singers, dancers, acrobats and comics.
On the night of April 23rd, 1896, the bill ended with something new.
After the live acts, the lights went down, and a projector threw moving pictures onto a large screen: six short films, each lasting about a minute.
Thomas Edison's company had been selling peep-show machines, where one person at a time bent over a box to watch a tiny film.
This was different.
A whole audience sat in the dark and watched the same images together, larger than life.
Others had projected films before, but this was the show that caught on, and the night is often remembered as the start of the movie business in America.
The machine was billed as Edison's Vitascope.
In fact, it was mostly the work of a young inventor named Thomas Armat.
The businessmen who bought the rights thought Edison's name would sell more tickets, and Edison agreed to manufacture it and take the credit.
He was in the audience that night.
The program included dancers, a comic boxing match and waves breaking on a beach in England, a sight that seemed astonishing on a screen.
Koster and Bial's closed in 1901 to make way for Macy's.
Look for a plaque on the Macy's building marking the spot.
Within a decade, storefront movie theaters called nickelodeons were spreading across the city, and the music halls that had launched the movies were losing their audiences to them.
You heard the giant balloons joined the Thanksgiving parade in 1927.
They came from a puppeteer.
Tony Sarg was a marionette maker who also designed Macy's holiday window displays, filled with moving puppets that drew crowds to the glass.
For the 1927 parade, he came up with huge figures filled with air, and worked with the Goodyear tire and rubber company to build them.
The first star was Felix the Cat, the most famous cartoon character of the day.
Sarg is said to have called his creations upside-down marionettes: instead of hanging from strings, they floated above the street, held down by handlers walking below.
Those first balloons were awkward, and handlers sometimes propped them up on poles.
For 1928, Sarg switched to helium, and Macy's tried a stunt.
At the end of the parade, the balloons were let go, to drift away over the city.
They were built to leak slowly and come down somewhere days later, and each carried a return address.
Macy's offered a reward of a hundred dollars to anyone who brought one back.
It didn't go smoothly.
By one account, of the first five released, two came down in the water, and a third was torn to shreds by neighbors fighting over it.
The aviator Clarence Chamberlin, famous for flying across the Atlantic, once snagged a balloon in midair with his plane.
The releases ended in the early 1930s.
The first parade, in 1924, had no balloons at all.
It had floats, bands and live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo.
Within a few years, the balloons had taken the animals' place.

Today, the balloons are still designed and built in Macy's own studio, and the night before the parade, crowds come to watch them being inflated near the American Museum of Natural History, a show of its own.
You heard the garment industry moved into this district in the 1920s.
It didn't simply drift here.
It was pushed.
In the early 1900s, as the industry outgrew the Lower East Side, many shops moved into new loft buildings along lower Fifth Avenue and the streets around it, and they kept creeping north.
At lunchtime and at the end of the day, thousands of garment workers poured onto the sidewalks of Fifth Avenue, which the avenue's fashionable stores considered their own.
The merchants decided the crowds were bad for business.
On March 5th, 1916, the Fifth Avenue Association, the merchants' organization, ran advertisements in the city's newspapers under the headline, Shall We Save New York?
The ads warned that the loft factories were swallowing the shopping district, and the merchants pledged to stop buying from manufacturers who stayed in the area around them.
The campaign fed into the zoning law the city passed that same year, the first comprehensive one in the country.

Besides shaping the skyscrapers, as you may have heard at the start of this tour, the law divided the city into districts for homes, for business and for industry, and helped keep new factories away from the shopping blocks.
So the garment makers moved west, to the blocks beyond Sixth Avenue, which included much of the old Tenderloin, a district of saloons, dance halls and brothels.
Developers put up tall new loft buildings for them, and by 1924, the lofts reached all the way to Ninth Avenue.
A new garment center rose here, close to Penn Station and the department stores of Herald Square, but out of sight of Fifth Avenue's customers.
It's an early example of how zoning could be used not just for light and air, but to decide who belongs where.
You heard that the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union was one of the most powerful unions in the city.
In 1937, it also produced a Broadway hit.
The union ran education and culture programs for its members: classes, choruses, sports teams and drama groups.
It took over a small theater, renamed it the Labor Stage, and asked a young songwriter, Harold Rome, to write a musical revue.
The cast was made up of union members, garment workers who rehearsed after work: cutters, basters and sewing machine operators.
The show was called Pins and Needles.
It opened on November 27th, 1937, and the opening number set the tone: Sing Me a Song with Social Significance.
The sketches and songs poked fun at bosses, at dictators abroad and at politicians at home.
Critics liked it, and audiences kept coming.
In March 1938, the cast performed at the White House for President and Eleanor Roosevelt.

The show was rewritten again and again to keep up with the news, moved to a larger Broadway house, the Windsor Theatre, in 1939, and closed in June 1940 after one thousand one hundred and eight performances, one of the longest runs Broadway had seen up to then.
The union kept singing.
Decades later, as garment jobs were moving overseas, its television commercials showed workers singing Look for the Union Label, urging shoppers to buy clothes made by union members in America.
By then the union was fighting a losing battle against cheaper imports.
But for a few years in the 1930s, the people who worked these sewing machines were the toast of Broadway.
You heard that New York is home to Fashion Week.
It began with a publicist and a war.
Before the Second World War, American fashion took its cues from Paris.
Manufacturers on Seventh Avenue sent buyers to the Paris collections and copied what they saw, and most American designers worked anonymously, their names hidden behind the manufacturers' labels.
Then, in 1940, Germany occupied Paris, and the flow of French fashion stopped.
Eleanor Lambert saw an opening.
She was a publicist who had worked with artists before turning to fashion, and she already ran the International Best-Dressed List, the annual ranking of the world's most stylish people.
In 1943, she staged what she called Press Week: a series of shows of American designers' collections, at the Plaza Hotel, for fashion editors from newspapers across the country.
To make sure they came, she paid for their travel.
The editors went home and wrote about American designers by name, many of them for the first time.
Press Week is the ancestor of today's New York Fashion Week.
Lambert spent the rest of her long life promoting American fashion.

In the early 1940s, she helped create the Coty awards for American designers, and in 1962, she founded the Council of Fashion Designers of America, which still gives the industry's top American awards.

The council also credits her as the force behind the Metropolitan Museum's Costume Institute benefit, today's Met Gala, and behind the Battle of Versailles, a fashion show at the palace in 1973 where, by most accounts, the Americans stole the show from the French.
In the 1990s, the shows gathered under big white tents in Bryant Park, the next stop on this walk, until they moved to Lincoln Center in 2010.
Lambert kept working into her late nineties and died in 2003, at the age of one hundred.
You heard about the Crystal Palace, the iron and glass hall built here for New York's world's fair in 1853.
Just across 42nd Street, the fair had a rival attraction.
It was the Latting Observatory, a wooden tower about three hundred and fifteen feet tall, put up by a promoter who guessed, correctly, that fairgoers would pay to look down on the city.
For three years, it was the tallest structure in New York, taller than the spire of Trinity Church.
From the top, visitors could look out over farms, rocky lots and shanties to both rivers.
But the fair lost money, the crowds faded, and in 1856, the tower burned.
The Crystal Palace lasted two years longer.
It was supposed to be fireproof, a building of iron and glass, but it had plenty of wood in its floors and fittings, and it was full of exhibits.
On October 5th, 1858, a fire broke out inside and spread with terrible speed.
By one account, the whole building was gone in about forty minutes, its great dome collapsing into the flames.
The cause was never settled.
For years afterward, the open ground beside the reservoir was known as Reservoir Square.
It was renamed for William Cullen Bryant in 1884, a few years after his death, and when the reservoir came down to make way for the library, the park began to take the shape you see now.

So as you sit here, picture the view in 1853: a glass palace glittering in the sun, a wooden tower rising beside it, and the massive stone walls of the reservoir, at what was then the northern edge of the city.
Walk toward Fifth Avenue and look a couple of blocks north.
In 1863, on Fifth Avenue between 43rd and 44th Streets, stood the Colored Orphan Asylum, a home and school for Black children.
It had been founded in 1836 by two Quaker women, and by the time of the Civil War, it was home to more than two hundred children.
That July, the federal government began drafting men for the Union army.
The law let a man buy his way out for three hundred dollars, a sum far beyond most working men, and anger at the draft exploded into one of the deadliest riots in American history.
For four days, mobs, many of them poor Irish immigrants, attacked draft offices, police, the homes of abolitionists and, above all, Black New Yorkers, who were beaten and murdered in the streets.
On the first day, July 13th, a huge crowd surrounded the orphanage.
The staff gathered the children, two hundred and thirty-three of them, and led them out a back door as rioters broke in the front, looted the building and set it on fire.
The children were taken to shelter, and the building burned to the ground.
The asylum never came back to Fifth Avenue.
It rebuilt uptown, first in Harlem and later in Riverdale, in the Bronx, and in 1944, it became the Riverdale Children's Association, carrying on its work with children under a new name.
It's hard to picture a mob burning an orphanage on this stretch of Fifth Avenue today.
But the attack became one of the defining images of the draft riots, a reminder that the Civil War was fought in New York's own streets too.
Look at the lawn in front of you.
Beneath it, and beneath the paths and the people, are the library's book stacks.
By the 1980s, the library had run out of room, and there was no space to expand on Fifth Avenue.
So during the park's restoration, the lawn was dug up, and workers excavated a vast underground storage space, about thirty feet deep.
The park was then rebuilt on top of it.
The first level of the new stacks opened in 1991.
A second, deeper level was fitted out years later and opened in the 2010s as the Milstein Research Stacks.
Together, they hold millions of volumes, kept at the cool, steady temperature and humidity that old paper needs.
Down there, the books aren't shelved by subject, as they are in most libraries.
They're shelved by size, which packs far more of them into the same space, and the library keeps track of exactly where each one sits.

When a reader in the Rose Main Reading Room asks for a book from the stacks, it rides up through the building on a book train, a system of small cars that run along tracks and climb between the stacks and the reading rooms.
The current train went into service in 2016, replacing an older conveyor.
So the people lounging on this lawn are sitting on top of one of the great research collections in the world.
In this park, the grass is a roof.
If you walk around to the library's Fifth Avenue steps, take a closer look at the two marble lions.
You heard Mayor La Guardia named them Patience and Fortitude.
They'd had other names before.
The lions were modeled by the sculptor Edward Clark Potter and carved by the Piccirilli Brothers, a family of Italian-born stone carvers who worked in the Bronx, from pink Tennessee marble.
They were unveiled in May 1911, when the library opened.
New Yorkers soon nicknamed them Lady Astor and Lord Lenox, after the library's founders, even though both lions have manes.
Patience sits on the south side, to your left as you face the building, and Fortitude on the north.
In December, they wear holiday wreaths.
Now look on either side of the entrance, at the two fountains set into the wall, by Frederick MacMonnies, the sculptor of the winged figures on the Washington Square Arch.
One is Truth, a man seated on a sphinx, the symbol of mystery.
The other is Beauty, a woman riding Pegasus, the winged horse.
For about thirty years, the fountains sat dry, until a restoration in 2015 got the water flowing again.
Then look up, above the columns, at the six figures by the sculptor Paul Wayland Bartlett.
They represent History, Drama, Poetry, Religion, Romance and Philosophy, a short list of what you'll find inside.
You heard that advertisers competed here to build the most spectacular signs.
For a quarter of a century, the most famous one blew smoke rings.
It was the sign for Camel cigarettes, on the side of the Hotel Claridge, on Broadway, and it went up around 1941.
It was the work of Douglas Leigh, a sign man who specialized in what the trade called spectaculars: signs that didn't just show a picture, but did something.
This one showed a giant face, and about every four seconds, a perfect ring of what looked like smoke puffed from its mouth and drifted out over the crowd.
It was really steam, pushed out in rings by a piston and a diaphragm behind the sign, a little like a drum being struck.
The face changed with the times.
During the Second World War, it was a man in uniform, and over the years, others took his place.
But the rings kept coming, day and night, until 1966, when the sign came down.
A few years later, cigarette ads were banned from American television, though tobacco signs hung on in Times Square for decades.
Look around you at the screens that flicker and move.
The idea that a sign should perform, not just sit there, runs straight from the smoking face to them.
You heard about the statue of Father Francis Duffy at the north end of the square.
Here's who he was.
Duffy was born in 1871 in Cobourg, Ontario, in Canada, came to New York as a young man, and became a Catholic priest.
When the United States entered the First World War, he went to France as chaplain of the 69th, New York's famous Irish regiment, which the army renamed the 165th Infantry.
It was part of the Rainbow Division, so called because it drew units from states across the country.
The regiment fought through some of the worst battles of 1918, and Duffy went with the men into the front lines, tending the wounded and burying the dead.
He came home one of the most decorated chaplains in the army.
Two other men of the regiment became famous.
One was William Donovan, a battalion commander nicknamed Wild Bill, who in the next war led the country's spy agency, the Office of Strategic Services.
The other was the poet Joyce Kilmer, the author of Trees, who had transferred into the 69th with Duffy's help.
Kilmer was killed in July 1918.
When Duffy published his memoir, Father Duffy's Story, in 1919, it included a historical appendix by Kilmer.
After the war, Duffy served as pastor of Holy Cross Church, a few blocks west on 42nd Street, until he died in 1932.
The statue, by Charles Keck, was dedicated in 1937, and two years later, this end of the square was named Father Duffy Square.
In 1940, Hollywood told the regiment's story in the film The Fighting 69th, with Pat O'Brien as Father Duffy and James Cagney as a fictional soldier.
Times Square is where New York comes to celebrate the New Year.
It's also where the city comes to hear big news together.
On November 7th, 1918, a wire service, the United Press, sent out a report from France that Germany had signed an armistice.
It wasn't true, but nobody knew that yet.
Across the country, offices emptied, whistles blew and crowds filled the streets.
In New York, so much paper rained down from office windows that the wire service was reportedly made to pay for the cleanup.
Four days later, on November 11th, the real armistice was signed, and the city celebrated all over again.
On August 14th, 1945, the crowds came for the end of the Second World War.
People packed the square, reading the news ticker that wrapped around the Times tower, and when word of Japan's surrender came that evening, the square erupted.
That day, the photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt caught a sailor bending a woman in a white uniform backward into a kiss.
Published in Life magazine, it became one of the best-known photographs of the century.
For decades, many people claimed to be the couple.
Most researchers now identify them as George Mendonsa, a sailor on leave, and Greta Zimmer Friedman, a dental assistant who had come to America as a teenage refugee from Austria.
They were strangers.
Years later, Friedman said it wasn't her choice and it wasn't romantic: he simply grabbed her.
The picture looks different once you know that.
Under your feet is the oldest stretch of the subway, and a door to a hotel.
You heard that the first subway line opened in 1904 with a station here.
It ran up the East Side to Grand Central, turned west under 42nd Street, and then headed north under Broadway.
In 1918, the line was split in two and each half was extended, creating the separate East Side and West Side lines riders use today.
The short crosstown piece under 42nd Street was left over, and it became the shuttle, running back and forth between Times Square and Grand Central.
When you ride it, you're on the tracks of the original 1904 subway.
Now look at the southeast corner of 42nd Street and Broadway, at the red-brick building with the steep mansard roof.

It opened in 1906 as the Knickerbocker Hotel, built by John Jacob Astor the Fourth, whom you may have heard about at the Empire State Building, and it was the first luxury hotel of the new Times Square.
The tenor Enrico Caruso lived there, and on Armistice Day in 1918, he is said to have come to his window and led the crowd below in the Star-Spangled Banner.
The hotel bar had a famous mural by Maxfield Parrish of Old King Cole.
When the hotel closed, around 1920, the mural moved, and it now hangs in the King Cole Bar of the Saint Regis, another Astor hotel, on 55th Street.
The Knickerbocker had its own entrance from the subway.
If you ride the shuttle, look on its Times Square platform for an old doorway with the word Knickerbocker above it.
The building has been a hotel again since 2015, but that door no longer opens for guests.
You heard that the Shubert brothers built the largest theater empire in America.
They built it by going to war.
At the turn of the century, the theater business was controlled by a combine called the Theatrical Syndicate, formed in 1896 by six men and led by the producers Marc Klaw and Abraham Erlanger.
The Syndicate controlled the bookings of first-class theaters across the country.
If a producer or a star wanted to tour, they played Syndicate houses on Syndicate terms, or they didn't play the big towns at all.
Even the great French actress Sarah Bernhardt, touring America without the Syndicate, famously played some of her dates in a circus tent.
The Shuberts started out managing theaters in Syracuse and came to New York around 1900, leasing theaters and producing shows.
Then, in 1905, Sam, the brothers' leader, died after a train wreck.
According to the family's account, when Lee went to Erlanger to confirm a deal Sam had made, Erlanger refused, saying he wouldn't honor an agreement with a dead man.
Lee and his younger brother, Jacob, known as J.J., set out to break the Syndicate.
They did it by building and buying theaters, in New York and in cities across the country, until stars and producers had somewhere else to go.
Within about a decade, the Syndicate's grip was broken.
But the Shuberts became what they had fought.
They grew so dominant that in the 1950s, the federal government took them to court under the antitrust laws, and they had to sell off some of their theaters.
Lee and J.J. were famously difficult, and they quarreled with each other for decades.
But between them, they ran the business for half a century.
You heard that A Chorus Line ran for fifteen years at the Shubert Theatre, right next to the alley.
It began with a tape recorder.
At midnight on January 26th, 1974, the director and choreographer Michael Bennett gathered twenty-two Broadway dancers in a studio.
They were gypsies, as chorus dancers call themselves, the performers who move from show to show without their names ever going up in lights.
Bennett turned on a tape recorder and asked them to talk about their lives: how they started dancing, their families, their fears, what they'd do when they couldn't dance anymore.
The session went on through the night, and there were more sessions afterward.
Those tapes became the raw material for the show.

The characters on stage, dancers auditioning for a few places in a chorus line and telling their stories to an unseen director, were built largely from the real stories on the tapes, and several of the dancers who had been in the room ended up in the cast, playing versions of themselves.
The show was developed downtown at Joseph Papp's Public Theater, which borrowed about one point six million dollars to produce it.
It opened there in April 1975, became the hottest ticket in town, and moved here to the Shubert that July.

It won the Pulitzer Prize for drama and nine Tony Awards, and when it closed in April 1990, after six thousand one hundred and thirty-seven performances, it was the longest-running show in Broadway history, a record it held until Cats passed it in 1997.
For the Public Theater, it was a gold mine: its share came to more than thirty-eight million dollars.
The dancers had signed away the rights to their stories for a dollar each, and later received a small share of the royalties.
Some of them felt they had given away far more than they got.
Theaters are full of superstitions, and Broadway has its share of ghosts.
These are stories, and they're told here as stories.
Start with the ghost light.
When a theater goes dark for the night, the last person out leaves a single bare bulb burning on a stand in the middle of the stage.
There's a practical reason: a pitch-black stage is dangerous, and someone could walk off the edge into the orchestra pit.
But theater people will also tell you the light is there for the ghosts, so they can perform when nobody's watching, or so they don't make mischief in the dark.
Now Broadway's most famous ghost.

A short walk east on 44th Street, on the far side of Broadway, is the Belasco Theatre, built in 1907 and renamed in 1910 for its owner, David Belasco, a producer and director known for astonishingly realistic stage sets.
He was a showman offstage too.
He dressed in a dark suit with a clerical collar, and people called him the Bishop of Broadway.
He kept a lavish private apartment upstairs in the theater.
Belasco died in 1931, but according to the stories, he never left.
Actors and staff reported a figure in clerical dress watching from his old box, and it was said that if he appeared on an opening night, the show would be a hit.
Some also reported a mysterious woman in blue.
The sightings are said to have stopped around 1970, about when a famously nude revue moved into the theater, which, the joke goes, was more than the old man could take.
Nobody has ever proven any of it.
But if you pass the Belasco late at night, glance up at the windows.
You heard that the first Grand Central was opened by Cornelius Vanderbilt in 1871.
Everyone called him the Commodore, and he earned the title on the water.
Vanderbilt was born on Staten Island in 1794.
As the family story goes, at sixteen he borrowed a hundred dollars from his mother to buy a sailboat, and ferried passengers and freight across the harbor.
He was tireless and tough, and by his twenties he was captaining a steamboat called the Bellona, between New Jersey and New York, for an owner named Thomas Gibbons.
There was a catch.
New York State had given a monopoly on steamboats in its waters to Robert Livingston and Robert Fulton, and Gibbons was running his boats in defiance of it.
For years, Vanderbilt dodged the officers who came aboard to serve him with court papers, reportedly hiding in a secret compartment.
The fight went to the Supreme Court, and in 1824, in Gibbons versus Ogden, the court ruled that trade between the states was for Congress to regulate, and the monopoly fell.
It's still one of the most important cases on the power of the federal government, and it opened the waters to competition.
Vanderbilt built his own fleet of steamships and became one of the richest men in America.
Then, late in life, he switched to railroads and took control of the New York Central.
When he died in 1877, he was worth about a hundred million dollars, and he left nearly all of it to his son William.
His biggest gift was a million dollars to found a university in Nashville, which was named for him: Vanderbilt University.
Step outside onto 42nd Street, and look up at the top of the terminal's front.
The sculpture group crowning the building is the Glory of Commerce, by the French sculptor Jules-Félix Coutan.
In the middle stands Mercury, the Roman god of commerce and travelers, in his winged helmet.
On one side is Hercules, though some say it's Vulcan, the god of the forge, and on the other is Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.
Together, they're about forty-eight feet high and weigh some fifteen hundred tons.
They were unveiled in 1914, a year after the terminal opened.
Just below Mercury is a clock thirteen feet across, made with glass from Tiffany.
It's often called the largest piece of Tiffany glass in the world.
Below that, above the viaduct that carries Park Avenue traffic around the building, stands the bronze statue of Cornelius Vanderbilt.
You may have heard in SoHo how it came here in 1929 from his old freight depot.
Now look for a smaller detail, and you'll find it everywhere: acorns and oak leaves, carved into the stone and worked into the metal, inside and out.
The acorn was a Vanderbilt family emblem, a reminder of the old saying, great oaks from little acorns grow, a fitting motto for a fortune that, by family tradition, started with one small boat.
Once you start spotting them, you won't stop.
You heard about the Whispering Gallery, downstairs near the Oyster Bar.
Look closely at what it's made of.
The low arches there, and the vaulted ceiling of the Oyster Bar beyond, are built of thin terracotta tiles laid in a herringbone pattern.
This is Guastavino tile, named for a Spanish builder, Rafael Guastavino, and his son, also named Rafael, who came to New York from Spain in the 1880s.

They brought with them an old Mediterranean way of building, the tile vault, with deep roots in the region of Valencia: several layers of thin tiles set in fast-drying mortar, which can span wide spaces, needs little support while it's being built, and won't burn.
In a city terrified of fire, that was a powerful selling point.
In 1889, they founded the Guastavino Fireproof Construction Company.
Their vaults are all over New York.
You may have heard about the tiles in the old City Hall subway station.
They also built the great vaulted ceiling of the registry room at Ellis Island, where millions of immigrants were processed, after an explosion in 1916 damaged the old roof.
When the room was restored decades later, only seventeen of its nearly thirty thousand tiles had to be replaced.
And they built the vaults under the Queensboro Bridge, at 59th Street.
The Oyster Bar opened in 1913, a few weeks after the terminal, under those tiles.
As for the whispering, the curved tile surfaces carry sound along the arch from one corner to the opposite one.
Nobody is sure whether the effect was planned, or whether the builders simply discovered it once the vault was up.
Somewhere north of here, beneath Park Avenue, is a platform that has become one of New York's favorite secrets.
When the railroad buried its tracks, its train yards stretched for blocks under Park Avenue, and new buildings went up on top of them.
When the new Waldorf-Astoria opened in 1931, on Park Avenue at 49th Street, it sat above part of the yards.
A siding there, known as Track 61, had a platform and a freight elevator big enough to carry a car up into the hotel.
The legend says this was a secret presidential entrance.

Franklin Roosevelt, who used a wheelchair and worked hard to hide it from the public, is said to have arrived in his own armored railroad car, had his automobile driven off the train and onto the elevator, and gone straight up into the Waldorf without anyone seeing him.
And down on the platform, the story goes, his armored car still waits.
Here's what's documented.
Roosevelt did use the siding, on October 21st, 1944, during his last campaign, arriving by train beneath the hotel.
The rest is mostly myth.
The old railroad car that has sat on the track for years is a baggage car, not Roosevelt's, and there's no evidence of a regular secret commute.
The legend survives because the place is real and the story is almost true.
Track 61 is still down there, closed to the public, under the traffic of Park Avenue.
You heard that Walter Chrysler started out as a railroad mechanic.
In a way, he never stopped being one.
Chrysler grew up in a railroad town in Kansas, the son of a locomotive engineer, and apprenticed as a machinist in the railroad shops, where, like many apprentices, he made his own tools.
He moved from railroad to railroad, rising to manage locomotive works.
In 1908, at an auto show in Chicago, he fell for a car, a Locomobile, that cost far more than he could afford.
He put in his savings, borrowed the rest, and bought it.
Then he did something odd.
He hardly drove it.
For about three months, he took the car apart, studied every piece, and put it back together, again and again, until he understood exactly how it worked.
That car was his education in the automobile business.
In 1912, he left the railroads, taking a big cut in pay, to run production at Buick, in Michigan, and he made its factories some of the most efficient in the industry.
He became Buick's president, left General Motors a rich man, and was hired to rescue struggling carmakers, which led him to found his own company.
When his tower opened, he put his past on display.
By one account, the tools he'd made as an apprentice were shown in a glass case near the observation floor, high in the building.
And from 1930, three floors near the top held the Cloud Club, a private lunch club where executives ate high above the city.
Chrysler died in 1940, at sixty-five.
The building that carries his name was paid for with his own money, a monument to a mechanic who never trusted a machine he hadn't taken apart himself.
You heard how William Van Alen won the race for the sky with a spire hidden inside his building.
His reward was a lawsuit.
Van Alen had trained in New York and in Paris, at the École des Beaux-Arts, and he had a reputation as a daring designer.
But he never signed a contract with Walter Chrysler.
When the building was finished, he asked for the usual architect's fee of the day, six percent of the construction cost, which came to roughly eight hundred and forty thousand dollars.
Chrysler refused to pay, and attacked Van Alen's character.
Van Alen took him to court, and won.
The victory cost him.
Clients were wary of an architect who had sued a famous millionaire, and the Depression had stopped most new building anyway.
Van Alen never landed another major commission.
He did get one more famous moment.
On January 23rd, 1931, the Society of Beaux-Arts Architects held its costume ball at the Hotel Astor, and several of the city's leading architects came dressed as their own buildings.
A well-known photograph shows them lined up like a little skyline.
Van Alen is dressed as the Chrysler Building, with its crown on his head, towering over the rest.
William Lamb, one of the architects of the Empire State Building, came dressed as his tower, the one that would take Van Alen's title only a few months later.
Others came as clubs and office buildings.
Look up at the crown again.
It has outlived the lawsuit, the Depression and the loss of the height record.
In the end, it's Van Alen's crown, not his fee, that people remember.
Here's a question most people never ask about a skyscraper: who owns the ground under it?
For the Chrysler Building, the answer is a college: Cooper Union, the school founded by Peter Cooper that you may have heard about in the East Village.
Cooper Union has owned this land since 1902.
Walter Chrysler built his tower on it under a long-term lease, and every owner of the building since then has paid the college rent for the ground beneath it.
There's more.

Because Cooper Union is a nonprofit, the land is exempt from property taxes, so the building's owners pay the college an amount equal to what the taxes would be, by one recent account more than twenty million dollars a year.
For a college that offered every student a free education for more than a century, the land under this tower has been a lifeline.
It has also made owning the building a roller coaster.
In 2008, an investment fund from Abu Dhabi paid eight hundred million dollars for most of the tower.
But the ground rent was set to jump, and between 2017 and 2018, it rose from about seven point eight million dollars a year to thirty-two and a half million, with more increases scheduled.
With rent like that, the building was worth far less.
In 2019, it sold for about a hundred and fifty million dollars, a fraction of what it had fetched eleven years earlier.
The new owners struggled too.
In 2024, after they fell more than twenty million dollars behind on the rent, Cooper Union moved to end the lease, and after a court fight, the college took the building back.
It has since been looking for a new partner to run it.
So one of the most admired skyscrapers in the world is, in a sense, a college's endowment, with a stainless steel crown on top.
You heard that John D. Rockefeller Junior leased this land from Columbia University.
How did a university come to own a slice of Midtown?
The answer is a garden.

In 1801, when this was open country far north of the city, a doctor named David Hosack bought about twenty acres here and planted the Elgin Botanic Garden, the first public botanical garden in the United States.
Hosack taught botany and medicine, and he's remembered for another reason too: he was the doctor who attended Alexander Hamilton after his duel with Aaron Burr in 1804.
At Elgin, he grew a great variety of plants, native and foreign, with greenhouses for tender species, so that medical students could learn to recognize the plants their medicines came from.
The garden was expensive, and Hosack couldn't keep paying for it.
In 1810, he sold it to New York State.
In 1814, the state handed the land to Columbia, in place of money it had promised the college.
The garden faded, and as the city grew north, the land became valuable beyond anyone's imagining.
By the 1920s, it was covered with brownstones, and when the opera plan came along, Columbia was the landlord.
Columbia kept the land through the building of Rockefeller Center and for half a century afterward.
In 1985, it finally sold the ground under the center for four hundred million dollars.
So the next time you walk among the flower beds of the Channel Gardens, remember that long before there was a Rockefeller Center, this ground was a garden.
You heard about Lunch atop a Skyscraper, the photograph of eleven ironworkers eating lunch on a beam high above the city.
It's one of the most famous pictures ever taken in New York, and almost everything about it is a mystery.
Start with how it happened.
The usual date is September 20th, 1932, when the building's frame was nearing the top.
The beam was real, and so was the drop, but the moment is believed to have been arranged.
Rockefeller Center was trying to rent office space in the depths of the Depression, and it ran its own publicity operation, with photographers on hand to show off the project.
Then, who took it.
The picture is most often credited to Charles Ebbets, who did publicity photography for the center.
But other photographers were up on the steel that day too, and nobody can say for certain whose shutter clicked.
And who's in it.
Over the years, many families have looked at those faces and recognized a father, an uncle or a grandfather.
In 2012, an Irish documentary followed claims that two of them came from the west of Ireland, and Native American families have claimed others.
Most of the eleven have never been identified for certain, and that may be part of the picture's power.
They aren't famous men.
They're the men who built the city.
Stand in front of 30 Rockefeller Plaza and look up over the main entrance.
The bearded figure leaning out of the clouds, holding a giant compass, is Wisdom, carved by the sculptor Lee Lawrie, who also made the Atlas on Fifth Avenue.
He's measuring out the universe, and the panels on either side, called Light and Sound, suit a building made for radio.
Below him runs a line from the book of Isaiah: Wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times.
It was a hopeful thing to carve over a door in the depths of the Depression.
Now turn toward Fifth Avenue and walk through the gardens that slope down to the plaza.
They're called the Channel Gardens, and the name is a little joke.
On one side stands La Maison Française, built for French businesses, and on the other, the British Empire Building.
Between France and Britain lies a channel, and so does this one.
Look above their doors for the gilded reliefs celebrating each country.
The center was built with an art program unlike any other commercial development of its time.
Dozens of artists made murals, mosaics, sculpture and metalwork for its buildings.

Look up as you walk, at the doorways, the lobbies and the tops of the walls, and you'll find gods, workers, airplanes, radio waves and planets, a whole Depression-era vision of the modern world in stone and metal.
You heard that Radio City Music Hall opened in 1932 as the largest indoor theater in the world.
It was the dream of one showman, Samuel Rothafel, known to everyone as Roxy.
Roxy had made his name running grand movie palaces, and he promised this one would top them all.
It opened on December 27th, 1932, with an enormous stage show, a parade of acts that included the dancer Martha Graham and the comic dancer Ray Bolger, later the Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz.
More than a hundred thousand people asked for tickets to the opening, for a hall with about six thousand seats.
Within two weeks, the hall was showing movies too, and for more than four decades, it paired first-run films with lavish stage shows.
Its most famous performers came from Saint Louis.
In 1925, a choreographer named Russell Markert put together a precision dance troupe called the Missouri Rockets, every dancer kicking in perfect unison.
Roxy brought them to New York, where they became the Roxyettes, and when he opened the Music Hall, he brought them with him.
In 1934, they became the Rockettes.
Their eye-high kicks in a long straight line, and their Christmas show, have made them one of the city's great traditions.
Step inside if you can, to see the great auditorium with its sunburst of arches, and the Art Deco lounges and furniture by the designer Donald Deskey.
In 1978, when the hall was in danger of closing, a public campaign saved it, and its interior was named a city landmark.
Go inside, and look for something hanging high overhead: wide, flat red hats with long tassels.
They're galeros, the hats once given to cardinals of the Catholic Church, and each one here belonged to a cardinal archbishop of New York.
The tradition goes back centuries.
When a cardinal died, his red hat was hung from the ceiling of his cathedral, above his tomb, and left there.
It was said that it would hang until it rotted and fell, a reminder that all earthly glory passes away.
In the late 1960s, as part of a reform of the church's ceremonies, the Vatican stopped giving out the galero altogether.
Four hang here.
The oldest belonged to John McCloskey, who in 1875 became the first American named a cardinal.
The others belonged to his successors John Farley, Patrick Hayes and Francis Spellman, the powerful archbishop who led New York's Catholics from 1939 to 1967.
During the cathedral's restoration in the 2010s, the old silk hats were taken down, carefully conserved and hung back up, which isn't quite the tradition, but saved them from falling to dust.
Beneath the altar, in the crypt you heard about, these cardinals lie with other archbishops of New York.
So when you look up at the hats, you're looking at the cathedral's own history: an immigrant church that built this place, and the men who led it as it rose to power in the city.
You heard that construction began in 1858.
The cathedral didn't open until 1879, with work halted for years during the Civil War, and money was short the whole way.
The evidence is over your head.
James Renwick designed the cathedral in the manner of the great Gothic cathedrals of Europe, with pointed arches, ribbed vaults and soaring piers, all clad in white marble outside.
In a true medieval cathedral, the vaulted ceiling is stone.
Stone vaults are enormously heavy, and they push outward on the walls, which is why medieval builders added flying buttresses, the stone arms that brace the walls from outside.
Renwick planned a masonry ceiling too.
But the money wasn't there, so the vault you see overhead was built as a lighter, cheaper ceiling of plaster on wood and lath, meant as a stopgap.
The stopgap became permanent.
And because a plaster vault weighs so little, the cathedral could do without the great flying buttresses that brace the stone vaults of Europe's cathedrals.
The restoration in the 2010s took on that old ceiling.
Workers raised scaffolding to the vaults, repaired the cracks, and kept the plaster fixed to its original timber laths.
So St. Patrick's is a little like the city that built it: a grand European idea, put up by an immigrant community on a budget, and made to last anyway.
In the early 1950s, one of the most popular stars on American television was a Catholic bishop who preached here.
Fulton Sheen was an auxiliary bishop of New York, a gifted speaker with piercing eyes, a flowing cape and a showman's timing.
In 1952, he began a weekly television program called Life Is Worth Living.
There was no choir and no altar, just Sheen in a study with a blackboard, talking for half an hour about love, fear, communism and the meaning of suffering, with jokes thrown in.
He was scheduled on Tuesday nights against the biggest star on television, the comedian Milton Berle, and few expected him to last.
Instead, he drew millions of viewers of every faith, won an Emmy as television's most outstanding personality, and in accepting it, is said to have thanked his writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Sheen later became bishop of Rochester, and then an archbishop.
When he died in 1979, he was buried in the crypt beneath the altar here, among the archbishops of New York.
But he had grown up in Peoria, Illinois, and the diocese there, which was leading the effort to have him declared a saint, wanted his body.
After years of legal fighting, with his family taking Peoria's side, the Archdiocese of New York gave way, and in June 2019, his remains were moved to the cathedral in Peoria.
So for forty years, the crypt beneath this altar held one of the first stars of television.
You heard that Paley Park stands on the site of the Stork Club.
For more than three decades, it was the most famous nightclub in America.
It was run by Sherman Billingsley, an Oklahoman who had been a bootlegger, and it began as a speakeasy during Prohibition.
In 1934, it moved to this block of 53rd Street and became the place where movie stars, socialites, politicians and writers all wanted to be seen.
Getting in was the game.
A doorman decided who passed the gold chain at the entrance, and the inner room, the Cub Room, had its own gatekeeper, nicknamed Saint Peter.
The club's most powerful regular was Walter Winchell, the gossip columnist and radio broadcaster, followed by tens of millions of Americans.
He held court at Table 50 in the Cub Room, and a mention in his column could make or break a career.
Billingsley and Winchell made each other famous.

Then, in October 1951, the singer and dancer Josephine Baker, an American star who lived in France, came in with friends, ordered dinner, and by her account waited about an hour for food that never came.
She was sure she was being refused service because she was Black.
Winchell had been in the room, and Baker publicly accused him of doing nothing.
Winchell said he had left before the trouble began, and turned on her in his column.
The NAACP picketed the club, and the quarrel played out in the newspapers for months.
The club's glamour faded in the years that followed.
It closed in 1965, the building was torn down, and the site became the little park where you can sit today.
On April 15th, 1958, the Museum of Modern Art caught fire.
Workers were renovating on the second floor, and a fire broke out among their materials, by the most common account from a workman's cigarette.
Thick smoke poured up through the building.

On the floor above hung a major exhibition of the paintings of Georges Seurat, including one of the most famous pictures in the world, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, lent by the Art Institute of Chicago.
Paintings were rushed to safety, and La Grande Jatte ended up next door in the Whitney Museum, which then stood beside the Modern.
It came through undamaged, but it was the first time Chicago had ever lent the painting, and it hasn't traveled since.
One workman died, and more than two dozen people, many of them firefighters, were hurt.
The greatest loss to the collection was a painting.
In 1955, the museum had bought one of Claude Monet's huge late paintings of water lilies, about eighteen feet long.
It was destroyed.
A smaller Monet came out scorched, looking, as one writer later put it, like a toasted marshmallow.
The museum's conservators worked on it for three years before declaring it beyond repair.
The museum didn't give up on Monet.
Soon afterward, it bought another of his enormous water lily paintings in Paris, a triptych of three panels that together stretch more than forty feet.
That's the painting you'll usually find in the galleries today, one of the most popular in the museum.
If you stand in front of it, you're looking at the museum's answer to the fire.
Two of the best outdoor rooms in Midtown are a block apart, and they're related.
The first is behind the museum: the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, named for one of the museum's founders.
It was designed by the architect Philip Johnson, who also ran the museum's architecture department, with the landscape architect James Fanning, and it opened in 1953.
Johnson laid it out like an open-air room, paved in marble, with pools of water, trees, and sculptures set against the sky and the surrounding towers.
