In 1964, he enlarged it, working with the landscape firm Zion and Breen.
If you go in, notice how the walls, the water and the trees make you forget the street outside.
The second is Paley Park, which opened three years later, designed by the same landscape firm, led by Robert Zion.
You can feel the family resemblance: a small room cut off from the city, with water, a canopy of trees, and chairs you can move.
Zion was a champion of what came to be called pocket parks, tiny parks tucked between buildings, and this one became the model for them.
What both gardens understand is that a city space doesn't have to be big.
It needs walls to hold you, something to look at, the sound of water, shade, and a place to sit.
Those are simple ingredients, and they're why these two small gardens are still full on a sunny day, more than half a century later.
You heard that Phyllis Lambert persuaded her father to hire Mies van der Rohe.
Here's how she did it.

In 1954, Lambert was twenty-seven and living in Paris when she saw the design her father, Samuel Bronfman, the head of Seagram, had in mind for the company's new headquarters on Park Avenue, a conventional tower by a commercial firm.
She was appalled.
She sat down and wrote him an eight-page letter, and by her own account, it began with the words No, no, no, no, no.
The rest was a passionate argument that a company's building is a public statement that will stand for generations, and that Seagram should build something great.
Her father did something unusual.
Instead of brushing her off, he put her in charge of finding a new architect.
She came back to New York and spent weeks meeting the leading architects of the day, with advice from Philip Johnson, and chose Mies, then in his late sixties and working in Chicago.
Johnson joined him on the project, designing interiors including the Four Seasons restaurant.
Lambert didn't stop there.
She went on to study architecture herself and became an architect, a preservationist and a fierce critic of careless development.
In 1979, she founded the Canadian Centre for Architecture in Montreal, one of the world's great architecture museums.
The Seagram Building turned out to be what she had promised her father: a landmark copied around the world, and a reminder of what one stubborn letter can do.

The Four Seasons restaurant, inside the Seagram Building, was meant to be a complete work of modern design: Mies's building, Philip Johnson's rooms, and on the walls, paintings by one of the greatest living painters.
Around 1958, Mark Rothko accepted a commission to paint a series of large murals for the restaurant.
He threw himself into the work, producing dozens of dark, brooding canvases in deep maroons and blacks.
But he had doubts.

He told a writer he met on a ship to Europe that he had taken the job with strictly malicious intentions, hoping to paint something that would ruin the appetite of every rich diner who ever ate in that room.
Then he went to dinner at the restaurant himself.
By most accounts, the expensive, showy atmosphere confirmed his fears, and he decided that his paintings would never hang there.
He withdrew from the commission and kept the murals.
Years later, he gave nine of them to the Tate in London, on condition that they hang together in a room of their own.
They arrived in London on the same day in 1970 that Rothko died in New York.
The restaurant got along without him.
For decades, a different masterpiece hung in its corridor: a huge stage curtain painted by Pablo Picasso for a ballet, Le Tricorne.
In 2014, after a dispute with the building's owner, the curtain was moved to the New-York Historical Society.
The Four Seasons left the building in 2016, and its famous rooms have since been taken over by new restaurants.
But the story of the Rothkos is a reminder that some art refuses to be decoration.
You heard that Lever House was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.
For decades, his was the only name most people knew.
Working beside him was Natalie de Blois.
De Blois was one of very few women in American architecture when she joined the firm in the 1940s, and she rose to become one of its senior designers.
On Lever House, she worked closely with Bunshaft, and colleagues and historians have since credited her with a large share of the design.
But when the building opened in 1952 and the praise poured in, it went to Bunshaft and the firm.
That was how big firms worked in those days, and it was doubly true for a woman.

She went on to help design other corporate towers of the era, including the Pepsi-Cola Building, a few blocks up Park Avenue, and, by most accounts, the Union Carbide Building, the tower at 270 Park Avenue you heard was torn down for JPMorgan Chase.
Later she taught architecture in Texas and spoke out for women in the profession, and she has slowly been written back into the story.
Lever House itself had to fight to survive.
Its low base and open courtyard used only a fraction of what the zoning allowed, which made it a tempting target for a bigger tower.
Preservationists rallied, and in 1982, when the building was barely thirty years old, the city named it a landmark.
It's still here, still green glass, still showing how much a building can give back to the street.
Look at the planted islands running down the middle of Park Avenue.
They gave the avenue its name.
This was once Fourth Avenue, and for much of the nineteenth century, its northern stretch was a railroad right-of-way, with trains running through an open cut and tunnels.
As the tracks were covered over, the avenue got landscaped medians on top, and with them a grander name: Park Avenue.

Over time, the name spread south along the old Fourth Avenue, all the way down to Union Square, and the medians became some of the most carefully tended strips of green in the city, with tulips in spring.
Every December, the medians get something else: a long line of Christmas trees, lit for almost fifty blocks.
The tradition began in 1945.
After the Second World War, a group of Park Avenue mothers arranged for lighted fir trees along the avenue, in memory of the sons the war had taken.
The trees came back the next year, and they've come back ever since.
Today, about a hundred and twenty trees are shipped down from Nova Scotia each year, and the lights are switched on at a ceremony at the Brick Presbyterian Church, uptown on Park Avenue.
Most people walking past in December think they're just decorations.
They began as a memorial.
You heard that Vanderbilt family mansions lined Fifth Avenue for blocks south of here.
The most famous party ever thrown in one of them was a social coup.
In the early 1880s, the Vanderbilts were among the richest people in America, but old New York society looked down on them as new money, descendants of a rough ferry captain.
Society's gatekeeper was Caroline Astor, known simply as the Mrs. Astor, and her circle, the one later nicknamed the Four Hundred, as you may have heard at Gramercy Park, kept the Vanderbilts out.
Alva Vanderbilt, the wife of the Commodore's grandson William Kissam Vanderbilt, set out to change that.
She had a new château built on Fifth Avenue at 52nd Street, designed by Richard Morris Hunt, and on March 26th, 1883, she threw a costume ball to show it off, for more than a thousand guests.
Society talked of nothing else for weeks.
Guests came as kings, queens and figures from history, and Alva's sister-in-law came dressed as Electric Light.
Now the story, as it's usually told, and it may have been polished.
Mrs. Astor's daughter, Carrie, was dying to go, and had been rehearsing a dance for the ball with her friends.
But no invitation came.
Alva let it be known that she couldn't invite someone whose mother had never paid a call on her.
So Mrs. Astor swallowed her pride, had her carriage driven to Alva's door, and left her calling card.
The invitation arrived the next day.
Whether or not it happened just that way, the ball worked.
The Vanderbilts were in.
Alva's château is long gone, but her ambitions were just getting started.
A few blocks south, at Fifth Avenue and 53rd Street, stands Saint Thomas Church.
In 1895, in the church that stood on that corner before the present one, Alva Vanderbilt married off her daughter.
Consuelo Vanderbilt was eighteen, and in love with an American.
Alva had other plans.
In the Gilded Age, rich American families married their daughters to European aristocrats: the families gained titles, and the aristocrats gained fortunes to prop up their estates.
The brides were called dollar princesses.
Alva chose the ninth Duke of Marlborough, who needed money for Blenheim Palace.
Consuelo resisted, and by her own later account, her mother kept her shut away and pressured her until she gave in.
On November 6th, 1895, she married the duke there, reportedly in tears, while crowds jammed Fifth Avenue to watch.
Her father settled a fortune in railroad stock on the marriage.
The marriage was miserable.
The couple separated and later divorced, and when the marriage came before a church court for annulment in 1926, Alva testified that she had forced her daughter into it.
Alva, meanwhile, had become a different person.
Earlier in 1895, she had divorced William Vanderbilt, a scandal in itself, and she soon married Oliver Belmont.
After his death in 1908, she poured her energy and money into the fight for women's votes.
In 1909, she founded the Political Equality Association, and as you may have heard on the Lower East Side, she backed the striking shirtwaist makers that winter.
Later, she bankrolled the most militant wing of the suffrage movement, the National Woman's Party, and served as its president.
The mother who forced her daughter into a loveless marriage ended her life as a champion of women's independence.
History doesn't always run in a straight line.
Look for the Harry Winston salon, at Fifth Avenue and 56th Street.
The jeweler who founded it once sent the most famous diamond in the world through the mail.
Harry Winston rose from his father's small jewelry shop to become known as the king of diamonds, trading in many of the world's great stones.
In 1949, he bought the Hope Diamond, a deep blue stone of about forty-five carats, along with the rest of the jewels of the Washington socialite Evalyn Walsh McLean, its last private owner.
For years, he took it on tour to charity events.
Then he decided it belonged to the public, and gave it to the Smithsonian Institution.
How do you deliver a priceless diamond to Washington?
Winston put it in a box, wrapped it in plain brown paper, and sent it by registered first-class mail.
The postage came to two dollars and forty-four cents, plus a hundred and forty-two dollars and eighty-five cents to insure it for a million dollars.
It rode to Washington in a mail car on the train, and a letter carrier delivered it to the museum on November 10th, 1958.
The Smithsonian still has the wrapping paper, stamps and all.
The Hope Diamond comes with a legend: that it carries a curse.
Its owners did include a French king who lost his head and a socialite whose family suffered terrible losses.
But the curse story seems to have been largely spread by jewelers and newspapers to make the stone more intriguing, and it may have helped sell it.
Winston owned it for nearly a decade and lived a long and prosperous life.
Today, the diamond is one of the most visited museum objects in the world, and it got there for the price of a postage stamp.
You heard that the gilded statue of General Sherman, by Augustus Saint-Gaudens, is considered one of the finest equestrian statues in America.
Look at the figure walking ahead of his horse.
She's Victory, striding forward with a palm branch in one hand and her other arm raised, wings spread, leading Sherman on.
Saint-Gaudens worked on the monument for more than a decade.
He had Sherman himself sit for a portrait bust in 1888, and the general's lean, weathered face came from those sittings.
The horse was modeled by another sculptor, Alexander Phimister Proctor, a specialist in animals.
Look down at its hooves: one of them treads on a branch of Georgia pine, a reminder of Sherman's march through Georgia to the sea.
For Victory, the sculptor's principal model was Hettie Anderson, a Black woman who was one of the most sought-after artists' models in New York in the 1890s.
She posed for Saint-Gaudens over several years, and her face and figure shaped one of the most admired allegories in American sculpture.
It's often said that she also posed for the figure of Liberty on the gold twenty-dollar coin that Saint-Gaudens designed a few years later, though that's harder to pin down.
For a long time, her name was left out of the story, and only recently has she been given her due.
Think about the pairing for a moment.
Sherman's armies helped bring an end to slavery.
Leading him in bronze and gold, at the corner of Central Park, is the likeness of a Black woman.
The monument was shown in Paris at the World's Fair of 1900 before it was unveiled here in 1903.
Its bright gilding has divided people almost from the start.
Some find it glorious, others gaudy, and each time it's been regilded, the argument has started all over again.
You heard that the fountain in front of the Plaza was paid for by a bequest from Joseph Pulitzer.
Its making was haunted by a death.

Pulitzer, whose newspaper campaign paid for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal, as you may have heard near City Hall, died in 1911 and left money in his will for a fountain at this corner of Central Park, in the spirit of the great fountains of Paris.
The design went to Thomas Hastings, of Carrère and Hastings, the architects of the New York Public Library, who drew a series of stone basins stepping down toward the plaza.
For the figure on top, the commission went to Karl Bitter, a Vienna-born sculptor who had become one of the busiest in New York.
You may have seen his bronze doors at Trinity Church.
Bitter chose Pomona, the Roman goddess of abundance, with a basket of fruit in her arms.
In April 1915, he had just finished the plaster model when he was struck by a car and killed.
He was forty-seven.
His widow and Hastings chose another sculptor, Isidore Konti, to carry the figure through to bronze, working with Bitter's young assistant, Karl Gruppe, and the fountain was dedicated in 1916.
In the 1930s, Gruppe led the parks department's campaign to restore the city's neglected monuments, cleaning and repairing statues all over town.
So the goddess of abundance at the edge of the park is a collaboration across a death: Bitter's model, finished by his colleagues, in a fountain paid for by a newspaperman's will.
Here's a story New Yorkers love to tell about the Pulitzer Fountain.
It may even be true.

In 1920, F. Scott Fitzgerald published his first novel, This Side of Paradise, became famous almost overnight, and married Zelda Sayre of Montgomery, Alabama, in the rectory of St. Patrick's Cathedral, down Fifth Avenue.
The two of them became the golden couple of the Jazz Age, and they lived the part: riding on the roofs of taxis, dancing on tables, getting asked to leave hotels.
And according to legend, one night Zelda, fully dressed, jumped into the fountain in front of the Plaza, with Scott perhaps right behind her.
Did it happen?
Nobody has pinned it down.
Other versions put Zelda's famous plunge in the fountain at Union Square or in Washington Square Park, and in her hometown, people tell a similar story about a fountain there.
It's exactly the kind of thing Zelda might have done, and exactly the kind of story people tell about the Fitzgeralds whether or not it happened.
So file it under legend.
What's certain is that the Plaza meant something to Scott.

The couple stayed here, and in The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the novel's great confrontation takes place in a sweltering suite at the Plaza, where Tom Buchanan finally faces down Gatsby over Daisy.
In the middle of the quarrel, the narrator, Nick Carraway, realizes that it's his thirtieth birthday.
If you've read the book, look up at the windows and picture that hot afternoon.
You heard that everyone from Mahler to Benny Goodman has played here.
Goodman's night is the famous one.
But he wasn't the first to bring this kind of music here.
On May 2nd, 1912, James Reese Europe led his Clef Club Orchestra onto this stage for a Concert of Negro Music, a benefit for the Music School Settlement for Colored People.
Europe was a Black bandleader and composer who had organized the Clef Club, a union and booking agency for Black musicians in New York.
His orchestra had more than a hundred players, with banjos, mandolins and pianos, and it played to a sold-out hall with a racially mixed audience.
Whether you call the music jazz or the ragtime that came just before it, it was the first time that sound filled this hall.
Europe went on to lead the band of the 369th Infantry, the Harlem Hellfighters, in the First World War, carrying the new American music to France.
Twenty-six years later, on January 16th, 1938, Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, brought his band here.
Swing was dance music, played in ballrooms and clubs, and many people thought it had no place in a concert hall.

Goodman's musicians included the Black pianist Teddy Wilson and vibraphonist Lionel Hampton, at a time when most bands were segregated, and he brought in guests from Count Basie's and Duke Ellington's bands.
Before the concert, asked how long an intermission he wanted, Goodman is said to have answered: I don't know.
How long does Toscanini take?
When the band tore into Sing, Sing, Sing, the hall went wild.
The recording of that night, released years later, became one of the best-selling jazz albums ever made.
Five years later, Duke Ellington premiered his long jazz symphony, Black, Brown and Beige, on this stage.
Jazz has had a home at Carnegie Hall ever since.
Look up above the hall.
For more than a century, the building's upper floors were full of artists.
A few years after the hall opened, two towers of studios were added, finished in the 1890s, with big windows and skylights for working artists.
They became one of the great creative addresses in New York.
Over the years, the tenants included painters, sculptors, dancers, singers, actors, teachers and photographers.
Marlon Brando lived in one as a young actor.
Leonard Bernstein lived in another early in his career, before he became the most famous conductor in America.
Students climbed the stairs for lessons, while the stars performed down below.

The best-known of the last tenants was Bill Cunningham, the photographer who for decades rode his bicycle around Manhattan photographing what people actually wore on the street, for the New York Times.
He lived and worked in a tiny studio here, crammed with filing cabinets full of negatives, for about sixty years.
In 2010, Carnegie Hall moved out its remaining residents to turn the towers into rehearsal rooms, classrooms and offices for its education programs.
Some of the longtime tenants fought it, and the papers wrote about the end of a bohemian era.
Today, young musicians practice where the artists once lived, which seems only fitting in a building where the answer to the old joke is practice.
Look above the entrance arches, and you'll find words carved in stone: Music Hall, founded by Andrew Carnegie.
That was the building's first name.
Its architect, William Tuthill, was not a famous one.

He was in his thirties, a gifted amateur cellist who sat with Carnegie on the board of the Oratorio Society, and before he drew the hall, he toured Europe to study the concert halls most admired for their sound.
Many people credit his musician's ear for the acoustics you heard about.
When the hall opened in May 1891, it was simply the Music Hall.
The opening was a five-day festival.

On the first night, after a speech by the Episcopal bishop of New York, Walter Damrosch conducted the orchestra, and then one of the most famous composers in the world stepped onto the stage: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, who had come from Russia to conduct his own music.
Two days later, on his fifty-first birthday, he conducted his Third Suite.
Tchaikovsky kept a diary of his American trip.
It's full of wonder at the city and the warmth of its people, and full of homesickness too.
He wrote that he seemed to be far more famous in America than in Europe.
And he could be blunt: sitting through a long choral work by Berlioz on opening night, he found it tedious until the very end.
The plain name didn't last.
The hall's board persuaded a reluctant Carnegie to let them use his.
The story goes that to European performers, a music hall meant a place for comic songs and variety acts, not symphonies.
By the mid-1890s, the Music Hall had become Carnegie Hall, though the old name is still carved over the door.
Its rooms have since taken on other names, many of them for donors, and the main auditorium is named for Isaac Stern, the violinist who saved the building.
But to musicians around the world, the whole place is simply Carnegie, the hall every young performer dreams of playing.
You heard that Frederick Law Olmsted had never designed a park when he and Calvert Vaux won the competition for this one.
That's true, and the life around it is one of the great American careers.
Olmsted was born in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1822.
A poisoning that damaged his eyes cut short his schooling, and for years he drifted.
He sailed to China as a young seaman, and ran a farm on Staten Island.
He walked through England and wrote a book about its farms and countryside, and near Liverpool, he saw a new public park, at Birkenhead, that he never forgot.
Then a newspaper sent him south.

In the 1850s, Olmsted traveled through the slave states for the paper that became the New York Times, and his dispatches, later collected in a book called The Cotton Kingdom, were a detailed and damning portrait of slavery and the society built on it.
In 1857, the commissioners of this park hired him as its superintendent, a writer and farmer who knew more about land and people than about design.
Vaux, the trained architect, invited him to enter the competition as his partner.
After Central Park, Olmsted kept going.
During the Civil War, he ran the Sanitary Commission, which cared for sick and wounded Union soldiers.
He managed a gold mine in California and helped protect Yosemite Valley.

He and Vaux designed Prospect Park, and Olmsted went on to shape the grounds of the United States Capitol, Boston's chain of parks called the Emerald Necklace, and the Biltmore estate in North Carolina.
Dementia clouded his last years, which he spent at McLean, a hospital outside Boston whose grounds he had helped to plan.
He died in 1903.
But you're standing in the work he's remembered for.
Look at the entrance at Fifth Avenue and 60th Street.
There's no gate, just an opening in the low stone wall.
That was a choice, and it took a fight.
In 1862, the park's commissioners decided to give the entrances names, and they turned down the obvious ideas: no war victories, no states or cities, no famous men.
Instead, the gates would honor the people of New York by their work.
Along the southern edge, this one became the Scholars' Gate, and to the west come the Artists', the Artisans' and the Merchants' Gates.
Farther up, there are gates for Engineers and Inventors, Mariners and Miners, Woodmen and Hunters, and for Women, Children, Boys and Girls.
There's even one for Strangers.
The park, the names said, belonged to everyone who worked in the city.
Then came Richard Morris Hunt, the Paris-trained architect you may have heard about on Fifth Avenue, who later designed Alva Vanderbilt's château.
Hunt drew grand, monumental gateways for the southern entrances, in the manner of imperial Paris, with sculpture, and the commissioners liked them.
Olmsted and Vaux were appalled.
To them, triumphal gates belonged to an emperor's capital, not a republic's park.
In 1863, partly over the gates, they resigned.
Hunt's gates were never built, and two years later, Olmsted and Vaux were back.
The names appeared on maps, but for well over a century, you couldn't see them anywhere at the entrances themselves.
Only around the year 2000 were they finally carved into the stone of the walls.
Look for this one as you go.
In J. D. Salinger's novel The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, the teenage narrator, Holden Caulfield, can't stop wondering about this pond.
He calls it the lagoon near Central Park South, and what bothers him is the ducks.
Where do they go in winter, when the water freezes over?
Does somebody come in a truck and take them away to a zoo, or do they just fly off?
Lonely and adrift in the city after being thrown out of his school, Holden asks two different taxi drivers.
The first looks at him as if he's crazy.
The second, a cabbie named Horwitz, gets angry and says the fish have it worse: they stay right there in the frozen water all winter, taking in their nourishment through their pores.
It's one of the funniest exchanges in the book, and one of the saddest, because the question isn't really about ducks.
Holden is a boy who has lost his younger brother, and he wants to know whether anyone looks after the creatures left out in the cold.
So, where do the ducks go?
Some of them don't go anywhere.
Mallards often stay in the park all winter, gathering wherever the water stays open, while other ducks leave for the south and new ones arrive from the north.
And the novel doesn't leave the park.
It ends a few minutes' walk from here, as you'll hear at the carousel.
On the morning of November 9th, 1874, New Yorkers opened the New York Herald to a horrifying story.
The animals of the Central Park menagerie, it said, had broken loose.
A rhinoceros had smashed its cage and set others free, and big cats and bears were roaming the streets, mauling people as they went.
The article ran on for columns, with lists of the dead and injured.
None of it was true.
As you may have heard on Park Row, New York's papers had a weakness for hoaxes, and this was one of the biggest.
The story's last paragraph admitted that the whole thing was invented.
But many readers never got that far.
Men took guns into the streets to hunt for escaped beasts.
The idea reportedly came from the Herald's managing editor, Thomas Connery, after he saw a leopard nearly get loose while it was being moved at the menagerie.
The paper claimed it wanted to warn the city that the cages were unsafe.
The Herald, then run by James Gordon Bennett Junior, whose owls you may have heard about at Herald Square, loved a stunt.
Rival papers were furious, and a group of citizens went to the district attorney to ask whether the Herald could be prosecuted.
It never was, and its sales didn't suffer.
The menagerie stayed beside the Arsenal for another sixty years, until Robert Moses replaced it with a proper zoo.
Walk a little north of the zoo, toward the East Drive at about 67th Street, and look for a bronze sled dog standing on a rock.
His back and ears have been rubbed shiny by generations of children climbing on him.
This is Balto, and in 1925, he was the most famous dog in America.
That January, diphtheria broke out in Nome, a remote town on the coast of Alaska.
Children were falling ill, and the town's supply of antitoxin was nearly gone.
The nearest serum was about a thousand miles away, in Anchorage.
So the serum went north by train to the end of the line, and from there, relay teams of mushers and sled dogs carried it nearly seven hundred miles, through blizzards and temperatures far below zero.
It reached Nome in less than six days.
Balto led the team that ran the last stretch into Nome, so he got the headlines, and in December 1925, this statue was unveiled with Balto himself in attendance.
The inscription honors all the dogs of the relay, for their endurance, fidelity and intelligence.
Here's where the legend and the record part ways.

The longest and most dangerous leg was run by a musher named Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog, Togo, who covered about twice the distance of any other team, including a crossing of the treacherous sea ice of Norton Sound.
Seppala felt that Togo had been robbed of the credit.
Lately, Togo has won some of it back, with books, a film, and a small statue in Seward Park, on the Lower East Side.
Balto himself ended up in a dime museum in Los Angeles, until the people of Cleveland raised money to bring him and his teammates to their zoo.
When you pat this bronze dog, spare a thought for Togo, too.
In the 1990s, the most famous animal in this zoo was a polar bear named Gus.
Gus was born at the Toledo Zoo in 1985 and came here in 1988, just as the rebuilt zoo opened.
Visitors could watch him swim through a window into his pool.
But in 1994, people began to notice something odd.
Gus swam the same pattern over and over, for hours a day, pushing off the same wall and turning at the same spot, around and around.
Behavior like this is common in wide-ranging animals kept in small spaces, and polar bears in the wild roam across vast stretches of sea ice.
Newspapers called Gus neurotic, and he became a symbol of a hard question: can a zoo ever be a good home for an animal like that?
The zoo took it seriously.
It brought in an animal behaviorist from California, at a cost of about twenty-five thousand dollars, and changed Gus's days.
Keepers froze his food into blocks of ice and hid treats in puzzles, and gave him new toys, so that he had to search and work and think.
The swimming eased.
Ideas like these, called enrichment, are now standard in good zoos everywhere, and Gus helped make them famous.
He lived here for twenty-five years, and more than twenty million people came to see him.
In 2013, at twenty-seven, he was found to have an inoperable tumor and was put to sleep.
New Yorkers mourned him like a neighbor.
You heard that swill milk, from cows fed on distillery waste, was blamed for the deaths of thousands of children.
How New York finally faced it is a story about a newspaper, and about a politician who tried to make it go away.
In May 1858, Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper began a crusade.

Its artists went into the distillery dairies of Manhattan and Brooklyn and drew what they found: hundreds of cows crammed into dark, filthy sheds, sick and covered in sores, fed on hot mash piped in from the distillery next door.
One engraving showed a dead cow being dragged out just after milking.
The thin, bluish milk was whitened with chalk and sold as pure country milk.
The city ordered an investigation and put an alderman named Michael Tuomey in charge.
Tuomey defended the distillers, and his committee cleared them.
Leslie's answered with a cartoon of politicians painting a sickly cow white, while a distiller slipped a bag of money into Tuomey's pocket.
From then on, he was known as Swill Milk Tuomey.
But the public's anger didn't fade, and in 1862, the state legislature passed a law against swill milk.
Enforcement stayed weak for decades, but the fight for safe food had begun.
And it explains why this little Gothic building, with its promise of clean milk from country cows, felt like a gift to the children of the city.
You heard that the Wollman Rink, down the hill to the south, opened in 1950.
In the 1980s, it became the setting for a very New York political story.
In 1980, the city closed the rink to rebuild it.
The work went badly wrong, with leaking pipes and endless delays, and six years and about twelve million dollars later, the rink was still shut.
In May 1986, a developer named Donald Trump wrote to Mayor Ed Koch offering to take over the job.
After a very public exchange of letters, Koch accepted.
Trump's team brought in experienced rink builders, and the rink reopened that November, about four months after work began and well under its budget of three million dollars.
The episode made Trump a symbol of private speed against public failure, and he told the story for years afterward.
Critics pointed out that the city paid for the work, and that Trump's company went on to run the rink as a profitable concession, so the deal was good business as well as good publicity.
His company managed the rink for decades, and later the carousel too.
In 2021, after the attack on the United States Capitol, the city moved to end its contracts with the Trump Organization, and his name came off the rink.
Whatever you make of the politics, on a winter night, the rink is one of the loveliest sights in the city.
Take a closer look at the carousel's horses.
They're big, muscular animals with flaring nostrils, and manes that whip back as if they're galloping into a gale.
That's the signature of their carvers, Solomon Stein and Harry Goldstein.
Stein and Goldstein worked as carvers in Brooklyn, in the years when Coney Island was the carousel capital of America.
In 1908, they built this one at their own shop in Williamsburg, which they called the Artistic Carousel Manufacturing Company.
Their horses are prime examples of what collectors call the Coney Island style: flashy, theatrical animals decked with jewels and gold.
This carousel spent its first decades in a trolley terminal at Coney Island, and it had been left there, abandoned, by the time the park needed a replacement for its own burned carousel.
Restored and brought here in 1951, it's officially named for Michael Friedsam, a president of the B. Altman department store, whose foundation helped pay for it.
If you've read The Catcher in the Rye, you may remember that the novel ends at the carousel on this spot.
On a rainy Sunday, Holden Caulfield walks his little sister, Phoebe, past the sea lions at the zoo and brings her here.
She rides around and around on a big brown horse, reaching for the gold ring, while he sits on a bench getting soaked, and feels, all of a sudden, so happy he could almost cry.
You heard that Sheep Meadow became a gathering place for protests against the Vietnam War.
The biggest began here on April 15th, 1967.
That Saturday, a coalition called the Spring Mobilization to End the War in Vietnam filled this lawn with an enormous crowd, ready to march to the United Nations.
Estimates of its size ran from about a hundred thousand to several hundred thousand.

At the front of the march were Martin Luther King Junior, who had come out publicly against the war just eleven days before, in a speech at Riverside Church, along with the singer Harry Belafonte and the baby doctor Benjamin Spock.
Before the march set off, something happened here that the organizers hadn't planned, and many of them didn't want.
A group of young men, many of them students from Cornell University in Ithaca, gathered in the meadow, and one after another, they set fire to their draft cards.
Burning a draft card was a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, and they did it in front of the cameras.
They claimed that nearly two hundred cards were burned, though nobody could check.
The next morning's New York Times headline read: Many Draft Cards Burned.
Eggs Tossed at Parade.
Then the crowd poured out toward the United Nations, where King spoke.
It was one of the largest antiwar protests the country had yet seen.
On June 17th, 1967, Barbra Streisand gave a free concert on this meadow.
She was twenty-five, and already a star of records, Broadway and television.
The crowd was enormous, by her own count about a hundred and thirty-five thousand people, spread across the grass as far as she could see.
The concert was filmed for a television special called A Happening in Central Park, and on film, it looks like a triumph.
But during the evening, she forgot the words to a song, and by some of her own accounts, to more than one.
In front of that sea of people, it was, as she later put it, an actor's nightmare come true.
The experience shook her badly.
Streisand has said it left her with stage fright so severe that for about twenty-seven years, she gave almost no public concerts, apart from a handful of benefits and political events.
When she finally went back on tour, in the 1990s, she relied on teleprompters, which she credited with giving her the confidence to face a crowd again.
The night of her biggest audience was also the night that kept Barbra Streisand off the concert stage for a generation.
Look toward the western edge of the meadow for the restaurant you heard about, Tavern on the Green.
Its story runs from sheep to glitter.
The building began in 1870 as the Sheepfold, designed by Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould in a Victorian Gothic style, a home for the flock and its shepherd.
In 1934, Robert Moses sent the sheep away and turned the building into a restaurant, which opened that October.
Then, in the 1970s, came Warner LeRoy.
He was the son of the Hollywood director Mervyn LeRoy, who had produced The Wizard of Oz, and he had a showman's taste for spectacle.

He took over the lease and spent about ten million dollars turning the Tavern into a fantasy, with chandeliers, stained glass, topiary animals on the lawn, and a glass-walled Crystal Room, unveiled in 1976.
Critics often sniffed at the food, but nobody came for the food alone.

Tourists, wedding parties, celebrities and birthday crowds packed it, and it became one of the highest-grossing restaurants in the United States, taking in about thirty-eight million dollars as late as 2007.
LeRoy died in 2001, and his family ran it until the city put the lease up for bid.
The family's company lost the lease and went bankrupt, and on the last night of 2009, the Tavern served its last dinners.
Even the chandeliers were auctioned off.
It has since reopened under new owners, and the old Sheepfold still stands: a building made for sheep that became a palace for parties.

On the Literary Walk, three of the writers need no introduction: Shakespeare, the statue the Booth brothers raised money for, as you may have heard at Gramercy Park, and the Scottish poets Robert Burns and Walter Scott.
The fourth, seated in bronze, is Fitz-Greene Halleck.
He's the only American on the walk, and in his day, he was one of the most popular poets in the country.
Halleck came to New York from Connecticut as a young man.
In 1819, he and his close friend Joseph Rodman Drake published a series of witty, satirical poems about the city's notables in the Evening Post, signed The Croakers, and all New York laughed along.
When Drake died the next year, at twenty-five, Halleck wrote an elegy for him with lines that people quoted for a century: Green be the turf above thee, friend of my better days.
None knew thee but to love thee, nor named thee but to praise.
Historians of gay New York have pointed to the depth of that friendship.
Halleck's poem about a Greek hero, Marco Bozzaris, was recited by schoolchildren across America.
And for years, he earned his living as the private secretary of John Jacob Astor, the richest man in the country.
When Halleck died in 1867, his admirers, led by the poet and editor William Cullen Bryant, raised money for this statue.
On May 15th, 1877, President Rutherford B. Hayes came to unveil it, with members of his cabinet, and the crowd was so big that it overwhelmed the stands.
Then the world forgot him.
Tastes changed, and his poems began to seem stiff and old-fashioned.
Halleck sits here as a lesson in the fickleness of fame: a president came to honor him, and today, hardly anyone stops to read his name.
Walk to the north end of the Mall, to the open plaza in front of the Naumburg Bandshell.
This was designed as the Concert Ground, and music was played here for sixty years before the bandshell was built.
It started with Jacob Wrey Mould, the architect behind so much of the park's decoration, who was also an amateur musician.
In the park's first years, Mould persuaded wealthy friends to pay for free band concerts in the Ramble.
The crowds were so big that the park's board took them over, and in 1862, it built Mould's Music Pavilion here, a Moorish fantasy in wood and cast iron, brightly painted and gilded.
Bands played there on fine Wednesday and Saturday afternoons.
By the 1920s, the old pavilion was worn out, and its sound was poor.
A retired banker named Elkan Naumburg, who loved music, had been paying for free orchestral concerts here since 1905, and in 1921, he offered the city a hundred thousand dollars for a new bandshell.
His nephew, William Tachau, designed the neoclassical shell you see, which opened in 1923.
The Naumburg concerts still go on every summer, one of the oldest series of free outdoor classical concerts in the country.
Now look around the edges of the plaza for the busts.
Beethoven is here, a gift from a German singing society in 1884, and so is Victor Herbert, the composer of operettas.
Nearby is the poet Friedrich Schiller, whose bust, by most accounts, was the very first sculpture placed in Central Park, in 1859.
On a summer weekend, walk west from the bandshell toward a short stretch of old roadway that no longer carries traffic, and listen for the music.
You'll probably find a circle of roller skaters, young and old, some of them gray-haired veterans, dancing, spinning and gliding to disco, funk and house music from a DJ's speakers.
The spot is called the Dead Road, and skaters have been gathering here since the late 1970s, when roller skating and disco were taking off together across the city.
A skate rental shop opened nearby, and soon this stretch of pavement became an open-air roller disco, where skaters of every background invented moves and showed them off.
The good times didn't last without a fight.
In the 1990s, after the area was repaved during the restoration of the Bandshell and Bethesda Terrace, the skaters faced the threat of being banned from the park.
They organized, forming the Central Park Dance Skaters Association, to keep the circle alive and to work things out with the city.
It worked.
Decades later, the circle still turns, with veterans who have skated here since the disco days teaching newcomers the moves.
It's one of the most joyful sights in the park, and a living reminder that a great public space is shaped not only by its designers, but by the people who make it their own.
You heard that Emma Stebbins, the sculptor of the Angel of the Waters, shared her life with the actress Charlotte Cushman.
Their story begins in Rome.
Stebbins came from a wealthy New York family, and in the 1850s, in middle age, she went to Rome to study sculpture, encouraged by her brother Henry.
There she met Cushman, the most celebrated American actress of the day, a commanding figure famous for playing Lady Macbeth, and for playing men, above all Romeo.
Cushman's household in Rome became the center of a circle of independent American women sculptors, working in marble, whom the novelist Henry James later described as a white, marmorean flock.
Stebbins and Cushman stayed together for the rest of Cushman's life.
The fountain was a remarkable commission for a woman in the 1860s, and not everyone thought Stebbins had won it fairly.
Her brother Henry had become president of the board that ran Central Park, and Cushman used her own connections on her behalf.
Stebbins modeled the angel in Rome over several years, and the casting in bronze was held up by the Franco-Prussian War.
When the fountain was finally unveiled in 1873, the reviews were mixed, and some critics were scornful.
Time has been kinder.
The angel, wings spread, blessing the water with one hand and holding lilies in the other, has become one of the best-loved figures in New York.
By then, Cushman was fighting breast cancer, and Stebbins nursed her until her death in 1876, then wrote a book about her life.
They lie far apart, Cushman near Boston and Stebbins in Brooklyn.
But here, at the heart of the park, the angel stands as their monument too.
Before you go down to the fountain, go back to the top of the terrace, along the road, and look closely at the carved stone posts and panels beside the staircases.
The theme was chosen by Calvert Vaux, and the carving was designed by Jacob Wrey Mould: the turning of the seasons and the hours of the day, told through plants, birds and animals.
Look for the seasons in flowers, fruit, leaves and birds.
Look for a rooster crowing in the morning, and an owl for the night.
Now find the most famous carving of all.
On the western face of one of the posts at the top of the terrace, a witch flies across the stone on her broomstick, and beside her is a jack-o'-lantern.
On the opposite face of the same post, the sun rises over the sea.
Night and day, back to back.
People have argued for years over whether the witch stands for Halloween, or simply for the night.
Either way, she's a wonderful surprise to find on a Victorian terrace.
Mould and his carvers covered the terrace in scene after scene like these, and most visitors walk right past them.
Over the decades, soot and weather wore many of them down, and restorers have since cleaned and repaired them with great care.
Take a few minutes to hunt for your favorite.
Bethesda Terrace is the architectural heart of the park, and above all, it's the work of Calvert Vaux.
Yet for more than a century, most of the park's fame went to his partner.
Vaux was born in London in 1824 and trained as an architect there.
In 1850, the American landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing, one of the first to call for a great park in New York, came to London looking for an architect, and hired him.
Two years later, Downing was killed when a Hudson River steamboat caught fire.
Vaux was left without his mentor in a new country, but he stayed, and he carried on Downing's dream of a park.
He named one of his sons Downing.
It was Vaux who saw the 1857 competition as a chance, and Vaux who asked Olmsted, then the park's superintendent, to join him.
Olmsted knew the ground, and Vaux knew design.
Their Greensward Plan won.
But Olmsted held the official title in charge of the work, and the newspapers and the public came to think of the park as Olmsted's.
Vaux fought, sometimes bitterly, to have his share recognized.
He went on to design Prospect Park and Morningside Park with Olmsted, and, with Mould, the first buildings of the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the American Museum of Natural History.
In November 1895, at seventy, Vaux went out for a walk near Gravesend Bay in Brooklyn, and didn't come home.
His body was found in the water two days later.
Whether he slipped or meant to go has never been settled.
Stand on the terrace and look out at what he made.
This is his monument.
You heard that Bow Bridge is one of the oldest cast-iron bridges in America.
Its ironwork came from a foundry that was working on something much bigger at the same time.
The firm was Janes, Kirtland and Company, an ironworks that turned out all kinds of ornamental iron.
In the years this bridge was being made, it was also building one of the great iron projects of the age: the new dome of the United States Capitol in Washington.
The company set up a big works in what's now the Bronx, and all through the Civil War, the giant iron dome rose piece by piece over the Capitol.
Bow Bridge, finished in 1862, is its little cousin in the park.
Look again at the bridge's railing of interlocking circles, and at the planters along the top.
Iron grows and shrinks with the temperature, and a bridge like this has to be free to move a little between a summer afternoon and a winter night.
That's where a favorite park legend comes in.
For years, people said that the bridge rests on cannonballs, set under one end so that the span could roll back and forth as it expands and contracts.
It's a lovely image: a bridge riding on ammunition.
But when the bridge was restored, workers went looking for the cannonballs, and found none at all.
The bridge still breathes with the seasons, just without the cannonballs.
You heard that in the nineteenth century, the Lake was the park's great skating pond.
Not all of it was open to everyone.
On winter days in the park's early years, tens of thousands of skaters crowded onto the ice.
For women in long skirts, a jostling crowd of strangers on skates could be daunting, so a small pond off the Lake's western arm was set aside as the Ladies' Pond, for women skaters.
On the rocky point called Hernshead, a little shelter called the Ladies' Cottage gave them a place to warm up and put on their skates.
In 1860, a young illustrator named Winslow Homer drew a scene for Harper's Weekly of women skating on the Ladies' Pond, in bonnets and wide skirts, gliding past the bare trees.
The Ladies' Pond was filled in long ago.
But look west across the water toward Hernshead for a delicate cast-iron pavilion with a lacy roof.
That's the Ladies' Pavilion, designed by Jacob Wrey Mould in 1871, and it didn't start out here.
It was built as a shelter for people waiting for streetcars at the park's entrance at Columbus Circle.
Around 1912, it was moved to Hernshead to make way for the Maine Monument, which still stands at that entrance.
By the 1970s, the pavilion was battered and broken.
Its restoration, celebrated in 1973, was one of the first projects in which private donors teamed up with the city to repair the park, years before the Conservancy was born.
So a former streetcar shelter helped point the way to the park's rescue.
You've heard Jacob Wrey Mould's name again and again on this walk: the carvings of Bethesda Terrace, the Music Pavilion, the Sheepfold, the Ladies' Pavilion, and this bridge.
Who was he?
Mould was born in England in 1825 and trained under Owen Jones, a designer famous for his studies of color and ornament, who spent years documenting the Alhambra, the great Moorish palace in Spain.
Mould is said to have helped him with that work, and the Moorish love of pattern and bright color stayed with him all his life.
You can see it in the tiles of the Bethesda arcade, and you once could see it in the gilded pavilion on the Mall.
He came to New York in the early 1850s to design a church, All Souls Unitarian, on Fourth Avenue at 20th Street.
Its bold stripes of brick and pale stone startled the city, and New Yorkers nicknamed it the Church of the Holy Zebra.
It was torn down long ago, but it made Mould's name.
Soon he was working beside Vaux in the park, designing much of its ornament, from carved birds to iron railings.
Mould was a gifted and unusual character, a lover of music who got the park's first concerts going.
In the 1870s, he spent several years working in Lima, Peru, before coming back to design for the city's parks.
He died in 1886.
Olmsted and Vaux gave the park its shape, and Mould gave it its sparkle.
Look for his touch in the curves of this railing.
This garden takes its name from a song, and the song takes its name from a real place in Liverpool.
As a boy, John Lennon lived with his Aunt Mimi in the Liverpool suburb of Woolton.
Nearby stood a Victorian mansion called Strawberry Field, which had become a children's home run by the Salvation Army.
Its grounds were a wild, overgrown garden, and young John would climb over the wall to play among the trees.
Every summer, the home held a garden party with a Salvation Army brass band, and he loved to go.
Mimi warned him he'd get into trouble for trespassing, and it's often said that her warning, that they'd hang him for it, is why the song says there's nothing to get hung about.
In late 1966, while filming in Spain, Lennon began writing a song about that garden, and about the dreamy, lonely feeling of a child who doesn't quite fit in.
The Beatles released Strawberry Fields Forever in February 1967, on a single with Paul McCartney's Penny Lane, another song about a real place in Liverpool.
Its swirling sound was made partly by splicing two different recordings together.
The children's home closed in 2005, and its famous red gates were later replaced with copies.
In 2019, the Salvation Army reopened the site with an exhibition about Lennon and the song.
So two gardens, an ocean apart, share a name: the one where a lonely boy played, and the one where the world comes to remember him.
You heard that John Lennon lived across the street, at the Dakota.
For a few years in the 1970s, the United States government tried to throw him out of the country.
Lennon and Yoko Ono moved to New York in 1971, and Lennon threw himself into radical politics.
He sang at rallies, befriended antiwar activists, and talked of a concert tour that would register young voters and campaign against President Nixon in the 1972 election.
The government moved against him.

A memo from Senator Strom Thurmond suggested that deporting Lennon might be a way to stop him, the FBI put him under surveillance, and in 1972, the immigration service began proceedings to send him out of the country.
The official reason was a conviction in Britain, in 1968, for possessing cannabis.
Lennon fought back, and the case dragged on for years.
In October 1975, a federal appeals court ruled in his favor.
The judge, Irving Kaufman, wrote that the courts would not condone selective deportation based upon secret political grounds.
Two days later, on Lennon's thirty-fifth birthday, Yoko Ono gave birth to their son, Sean.
In July 1976, Lennon finally received his green card, which let him stay in the United States for good.
He called New York home for the rest of his life.
Years later, the FBI's files on him were released, showing just how closely he had been watched.
After Sean was born in 1975, John Lennon did something almost unheard of for a rock star at the height of his fame.
He stopped.
For five years, Lennon released no new music.
He stayed home at the Dakota and raised his son, while Yoko Ono ran the family's business affairs.
He baked bread, and was proud of it, and later joked that after all that work, he felt he deserved a gold record.
He called himself a househusband, an unusual word at the time, and he meant it.
He spent his days with Sean, read, drew and traveled, and, by many accounts, walked in the park across the street.
In 1980, he and Ono recorded a new album, Double Fantasy, released that November, with songs about family and this quiet life.
In one, Watching the Wheels, he sings about the people who told him he was crazy to give it all up, while he was happy just sitting there, watching the wheels go round and round.
In another, Beautiful Boy, a lullaby for Sean, he sings a line that has become one of his most quoted: life is what happens to you while you're busy making other plans.
Three weeks after the album came out, he was killed outside his home.
Strawberry Fields is a memorial to a Beatle, but it's also a memorial to a father who chose, for a while, to step away from the world and stay home.
Stand by the mosaic and imagine him crossing the street on an ordinary afternoon, with a little boy by the hand.
You heard that Olmsted called the Ramble a wild garden, and that its rocks and paths were all placed.
Olmsted set the idea.
The man who chose and planted much of what grew here was the park's chief gardener, Ignaz Pilat.
Pilat was born in Austria in 1820 and trained as a gardener in Vienna's botanical gardens.
The upheavals of 1848, when revolutions swept across Europe, sent him abroad, and he ended up in America.
By the late 1850s he was working on the new park under Olmsted, and he rose to be its chief gardener, in charge of the groves, the shrubs, the vines, and the flower beds.
The planting design of the Ramble is credited to him.
In 1863, Olmsted crossed the Isthmus of Panama by train, on his way to a job in California.
He was dazzled by the jungle passing his window, by forests draped in vines, and he sent Pilat a long letter about it, full of ideas for the park.
He wanted something of that mystery and abundance here, made with plants tough enough for a New York winter.
You can feel the idea around you: shrubs layered under trees, vines over rocks, and paths that vanish around a bend.
Pilat didn't live to see the park grow up.
He died of tuberculosis, then called consumption, at his home in New York in 1870, at about fifty.
Woods take decades to fill in, and what you're walking through is the result he and Olmsted were after: a garden designed so carefully that it seems no one designed it at all.
You heard that a Eurasian eagle-owl named Flaco lived free in the park for a year.
Here's how that year began, and what his death revealed.
Eagle-owls are among the largest owls in the world, with orange eyes, feathered ear tufts, and wings that can stretch close to six feet.
Flaco had lived for more than a decade in an enclosure at the Central Park Zoo.
On February 2, 2023, someone cut the steel mesh of his exhibit, and he flew out.
Zoo staff worried that he would starve, since he had never hunted for himself, and they tried to lure him back.
But people soon watched him catch and eat the park's rats, and the zoo eventually stopped trying to recapture him.
He became a celebrity.
Birders and photographers followed him through the park, and later through the streets, where he perched on water towers and fire escapes and hooted into the night.
On February 23, 2024, Flaco flew into a building on West 89th Street and died.
The final report on his death found more than a crash.
He had a severe infection of pigeon herpesvirus, picked up from eating the city's feral pigeons.
And his body held four different rat poisons, the kinds commonly used across New York.
The zoo said the illness and the poisons would likely have killed him anyway, and may be why he hit the building.
Those poisons work by stopping blood from clotting, and they can build up in any hawk or owl that eats a poisoned rat.
Flaco escaped his cage, but not the city's food chain.
You heard that birders crowd the Ramble every spring.
On the morning of May 25, 2020, one of them, Christian Cooper, was out here when he saw a dog running loose.
In the Ramble, dogs must always be on a leash, to protect the birds and the plants.
Cooper, a birder since childhood and a former editor at Marvel Comics, asked the dog's owner, a white woman, to leash it.
She refused.
He took out some dog treats, a tactic he used to get owners to leash their dogs, and started recording on his phone.
She told him she was going to call the police and say that an African American man was threatening her life.
Then she did.
His video, shared online that day, was watched by millions.
It was the same day George Floyd was killed by a police officer in Minneapolis, and the two videos became part of the same national reckoning.

Within days, a group of young Black scientists organized the first Black Birders Week, to celebrate Black people who study and love the outdoors, and to talk honestly about the dangers they can face there.
Cooper became the most famous birder in America almost overnight.
In 2023 he published a memoir, Better Living Through Birding, and began hosting a National Geographic television series, Extraordinary Birder.
So when you see someone here with binoculars, waiting for a warbler, remember that the Ramble's quiet belongs to everyone.
You heard that the official weather for Central Park is measured here.
The park's weather record is one of the longest in the country, and it didn't begin at the castle.
In 1869, New York State authorized a weather observatory in Central Park.
For its first half century it was based at the Arsenal, near Fifth Avenue and 64th Street, which you may have passed on the southern park tour, with its instruments on the roof.
In 1919, as you heard, the Weather Bureau moved into the castle, and from the start of 1920 this was the official site.
The instruments didn't stay put.
As the trees grew, they were shifted around the grounds to keep them in the open, and today they sit in a fenced enclosure nearby, screened by trees.
Some meteorologists grumble that the leaves shade the sensors and block the breeze, so the park can read differently from the airports.
But the park's record is prized for its length: it lets you compare a hot afternoon this summer with one in the 1870s.
Nearly everything is automated now, with one exception.
When it snows, a person still goes out to a flat white board set on the ground, measures the snow with a ruler, and wipes the board clean to start again.
That job has passed through several hands over the years.
Since 2015, it has belonged to the staff of the Central Park Conservancy.
So when the news says Central Park got six inches, someone in boots probably measured it by hand.
You heard that the castle sits on Vista Rock.
Look down at the rock itself, wherever it breaks through the ground around you.
This is Manhattan schist, the bedrock of much of the island.
It began as mud and sand on the floor of an ancient sea.
Roughly four hundred fifty million years ago, as continents collided and pushed up a range of mountains, those layers were buried, squeezed, and heated until their minerals grew into new crystals.
Geologists call rock like this metamorphic, which means changed in form.
Look closely and you can see the change.
The rock glitters, because it's full of mica, a mineral that forms thin, flat flakes, like tiny shards of a broken mirror.
In places you may spot small dark red specks.
Those are garnets.
And notice that the rock has a grain, a layering, often tilted at a steep angle.
That's the squeezing, frozen in place.
Now look at the tops of the outcrops.
In spots they're smooth, almost polished, and scored with long, straight scratches.
Those were made by ice.
In the last ice age, tens of thousands of years ago, a great ice sheet covered this whole region.
As it ground slowly south, stones frozen into its base worked like sandpaper and chisels on the bedrock.
The ice left things behind, too.
Scattered around the park are boulders that don't match the ground they sit on, carried here by the ice and dropped when it melted.
Geologists call them erratics.
Olmsted and Vaux didn't blast this away.
They made it part of the scenery, and set the castle on top of it, so it seems to grow from the rock.
A short walk west of the castle, near 79th Street, stands a small wooden building with a steep roof that looks as if it wandered in from a Scandinavian village.
In a way, it did.

The Swedish Cottage was built in Sweden in 1875 as a model schoolhouse, shipped across the Atlantic, and put up at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia in 1876, the world's fair for the hundredth birthday of American independence.
When the fair closed, the city of New York bought it, and in 1877 it was taken apart again and rebuilt here.
Accounts differ on how much Olmsted himself had to do with that.
For decades, the park used it for whatever was needed, including as a tool shed.
Then, in 1947, it found its calling.
The Parks Department had a traveling marionette troupe that put on puppet shows around the city, and that year the troupe moved into the cottage.
In the 1970s, it was remodeled with a permanent stage.
Generations of New York children have seen their first play here, watching marionettes act out fairy tales on strings.
It's said to be one of the last public marionette theaters in the country.
It makes a nice pair with the Delacorte, a short walk away.
Two theaters share this corner of the park: one for Shakespeare under the stars, and one for the park's smallest actors and its youngest audiences.
You heard that Simon and Garfunkel reunited here in September 1981.
It's worth knowing how unlikely that was.
Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel had split up more than a decade earlier, after Bridge Over Troubled Water, and had rarely performed together since.
The show on September 19, 1981, was a free benefit to help pay for the restoration of the park, which was badly run down.
The two men expected a modest crowd.
About half a million people came, and the concert was filmed and recorded for a live album.
The most charged moment didn't make the album.
Nine months earlier, John Lennon had been shot outside the Dakota, on the edge of the park, as you may have heard at Strawberry Fields.
Simon had written a new song, The Late Great Johnny Ace, about the death of a 1950s rhythm and blues singer and about the night he heard that Lennon had died.
He sang it here.
In the middle of the song, a man climbed onto the stage and rushed toward him.
Security pulled the man away before he reached Simon, and Simon kept singing.
The song was left off the record, though you can see the moment in the concert film, and a studio version came out two years later.
The reunion didn't last.
The two toured together and began a new album, but it was finished as a Paul Simon solo record.
Still, for one night, half a million people sat on this lawn and sang along, and the night became part of the story of the park's comeback.
You heard that about a million people gathered here in June 1982 to protest nuclear weapons.
It's widely called the largest antinuclear demonstration in American history.
The date, June 12, 1982, was chosen to coincide with a special session of the United Nations General Assembly on disarmament, meeting a few miles away on the East River.
The early 1980s were a frightening time.

The Cold War had turned icy again, both superpowers were building new weapons, and a grassroots campaign was calling for a freeze: a halt by both sides to testing, building, and deploying nuclear weapons.
Marchers filled the streets of Midtown on their way to the park.
By mid-afternoon, police estimated the crowd at more than seven hundred fifty thousand, and by the end of the day, about a million.
They came from across the country and from overseas.
On the stage, Bruce Springsteen sang with Jackson Browne, and James Taylor, Joan Baez, Linda Ronstadt, and Peter, Paul and Mary performed.
Did it work?
The freeze itself never became policy.
But within a few years, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev were negotiating the first treaty to actually eliminate a whole class of nuclear weapons.
Historians still argue over how much credit the marchers deserve.
But for one day, this lawn, packed from edge to edge, showed how many people were afraid, and how many wanted something done.
You heard that the Great Lawn drew enormous crowds for free concerts.
One of the most remembered took place in a downpour.
On July 21, 1983, Diana Ross, by then more than a decade into her solo career and one of the biggest stars in the world, gave a free concert here, which was being filmed for television.
Less than half an hour in, a violent storm swept over the park.
Ross stayed on stage, soaked through, and kept singing, then urged the vast crowd to leave slowly and calmly so that no one would be hurt.
She came back the very next evening, at six o'clock, for an unplanned second show.
The concerts were supposed to raise money for a playground in the park.
Instead, the costs of putting on a second show, and the lawsuits that followed, swallowed the profits.
In the end, Ross handed Mayor Ed Koch a check for two hundred fifty thousand dollars.
The playground got built.
Ground was broken in 1986, at the west edge of the park near 81st Street, not far from here, and it's called the Diana Ross Playground.
If you pass it, and hear children shrieking on the slides, that's partly thanks to a singer who refused to leave the stage in a thunderstorm.

On a small hill just east of the Great Lawn, behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art, stands the oldest man-made object in Central Park, and one of the oldest outdoor monuments anywhere in the Americas: a granite obelisk nicknamed Cleopatra's Needle.
It has nothing to do with Cleopatra.
It was carved around 1450 BC, more than a thousand years before Cleopatra's time, for the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose the Third, and erected at the temple city of Heliopolis.
Look for the hieroglyphics carved on its sides, though they're badly weathered on some faces.
Around 12 BC, the Romans moved it to Alexandria, where it stood outside a temple built by Cleopatra in honor of Julius Caesar, or Mark Antony, depending on the source.
That's how it got its nickname.
In the 1870s, the ruler of Egypt, Khedive Ismail Pasha, offered the obelisk to the United States as a gift, hoping to win friendship and support.
A similar obelisk had gone to London.
The cost of moving it, more than one hundred thousand dollars, was paid by William Henry Vanderbilt, the son of the Commodore.
A Navy officer named Henry Gorringe engineered the move.

The obelisk, about seventy feet tall and weighing over two hundred tons, was lowered, loaded into the hold of a steamship through a hole cut in its hull, shipped across the Atlantic, floated to the Hudson River, and hauled across Manhattan on a special railway over several months.
Its cornerstone was laid in October 1880, in a Masonic ceremony attended by thousands, and the obelisk itself was raised here in January 1881.
New York's climate, with its freeze-thaw cycles and air pollution, has been much harder on the stone than three thousand years in Egypt.
Some of the hieroglyphics have eroded significantly since it arrived.
Look at the base, at the corners.
You'll see bronze crabs.
They're replicas of crabs the Romans placed under the obelisk to support it when they moved it to Alexandria.
The originals are in the Met.
Speaking of which, the massive building next to you is the back of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Look for the glass wall of the Sackler Wing.

Inside, visible through the glass, is the Temple of Dendur, an Egyptian temple built around 15 BC, given to the United States by Egypt in the 1960s, in gratitude for American help in saving monuments threatened by the Aswan High Dam.
So here, two ancient Egyptian monuments face each other across a park in Manhattan.
You heard that the obelisk was carved for Thutmose the Third.
Look at the face where the hieroglyphics are clearest, and you'll find that he wasn't the only pharaoh to sign it.
The obelisk is a single piece of red granite, quarried far up the Nile at Aswan.
Down the center of each face runs one column of hieroglyphics for Thutmose.

About two centuries later, Ramesses the Second, the most self-promoting of all the pharaohs, had two more columns carved on each face, one on either side of the original, celebrating his own military victories.
So the stone carries two kings' names, cut by different hands, generations apart.
Look for the ovals called cartouches, which frame a royal name.
Look for birds, including the falcon, the symbol of the god Horus and of kingship.
On some faces, the carving is almost gone.
In January 2011, Zahi Hawass, then Egypt's chief of antiquities, wrote to the mayor and the Conservancy that the obelisk had weathered badly.
If New York could not care for it properly, he wrote, he would take the necessary steps to bring it home.
City officials disputed that it was being neglected, and experts who studied it found no sign of significant ongoing erosion.
Hawass had sent a similar complaint a few years before.
Still, in May 2014, conservators began a careful cleaning.
Before they started, photographers from the Met documented the stone in detail from a lift.
As one official put it at the time, the obelisk was clearly not falling apart, but it could definitely use a good cleaning.
You heard that the obelisk's cornerstone was laid in a Masonic ceremony.
The Masons had a particular reason to care.

When Henry Gorringe lifted the obelisk from its base in Alexandria, he reported finding objects in the foundation that seemed to him clearly Masonic: a rough altar of red granite, a polished cube, a square, and an iron trowel.
A committee of Masons in Egypt, including Egyptologists, reportedly agreed that the emblems were Masonic.
Others were doubtful.
Albert Pike, a leading American Freemason, reportedly said they bore no resemblance to Freemasonry at all.
Whether the obelisk's builders had anything to do with the Masons is a legend, not history.
But when the obelisk was raised here, the emblems were set back exactly as they had been found in Alexandria.
The cornerstone ritual was led by the Grand Master of New York's Masons, Jesse B. Anthony.

Inside the stone, they sealed a time capsule: a copy of the 1870 census, a Bible, Webster's Dictionary, the complete works of Shakespeare, a guide to Egypt, and a copy of the Declaration of Independence.
And one more thing, a small box placed by one of the men who arranged for the obelisk to come to New York, whose contents were never made public.
No one has opened it since, and the Conservancy has said it has no plans to.
So somewhere beneath your feet is a box that, as far as anyone knows, no one living has seen inside.
What's in it is anyone's guess.
You heard that a similar obelisk went to London.
It's this one's twin.
The two stood as a pair, first at Heliopolis, then in Alexandria.
Paris has an obelisk too, but it came from a different temple, at Luxor.
The London obelisk had a far harder journey.
It had toppled long ago and lay half buried in the sand.
Egypt's ruler gave it to Britain in 1819, but for nearly sixty years no one wanted to pay to move it.
When the British finally did, they sealed it inside an iron cylinder, just big enough to hold it, with a small deck, a mast, and a cabin on top.
The strange vessel was named Cleopatra, and a steamship called the Olga was to tow it to England.
They left Alexandria in September 1877.
On October 14, in a storm in the Bay of Biscay, the cylinder began to roll out of control.
The Olga sent six volunteers in a small boat to rescue the Cleopatra's crew.
The boat was swamped, and all six drowned.
The Olga's captain finally brought his ship alongside and took off the Cleopatra's captain and five crewmen, and the cylinder was left to the sea.
It didn't sink.
It was found drifting, towed into a Spanish port, and eventually brought to London, where the obelisk was raised beside the Thames, on the Victoria Embankment, in 1878.
The names of the six sailors who died are remembered on a plaque at its base, and its bronze sphinxes still carry shrapnel scars from a German air raid in the First World War.
This obelisk, as you heard, made its own crossing three years later, tucked in the hold of a steamship.
You heard that Seneca Village had three churches.
One of them was All Angels' Church, an Episcopal congregation where Black and white New Yorkers worshipped together.
Its porter and sexton, the man who looked after the building and grounds, was William Godfrey Wilson.
When a state census taker came through in 1855, Wilson was forty-one.
He lived next to the church with his wife, Charlotte, and their eight children, in a three-story wood-frame house with a stone foundation and a brick chimney.
That isn't a shanty.
It's a substantial family home.
When archaeologists dug here in 2011, they went looking for two houses they had found in the archives, and the Wilson house was among the most important.
They found pieces of its metal roofing, kitchen utensils, scraps of clothing, and a stoneware beer bottle.
Why did so much survive?
Because when the city cleared the village, its crews took away what stood above the ground, often salvaging the wood, and left what lay below.
Foundations, cellars, and whatever had fallen into them stayed where they were, under the new park's soil, for a century and a half.
The findings were published in 2018, in a report called Seneca Village, A Forgotten Community.
Remember the Wilsons the next time you hear the village described as a cluster of shacks.
The record says something else: a father with a steady job at his church, a big family, and a three-story house with a brick chimney, on land the city decided it needed more.
You heard that residents were compensated for their land, though many said the amounts were too low.
One document shows what that looked like.
Andrew Williams, the young shoeshiner who bought the village's first lots in 1825, had paid one hundred twenty-five dollars for his land.
Three decades later, he had a house on it.
In 1856, as the city's commissioners set the prices for the land they were taking, Williams swore out an affidavit.
He valued his house and lots at four thousand dollars.
He had been offered thirty-five hundred, he said, and he had refused.
The document survives in the city's Municipal Archives.
It's a small piece of paper, but it says a lot.
Williams wasn't a squatter pleading to stay.
He was a property owner, arguing over a price, using the legal tools available to him.
And remember the two hundred fifty dollar rule that applied only to Black voters.
A man with four thousand dollars of property had cleared it many times over.
When the city took the land, it took the property that qualified him.
Unless he bought property somewhere else, he could lose his vote along with his home.
You heard that Seneca Village was one of the first communities of Black property owners in New York.
Across the East River, a similar community did better.
In the 1830s, on farmland at the eastern edge of Brooklyn, a free Black man named James Weeks bought land, and the settlement that grew around it took his name: Weeksville.
Like Seneca Village, it was a place where Black families could own property, and with it, for Black men, the right to vote.
It grew much larger than Seneca Village, with its own churches and schools.

During the Draft Riots of 1863, when mobs attacked Black New Yorkers in Manhattan and burned the Colored Orphan Asylum you may have heard about on the Midtown tour, some families fled to Weeksville for safety.
But Weeksville, too, was nearly forgotten, as Brooklyn's streets grew over it.
Then, in 1968, a researcher named James Hurley and a pilot named Joseph Haynes flew over the neighborhood, looking for traces of the old settlement.
From the air, they spotted a few old wooden houses that stood at an odd angle to the modern streets, because they had been built along an old country lane called Hunterfly Road.
Neighbors, led by a woman named Joan Maynard, organized to save them.
The houses became city landmarks, and in 1973, the community's society bought them.
Today they're the heart of the Weeksville Heritage Center in Crown Heights.
If Seneca Village makes you wonder what was lost here, Weeksville shows you what might have been.
You heard that the track around the Reservoir is one of the most famous running paths in the world.
The world's biggest marathon began a short distance from here.
On September 13, 1970, the first New York City Marathon was run entirely inside Central Park, around and around the park's loop drive.
The organizers, Fred Lebow and Vince Chiappetta, had a budget of about a thousand dollars.
The entry fee was one dollar.
A hundred twenty-seven runners started, and fifty-five finished.
One woman entered, and she had to drop out.
The winner, a city firefighter named Gary Muhrcke, crossed the line in about two hours and thirty-one minutes.
Lebow was a Romanian-born immigrant who worked in the garment industry, and he had a showman's instincts.
In 1976, for the nation's bicentennial, the race left the park and ran through all five boroughs.
It became a sensation.
Today it has more than fifty thousand finishers, and it still ends here in Central Park.
In 1992, ill with brain cancer, Lebow ran the course himself, alongside Grete Waitz of Norway, who won the women's race here nine times.
He finished in about five and a half hours.
He died two years later.
Look for his statue at Engineers' Gate, the park entrance at Fifth Avenue and 90th Street, just east of the Reservoir.
He's in running clothes, checking his watch, as if timing every runner who passes.
You heard that the Reservoir was retired in 1993, after a newer system of water tunnels made it obsolete.
One of those tunnels passes deep beneath this part of the park.
