New York's drinking water comes mostly from reservoirs upstate, and it reaches the city through enormous tunnels bored through solid rock, hundreds of feet down.
City Tunnel Number One opened in 1917, and Number Two in 1936.
For decades, neither could be shut down for inspection, because there was no backup.
So in 1970, the city began City Water Tunnel Number Three.
Its first stage runs about thirteen miles, from Hillview Reservoir in Yonkers, under the Bronx, under Manhattan and beneath Central Park, then under the East River and Roosevelt Island into Queens.
It was put into service in 1998, at a cost of about a billion dollars.
The new tunnel was built partly so that the two old ones could, at last, be shut down and repaired.
Later stages have followed, and the tunnel is still not finished.
The digging was done by sandhogs, the same trade you may have heard about at the Holland Tunnel, with drills and dynamite and, later, giant boring machines.
Twenty-four people have died on the project since 1970, most of them sandhogs.
So as you walk around the Reservoir, the water in front of you is just for looking at.
The water the city drinks is moving far below your feet.
You may have heard on the southern park tour that Olmsted and Vaux gave carriages, riders, and walkers separate paths.
The Reservoir is circled by one of those riding paths, a soft dirt bridle path just outside the runners' track.
Before the automobile, horses were everywhere in New York, and stables were as common as garages are today.
For more than a century, a stable a couple of blocks west of the park, at 175 West 89th Street, sent horses out onto these paths.
The building, designed by Frank A. Rooke, went up in 1892 as a stable, and in time became the Claremont Riding Academy, where generations of New Yorkers learned to ride.
Riders led their horses out of the building, down the street and across the avenues, into the park.
Claremont was the oldest continuously operated stable in New York City and the last public stable in Manhattan.
Rising costs and fewer riders finally closed it, at five in the afternoon on April 29, 2007.
The building, on the National Register of Historic Places, now belongs to a school.
The bridle path is still here, and it belongs mostly to runners now, who like its soft surface.
But it was built for hooves, and for a hundred years, the clatter of horses on 89th Street was as much a part of this neighborhood as the joggers are today.
As you may have heard at the Pond, the park's entrances were named in 1862 for the people of the city: artisans, scholars, mariners, and more.
In 2022, for the first time since then, a new name was added, on 110th Street between Malcolm X Boulevard and Fifth Avenue: the Gate of the Exonerated.
On April 19, 1989, a young woman jogging in the park was attacked and raped near the 102nd Street Cross Drive.
Five teenagers from Harlem, Black and Latino, aged fourteen to sixteen, were arrested: Antron McCray, Kevin Richardson, Yusef Salaam, Raymond Santana, and Korey Wise.
After hours of police questioning, they gave confessions that they soon took back, confessions that didn't match one another or the evidence.
Much of the press treated them as guilty from the start, and Donald Trump, then a real estate developer, bought full-page newspaper ads calling for the death penalty.
All five were convicted in 1990 and spent between about six and thirteen years in prison.
In 2002, Matias Reyes, a man already imprisoned for other crimes, confessed that he alone had committed the attack, and his DNA matched the evidence.
That December, the five men's convictions were thrown out.
In 2014, the city settled their lawsuit for forty-one million dollars, and in 2023, Yusef Salaam was elected to the City Council, representing Harlem.
The gate was dedicated on December 19, 2022, twenty years to the day after the convictions were vacated.
It honors the five, and everyone who has been wrongly convicted.
You heard about McGown's Pass Tavern, on the hill near the park's eastern edge.
Before the park, that hill had another life, as a convent and a school.
In the 1840s, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul acquired the property and founded a school for girls there, the Academy of Mount Saint Vincent.
When the park took the land, the Sisters moved north to an estate in the Bronx overlooking the Hudson, called Font Hill, where their college stands to this day.
Their old buildings stayed behind.
During the Civil War, from 1862 to 1865, they served as a military hospital for Union soldiers.
Mother Mary Jerome Ely sent fifteen sisters back to nurse the wounded, and the place was known as Saint Joseph's Military Hospital.
After the war, the old convent became a restaurant and hotel, and kept the Mount Saint Vincent name.
After a fire in 1881, it was rebuilt.
The Sisters, it's said, didn't want their name over a place they considered unsanctified, so the new building was named after the old tavern of the Revolutionary era: McGown's Pass Tavern.
So the name you heard at this stop has layers.
A Revolutionary-era tavern gave its name to a pass and a hill, the hill held a convent, the convent became a hospital, the hospital became a hotel, and the hotel took the tavern's name again.
You heard that the Loch's water comes from the city supply, and that the stream is artificial.
But it follows a real one.
Before the park, a natural brook ran through this area, called Montayne's Rivulet.
Its name is spelled several ways in old records.
It was one of the very few natural streams on the land that became Central Park.
Olmsted and Vaux dammed and reshaped it, sending its water northeast through a chain of water features.
First comes the Pool, near 100th Street, then the Loch, through the ravine, and finally the Harlem Meer.
They were built between 1862 and 1865, with dams and weirs.
Before the park, the low ground where the Meer is now was fed by more than one stream, including Harlem Creek, flowing down from the north.
This whole corner wasn't in the original park plan at all.
The park first ended at 106th Street, and the land up to 110th Street was added in 1863.
Outside the park, the old stream was buried in sewers as the city grew over it.
And for decades, the pool and rink built in the 1960s at the foot of the ravine cut off the natural link between the Loch and the Meer.
The new complex you'll see at the next stop reopens that link, so water can run from the ravine to the lake again, as the designers intended.
Before you leave, walk to the plaza at the park's northeast corner, at Fifth Avenue and 110th Street.
Here stands a monument to Duke Ellington, who, as you'll hear on the Harlem tour, became famous playing at the Cotton Club.
The memorial was the idea of Bobby Short, the cabaret singer and pianist who for decades played the Café Carlyle on the Upper East Side.

Short conceived it in 1979, did the fundraising himself, and chose the sculptor, Robert Graham, a Mexican-born artist based in Los Angeles, whose other works include the giant bronze fist in Detroit honoring the boxer Joe Louis.
The memorial took nearly twenty years.
Ellington had died in 1974.
Short lived to see it finished, and died in 2005.
When it was dedicated, on July 1, 1997, it was the first statue honoring Ellington anywhere in the United States, and it was hailed at the time as the city's first monument to a Black artist.
Look up.
It's about twenty-five feet tall.
At the top, Ellington stands beside a grand piano.
They're held up by three columns, and on top of each column stand three nude women, nine in all: the Muses of Greek myth, goddesses of the arts, balancing the piano and its player on their heads.
It's a bold, slightly startling piece, as unconventional as Ellington's music was in its day.
The circle itself is now called Duke Ellington Circle.
It sits where Central Park, Fifth Avenue, Harlem, and East Harlem all meet, which suits a composer who wrote for every corner of the city.
And a few blocks south, across Fifth Avenue, are the Museum of the City of New York and El Museo del Barrio, at the northern end of Museum Mile.
You heard that the Conservatory Garden's north garden has a fountain with three dancing maidens, and the south garden a statue of two children.
Both have stories.
The dancers are a bronze cast of Three Dancing Maidens, by the German sculptor Walter Schott, completed before 1910.
They came from Yonkers, just north of the city.

The family of Samuel Untermyer, the lawyer who famously questioned J. P. Morgan before Congress in 1912 about the power of the big banks, bought the piece from Schott's workshop and set it in the gardens of their estate overlooking the Hudson, gardens that are now a public park.
The sculpture came to Central Park and was placed here in the late 1940s.
Walk around it, and watch the three girls lean back as they dance in a ring, their dresses swirling as if caught in mid-turn.
Then find the small pool in the south garden with its two bronze children.
This is the Burnett Fountain, by the American sculptor Bessie Potter Vonnoh, a memorial to Frances Hodgson Burnett, the author of The Secret Garden.
The children are Mary and Dickon, from the novel.
In the book, Dickon charms wild animals by playing a pipe, and the statue shows him playing one.
The Secret Garden is a story about a neglected, walled garden that two children bring back to life.
That's worth keeping in mind here, because this garden, too, was once neglected and forgotten.
You heard that the Conservatory Garden was restored in the 1980s.
The person who led that work was Lynden Miller.
In 1982, the garden had long been neglected and was battered by vandalism.
Miller took on its rescue for the young Central Park Conservancy, and it took five years of replanting, rebuilding, and fundraising.
The work was completed in 1987.
Her argument, which she made for the rest of her career, was that beautiful, well-tended plantings change how people feel about a public place.
A garden that looks cared for draws people in, and a park full of people feels safer.
She later laid out the case in a book, Parks, Plants, and People.
She went on to put that idea to work across the city.
She designed the gardens of Bryant Park when it reopened in 1992, after the rescue you may have heard about on the Midtown tour.

She also worked at the New York Botanical Garden, Battery Park City, Hudson River Park, Fort Tryon Park, the planted mall on Park Avenue at 97th Street, and the British Garden in Hanover Square downtown.
The Conservatory Garden has since had another major restoration, completed in 2025.
If you come in late April or early May, walk the two long rows of crabapple trees that line the central lawn, when they're in full pink and white bloom.
Much of what you see began with a decision, more than forty years ago, that a forgotten garden at the top of the park deserved the same care as anything at its famous southern end.
Walk a block south and half a block west, to East 65th Street between Park and Madison Avenues.
Look for a wide, red brick townhouse with two front doors.
It's really two houses built as one, and for a time it was the home of a future president.
In 1908, Sara Delano Roosevelt, a wealthy widow, had the architect Charles A. Platt design a double townhouse.
She took Number 47 for herself, and gave Number 49 to her son, Franklin, and his wife, Eleanor.
She also chose their furniture and decoration, and hired their household staff.
The two houses were joined by doors on several floors, and Eleanor later recalled that she was never quite sure when she would be alone.
In August 1921, Franklin was struck by polio.
After two months in the hospital, he insisted on coming here, rather than to the family estate at Hyde Park, and in these rooms he began the long, private struggle to rebuild his strength.
Eleven years later he was elected president.
In the months before he took office, this house was his base in New York while he assembled his administration.
Sara died in 1941.
Hunter College, a few blocks away, acquired the house, and in November 1943 dedicated it as the Sara Delano Roosevelt Memorial House, a center for interfaith and interracial understanding.
Today it's the home of Hunter's Roosevelt House Public Policy Institute.
You heard that many of the apartment buildings along Park Avenue were designed by Rosario Candela.
He led a remarkable double life.
Candela was born in Sicily, came to New York as a young man, and studied architecture at Columbia.
In the 1920s, as the old mansions gave way to apartment houses, he became the architect the rich trusted most.
His specialty was the apartment that felt like a mansion: grand entrance galleries, high ceilings, and duplexes, fitted together inside the building like pieces of a three-dimensional puzzle.
His most famous building is 740 Park Avenue, at 71st Street, where John D. Rockefeller Junior lived, and where a young Jacqueline Bouvier, the future Jacqueline Kennedy, spent part of her childhood.
In the 1930s, with the building boom over, Candela threw himself into another passion: codes.
He studied the ciphers of a French army officer, Commandant Étienne Bazeries, and decrypted messages Bazeries had encoded in 1898.
Starting in 1941, he taught a class in cryptography and cryptanalysis at Hunter College, a few blocks north of here, said to be the only course of its kind open to the public anywhere in the country.
When the war came, he reportedly put those skills to work for the government.

So the next time you pass a Candela building, with its orderly rows of windows and its interlocking apartments hidden behind them, think of a man who saw both buildings and secret messages as puzzles to be solved.
You heard that the Seventh Regiment was nicknamed the Silk Stocking Regiment.
In the First World War, its men paid a terrible price.
When the United States entered the war, the regiment was reorganized as the 107th Infantry, part of a division made up of New York troops.
On September 29, 1918, it attacked the Hindenburg Line, the great German defensive line in northern France, near the Saint Quentin Canal.

Over the course of the war, the 107th counted nearly two thousand casualties: four hundred thirty-seven men killed, more than thirteen hundred wounded, and ninety-eight more who later died of their wounds.
Much of that toll came in the one assault in September.
After the war, a memorial was commissioned, and the sculptor chosen was Karl Illava, who had served in the regiment as a sergeant.
It was dedicated in 1927, on the ninth anniversary of the attack.
You can see it a few blocks west of here, on Fifth Avenue at 67th Street, set into the stone wall of Central Park.
It shows a group of soldiers surging forward with their rifles, some of them helping wounded comrades along.
The faces are specific, tired, and determined, because the man who sculpted them had seen the real thing.
The drill hall behind you, where the regiment drilled for generations, now hosts art.
It's worth remembering that its first purpose was to prepare young New Yorkers for exactly this.
At Fifth Avenue and 70th Street, facing Central Park, stands a low, elegant mansion of limestone set back behind a garden.
This is the Frick Collection.
It was built between 1912 and 1914 as the home of Henry Clay Frick, designed by Thomas Hastings of Carrère and Hastings, the architects of the New York Public Library.
Frick was one of the most ruthless industrialists of the Gilded Age.
He made his fortune producing coke, a fuel used in steelmaking, in western Pennsylvania, and became the chairman of Carnegie Steel, Andrew Carnegie's company.
In 1892, during a strike at the Homestead steel works near Pittsburgh, Frick brought in hundreds of armed Pinkerton agents.
A battle broke out between the strikers and the Pinkertons, and people were killed on both sides.
The state militia then occupied the town, and the strike was broken.
Weeks later, an anarchist named Alexander Berkman burst into Frick's office, shot him twice and stabbed him.
Frick survived, and reportedly returned to work within about a week.
Frick and Carnegie eventually had a bitter falling out.
Frick moved to New York, and built his mansion on Fifth Avenue, about twenty blocks south of Carnegie's.
Some say he wanted to make Carnegie's house look like a miner's shack.
Frick spent his later years collecting European art, and he intended from the beginning that his house and collection would become a museum after his death.
He died in 1919, and the museum opened in 1935.

The Frick has an extraordinary collection, including works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein, Goya, Titian, and Turner, displayed as they would have been in a private home, among furniture and decorative objects.
Many visitors find it the most intimate and beautiful museum in the city.
The Frick underwent a major renovation and expansion in the early 2020s, opening up the second floor of the mansion, where the family's private rooms were, for the first time.
During the renovation, the collection was displayed temporarily in the Breuer building on Madison Avenue, the former home of the Whitney Museum.
You heard that the Frick's paintings hang as they would in a private home.
Two of them hang in what may be the most pointed arrangement in any museum in New York.
In the room called the Living Hall, on either side of the fireplace, hang two portraits by Hans Holbein the Younger, the great painter of Henry the Eighth's court.
On one side is Sir Thomas More, the king's chancellor, in a fur collar and a heavy gold chain of office, his face intelligent and wary.
On the other is Thomas Cromwell, the king's chief minister, heavy-set and watchful, clutching a document.
They face each other across the room.
In life, they were enemies.
More refused to accept Henry's break with the Church of Rome, and Cromwell helped bring about his downfall.
More was beheaded in 1535.
Five years later, Cromwell himself fell from favor and was beheaded too.
Between them, above the fireplace, hangs El Greco's portrait of Saint Jerome, a scholar and a saint, as if keeping the peace.
While you're inside, look for Frick's three paintings by Vermeer.
Only about three dozen paintings by Vermeer survive, and this house holds three of them.
One, Mistress and Maid, was the last painting Frick ever bought, in 1919, the year he died.
You heard that Frick and Carnegie had a bitter falling out.
The story of how it ended is one of the most quoted lines of the Gilded Age, and it may be a legend.
The partnership had made both men enormously rich.
But after Homestead it frayed, and around 1900 it collapsed in a fight over money.
Carnegie tried to force Frick out of the company and buy back his share at a price Frick considered far too low.
Frick took him to court, and in the end the dispute was settled with Frick still a very rich man.
As far as anyone knows, the two never made peace.
Then comes the story.
Years later, the tale goes, Carnegie, old and frail, sent word to Frick suggesting it was time they met and were reconciled.
Frick sent back his answer: Tell him I'll see him in hell, where we both are going.
Did he really say it?
The line turns up in many books, in slightly different words, and it has become more myth than record.
What is certain is that Carnegie made more than one attempt at reconciliation, and that it never happened.
And both men died in the same year, 1919, Carnegie in August and Frick in December.
As for the idea that Frick built this house to make Carnegie's mansion look like a miner's shack, you can judge for yourself.
Carnegie's house is about twenty blocks up Fifth Avenue, at 91st Street, on this tour.
Look at the walled garden beside the museum on East 70th Street, with its lawn, its pool, and its carefully placed trees and shrubs, seen through iron railings.
It's a viewing garden, meant to be looked at, not walked in.

It was designed by Russell Page, one of the most admired English garden designers of the twentieth century, and it was created in 1977, along with a new reception pavilion, after the museum demolished three row houses on the site.
Page composed it to be enjoyed from the sidewalk, in every season, like a picture in a frame.
In 2014, the Frick announced an expansion plan with a six-story addition that would have replaced the garden.
Opposition grew quickly.
Critics, including a former director of the museum, Everett Fahy, argued that the garden had been promised as permanent when the city's landmarks commission approved it in the 1970s.
In June 2015, the Frick dropped the plan.
The museum came back with a smaller design that left the garden where it is, and the renovation you heard about went ahead.
The new plan also called for the garden to be restored by Lynden Miller, the garden designer you may have heard about at the Conservatory Garden in Central Park.
It's a small victory, but a telling one.
A little garden that no one is allowed to walk into turned out to be something New Yorkers would fight for.
On November 15, 1961, a crowd packed an auction room at the Parke-Bernet Galleries on Madison Avenue, a few blocks from here.
The prize was Rembrandt's Aristotle with a Bust of Homer, from the collection of the late advertising executive Alfred Erickson.
The bidding was over in minutes.
The Metropolitan Museum won the painting for two point three million dollars, the highest price ever paid for a painting at auction up to that time.
When it went on display here, crowds lined up to see the record-breaking painting.
Look for it upstairs in the European paintings galleries.
The philosopher Aristotle, in a broad black hat and white sleeves, wears a heavy golden chain across his chest, and rests his hand on a marble bust of the poet Homer.
On the chain hangs a medallion that probably shows Alexander the Great, Aristotle's most famous pupil.
Rembrandt painted it in 1653, for a Sicilian nobleman who had asked for a philosopher.
It's a painting about three great men, the poet, the philosopher, and the conqueror, and about what lasts.
Aristotle seems to be weighing the gold on his chest against the blind poet under his hand.
Three centuries later, the painting itself became a test of what a museum should pay for a masterpiece, and the Met decided it was worth the price.
You heard that the Met's collection spans five thousand years.
Some of it, it turns out, came out of the ground illegally, and the museum has had to give it back.
In 1972, the Met bought a painted Greek vase called a krater, used for mixing wine with water, made around 515 BC and painted by Euphronios, one of the masters of Athenian vase painting.
It cost about a million dollars, an astonishing sum for a vase, and the press nicknamed it the hot pot.
Italian investigators believed it had been dug up illegally from an Etruscan tomb near Rome.
Over the following decades the evidence piled up, and in 2008 the Met returned it to Italy.
In 2017, the Met paid about four million dollars for a gleaming gilded coffin made for an Egyptian priest named Nedjemankh, more than two thousand years ago, and built an exhibition around it.
Then investigators from the Manhattan District Attorney's office showed that it had been looted from Egypt and sold with forged documents.
In February 2019, the museum handed it over to be returned to Egypt, and said it had been deceived.
Those cases are part of a much larger reckoning.

The district attorney's antiquities investigators have since seized many more objects from New York collectors, dealers, and museums, and museums now research where an object has been far more carefully before they buy it.
Underneath it all is a question that's political as well as legal: who owns the past?
In 1989, a poster appeared that New Yorkers still quote.
It showed a reclining nude, borrowed from a famous painting by Ingres, wearing a snarling gorilla mask.
Its headline asked: Do women have to be naked to get into the Met Museum?
Underneath, it said that less than five percent of the artists in the museum's modern art sections were women, but eighty-five percent of the nudes were female.

It was the work of the Guerrilla Girls, an anonymous group of women artists formed in New York in 1985, after the Museum of Modern Art mounted a huge survey of contemporary art in which only a small fraction of the artists were women.
The members appear in public in gorilla masks, and take the names of dead women artists, like Frida Kahlo and Käthe Kollwitz.
Their method is simple: they count.
The poster was designed as a billboard for a public art program, which turned it down.
So the Guerrilla Girls rented advertising space on New York City buses instead, until the bus company canceled the ads.
They have gone back to count again more than once, and found the numbers stubborn.
Their posters now hang in major museums around the world.
As you walk through the galleries here, try counting for yourself.
You heard that Solomon Guggenheim was advised by an artist, the Baroness Hilla von Rebay.
Without her, the building in front of you would not exist.
Rebay was a German painter from an aristocratic family.

She met Guggenheim in 1927, when she was commissioned to paint his portrait, and she persuaded the copper magnate, then in his sixties, to collect what she called non-objective art: pure abstraction, which she believed could lift the human spirit.
She steered him toward Kandinsky, and the collection grew.
She kept painting, too, and her own abstract canvases are in the collection.
In 1939, the foundation opened the Museum of Non-Objective Painting in rented space in Midtown, with Rebay as its first director.
In 1943, she and Guggenheim wrote to Frank Lloyd Wright, asking him to design a permanent home for the collection.
What she wanted, she said, was a temple of the spirit.
She had considered other architects, among them Walter Gropius and Le Corbusier.
According to one account, she wasn't even sure Wright was still alive, and it was Guggenheim's wife, Irene, who knew better.
The next year, they bought the land here on Fifth Avenue.
But after Solomon Guggenheim died in 1949, the family pushed Rebay out, and in 1952 the museum took his name.
By the time Wright's building opened in 1959, the woman who had dreamed of it was no longer part of the story, and for decades her role was largely forgotten.
As you look at the spiral, remember that it began with a baroness asking for a temple.
The Guggenheims were a large family, and Solomon was not the only one who collected modern art.
His niece Peggy did too, in a completely different spirit.
Peggy Guggenheim was the daughter of Solomon's brother Benjamin, who went down with the Titanic in 1912.
As the ship sank, he reportedly changed into evening clothes and said he was prepared to go down like a gentleman.
She inherited a much smaller fortune than her uncles, moved to Europe, and threw herself into the world of the avant-garde, at one point setting out to buy a picture a day.

When the Second World War broke out, she shipped her collection to New York, and in 1942 she opened a gallery on West 57th Street called Art of This Century, with walls and lighting as unconventional as the art.
There she gave a young painter named Jackson Pollock his first solo show, paid him a monthly stipend, and commissioned a huge canvas for her apartment, which he called Mural.
Her gallery was a launching pad for the painters who would make New York, not Paris, the capital of the art world.
After the war, Peggy moved to Venice, to an unfinished palace on the Grand Canal, where she lived among her paintings and her little dogs until her death in 1979.
Today the palace is a museum, run by the foundation named for her uncle.
So in the end, the two Guggenheim collections, the uncle's and the niece's, ended up in the same family.
You heard that the building is a single spiral ramp under a skylight.
Look again, with Wright's own words in mind.
Wright called it an optimistic ziggurat.
The ziggurats of ancient Mesopotamia were stepped towers that grew narrower as they rose.
Wright turned the idea upside down, so the building grows wider as it climbs, opening toward the sky.
Inside, he meant the outer walls of the ramp to lean back slightly, so that paintings would lean back too, as if resting on an artist's easel.
That was one of the features that angered painters, and in 1956, before the building even opened, a group of artists signed a letter of protest.
Curators have been working with, and around, those walls ever since.
Now step back and look at the whole block.
Along the facade, look for the museum's name, spelled out in lettering Wright designed himself.
The tall, plain building rising behind the spiral is a tower added in 1992, by the architects Gwathmey Siegel, to give the museum more gallery and office space.
Beside the spiral, look for the smaller round building, which Wright called the Monitor.
It now holds the Thannhauser Collection, a gift of Impressionist and early modern paintings, including works by Picasso.
Between 2005 and 2008, the museum restored the spiral's exterior, repairing cracks in the concrete and stripping away many layers of old paint.
In 2019, the Guggenheim was added to the World Heritage List, along with seven other buildings by Wright, the first modern architecture in the United States to be honored that way.
So the building that critics once compared to a washing machine now sits on the same list as the Taj Mahal.
You heard that Carnegie devoted himself to giving his fortune away.
The gift people remember most is libraries.
As a boy near Pittsburgh, Carnegie worked long hours and had no money for books.
A local man, Colonel James Anderson, opened his private library of a few hundred books to working boys on Saturdays, and young Andrew borrowed a book each week.
He never forgot it.

Starting in the 1880s, Carnegie paid for public library buildings across America and around the English-speaking world, more than twenty-five hundred in all, about seventeen hundred of them in the United States.
His usual bargain was that he paid for the building, and the town provided the land and promised to stock and run it.
In 1901, he made that offer to New York City on a grand scale: five point two million dollars for sixty-five branch libraries.

The city hired a handful of leading architectural firms, among them McKim, Mead and White and Carrère and Hastings, to design them in a shared, dignified style, so a Carnegie branch is easy to spot in any neighborhood.
Most still stand, and many are still in use, recognizable by their classical fronts and tall windows.
One of the first to open, in 1902, is the Yorkville branch on East 79th Street, a short walk from the next stop.
Not everyone was grateful.
Some towns turned his money down, and some workers said they would rather have had better wages than libraries with Carnegie's name on them.
But generations of immigrant children learned English, and much else, at those reading tables.
You heard that the design museum in this house was founded by three granddaughters of Peter Cooper.
Two of them, Sarah and Eleanor Hewitt, were its driving force.

Their father was Abram Hewitt, an iron manufacturer who served as mayor of New York in the late 1880s, and their grandfather Peter Cooper had founded Cooper Union, the free college you may have heard about on the East Village tour.
Their family's country home, Ringwood Manor in northern New Jersey, is now a state park.
The sisters, who never married, traveled in Europe and admired its museums of decorative arts, where designers and students could study real objects up close.
In 1897, they opened their own museum, in their grandfather's building downtown.
They collected relentlessly: textiles and lace, wallpapers and drawings, furniture and metalwork, anything that could teach a designer how things had been made and decorated over the centuries.
Today the collection numbers more than two hundred thousand objects.
Their museum was meant to be a working library of objects, not a treasure house.
The museum outlived them.
In the 1960s, Cooper Union decided it could no longer afford it, and designers and supporters rallied to save it.
The Smithsonian Institution took over the collection, and in 1976 it reopened here, in Carnegie's mansion.
So the steel king's house holds a museum started by two determined sisters.
It's also a fitting home for design: as you heard, Carnegie's house was itself a showcase of the newest technology of its day.
You heard that the Jewish Museum, a block north, was the mansion of the banker Felix Warburg.
The family behind it shaped finance and philanthropy on two continents.
Felix Warburg came from a banking family in Hamburg, Germany.
In New York he married Frieda Schiff, the daughter of Jacob Schiff, the head of the investment bank Kuhn, Loeb, and one of the most powerful bankers in America.
Schiff's money also helped Lillian Wald open the Henry Street Settlement, as you may have heard on the Lower East Side.
And in 1904, when Japan went to war with Russia, Schiff helped Japan raise enormous loans, in part to strike at the czar, whose government persecuted Russian Jews.
Japan won, and its emperor honored him.
Felix joined his father-in-law's firm and became one of the great philanthropists of his time.

His brother Paul, also a banker in New York, was one of the men at the secret Jekyll Island meeting you may have heard about in the Financial District, and became one of the chief architects of the Federal Reserve.
In 1914, Felix became the first chairman of the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, which sent aid to Jews suffering in Europe and beyond.

The house was designed by C. P. H. Gilbert, who built mansions for many of the era's richest families, in the style of a French Gothic château, reportedly to the dismay of Jacob Schiff, who thought it too showy.
After Felix died in 1937, Frieda gave it to the Jewish Theological Seminary, and in 1947 it opened as the Jewish Museum.
Look at the carved stonework: a château built by a German Jewish banker on Fifth Avenue, now devoted to Jewish art and culture.
You heard that the pro-Nazi German American Bund held rallies here on 86th Street.
Its biggest night in New York came not here but at Madison Square Garden, on February 20, 1939.
About twenty thousand people filled the arena.
The Bund billed the event as a celebration of George Washington's birthday, and a giant portrait of Washington hung above the stage, flanked by swastika banners.
Uniformed Bund guards lined the aisles.
Speakers attacked Jews and mocked President Roosevelt, to roars of approval.
Outside, thousands of counter-protesters gathered, and a huge force of police kept the two sides apart.
During the speech by Fritz Kuhn, the Bund's leader, a young Jewish plumber's helper from Brooklyn named Isadore Greenbaum rushed the stage.
Bund guards tackled him and beat him, tearing at his clothes as the crowd laughed and cheered, until police pulled him away.
He was arrested and fined.
Film of the rally sat largely forgotten for decades, until the filmmaker Marshall Curry turned it into a short documentary, A Night at the Garden, in 2017.
It's only a few minutes long, and many who see it are shocked that it happened in New York at all.
Later that year, as you heard, Kuhn was convicted of embezzling the Bund's money, and the movement collapsed.
But for one night, twenty thousand people cheered for it in the middle of Manhattan, and one man from Brooklyn tried to stop them.
Walk a few blocks northwest of here, to East 93rd Street between Lexington and Third Avenues.
In a modest walk-up at Number 179, the Marx Brothers grew up.
There were five of them: Chico, Harpo, Groucho, Gummo, and Zeppo, born Leonard, Adolph, Julius, Milton, and Herbert.
Their father, Sam, was a tailor from Alsace, famously not a very good one.
The real force in the family was their mother, Minnie, who was determined to put her boys on the stage.
Show business ran in her family: her brother, Al Shean, was a vaudeville star, half of the comedy team Gallagher and Shean.
The family lived here around the turn of the twentieth century, when Yorkville was crowded with immigrant families like theirs.
Harpo left school early and taught himself the harp, in his own unorthodox way.
Chico played piano in saloons and hustled at pool.
Groucho had wanted to be a doctor, but his mother had other plans.
Their famous nicknames reportedly came from a fellow vaudevillian, during a card game in the 1910s.

Minnie managed them through years of small-time vaudeville, until their act grew into the anarchic, fast-talking comedy that took Broadway by storm in the 1920s, and then Hollywood, with films like Animal Crackers and Duck Soup.
The building still stands.
It's an ordinary tenement on an ordinary block, which is exactly the point: some of the most famous comedians in American history learned their timing in rooms like these.
You heard that Yorkville was home to Czechs, Slovaks, and Hungarians as well as Germans.
A short walk south, at 321 East 73rd Street, the Czech community left a monument.
Many of the Czech immigrants who settled here worked in the cigar trade, rolling tobacco in factories and in their own tenement apartments.
The Bohemian National Hall was built in the 1890s by Czech immigrants, designed by the architect William C. Frohne in a Renaissance Revival style.
It was a social center for the whole community, with a ballroom, meeting rooms, and a restaurant, and for decades it hosted dances, plays, and lectures.
As the Czech community moved away, the building declined.
In 2001, the old Czech benevolent association that owned it transferred it to the Czech Republic, which restored it.
Today it houses the Czech consulate and a Czech cultural center, along with the original association, and a society devoted to the composer Antonín Dvořák.
Dvořák lived in New York in the 1890s, as director of a music conservatory, and it was here that he wrote his Symphony From the New World.
It had its premiere at Carnegie Hall in December 1893, and became one of the most loved symphonies ever written.
The hall is a city landmark now, a reminder that Yorkville's immigrant story was never only German.
You heard that Archibald Gracie built his country house here in 1799.
He wasn't the first to build on this point, and the first house here ended in gunfire.
Around 1770, a merchant named Jacob Walton, a Loyalist, built a house on the site.
When the Revolution began, Washington's army took over the property, and American troops built a fort on the lawn, with cannons facing the East River and Hell Gate.
On September 8, 1776, British guns across the water bombarded it, destroying the ramparts and the Walton house.
In 1798, Gracie bought the land from Walton's heirs.
The Gracie name lived on in an unexpected way.
Archibald Gracie's great-grandson, Colonel Archibald Gracie the Fourth, was a passenger on the Titanic in April 1912.
He helped load women and children into the lifeboats, went down with the ship, and survived by clinging to an overturned collapsible boat in the freezing water.
He wrote a book about the disaster, The Truth About the Titanic, but he never recovered his health, and died that December, before it was published.
The house his great-grandfather built is now one of the oldest surviving wooden houses in Manhattan.
So the house you see stands on the ruins of a Revolutionary battery, and carries the name of a family whose story runs from a merchant's country estate to the deck of the Titanic.
You heard that Carl Schurz fled Germany after the failed revolutions of 1848.
His escape, and what he did next, reads like an adventure novel.
As a student at the University of Bonn, Schurz joined the revolutionary movement along with his professor and mentor, Gottfried Kinkel.
When the revolution was crushed in 1849, Schurz escaped from the besieged fortress of Rastatt through a sewer and fled to Switzerland.
Kinkel was captured and sentenced to life in prison.

In November 1850, Schurz, just twenty-one, slipped back into Germany under a false name, bribed a guard at Spandau prison outside Berlin, and helped Kinkel climb out of the building at night and down a rope.
The two raced to the coast and escaped by ship to Britain.
The rescue made Schurz famous across Europe.
In London he married Margarethe Meyer, and the couple sailed for America.
In Watertown, Wisconsin, in 1856, Margarethe opened what's considered the first kindergarten in the United States, for German-speaking children.
Carl rose quickly too: a campaigner for Lincoln, minister to Spain, a Union general, a senator, a cabinet secretary, and a crusading reformer.
In 1910, the city renamed this park for him.
The dignified statesman it honors was, as a young man, a jailbreaker.
His formal monument, by Karl Bitter, the sculptor you may remember from the fountain at the Plaza, stands across town on Morningside Drive at 116th Street.
You heard that Hell Gate's rocks wrecked hundreds of ships.
One of those wrecks has drawn treasure hunters for more than two centuries.
In 1780, during the Revolutionary War, the British frigate Hussar tried to pass through Hell Gate.
It struck a hidden rock called Pot Rock and sank.
According to the legend, the ship was carrying the British Army's payroll in gold coin, by some accounts worth around two million pounds.
The British, the story goes, insisted there was little of value aboard.
Hardly anyone believed them.
For generations, salvagers came looking, with divers in primitive suits, diving bells, and dredges, and later with new underwater machines.
The gold, if it was ever there, has never been found.
Was it really there?
No one knows for sure.
The rocks of Hell Gate were blasted away long ago, and if anything is left of the Hussar, it lies somewhere in the mud of the East River.
So as you watch the water churning past the promenade, there may or may not be a king's fortune somewhere beneath it.
That's what makes it a good legend.
The promenade you're standing on, built over the highway along the river, has a name: the John Finley Walk.
Finley was the president of City College and later an editor at The New York Times, and a great lover of walking the city.
The walk was dedicated in 1942, two years after his death.
Now look for a small bronze statue of Peter Pan in one of the park's quiet gardens.
It was made in 1928 by the sculptor Charles Andrew Hafner, for the lobby of the Paramount Theater in Times Square, when that was one of the grandest movie palaces in the world.
Peter Pan himself was still fairly new then, by stage standards: the play had opened on Broadway in 1905, with Maude Adams as the boy who wouldn't grow up.
At the Paramount, in the 1940s, crowds of screaming teenagers lined up around the block to see a young Frank Sinatra.
The statue came to this park in 1975.
In 1999, vandals pried it loose and threw it into the East River.
It was recovered and put back on its pedestal, this time more securely.
There's a good match between the two.
A man who loved to walk, and a boy who never grew up, side by side above the river.
Turn toward the park.

At the corner entrance stands a tall stone pylon crowned by a gilded group: a woman riding in a chariot shaped like a seashell, pulled by three hippocamps, the half horse, half fish creatures of Greek myth.
This is the USS Maine National Monument, and its story is as political as the statue in the middle of the circle.
On the night of February 15th, 1898, the American battleship Maine exploded in the harbor of Havana, in Spanish-ruled Cuba.
More than two hundred and fifty men died.
Nobody knew what had caused the blast, but William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal blamed Spain at once, and its rival, Joseph Pulitzer's World, joined in.
Remember the Maine became a slogan, and two months later the United States was at war with Spain.
It's the war whose most famous battle may have given San Juan Hill, your next stop, its name.
Hearst's paper also started the collection for a memorial, and it took fifteen years to finish.
The monument was dedicated in 1913.
The architect was Harold Van Buren Magonigle, and the sculptor was Attilio Piccirilli, of the Bronx family of stone carvers who carved the lions at the Public Library on the Midtown tour.
The gilded figure at the top is Columbia Triumphant, and her bronze is said to come partly from metal salvaged from the Maine itself.
If you took the Civic Center tour, you may remember Audrey Munson, the model who is said to have posed for her.
So what did sink the Maine?
A navy inquiry in 1898 blamed a mine.
In 1976, a study led by Admiral Hyman Rickover concluded that the likeliest cause was a fire smoldering in a coal bunker, which set off the ship's own ammunition.
Historians are still arguing about it.
You heard that Italian immigrants faced intense discrimination when the Columbus statue went up.
One event, the year before it was unveiled, shows just how intense.
In October 1890, the police chief of New Orleans, David Hennessy, was shot near his home and died the next day.
He's said to have blamed Italians, and the police rounded up more than a hundred Italian immigrants.
Nineteen men were indicted.
In March 1891, a jury acquitted some of them and could not reach a verdict on others.
The next morning, a crowd of thousands, led by some of the city's most prominent men, broke into the parish prison and killed eleven Italian prisoners, shooting most of them and hanging two.
It's often called the largest single lynching in American history.
Italy recalled its ambassador, and for a time there was talk of war.
In the end, the United States paid Italy an indemnity of twenty five thousand dollars.
And in 1892, President Benjamin Harrison proclaimed a national celebration of the four hundredth anniversary of Columbus's voyage, which many historians see as a gesture toward Italian Americans.
New York held days of parades that October, and this statue was unveiled in the middle of them.
Columbus Day became a national holiday under Franklin Roosevelt in the 1930s.
And in 2019, the mayor of New Orleans formally apologized to Italian Americans for the lynching.

So when you hear the arguments about this statue, remember that it carries two histories at once: the Indigenous people Columbus harmed, and the immigrants who put him up here to say that they belonged.
Look up the column.
Bronze ships' prows jut from its sides, for the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María, and near its foot, a winged marble figure leans over a globe, as if working out the route.
Columbus himself stands at the very top, far above the traffic, too high for anyone on the ground to see his face.
Except for a few weeks in 2012.
That fall, the Japanese artist Tatzu Nishi, working with the Public Art Fund, wrapped the top of the monument in scaffolding and built a living room around the statue.

Visitors with free timed tickets climbed a long staircase up the scaffolding and stepped into a furnished apartment, with sofas, lamps, a television, and wallpaper Nishi designed, patterned with images from American popular culture.
In the middle of the room, standing on the coffee table, was Columbus.
The piece was called Discovering Columbus, and for the first time since 1892, people could look him in the eye.
Nishi has built rooms like this around monuments in other cities, and the idea is always the same: something distant and official becomes, for a moment, a very large houseguest.
The circle around you was remade too, in the 2000s, with fountains, benches and plantings.
For most of the twentieth century, it was a roaring traffic circle that people on foot crossed at their peril.
You heard that the Metropolitan Opera House anchors this plaza.
The company is much older than its home.
It was founded in 1883 by new money, families like the Vanderbilts, who couldn't get boxes at the old Academy of Music on 14th Street, where old New York held the best seats.
So they built their own opera house, on Broadway at 39th Street, with a ring of private boxes that came to be called the Diamond Horseshoe.
Critics called the building the yellow brick brewery, but for more than eighty years it was the center of opera in America.
The new house here opened on September 16th, 1966, with an opera written for the night: Samuel Barber's Antony and Cleopatra, starring the soprano Leontyne Price.
Price had grown up in Laurel, Mississippi, and when she made her Met debut in 1961, the audience reportedly applauded for more than forty minutes.
Now she was opening the company's new home.
The production, staged by the Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, was colossal, with a huge cast and a giant revolving stage that broke down in rehearsal.
On the night, the critics praised Price and panned almost everything else.
Barber was devastated, and years later he revised the opera into a leaner version.
The old house on 39th Street was torn down in 1967, despite protests.
Look through the Met's five arched windows.
The two huge paintings inside are by Marc Chagall, each about three stories tall: The Triumph of Music, mostly in reds, and The Sources of Music, mostly in yellows.
Look for the floating musicians, the dancers, the angels and the birds.
Chagall was nearly eighty when he painted them.
In 2009, in the depths of the recession, the Met pledged them as collateral for a loan.
Then look up at the chandeliers, spiky crystal globes like bursting stars.
They were a gift from the government of Austria, in thanks for American help in rebuilding the country after the Second World War, and they were made in Vienna by the glassmakers Lobmeyr.
If you go to a performance, watch the ones in the auditorium.
Just before the music starts, they rise slowly to the ceiling as the lights dim, so that everyone in the upper tiers can see the stage.
It's one of the loveliest little rituals in New York.
You heard that the New York Philharmonic plays in David Geffen Hall, to your right.
It's the hall's third name, and its third interior.
It opened in 1962 as Philharmonic Hall, the first building at Lincoln Center to be finished, designed by Max Abramovitz.
Leonard Bernstein conducted the opening concert, broadcast live on television, with the First Lady, Jacqueline Kennedy, in the audience.
Almost at once, musicians and critics complained about the sound.
The players couldn't hear one another, and the bass seemed to vanish.
For years, engineers fiddled with panels and ceilings.
In 1973, the audio pioneer Avery Fisher, who had made a fortune selling high fidelity equipment, gave the hall about ten million dollars, and it was renamed for him.
In 1976 the whole interior was torn out and rebuilt, with the architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee and the acoustician Cyril Harris.
It was better, but it never won many hearts.
In 2015, the entertainment mogul David Geffen gave a hundred million dollars, and Fisher's family was paid fifteen million to give up the name.
The hall was rebuilt once more and reopened in October 2022, with the stage pushed forward and the seats wrapping around the orchestra.
Among the music written for the reopening was a piece by the trumpeter Etienne Charles called San Juan Hill: A New York Story, a portrait of the neighborhood that was cleared to build this place.
You heard that thousands of families were displaced.
The estimates are startling.

The Lincoln Square project cleared about eighteen blocks, and historians put the number of families who lost their homes at about seven thousand, most of them Black, Puerto Rican or from the Caribbean, along with some eight hundred businesses.
The Housing Authority moved many of the families into public housing elsewhere, and a large share ended up in Brownsville, in Brooklyn, far from the jobs and churches they had known.
The neighborhood didn't go quietly.

Residents and shopkeepers took the city to court, arguing, among other things, that public power was being used to clear land for private institutions, including a Catholic university, Fordham, which got a campus just north of here.
The courts let the project go ahead.
One piece of the old neighborhood's housing survived.
The Amsterdam Houses, public housing finished in the late 1940s, still stand just west of Amsterdam Avenue, between 61st and 64th Streets.
And the memory is coming back.
In 2024, the filmmaker Stanley Nelson's documentary San Juan Hill: Manhattan's Lost Neighborhood had its premiere here, at the institution that replaced it.
You heard that the Dakota was built by Edward Clark, the head of the Singer company.
If you took the SoHo and Tribeca tour, you met Isaac Singer, the inventor with several families at once.
Clark was his opposite, a careful lawyer from upstate New York who took a share of the business in return for his legal work, and ended up running it.
Clark's great idea was about money, not machinery.
A sewing machine cost more than most families could pay at once, so in the 1850s, Clark began letting customers buy one with a small payment down and the rest in installments.
It's often called one of the first installment plans in American selling.
Sales soared, and Singer became one of the first great American multinational companies, with factories in Scotland and agents around the world.
Clark died in 1882, two years before the Dakota opened, so he never saw it finished.
But the family's money went on to shape American culture in unexpected places.
One grandson, Stephen Clark, founded the National Baseball Hall of Fame, which opened in 1939 in Cooperstown, the upstate village where the family had long kept a home.
Another, Sterling Clark, collected French paintings, especially Renoirs, and founded the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts.
So there's a little sewing machine money behind Cooperstown's plaques and the Clark's galleries.
Before you move on, look near the top of the arched entrance on 72nd Street for a carved stone head of a Native American.
Whatever the true origin of the building's name, Clark clearly enjoyed it.
You heard that Leonard Bernstein lived here.
He spent the last years of his life in the Dakota, and of all its famous residents, none was more closely tied to the music of the West Side.
If you took the Fifth Avenue tour, you heard that as a young man he lived in a studio above Carnegie Hall.
Bernstein became famous overnight in November 1943, when he was a twenty five year old assistant conductor of the New York Philharmonic.
The guest conductor, Bruno Walter, fell ill, and Bernstein stepped in on a few hours' notice, with no rehearsal, for a concert broadcast across the country.
The next day, he was on the front page of the New York Times.
In 1957 came West Side Story.
The idea had begun years earlier as East Side Story, about a Jewish girl and a Catholic boy on the Lower East Side.
By the time it reached Broadway, the story had moved to the West Side, with Puerto Rican and white gangs, in streets like the ones you heard about at Lincoln Center.

The next year, Bernstein became music director of the Philharmonic, the first American-born conductor to hold the job, and on television, his Young People's Concerts taught millions of children how to listen.
Bernstein died in his apartment here in October 1990.
As his funeral procession left the Dakota and made its way through the streets, it's said that construction workers along the route took off their hard hats, waved, and called out, Goodbye, Lenny.
You heard that the twin towers of Central Park West make one of the city's best known skylines.
They're there because of a law.
For decades, the rules had capped how tall an apartment house could be.

Then in 1929, New York State passed the Multiple Dwelling Law, which let apartment buildings on very large lots rise much higher, as long as the upper floors took the form of towers set back from the street.
On Central Park West, where whole blockfronts faced the park, several architects chose to build two towers instead of one, giving more apartments views, light and air.
The San Remo, at 74th Street, finished in 1930, was designed by Emery Roth.

Each of its towers is crowned with a small round temple of columns, modeled on an ancient monument in Athens, the Choragic Monument of Lysicrates, the same model as the Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument at the end of this walk.
Roth also designed the Eldorado, up at 90th Street.
The Majestic, at 71st Street, and the Century, at 62nd, were designed by Irwin Chanin, in sleek Art Deco, and both were finished in 1931.
The Century took its name from the Century Theatre, a grand and money-losing playhouse that stood on its site until 1930.
The Majestic had a famous tenant: the mob boss Frank Costello.
On the night of May 2nd, 1957, as Costello walked into the lobby, a gunman stepped out, said, This is for you, Frank, and fired at his head.
The bullet only grazed him.
A young enforcer named Vincent Gigante was tried for the shooting, but Costello told the court he couldn't identify the man, and Gigante was acquitted.
Costello soon stepped back from the rackets.
You heard that William Earl Dodge Stokes kept a farm on the Ansonia's roof.
That was among the milder things about him.
Stokes was a restless, combative millionaire who poured much of his inheritance into West Side real estate.
He also bred trotting horses on a stock farm in Kentucky, and he believed that what worked for horses would work for people.
In 1917 he published a book called The Right to Be Well Born, subtitled Horse Breeding in Its Relation to Eugenics, arguing for the now discredited idea of breeding better human beings.
His private life filled the newspapers.
Both of his marriages ended in bitter, public divorces.
And in June 1911, he went to an apartment a few blocks north of here, at Broadway and 80th Street, where two young women, Lillian Graham and Ethel Conrad, lived.
He said they had lured him there with an offer to return letters he had written to Graham.
They said they had acted in self-defense.
Either way, they fired at him, and he was hit in the legs.
The papers called them showgirls, and the case was a sensation for months.
That December, a jury acquitted them both, and by then they had already gone on the vaudeville stage as a double act.
Stokes recovered, and went on building, suing and quarreling until his death in 1926.
The Ansonia, which he meant as his monument, has outlasted the scandals by a century.
Step into the little park and look at the monument.
Verdi stands on top in white marble, and around the base sit four of his characters, each facing a different way.
There's Aida, the Ethiopian princess enslaved in Egypt.
There's Otello, the general destroyed by jealousy.
There's Leonora, the doomed heroine of La forza del destino, The Force of Destiny.
And there's Falstaff, the fat, boastful knight of his last opera, a comedy he wrote when he was nearly eighty.
The sculptor was Pasquale Civiletti, from Sicily, and the monument was unveiled in October 1906, five years after Verdi's death.

The money came from Italian New Yorkers, through a campaign led by the same man behind the Columbus statue at the start of this walk, Carlo Barsotti, the founder of the newspaper Il Progresso Italo-Americano.
Barsotti also championed statues of Giovanni da Verrazzano, in Battery Park, and of Dante, in the small park across the street from Lincoln Center.
Each one was a claim, in stone and bronze, that Italian culture belonged in New York.
Verdi was the obvious choice for a monument.
In Italy he was a national hero.

A famous story says that in the years before Italy was united, patriots scrawled Viva Verdi on walls as a code, the letters standing for Vittorio Emanuele, Re d'Italia, Victor Emmanuel, King of Italy.
Historians suspect the slogan owes more to later legend than to the time itself, but the story tells you what Verdi meant to the immigrants who paid for this statue.
The little park was the northern end of Sherman Square until 1921, when it was named for Verdi.
It's now one of the city's scenic landmarks, a rare honor for a patch of ground this small.
You heard that this square was once called Needle Park.
The name came from the street, and so did the film.
In 1965, Life magazine ran a photo essay by Bill Eppridge about a young couple addicted to heroin, who spent their days around these few blocks of Broadway.
The writer James Mills, who reported the story, turned it into a book, The Panic in Needle Park.
The nickname covered both little triangles at this intersection, Verdi Square and Sherman Square, just to the south.
The 1971 film was directed by Jerry Schatzberg and written by Joan Didion and her husband, John Gregory Dunne, and much of it was shot on these streets.
Kitty Winn won the best actress prize at the Cannes Film Festival for playing the young woman.
She played Helen, a young woman who drifts into the life, and her costar, as Bobby, a small-time dealer, was a little-known actor named Al Pacino, in his first leading role.
A year later, he was Michael Corleone in The Godfather.
The film came out as the city's heroin crisis was at its worst.
In those years, upper Broadway was lined with cheap single room occupancy hotels, and many of the grand old buildings around you had fallen on hard times.
The neighborhood's turnaround came slowly, through the 1980s and 1990s, and today the old days are hard to picture.
But West Siders who lived through them still remember the park by its old name.
You heard about the Roosevelt statue that was removed from the front steps.
The museum's own history holds a harder story, about a boy named Minik.

In 1897, the explorer Robert Peary came back from northern Greenland with an enormous iron meteorite, which you can still see in the museum, and with six Inuit people, brought to New York partly so the museum's scientists could study them.
Among them were a man named Qisuk and his son, Minik, who was about seven.
They were lodged at the museum, and within months most of them were sick.
By the spring of 1898, four had died, including Qisuk.
The museum staged a funeral for the boy's sake.
Minik watched a coffin being buried on the grounds, not knowing it held no body.
His father's remains had been kept for study, and the skeleton went into the museum's collection.
Minik was taken in by the museum's building superintendent, William Wallace, and grew up in New York as Minik Wallace.
Years later, newspapers revealed that Qisuk's skeleton was at the museum, and Minik begged for his father's body.
The museum refused.
Minik went home to Greenland, came back to the United States, and died in the flu pandemic of 1918, while working at a lumber camp in New Hampshire.
Only in 1993, after years of pressure, did the museum send the remains of Qisuk and the three others back to Greenland, where they were finally buried.
The dioramas you heard about owe the most to one man, Carl Akeley, a farm boy from upstate New York who reinvented taxidermy.
Older taxidermists stuffed skins with straw and rags.
Akeley sculpted the animal's body, muscle by muscle, made a light form from the sculpture, and stretched the skin over it, so the animals looked alive.
Early in his career, he mounted P. T. Barnum's famous elephant, Jumbo, after it was killed by a train in 1885.
He was no armchair naturalist.
In Somaliland in 1896, a wounded leopard sprang at him, and he killed it with his bare hands.
In 1921, Akeley went to the volcanoes of central Africa to collect mountain gorillas for the museum, and watching them changed him.
He came home convinced they had to be protected, and he persuaded King Albert of Belgium to set aside their mountains.
Albert National Park, created in 1925, was the first national park in Africa.
Akeley died there in 1926, on his next expedition, and he's buried on the slopes of Mount Mikeno, in what's now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
His wife, Mary Jobe Akeley, carried on his work.
The great hall that bears his name, with its herd of elephants in the center, opened in 1936.
Two of the museum's greatest finds came from its own fossil hunters, and one came with a surprise ending.
Barnum Brown, reportedly named for the showman P. T. Barnum, was the museum's star collector.
In 1902, in the Hell Creek badlands of Montana, he found the first partial skeleton of a giant meat eater that the museum's leading paleontologist, Henry Fairfield Osborn, named Tyrannosaurus rex.
In 1908, Brown found a far more complete one, and that's the skeleton on display today.
In 1941, the museum sold the first one to the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, reportedly in part from fear that New York might be bombed in the war.
In the 1920s, the explorer Roy Chapman Andrews led the museum's expeditions into the Gobi Desert of Mongolia, in a convoy of cars supplied by camel caravans.
In 1923, at a place called the Flaming Cliffs, his team found nests of fossil eggs, the first dinosaur eggs recognized by science.
They were thought to belong to a plant eater called Protoceratops.
Nearby lay a toothless skeleton, which Osborn named Oviraptor, the egg seizer, assuming it had died raiding the nest.
Seventy years later, in 1993, a museum expedition found a tiny embryo inside one of the same kind of eggs.
It was an oviraptor.
Later finds showed oviraptor relatives sitting on their nests with their arms spread, like brooding birds.
The egg thief had been a parent all along.
On the night of October 29th, 1964, three young men from Florida climbed into the museum through a window that had been left open, and made their way into the hall of gems.
The alarm on the case holding the most famous stone, the Star of India, had a dead battery.
The ringleader was Jack Murphy, a surfer known as Murph the Surf.

They took about two dozen gems, among them the Star of India, a blue star sapphire of more than five hundred and sixty carats, about the size of a golf ball, along with the DeLong Star Ruby and the Eagle Diamond.
The police caught up with them within days.
In January 1965, the Star of India and most of the other stones turned up in a locker at a Miami bus station.
The DeLong ruby came back later, after a ransom of twenty five thousand dollars was paid.
The Eagle Diamond was never found.
The Star of India, a gift to the museum from J. P. Morgan, is back on display, under better security.
You heard that the Zabar family still runs the store.
Louis Zabar died in 1950, at only forty nine, and his son Saul, in his early twenties, took over, and his brother Stanley later joined him.
Their youngest brother, Eli, would go his own way and build a food business of his own on the East Side.
The man who made Zabar's famous for its prices was Murray Klein, a former employee who came back as a partner around 1960 and stayed for more than thirty years.
Klein loved a price war.
In the 1970s, he picked a fight with Cuisinart by selling its new food processors at a deep discount.
His most famous battle came in the holiday season of 1983, against Macy's.
It started with Pommery mustard, moved on to Lindt chocolate, and ended with Beluga caviar.
Macy's put fourteen ounces of Beluga on sale for one hundred and forty nine dollars.
Klein cut Zabar's price to one hundred and nineteen, selling at a loss rather than lose.
The papers called it the caviar war, and the Zabars always said they won.
Klein retired in 1994.
Saul Zabar became a legend in his own right as the store's master of smoked fish, and the bright orange bags still carry the family name.
As you may have heard on the Lower East Side tour, Isaac Bashevis Singer's stories first appeared in Yiddish, in the Forward.
For most of his American life, though, he was an Upper West Sider.
Singer was born in Poland and came to New York in 1935, following his older brother, the novelist Israel Joshua Singer.
He kept writing in Yiddish all his life, even as the number of its readers shrank, and he found a far larger audience in English translation, one of the first by the novelist Saul Bellow.
In 1965 he moved into the Belnord, the huge courtyard building that fills the block between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue at 86th Street, six blocks north of here, and he lived there for decades.
He was a vegetarian, and he ate in the neighborhood's dairy restaurants and cafeterias, which turn up in his fiction.
His story The Cafeteria is set in one on Broadway.
And he fed the pigeons on the Broadway median, a habit that found its way into his stories too.
In 1978 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the only writer in Yiddish ever to receive it.
In his Nobel lecture, he joked that he liked to write ghost stories, and nothing suits a ghost better than a dying language.
A few years later, his story Yentl became a film with Barbra Streisand, which Singer made no secret of disliking.
In 1990, the year before he died, the city named the stretch of West 86th Street between Broadway and Amsterdam Avenue Isaac Bashevis Singer Boulevard.
Look for the sign if you walk that way.
You heard that William Waldorf Astor built the Apthorp.
He borrowed its name from the neighborhood's colonial past.
Charles Ward Apthorp was a rich merchant who, in 1764, built a country house about a dozen blocks north of here, near today's Columbus Avenue and 91st Street.
It was known as Elmwood, after its trees, and a lane connected it to the Bloomingdale Road.
In the Revolution, Apthorp stayed loyal to the King.
In September 1776, after the defeat on Long Island, George Washington used the house briefly as his headquarters while the American army fell back.
According to one account, the British moved in within hours of his leaving.
A few years after Apthorp's death, in 1799, the house was sold to a wealthy Englishman named William Jauncey, and the lanes leading to it took his name.
Later in the 1800s, the old grounds became Elm Park, a picnic ground and beer garden.
On July 12th, 1870, Irish Protestants of the Orange Order held a picnic there to celebrate an old Protestant victory in Ireland, and it ended in a battle with Irish Catholic laborers.
Several people were killed, in the first of the city's two Orange Riots.
The house came down in the 1890s.
Astor's apartment house revived the name in 1908, when a whiff of old New York was a selling point.
Look at the freestanding mansion on the corner of 89th Street, facing the park.
This is the Isaac L. Rice Mansion, finished in 1903, one of only two freestanding mansions left on Riverside Drive.

Isaac Rice was a lawyer and entrepreneur who founded the Electric Boat Company, which built the Navy's first submarines, and he was such a devoted chess patron that an opening, the Rice Gambit, carries his name.
The more famous Rice, though, was his wife, Julia Barnett Rice.
She had earned a medical degree, though she never practiced, and she was convinced that noise was a danger to health.
All night, the tugboats on the Hudson blew their whistles outside her windows, many of them, she was sure, for no reason at all.
So she recruited students from Columbia to sit up and count.
Their tallies ran to thousands of blasts in a single night.
In 1906 she founded the Society for the Suppression of Unnecessary Noise.

In 1907, Congress passed a law against needless whistling by boats in the harbor, and the society went on to win quiet zones around the city's hospitals, and later its schools, with a children's branch in the public schools.
It was one of the first organized campaigns against noise in America.
Since 1954, the house has been a yeshiva, a Jewish school.
You heard that trains still run in a tunnel beneath this park.
After the last freight trains stopped using it, around 1980, the tunnel went dark, and homeless New Yorkers moved in.
They built shacks and even small houses along the tracks, lit by the shafts of daylight that fall through the grates in the park above you.

A graffiti artist named Chris Pape, who signed his work Freedom, used the long concrete walls as his canvas, painting enormous murals in those shafts of light, and the tunnel came to be known by his name.
In 1991, Amtrak began running passenger trains through again, bringing its trains from Albany straight into Penn Station, and the people living inside faced eviction.
A young Englishman named Marc Singer, who had lived among them, made a documentary about the community, Dark Days, shot in black and white with a crew drawn from the tunnel's own residents.
It came out in 2000 and won awards at the Sundance Film Festival.
By the time the last residents left, many had been helped into apartments with housing vouchers.
Amtrak trains still rumble beneath the park.
Stand near a grate long enough and you may hear one.
Four blocks north, at 93rd Street, Joan of Arc rides into battle in bronze, in full armor, raising her sword.
The sculptor, Anna Hyatt Huntington, was one of the finest animal sculptors in America.
She worked on her model in Paris, where it won an honorable mention at the Salon in 1910, and the statue was dedicated in December 1915, while France was fighting for its life in the First World War.
Look closely at the pedestal.

The committee behind the statue, which included Tiffany's famous gem expert, George Frederick Kunz, learned in 1912 that the tower in Rouen where Joan was imprisoned before she was burned at the stake was being cleared away.
They bought more than two hundred of its stone blocks, which crossed the Atlantic in 1914.
A fragment of the cathedral at Reims, where Joan saw her king crowned, is set into the base too.
It's often called the first statue in New York of a real woman, rather than a goddess or an allegory.
Look across the Hudson at the Palisades, the wall of cliffs running north along the New Jersey shore.

They were born underground about two hundred million years ago, when molten rock forced its way between layers of sandstone and shale and cooled slowly into a thick sheet of hard, dark stone called diabase.
As it cooled, it shrank and cracked into tall columns.
Over millions of years, the softer rock wore away, and the columns were left standing like a fence of logs.
That's the name: a palisade is a wall of upright stakes, like the one that gave Wall Street its name on the Financial District tour.
By the 1890s, quarries were blasting the cliffs apart for crushed stone.
The campaign to stop them was led by the women's clubs of New Jersey, and in 1900, New York and New Jersey created the Palisades Interstate Park Commission.
J. P. Morgan put up money to buy out the worst of the quarries.
Later, John D. Rockefeller Junior bought land along the clifftops and gave it to the park, partly to protect the view from the Cloisters, the museum he paid for in northern Manhattan.
So the view from this terrace is no accident.
It was saved.

At the foot of the park, where Manhattan Avenue meets Morningside Avenue at 114th Street, a bronze pair stands on a stone pedestal: George Washington and the Marquis de Lafayette, in uniform, clasping hands.
The sculptor was Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, who designed the Statue of Liberty, and if you took the Union Square tour, you may have met his Lafayette there.
This group is a twin.
The original was commissioned by Joseph Pulitzer, the publisher of the New York World, the same Pulitzer who raised the money for Liberty's pedestal, as a gift from Americans to France.
It was unveiled in Paris in 1895, in the Place des États-Unis.
New York's copy came five years later, in April 1900.
It was the gift of Charles Broadway Rouss, a merchant who had made his fortune selling dry goods on Broadway, and who reportedly loved the street so much that he took its name as his middle name.
Look at the two faces.
The friendship was real.
Lafayette arrived in America in 1777 as a nineteen year old volunteer, and Washington, who had no children of his own, treated him almost as a son.
Lafayette's own father had been killed in battle when the boy was not yet two.
Years later, Lafayette named his only son Georges Washington.
You heard that the 1968 protesters took over the president's office in Low Library.
Twenty years earlier, Columbia had a very different kind of president.
Look up to the top of the cliff, at Morningside Drive and 116th Street.
The house on that corner is the official home of Columbia's presidents, and from 1948 to the start of 1953, it was the home of General Dwight Eisenhower.
Eisenhower had led the Allied armies in Europe in the Second World War, and he was perhaps the most admired man in America.
Columbia's trustees offered him the presidency, and he took it.
He was an odd fit.
He was a soldier, not a scholar, and many professors never warmed to him, or to his friends among oilmen and businessmen.

A story often told on campus has the physicist Isidor Rabi, a Nobel Prize winner, correcting him when he spoke of the faculty as employees of the university: the faculty, Rabi said, are the university.
Still, Eisenhower left his mark.

In 1950 he founded the American Assembly, a forum where leaders from business, government and universities met to work through national problems, and he called it the most important step he took as Columbia's president.
Within months, President Truman called him back to Europe to command the new NATO forces, and Columbia gave him leave.
In 1952 he ran for president of the United States, and he won.
He resigned from Columbia the day before his inauguration.
Six years later, as president, he came back uptown to break ground for Lincoln Center, as you may have heard on the Upper West Side tour.
You heard that Columbia's plan for a gym in this park died in 1968.
Forty years later, the university looked north instead, across 125th Street, to Manhattanville, a valley of warehouses, garages and auto shops in West Harlem.
In the 2000s, Columbia set out to build a new campus there, on seventeen acres, in a project budgeted at more than six billion dollars.
Most owners sold.
A few refused, among them Nick Sprayregen, whose family's Tuck-It-Away storage warehouses stood on the site.
The state agreed to take their land by eminent domain, after declaring the area blighted, and the owners went to court.
In December 2009, a divided appeals court ruled for them.
In June 2010, the state's highest court unanimously reversed that ruling, and the United States Supreme Court declined to hear the case.

Columbia signed a community benefits agreement with local groups, promising about one hundred and fifty million dollars for West Harlem over the years, and it designed the new campus to be more open than the old one.
The first buildings, by the architect Renzo Piano, opened in 2017, with glass-walled ground floors meant to welcome the neighborhood in.
Some neighbors see Manhattanville as the gym fight ending better this time.
Others see the same story, told again.
Either way, the cliff you're standing beneath is no longer the only line between Columbia and Harlem.
Before Ralph Adams Cram turned this cathedral Gothic, it held a jewel in a very different style.

At the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago, Louis Comfort Tiffany showed off an entire chapel, a glittering Byzantine interior of mosaics, colored glass and carved stone, designed to show what his studios could do.
Crowds lined up to see it.
A wealthy widow, Celia Whipple Wallace, bought the chapel for fifty thousand dollars and gave it to this cathedral, which was just rising.
It was installed in the crypt, beneath the eastern end, and it was one of the first parts of the building to be used.
But when the design turned Gothic, the Byzantine glitter fell out of favor, and the chapel was left in the basement, neglected.
In 1916, Tiffany bought it back and moved it to Laurelton Hall, his estate on Long Island.
