Laurelton Hall burned in 1957, and pieces of the chapel ended up in storage and in packing crates.

They were finally gathered and reassembled at the Charles Hosmer Morse Museum of American Art in Winter Park, Florida, where the chapel opened to the public in 1999, for the first time since the Chicago fair.
So one of this cathedral's first treasures now glows about a thousand miles to the south.
If you're ever in central Florida, you can stand in the room New Yorkers once worshipped in, in the crypt of this cathedral.
You may have heard on the Financial District tour about Philippe Petit, the French high-wire artist who walked between the Twin Towers in 1974.
Petit has a second New York home: this cathedral.
Not long after the towers, Petit strung a wire inside the cathedral and walked high above the nave without permission.
The cathedral's dean, James Parks Morton, made him artist in residence on the spot, reportedly to keep the police from arresting him.
He has held the title for decades.
In September 1982, construction on the cathedral started up again after some forty years, and Petit opened the celebrations in his own way.
He walked a wire stretched from a building across Amsterdam Avenue to the cathedral's west front, about a hundred and fifty feet above the street, while the crowd watched from below.

He has walked inside the cathedral several times since, including in 1992, for the hundredth anniversary of the cornerstone, and in August 2024, at the age of seventy four, he performed here again, in a show marking fifty years since his walk between the towers.
Morton, his patron, ran the cathedral from 1972 until 1996, and filled it with artists, musicians, scientists and causes.
The Blessing of the Animals you heard about is part of the spirit he brought: a cathedral that belongs to the whole city, not just its Episcopalians.
The cathedral's vast nave has made it the city's stage for its biggest goodbyes.
On May 27th, 1974, Duke Ellington's funeral was held here.
More than twelve thousand people came, filling the nave and the streets outside, and Ella Fitzgerald sang.
If you heard about Ellington on the Fifth Avenue and Central Park tours, this is where his story in New York ended.
In May 1990, the memorial service for Jim Henson, the creator of the Muppets, filled the cathedral with more than five thousand mourners.
Henson had asked, it's said, that no one wear black.
Big Bird came, and sang It's Not Easy Being Green, Kermit's song, and many in the cathedral wept.
The writers are remembered here too.
Since 1984, the cathedral has kept an American Poets' Corner, modeled on the famous one in Westminster Abbey in London, where the names of great American writers are carved in stone.
The first, in 1984, included Walt Whitman and Emily Dickinson.
Look for it in a side bay of the nave, if the cathedral is open.
And look up as you leave the crossing, where the great central tower was meant to rise.
Instead there's a dome of Guastavino tile, the thin, fireproof tiles you may remember from Grand Central on the Midtown tour.
It was built in 1909 as a temporary covering, until the tower could be finished.
More than a century later, it's still there.
Long before the cathedral, these grounds belonged to an orphanage, and its building is still here.
On the cathedral grounds, look for a much older building in the Greek Revival style, with a portico of stone columns.
It was finished in 1843 as the Leake and Watts Orphan House, designed by Ithiel Town, and it's the oldest building on Morningside Heights.
The orphanage's double name hides a story.

As it's usually told, a wealthy New Yorker named John George Leake, who had no children, left his fortune to the son of a friend, Robert Watts, on the condition that the young man take the name Leake.
The heir died soon after, and his father, John Watts, used the inheritance, and money of his own, to found a home for orphans, carrying both families' names.
When the diocese bought the land for its cathedral, the orphanage moved north to Yonkers, where its successor still works with children today.
The old building stayed behind, with the cathedral rising around it.
You heard in the introduction to this walk that Washington's army won a small victory here in September 1776, at the Battle of Harlem Heights.
Here's how it went.
It was the morning of September 16th, the day after the British had landed at Kips Bay and sent the Americans fleeing north in disarray.
Washington sent a company of scouts, Knowlton's Rangers, under Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Knowlton, to probe the British lines.
They ran into British light infantry and fell back.
As the British came on, their buglers sounded the call a fox hunter blows when the fox is on the run, a deliberate insult.
One of Washington's officers wrote that nothing had ever stung him like it.
Washington set a trap: a feint from the front, while Knowlton's men circled around to hit the British from the side.
The flanking attack went in too early, and both Knowlton and Major Andrew Leitch were mortally wounded.
But the fight grew, and in a buckwheat field in the blocks where Barnard College now stands, up toward 120th Street, the Americans drove back the British regulars.
Then Washington called off his men before British reinforcements could arrive.
For an army that had only known retreat, it was a huge lift.
On the Broadway side of the campus, on the wall of Mathematics Hall, look for a bronze plaque placed in 1897 by the Sons of the Revolution, with figures of Knowlton and Leitch.
And one more connection: Knowlton's Rangers had included a young captain named Nathan Hale, who had set out on a spying mission a few days before the battle.
As you may have heard on the Financial District tour, the British hanged him six days after it.
Look across Broadway at the gates of Barnard College.
In the 1880s, Columbia would not admit women.
Its president, Frederick Barnard, argued for years that it should, and when he died in 1889, the trustees still said no.

That same year, a young New Yorker named Annie Nathan Meyer, who had been allowed to take Columbia's exams but not to attend its classes, raised the money to found a separate college for women, affiliated with Columbia, and named it for Barnard.
There was a twist in her politics: Meyer opposed giving women the vote, while her own sister, Maud Nathan, was a leading suffragist.
Barnard's most famous student of the 1920s came by way of Meyer's help.
Zora Neale Hurston arrived in 1925, the college's only Black student at the time.
She joked that she was Barnard's sacred black cow.
She studied anthropology with Franz Boas, the great Columbia professor, who sent her back to the South to collect the stories, songs and folk beliefs of Black communities.
That work became her book Mules and Men, and it fed the novels, like Their Eyes Were Watching God, that made her one of the great American writers.
She graduated in 1928, the first Black woman known to have graduated from Barnard.
Today Barnard is still an independent women's college, with its own faculty and president, but its students take classes across Broadway, and the gates stay open both ways.
As you may have heard on the Greenwich Village tour, the Beat writers made their name downtown in the 1950s.
They found each other up here, in the 1940s.
Jack Kerouac came to Columbia in 1940 on a football scholarship, broke his leg in his first season, and drifted away from the team and the college.
Allen Ginsberg arrived in 1943, a seventeen year old from New Jersey who planned to become a labor lawyer.
Through a charismatic student named Lucien Carr, they met each other, and an older friend of Carr's from Saint Louis, William Burroughs.
They spent long nights talking at the West End, a bar on Broadway near 114th Street.
In August 1944, the circle was shattered.
Carr killed David Kammerer, an older man who had followed him obsessively for years, in Riverside Park, and dumped the body in the Hudson.
Kerouac was arrested as a material witness for helping him get rid of evidence, and Carr pleaded guilty to manslaughter.
Kerouac and Burroughs wrote a novel about it, And the Hippos Were Boiled in Their Tanks, which wasn't published until 2008.
Ginsberg was later suspended for scrawling obscenities in the grime of his dorm window, but he came back and graduated in 1948.
Out of those years came the friendships, and the restlessness, that produced On the Road and Howl.
You heard that Fermi worked here on chain reactions.
To keep one going, you have to slow the neutrons down, and Fermi's material of choice was graphite, the stuff in pencil leads, in enormous quantities.
In 1941 and 1942, in Schermerhorn Hall, a few steps from here, his team stacked tons of graphite bricks and uranium into tall piles and measured how the neutrons multiplied.
The work was heavy and filthy, and the physicists weren't built for it.
So, as Fermi later told the story, the university hired members of the football team, strong young men who hauled the graphite around as if it were nothing.

In 1942 the work moved to Chicago, where Fermi's team built the first nuclear reactor in a squash court under the stands of the university's football stadium, and on December 2nd, 1942, achieved the first controlled chain reaction.
Columbia stayed in the bomb business.

A secret laboratory with a deliberately dull name, the Substitute Alloy Materials Laboratories, worked on separating the rare uranium 235 that a bomb needed from the far more common uranium 238, by pumping uranium gas through fine barriers.
It was led by Harold Urey, who had won a Nobel Prize for discovering heavy hydrogen right here at Columbia.
Some of the work went on in a former car dealership on Broadway at 133rd Street.
The method they developed was used in the giant K-25 plant at Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
One of the physicists in Columbia's secret wartime labs was a young woman from China, Chien-Shiung Wu.

She was born in 1912 near Shanghai, the daughter of a schoolmaster who started one of the first schools for girls in China, and she had come to America in 1936 to study at Berkeley, and she joined the project at Columbia in 1944, working on radiation detectors and on uranium separation.
She's said to have helped solve a problem that nearly shut down the great reactor at Hanford, in Washington State, where a byproduct, xenon, was soaking up neutrons.
She stayed at Columbia for the rest of her career.
In 1956, two young theorists, Tsung-Dao Lee of Columbia and Chen-Ning Yang, asked whether nature truly treats left and right the same, a principle physicists called parity.
Wu designed the experiment to find out, cooling radioactive cobalt to nearly absolute zero at a laboratory in Washington.
Early in 1957, she showed that parity is broken: in one of nature's fundamental forces, the universe can tell left from right.
Lee and Yang won the Nobel Prize that same year.
Wu did not, an omission many physicists still call one of the great injustices in the prize's history.
She was honored in other ways.
She became the first woman to lead the American Physical Society, and in 2021, she was put on a postage stamp.
Her colleagues called her the First Lady of Physics, a title she earned in these buildings.
Michael Pupin's most brilliant student was Edwin Howard Armstrong, a Columbia engineer who changed radio three times.
As a student, in 1912, he invented the regenerative circuit, which made faint radio signals loud enough to hear.
As an army officer in Paris in the First World War, he invented the superheterodyne receiver, the basis of almost every radio since.
And in the early 1930s, in the basement of Philosophy Hall, just across the campus, he invented FM radio, which cut through static and carried music with startling clarity.
His friend David Sarnoff, the head of RCA, watched the demonstrations and decided to put RCA's money into television instead.
So Armstrong built his own FM station, on the Palisades at Alpine, New Jersey, and spent years in court.
His tower still stands on those cliffs.
If you took the Upper West Side tour, you looked across the river at them from Riverside Park.
First he fought the inventor Lee de Forest over the regenerative circuit, and lost in the Supreme Court in 1934.
Then he fought RCA over FM.
In 1954, worn down by the fight, he died by suicide.
His widow, Marion, carried on the lawsuits, and over the next thirteen years she won them, one company at a time.
Philosophy Hall is now a National Historic Landmark, for the invention made in its basement, and FM radio is everywhere.
You heard that Harry Emerson Fosdick was forced out of his old pulpit.
This is the sermon that did it.
In May 1922, preaching as a Baptist guest at the First Presbyterian Church on Fifth Avenue in Greenwich Village, Fosdick asked a question: Shall the fundamentalists win?
He argued that Christians could accept evolution and modern scholarship about the Bible without losing their faith, and that the church had room for people who disagreed.
The sermon was printed and mailed to ministers across the country, with the costs paid by an admirer, John D. Rockefeller Junior.
Conservatives in the Presbyterian Church, with the support of William Jennings Bryan, pressed Fosdick to either join the denomination and accept its creed or leave.
In 1925, he left.
Rockefeller offered him the pulpit of his own church, Park Avenue Baptist.

Fosdick reportedly set conditions: the church would accept members without requiring baptism by immersion, it would be open to Christians of any denomination, and it would move away from the wealthy East Side.
Rockefeller agreed, and this church was the result, rising near the universities and within sight of Harlem.
For the church's dedication, Fosdick wrote a hymn, God of Grace and God of Glory, and it's still sung in churches around the world.
He preached here until 1946, and his radio sermons, on a national program called National Vespers, reached millions of listeners.
The connection to Rockefeller ran in the family: Fosdick's brother, Raymond, was one of Rockefeller's closest advisers and later the president of the Rockefeller Foundation.
You heard that Martin Luther King Junior spoke out against the Vietnam War from this pulpit.
He had been moving toward it for two years, and his advisers had warned him off.
It would anger President Johnson, who had just signed the great civil rights laws, and it could split the movement.
The event was organized by a group called Clergy and Laymen Concerned About Vietnam, and King began by quoting their own statement: A time comes when silence is betrayal.
Much of the text was drafted by a young historian and activist, Vincent Harding.
In it, King warned against what he called the giant triplets of racism, extreme materialism and militarism, and he called for a revolution of values.
The reaction was savage.
The New York Times published an editorial called Doctor King's Error.
The Washington Post said he had diminished his usefulness to his cause, to his country and to his people.
Life magazine called the speech demagogic slander that sounded like a script for Radio Hanoi.
The board of the NAACP voted against merging the civil rights and antiwar movements.
King didn't back down.
Eleven days later, he marched at the head of a vast antiwar protest from Central Park to the United Nations, as you may have heard on the Central Park South tour.
Today, the speech many papers condemned is studied as one of the most important he ever gave.
Just north of the church, between it and Grant's Tomb, is a small, quiet park called Sakura Park.
Sakura is Japanese for cherry blossom.
In 1912, the Japanese residents of New York gave the city a large gift of cherry trees, and on an April day that year, the city held a planting celebration here.
It was the same spring that Tokyo's famous gift of cherry trees was planted in Washington.
The little park, until then called Claremont Park, took its new name.
Look for the stone lantern, a gift from the city of Tokyo, dedicated in October 1960, with Japan's crown prince and princess, Akihito and Michiko, in attendance.
They later became emperor and empress.
In the southeast corner stands a bronze general, Daniel Butterfield, by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor of Mount Rushmore.
Butterfield's later career had a shadow: as a Treasury official in New York under President Grant, he was caught up in the Black Friday gold scandal of 1869.
But his lasting claim is musical.
In July 1862, in a Union camp in Virginia, he reworked an older bugle call into the tune we know as Taps, to signal lights out.
It spread through both armies and became the call played at military funerals across the country.
So in spring, walking from the church to the tomb, you pass through cherry blossoms, under the eyes of the man who gave America its saddest twenty four notes.
Grant died in July 1885, at a cottage on Mount McGregor in upstate New York, just days after finishing his memoirs.
New York gave him the largest funeral the city had ever seen.

On August 8th, a procession many miles long, with tens of thousands of marchers, carried his coffin, on a black-draped funeral car drawn by twenty four black horses, from City Hall up to Riverside Park, past crowds often estimated at more than a million people.
Look at who carried him.
Among the pallbearers were his old generals, William Tecumseh Sherman and Philip Sheridan, and two Confederate generals, Joseph Johnston and Simon Bolivar Buckner.
Buckner had been Grant's friend at West Point.
In 1854, when Grant left the army broke and far from home, Buckner lent him money to get back east.
In 1862, Buckner had to surrender Fort Donelson to Grant, who demanded unconditional surrender, the words that first made Grant famous.
And in the summer of 1885, Buckner came to Mount McGregor to sit with his dying friend.
As for Johnston, six years later he was a pallbearer again, at Sherman's funeral in New York.
He stood bareheaded in a cold rain out of respect for his old enemy, caught pneumonia, and died a few weeks later.
For twelve years, Grant's coffin rested in a temporary brick tomb near here, while New York struggled to raise the money for this one.
You heard about Grant the general and Grant the writer.
Grant the president was long remembered mainly for the scandals of his administration.
In recent decades, historians have looked again, largely because of what he did in the South.
After the Civil War, the Ku Klux Klan and groups like it waged a campaign of terror against freed Black Southerners and their white allies, whipping and murdering people to keep them from voting.
In 1870, under Grant, the Fifteenth Amendment, protecting the vote for Black men, was ratified, and the new Department of Justice was created.
Congress passed the Enforcement Acts and the Ku Klux Klan Act, and Grant signed them.
His attorney general, Amos Akerman, prosecuted hundreds of Klansmen.
In October 1871, Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine counties of South Carolina, and federal troops and marshals made mass arrests.
Within a year or so, the first Klan was broken.
It didn't last.
As the North lost interest and the violence returned, Reconstruction collapsed in the years after Grant left office.
But Frederick Douglass, who knew every president from Lincoln on, praised Grant as a steadfast friend of Black Americans.
Above the tomb's entrance, look for the words Let Us Have Peace.
It was the slogan of Grant's first campaign for president, in 1868.
Grant's wife, Julia Dent Grant, lies beside him in the crypt.
She grew up at White Haven, her family's plantation outside Saint Louis, where the Dents held people in slavery, and Grant married into that household in 1848.
Before the war, struggling as a farmer near Saint Louis, he came to own one enslaved man, William Jones.
In 1859, though Grant badly needed money, he freed him rather than sell him.
Julia was born with strabismus, a condition in which the eyes don't line up, and she was self-conscious about it all her life, which is why photographs usually show her in profile.
When she was First Lady, she considered an operation, but Grant, as the story goes, told her he had fallen in love with her as she was.
The memoirs he finished as he was dying left her comfortable.
She wrote her own memoirs too, the first by a former First Lady, but they weren't published until 1975.
She died in 1902 and was placed here beside him.
It's said that one reason Grant chose New York for his grave, rather than West Point, was that there, she could not have been buried at his side.
You heard that about ninety thousand people paid for this tomb.
Raising the money took twelve years, and newspapers in other cities mocked New York for being so slow, some suggesting the body be moved to Washington.
The Grant Monument Association was formed within days of Grant's death, with former President Chester Arthur at its head.

Its first secretary, from 1885 to 1892, was Richard Theodore Greener, the first Black graduate of Harvard, a lawyer, scholar, and political supporter of Grant, who did much of the work of the early campaign.

During Reconstruction, Greener had been the first Black professor at the University of South Carolina, and he later led the law school at Howard University and served as an American diplomat in Russia.
Now look for two trees near the tomb, inside a small enclosure with a plaque.
On his trip around the world in 1879, Grant met Li Hongzhang, the leading Chinese statesman of the day, and the two men became friends.
When Li visited New York in 1896, he came to pay his respects at Grant's temporary tomb.
And in May 1897, a ginkgo, a tree native to China, was planted near the tomb on Li's behalf, by China's former minister to the United States.
So among all the monuments in this neighborhood, one of the most personal is alive: a tree from one old statesman to another.
By the 1980s, this monument was in sorry shape, scrawled with graffiti, littered, and widely seen as unsafe after dark.
Around 1990, a Columbia undergraduate named Frank Scaturro began volunteering here with the National Park Service.
He documented the damage and wrote reports, and when he took his complaints public, the Park Service dismissed him as a volunteer, in 1993.
He didn't give up.
He revived the Grant Monument Association, the same group that had built the tomb, and invited Grant's descendants onto its board.
The association prepared a lawsuit to force the federal government to restore the site, and some of Grant's descendants even talked about moving the bodies elsewhere.
The New York Times ran an editorial backing him, under the title Dishonor for a Hero President.
It worked.
The money was found, and the tomb was cleaned and restored in time for its hundredth anniversary, in April 1997.
The National Park Service still runs it, and visiting is free.
Scaturro went on to become a lawyer, and he wrote a book arguing that Grant's presidency deserved far more respect than it had been given.
So the next time someone asks you who's buried in Grant's Tomb, you can tell them about the student who made sure it was worth visiting.
You heard that Garvey filled Harlem's streets with parades.
The greatest came in August 1920, when the UNIA opened its first International Convention of the Negro Peoples of the World.
Delegates came from across the United States, the Caribbean, Central America and Africa.
They marched through Harlem in uniform, with bands and banners, and that night about twenty-five thousand people packed the old Madison Square Garden to hear Garvey speak.
Over the following weeks, the convention adopted a Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World, protesting lynching, segregation and colonial rule.
It named Garvey Provisional President of Africa, a continent he never set foot on.
And it chose colors for the movement: red, black and green.
Look around Harlem, on flags, murals and vendors' tables, and you'll still see them.
That flag is Garvey's, known today as the Pan-African flag.
Not every Black leader admired him.
A socialist magazine edited by A. Philip Randolph ran a campaign called Garvey Must Go.
W. E. B. Du Bois, who later lived on Sugar Hill, at the end of this walk, wrote in 1924 that Garvey was either a lunatic or a traitor.
Garvey answered with insults of his own, and the feud divided Harlem for years.
After his deportation, Garvey kept organizing, first from Jamaica and then from London, but the movement never regained its size.
He died in London in 1940.
As the story is usually told, newspapers had already printed his obituary by mistake, describing him as broke and forgotten, and reading it brought on the stroke that killed him.
He was not forgotten.
In 1964, his body was brought home to Jamaica, which named him its first National Hero.
And in January 2025, President Joe Biden granted Marcus Garvey a posthumous pardon, more than a century after his conviction.
Look up at the fire watchtower again.
It's often credited to James Bogardus, the cast iron pioneer you may have heard about in SoHo.
But in 1855, when the city held a competition for a bell tower on this hill, the winning design came from a little-known German-born engineer named Julius Kroehl.
Kroehl's real ambitions lay underwater.
During the Civil War, in Brooklyn, he began building an iron submarine called the Sub Marine Explorer, about thirty-six feet long, for a company that hoped to harvest pearl oysters.
Its crew could fill a chamber with compressed air, open hatches in the floor, and reach the sea bed while the craft rested on the bottom.
In 1866, it was taken apart, shipped to Panama, and put back together in the Pearl Islands, in the Pacific.
The dives worked, at first.
But in September 1867, Kroehl died in Panama, of what was recorded as a fever.
Some researchers now suspect decompression sickness, the bends, which nobody then understood.
When others took the submarine out again, they fell ill too, and it was left on a beach.
There it stayed, rusting between the tides.
Local legend had it that it was a Japanese submarine from the Second World War.
Then, in 2001, the maritime archaeologist James Delgado identified it as Kroehl's Explorer, one of the oldest submarines known to survive anywhere.
So the man behind this tower, built to watch the skies over Harlem for smoke, also built a machine to walk the bottom of the sea.
In the summer of 1969, while the world watched astronauts land on the moon, this park hosted one of the great music festivals of the decade.
Then the world forgot it.
The Harlem Cultural Festival was a series of free concerts, spread over six weekends, organized and hosted by a singer named Tony Lawrence.

The lineup was astonishing: a nineteen-year-old Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone, B. B. King, Gladys Knight and the Pips, Sly and the Family Stone, the Fifth Dimension, Hugh Masekela, Mongo Santamaría, and the gospel queen Mahalia Jackson, who shared the microphone with a young Mavis Staples to sing Precious Lord, Take My Hand.
By some counts, about three hundred thousand people came over the summer.
A television producer named Hal Tulchin filmed nearly all of it, and tried to sell it as the Black Woodstock.
Hardly anyone was interested.
The tapes sat in his basement for about fifty years.
In 2021, the drummer and producer Ahmir Questlove Thompson turned that footage into a documentary, Summer of Soul.
It won the Academy Award for best documentary feature, and a forgotten summer in Harlem became famous all over again.
Watch it, and you'll see this park packed with people in the summer heat.
In one scene, people in the crowd are asked what they think of the moon landing.
Several shrug.
The money, they say, would be better spent on the people of Harlem.
Look across 125th Street and a little to the east, to number 230.
For decades, this was Blumstein's, the biggest department store in Harlem.
You heard about the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work campaign.
Blumstein's was its most famous target.
In the summer of 1934, picketers marched outside, urging shoppers to stay away from a store that took Black customers' money but wouldn't hire Black salesclerks.
Blumstein's gave in and hired Black saleswomen, and the victory spread the campaign up and down the street.

Twenty-four years later, on a Saturday afternoon in September 1958, a young minister named Martin Luther King Junior sat at a table inside Blumstein's, signing copies of his first book, Stride Toward Freedom, about the bus boycott in Montgomery, Alabama.
A woman stepped up and asked whether he was Martin Luther King.
When he said he was, she plunged a steel letter opener into his chest.
King was rushed to Harlem Hospital, on Lenox Avenue, with the blade still in him.
Surgeons found its tip resting against his aorta, the body's main artery, and removed it with great care.
The papers reported that if he had so much as sneezed, he would have died.
His attacker, Izola Ware Curry, was found to be mentally ill and committed to a hospital.
King said he felt no ill will toward her.
Ten years later, in Memphis, on the night before he was killed, King remembered that day.
Many letters came to him in the hospital, he said, but the one he would never forget came from a ninth-grade girl at White Plains High School.
She wrote that she was so happy he hadn't sneezed.
Then he told the crowd all that he would have missed if he had.
The street outside now carries his name.
Twice in the twentieth century, a false rumor set 125th Street alight.
The first came on March 19th, 1935, at a Kress five-and-ten store on this street.
A sixteen-year-old Puerto Rican boy named Lino Rivera was caught slipping a penknife worth ten cents into his pocket.
Store workers grabbed him, there was a struggle, and the police took him out through the back and let him go.
But shoppers had seen the struggle, and word spread that the boy had been beaten to death.
When a hearse happened to pull up nearby, it seemed to prove it.
By nightfall, crowds were smashing store windows along 125th Street.
Three people died.
Mayor Fiorello La Guardia appointed a commission to find out why, with the sociologist E. Franklin Frazier leading its research.
Its answer was not the rumor, but years of discrimination in jobs, housing, relief and policing.
La Guardia never released the report, but the Amsterdam News, Harlem's newspaper, printed it.
Eight years later, in August 1943, in the lobby of the Hotel Braddock on 126th Street, a white police officer shot a Black soldier, Private Robert Bandy, in the shoulder during a scuffle.
A rumor flew that the soldier had been killed, in uniform, defending his mother.
Again the windows went.
This time, six people died.
That week, a young Harlem writer buried his father.

In his essay Notes of a Native Son, James Baldwin recalled that the funeral fell on his nineteenth birthday, and that they drove his father to the cemetery through a wilderness of smashed plate glass.
For Baldwin, his father's bitterness and the fury in the streets were part of the same story.
You heard about the Executioner, who sweeps unlucky acts off the Apollo stage.

Amateur Night itself was the creation of Ralph Cooper, an actor, dancer and emcee, who had run an amateur show at the Lafayette Theatre and brought it here in 1934, with a radio broadcast that carried it far beyond Harlem.
He hosted it, on and off, for many years.
The most famous Executioner was a tap dancer named Howard Sims, called Sandman because he danced on sand scattered over a board, so that his feet hissed and scraped like brushes on a drum.
He knew the crowd from the other side.
As the story goes, he was booed off this stage several times before he ever won.
Later, the theater hired him to chase away the acts the crowd rejected, with a broom or a long hook, to the audience's delight.
Winning was never easy.
One night in 1964, a young guitarist named Jimi Hendrix took first prize, a few years before the world knew his name.
And the Apollo is where Harlem says goodbye.
When James Brown died on Christmas Day, 2006, his body was carried up 125th Street in a white carriage drawn by horses, and laid in a gold casket on this stage.
Thousands lined up to file past the hardest-working man in show business, in the house where he had recorded Live at the Apollo.
Look up at the Theresa.

It went up in 1912 and 1913 for Gustavus Sidenberg, a German-born stockbroker, and was designed by the brothers George and Edward Blum, who designed many of Manhattan's apartment houses in those years.
At thirteen stories, it towered over the brownstones and tenements of 125th Street, and for decades it was one of the tallest buildings in Harlem.
The Blums clad it in white brick and white terra cotta, clay that was molded, glazed and fired, so that it kept its brightness and could be washed clean.
On a gray day, it still seems to glow.
It was built as a grand hotel for a Harlem that developers expected to stay white, and prosperous.
The neighborhood changed around it, but the hotel's rules didn't.
For more than two decades, the Theresa turned Black guests away, even as Harlem became the capital of Black America.
Then, in the late 1930s, a Black businessman named Love B. Woods bought it, and in 1940 the whites-only rule was gone.
Black travelers were still refused at most hotels downtown, but Harlem now had a first-class hotel of its own, and one of its tallest buildings was finally one its people could walk into.
After the hotel closed, the building was turned into offices, and it still is.
In 1993, the city named it a landmark.
You heard that Fidel Castro moved his whole delegation here in September 1960, after a dispute with his Midtown hotel.
Here's the dispute, and the legend that grew out of it.
The hotel was the Shelburne, on Lexington Avenue.
According to Castro, its managers demanded ten thousand dollars in cash, in advance, to cover any damage.
He called it an insult, swept out, and threatened to pitch tents in Central Park.
Instead, late that night, his motorcade drove up to 125th Street, and the Theresa took them all in.
New York's tabloids had a field day.
Stories spread that the Cubans had been thrown out of the Shelburne for keeping live chickens in their rooms, killing them, plucking them and cooking them on the spot.
In some versions, the chickens were for religious rites.
And in the papers, at least, the chickens followed the Cubans to Harlem, along with tales of feathers in the hallways of the Theresa.
Nobody has ever produced good evidence for any of it, and historians have called the stories politically motivated.
But a picture of bearded revolutionaries cooking chickens in a hotel room was too good to let go, and the tale is still told, sometimes as fact.
What is documented is how well the move worked for Castro.
By choosing Harlem, he turned a hotel bill into a statement about race in America, and the newspapers could hardly stop writing about it.
He came back to Harlem decades later, in 1995, to speak to a packed house at Abyssinian Baptist Church, a few blocks north of here.
You heard that Malcolm X rented offices here.
His rise as a leader in Harlem began on a spring night in 1957.
Malcolm was then minister of the Nation of Islam's Temple Number Seven, on Lenox Avenue at 116th Street.
One evening in April, police officers were clubbing a man on a Harlem street when a member of the temple, Johnson Hinton, objected.
The officers turned on him, beat him badly with their nightsticks, and took him to the station house.
Within hours, Malcolm was at the station, demanding to see him.
Outside, dozens of the temple's men stood in silent, disciplined ranks.
Behind them, a crowd of Harlem residents grew into the hundreds, and by some accounts into the thousands.
The police let Malcolm see Hinton, who was badly hurt, and agreed to send him to Harlem Hospital.
Malcolm stepped outside and gave a small signal with his hand.
The ranks turned and marched away, and the crowd melted into the night.
A police official who watched it reportedly said that no one man should have that much power.
Harlem had a new leader, and the police had a new worry.
Hinton survived, and a jury later awarded him damages from the city.

Seven years later, after his split with the Nation of Islam and a pilgrimage to Mecca, Malcolm set up his new organization in this building, and he often spoke at rallies on the corner below, at 125th Street and Seventh Avenue, Harlem's open-air forum.
You heard how a teacher's remark set Arturo Schomburg on his life's work.
What paid for it was a day job.
For more than twenty years, Schomburg worked at the Bankers Trust Company, downtown, where he rose to supervise the bank's mail for Latin America and the Caribbean.
In the evenings, on weekends and on his vacations, he hunted through bookshops, auctions and dealers' catalogs, at home and abroad.
He had come to New York as a young activist.
In the 1890s, he joined the movement to free Cuba and Puerto Rico from Spain, and helped found a club called Las Dos Antillas, the Two Antilles.
In 1911, with the journalist John Edward Bruce, he founded the Negro Society for Historical Research, to gather the very evidence his teacher had said didn't exist.
And in 1925, he wrote an essay called The Negro Digs Up His Past, arguing that Black history had been buried, ignored, or credited to others, and had to be recovered.

By the time the library bought his collection, for ten thousand dollars, it held some ten thousand items: books, manuscripts, prints and pamphlets, including rare works by Black writers going back to the sixteenth century, like the Latin poems of Juan Latino, a scholar of African descent who taught in Spain.
Selling it didn't mean letting go.
In 1932, Schomburg became curator of his own collection, here, and stayed until his death in 1938.
The library that grew from it now holds millions of items, and bears his name.
This library was never just a reading room.
In 1920, it got a new head librarian, Ernestine Rose, a white woman who set out to make it a branch that truly served Harlem.
She hired Black librarians at a time when the city's library system had almost none.
One was Catherine Latimer, the first Black librarian in the New York Public Library.
Another was Nella Larsen, who went on to write two acclaimed novels of the Harlem Renaissance, Quicksand and Passing.
The branch hosted lectures, readings and exhibitions of Black artists.
And in its basement was a small theater.
In 1940, the playwright Abram Hill and the actor Frederick O'Neal founded the American Negro Theatre there, a company where Black actors could play real people, not caricatures.
That basement stage launched remarkable careers.
As Harry Belafonte told it, he was working as a janitor's helper when he was given two tickets to one of its shows as a tip, and he was hooked.
A teenage dishwasher from the Bahamas named Sidney Poitier auditioned and was thrown out, for his thick accent and halting reading.
He practiced by reading newspapers aloud and imitating radio announcers, came back, and got in.
Ruby Dee, Alice Childress and Earle Hyman worked there too.
One of the company's productions, Anna Lucasta, moved to Broadway in 1944 and became a long-running hit.
Not bad for a theater under a library.
Walk around the corner onto 136th Street.
Just behind the Schomburg is the Countee Cullen branch library, named for the poet.
It stands where a grand townhouse once belonged to one of the richest Black women in America.
Sarah Breedlove was born in Louisiana in 1867, the first child in her family born into freedom.
Orphaned at seven, married at fourteen, and widowed at twenty, she spent years as a washerwoman.

Then, struggling with hair loss, she began developing hair care products, and as Madam C. J. Walker, she built a business that sold them across the country through thousands of Black women she trained as sales agents, giving them incomes of their own.
She's often called the first self-made female millionaire in America, though just how rich she was is still debated.
Walker and her daughter bought the townhouse here around 1913.
Later she built a mansion on the Hudson, Villa Lewaro, designed by Vertner Tandy, the first Black architect licensed in New York State.
She died there in 1919.
Her daughter, A'Lelia Walker, made the 136th Street house famous.
In 1927, she opened part of it as a salon for writers and artists, and called it the Dark Tower, after a column Countee Cullen wrote.
Langston Hughes remembered A'Lelia as the joy goddess of Harlem's 1920s.
The Dark Tower lasted only a couple of years, undone by money troubles, and A'Lelia died in 1931.
The house was later torn down, and the library took its place.
You heard that Adam Clayton Powell Junior was expelled from Congress in 1967.
Here is how he fell, and how Harlem stood by him.
In Washington, Powell was a crusader.
For years, he tacked what became known as the Powell Amendment onto bill after bill, barring federal money from segregated schools and programs.
Southern members hated it, and some liberal allies complained that it sank bills Black Americans needed.
Powell kept at it.
He also loved the high life: fine clothes, nightclubs, trips abroad at public expense, and a retreat on the island of Bimini, in the Bahamas.
Then, in 1960, in a television interview, he called a Harlem widow named Esther James a bag woman, someone who carried bribes for crooked police.
She sued him for libel and won.
Powell refused to pay.
The courts held him in contempt, and in New York he faced arrest, except on Sundays, when the law didn't allow it.
So for a time, Harlem's congressman came home only on Sundays, preached from this pulpit, and left before Monday.
In 1967, the House voted to exclude him.
Harlem's answer was to reelect him that spring, in a special election, and again the next year.
In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled that the House had no right to bar a member the voters had duly elected.
But his power was gone.
In 1970, he narrowly lost the Democratic primary to a young state assemblyman named Charles Rangel, who went on to represent Harlem in Congress for more than forty years.
Powell died in 1972.
Through all his troubles, he had a farewell line for crowds and reporters, and it became his motto: Keep the faith, baby.
Abyssinian helped raise one of the great entertainers of the jazz age.
Thomas Waller was born in Harlem in 1904.
His father, Edward, was a lay preacher at this church, a strict man who reportedly called jazz music from the devil's workshop.
His mother loved music and encouraged him, and as a boy he played the organ here for services.
By fifteen, he was playing the organ at the Lincoln Theatre on 135th Street, accompanying silent films.
After his mother died, he left home, and fell in with the masters of Harlem stride piano, especially James P. Johnson, who took him on as a pupil.

By the 1930s, Fats Waller was a star: a dazzling pianist, the composer of songs like Ain't Misbehavin' and Honeysuckle Rose, and a comedian who could turn a sappy ballad into a joke with a raised eyebrow and a muttered aside.
As one story goes, in Chicago in 1926, gunmen shoved him into a car, and he was sure he was about to be killed.
Instead, they delivered him to Al Capone's birthday party, where he played for three days, and went home with his pockets full of cash.
In December 1943, on his way home from California, he died of pneumonia on a train near Kansas City.
He was thirty-nine.
His funeral was held here, and more than four thousand people came.
Adam Clayton Powell Junior gave the eulogy.
Fats Waller, he reportedly said, always played to a packed house.
The Powells were not Abyssinian's last famous pastors.
In 1989, Calvin Butts, who had come to the church as a young assistant minister in the 1970s, became its pastor, and he led it for more than thirty years.
Butts believed in direct action.
In 1990, he led church members around Harlem with buckets of white paint, covering billboards that advertised cigarettes and liquor, ads he said targeted Black neighborhoods.
His bigger project was rebuilding.
In the 1980s, Harlem was full of abandoned buildings, many of them taken over by the city after landlords walked away.

The church founded the Abyssinian Development Corporation, which restored and built hundreds of apartments, and in 1999 brought a big Pathmark supermarket to 125th Street, at a time when Harlem had few places to buy fresh food.
For many years, Butts was also president of a state college on Long Island, while still preaching here on Sundays.
He died in 2022.
His work is part of the Harlem revival you heard about at the start of this walk, with all its arguments.
To some, the new housing and stores were the neighborhood rescuing itself.
To others, they opened the door to rising rents that pushed longtime residents out.
On February 17th, 1919, Lenox Avenue saw the greatest homecoming in Harlem's history.
The 369th Infantry Regiment, Black soldiers from New York, had come home from the First World War.
The regiment began as the 15th New York National Guard, and many of its men were from Harlem.
In France, the American army wouldn't let them fight beside white troops, so it lent them to the French army.
They spent longer in the front lines than almost any other American unit, and it's said the Germans gave them the name that stuck: the Hellfighters.
The most famous was Private Henry Johnson, a former railroad porter from Albany.
One night in May 1918, a German raiding party attacked his outpost.
Wounded again and again, Johnson fought them off with grenades, the butt of his rifle and a knife, and saved a fellow soldier from being carried off.
France awarded him its Croix de Guerre.
His own country took almost a century: in 2015, long after his death, President Obama awarded him the Medal of Honor.
That February day, the regiment marched up Fifth Avenue behind its famous band, led by James Reese Europe, whom you may have heard about at Carnegie Hall on the Fifth Avenue tour.
At 110th Street, the parade swung over to Lenox Avenue, and Harlem went wild.
The band struck up a popular tune, Here Comes My Daddy Now, and families broke into the ranks to embrace their men.
Johnson rode in an open car, to the loudest cheers of all.
Three months later, Europe was dead, stabbed by one of his own drummers after a quarrel at a concert in Boston.
The regiment lives on in its armory, a short walk east of here, on Fifth Avenue at 142nd Street.
You heard that Frankie Manning invented the Lindy Hop's first air steps here.
His later life is one of Harlem's great second acts.
In the 1930s, the best dancers at the Savoy formed a troupe managed by a Savoy bouncer named Herbert White, known as Whitey.

Whitey's Lindy Hoppers toured the country and Europe, danced in shows and nightclubs, and in 1941 appeared in a Hollywood comedy, Hellzapoppin', in a few minutes of high-speed, airborne dancing, choreographed by Manning, that still looks impossible.
Then came the war.
Manning was drafted, and by the time he came home, the swing era was fading.
He kept a troupe going for a while, then gave up and took a job at the post office, where he worked for about thirty years.
In the 1980s, young swing dancers in California and Sweden, studying old films, went looking for the people in them.
They found Frankie Manning in New York, in his seventies, and asked him to teach.
He said yes.
He taught all over the world, choreographed the Broadway revue Black and Blue, which won him a Tony Award in 1989, and created dances for Spike Lee's film Malcolm X.
On his birthdays, he would dance with one partner for every year of his age.
He died in 2009, a month before his ninety-fifth birthday, and the celebration planned for it went ahead in his honor.
Today, Lindy Hop is danced in cities all over the world, largely because a retired postal worker from Harlem agreed to teach it.
After the clubs and ballrooms closed, Harlem got hungry.
And one of its favorite answers became chicken and waffles.
The story usually told goes like this.
In 1938, a restaurant called Wells opened on Seventh Avenue, in the low 130s, a short walk from here.
Musicians and dancers finishing their last sets came in at three or four in the morning, too late for dinner and too early for breakfast.
So the kitchen gave them both: fried chicken from the dinner menu, with a waffle from the breakfast menu.
Wells grew into a supper club with a big dining room, and stayed in business for decades, famous for that plate.
As with most good food stories, the details are disputed.
Sources disagree about who exactly founded Wells, and when it finally closed.
A dancer named Dickie Wells, no relation, who ran his own Harlem nightspot, sometimes gets the credit instead.
And chicken and waffles were eaten together long before, in Pennsylvania Dutch country, where stewed chicken and gravy were spooned over waffles.
What Harlem can claim is the version most people know today: crisp fried chicken, a waffle and syrup, eaten in the small hours, after the music.
Harlem is widely credited with spreading it to soul food restaurants across the country.
Order it nearby, and you're eating a small piece of the swing era.
You heard that a developer named David King built these blocks.
King was one of the most successful builders in New York.
His firm built the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty, whose fundraising you may have heard about in the Financial District, and Stanford White's Madison Square Garden.

In 1891, King set out to build something new for Harlem: not a row of houses for single buyers, but a planned enclave on two blocks, marketed as the King Model Houses, with three of the best architects in the city, and shared service alleys to keep deliveries and horses off the street.
His timing could hardly have been worse.
Harlem was overbuilt, and in 1893 the country fell into a deep depression, set off by a financial panic.
The houses didn't sell.
King defaulted, and the Equitable Life Assurance Society, which had lent him the money, ended up with most of them.
The insurance company held on for a generation.
As Harlem around it became Black, Equitable would sell or rent the houses only to white families, and some stood empty for years.
Finally, in 1919, it gave in, and opened them to Black buyers.
They came, as you heard, the doctors, lawyers and musicians of Black Harlem, and bought the houses white buyers had passed over.
So the blocks King built for the white upper middle class became, through his failure and an insurance company's stubbornness, the showplace of Black Harlem.
You heard that the surgeon Louis T. Wright lived on Strivers' Row.
His career was a string of firsts, each won against resistance.
Wright was born in Georgia in 1891, and graduated from Harvard Medical School in 1915, near the top of his class.
In the First World War, he served as an army doctor in France, was gassed, and introduced a better method of vaccinating troops against smallpox.
In 1919, he joined the staff of Harlem Hospital, the first Black doctor appointed there.
Some white colleagues protested, but Wright stayed, and over the next three decades he helped make Harlem Hospital a place where Black doctors and nurses could train and rise.
He became its director of surgery.
In 1929, he became the city's first Black police surgeon.
He was an expert in head injuries and fractures, and designed a brace for broken necks.
In 1948, he led the team that first tested the new antibiotic Aureomycin on human patients.
Outside the hospital, he chaired the board of the NAACP for years, and fought segregation in American medicine.
And he passed his calling on.

His daughter, Jane Cooke Wright, joined him at Harlem Hospital, and went on to become a pioneer of cancer chemotherapy, testing drugs on cells from a patient's own tumor to find which would work best.
Strivers' Row was the exception.
A few blocks away, most Harlemites lived in crowded apartments, and paid dearly for them.
In the 1920s, landlords knew Black tenants had few other places to go, and studies found that Harlem families paid more than white New Yorkers for the same kind of housing.
Many took in lodgers to make ends meet.
And many threw parties.
A house-rent party worked like this.
You printed a little card, often with a rhyme on it, inviting guests to a social whist party on Saturday night.
Guests paid a small admission at the door, maybe a quarter, then paid again for plates of fried chicken, chitterlings and potato salad, and for drinks, bootleg during Prohibition.
By morning, with luck, the rent was covered.
The music was the draw.

Harlem's stride pianists, James P. Johnson, Willie The Lion Smith, and a young Fats Waller, went from party to party through the night, competing to outplay each other on whatever upright piano the host had.
The rent party was a proving ground for a whole style of jazz piano.
Langston Hughes went to many of them, and wrote about them fondly in his memoir, The Big Sea.
So while the strivers held their formal dinners behind these handsome doors, much of Harlem was paying its rent with music.
You heard that Hamilton built the Grange as a country retreat.
In a letter to a friend at the end of 1802, he explained why, with a wry line: A garden, you know, is a very usual refuge of a disappointed politician.
His party had lost power, his reputation was battered, and he threw himself into planning gardens and orchards, asking friends for seeds and plants.
Out of that garden grew Harlem's favorite tree story.
As it's usually told, Hamilton planted a grove of thirteen sweet gum trees near the house, one for each of the original states, a living monument to the union he had worked to build.
In some versions, the saplings were a gift from George Washington.
It's a lovely story, and that may be all it is.
The National Park Service, which runs the Grange, treats it as a claim, not a fact.
Even in the 1800s, people argued about it in the newspapers, and one account had Hamilton's own son saying the trees were already standing when his father bought the land.
Whatever their origin, by 1908 the old grove was gone.
The legend outlived the trees.
In recent years, new sweet gums have been planted beside the house.
Look for their star-shaped leaves, which turn red, orange and purple in the fall, and the spiky seed balls that litter the ground beneath them.
Whoever planted the first ones, Hamilton would surely have enjoyed the story.
Look up the hill at City College's Gothic towers.
In 1950, the college's basketball team did something no team had done before, or has done since.
The City College Beavers were New York kids, Jewish and Black players from the city's public high schools, coached by Nat Holman, who had been a star of the early professional game.
In March 1950, playing at Madison Square Garden, they won the National Invitation Tournament, then the most prestigious in the country.
Days later, they won the NCAA tournament too, beating the same team, Bradley University, in both finals.
No other team has won both in the same season, and under today's rules, no team can.
Less than a year later, it fell apart.
In February 1951, several City College players were arrested.
They had taken money from gamblers to shave points: to win by less than the betting line, or to lose games they were expected to win.
The scandal spread to other colleges, including Long Island University, New York University, Bradley and Kentucky, and dozens of players were caught up in it.
The players involved were barred from the NBA.
City College gave up big-time sports and dropped to the small-college level, where it remains.
For years, the double championship was a source of pride the college hardly mentioned.
Now it's remembered as both, a glorious season and a warning.
You heard that Paul Robeson, Count Basie and Joe Louis lived at 555 Edgecombe Avenue, about twenty blocks north of here, at 160th Street.
People in the neighborhood call it the Triple Nickel.
And it still has music in it.

Every Sunday afternoon, for more than thirty years, a pianist and actress named Marjorie Eliot has opened the door of her apartment there, 3F, to anyone who wants to come in, for a free afternoon of jazz.
Musicians play in her parlor, chairs fill the rooms and the hallway, and visitors from around the world sit beside neighbors from down the hall.
There's no ticket.
You can leave a donation if you like.
She began the concerts after the death of her son, as a way to turn grief into something she could share.
Reports over the years agree that she has hardly ever missed a Sunday.
If you're here on a Sunday, check the time, then walk up Edgecombe Avenue in the afternoon and follow the sound of the piano.
It's a living piece of the Sugar Hill story: music made at home, for whoever comes to listen.
The name Sugar Hill, for the sweet life on this ridge, has traveled far.
In 1979, across the Hudson in Englewood, New Jersey, a singer turned record producer named Sylvia Robinson started a record label and named it after this neighborhood: Sugar Hill Records.
That year, she brought together three young rappers, called them the Sugarhill Gang, and released a track nearly fifteen minutes long, called Rapper's Delight.
It became the first rap record to reach the American Top 40, and for millions of listeners, it was the first rap they had ever heard.
Three years later, the label put out Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five's The Message, a stark portrait of life in a struggling New York.
So the name that once meant the comfortable life of Black Harlem's elite carried the new sound of the Bronx out to the world.
You heard that George Washington made this house his headquarters in 1776.
He knew the man who built it.

Twenty-one years earlier, in 1755, Roger Morris and a young Virginia officer named George Washington had served together as aides to the British general Edward Braddock, on his march against the French in western Pennsylvania.
The march ended in disaster near Fort Duquesne, where Pittsburgh stands today.
Braddock was killed, and Morris was wounded.
If an old story is true, the two men had something else in common.
In 1756, Washington passed through New York and spent time with the family of Mary Philipse, an heiress from one of the richest families in the colony.
Legend says he fell for her.
The evidence is thin: a few teasing letters from a friend, hinting at Washington's interest.
Washington's own side of the correspondence has never been found.
What is certain is that in 1758, Mary married Roger Morris, and a few years later they built this house.
Then came the Revolution, and the old comrades ended up on opposite sides.
The Morrises stayed loyal to the king and left the house in 1775.
In 1779, New York confiscated the estates of leading loyalists, theirs among them, and the couple ended their lives in England.
When Washington came back to dine here in 1790, as you heard, he noted in his diary that the house had been confiscated and was now occupied by a farmer.
The young officer who had once ridden beside its builder was now the President of the United States.
You heard that Aaron Burr married Eliza Jumel in this house when he was seventy-seven.
How did the man who shot Alexander Hamilton end up here?
After the duel in 1804, Burr was indicted for murder in both New York and New Jersey, though he was never tried, and he finished his term as vice president.
Then he went west.
What exactly he planned there is still argued over: perhaps an invasion of Spanish Mexico, perhaps a new nation carved from the western territories.
In 1807 he was arrested and tried for treason in Richmond, Virginia, with Chief Justice John Marshall presiding.
He was acquitted, but his reputation was ruined.
He spent the next four years in Europe, trying to interest the British and the French in his schemes, and living for a time in near poverty in Paris.
In 1812, he slipped back into New York and quietly practiced law.
Then came the blow he never recovered from.
His only child, Theodosia, whom he adored and had educated as carefully as any son, had just lost her own young son.
At the very end of 1812, she sailed from South Carolina to join her father in New York.
Her ship, the Patriot, vanished.
Legends have filled the silence ever since: a storm off Cape Hatteras, wreckers who lured ships onto the shoals, pirates who made her walk the plank.
None has ever been proven.
So the man who married the rich widow in 1833 was a lonely survivor, and the couple separated within months.
Burr died on Staten Island in 1836, and was buried at Princeton, near his father, who had been president of the college there.
Eliza Jumel never won the acceptance she wanted.
Rumors about her past followed her all her life: that she had been desperately poor, that she had been a kept woman, that she had married Stephen Jumel for his money.
Fashionable New York kept its distance, even as she grew richer, managing her own property and investments.
In 1832, Stephen Jumel was injured in a carriage accident, and died soon after.
A darker story spread: that Eliza had torn off his bandages and let him bleed to death.
There was never any evidence for it, but the tale has clung to her ever since.
She lived on here until 1865, when she died at about ninety.
And then, the story goes, she stayed.
The mansion has a reputation as one of the most haunted houses in New York.
The best-known tale comes from the 1960s, when a group of noisy schoolchildren waiting outside were told to hush by a woman in old-fashioned clothes on the balcony.
Inside, the story goes, they recognized her in a portrait.
It was Eliza.
Around the same time, a well-known ghost hunter, Hans Holzer, held a séance here, and claimed he'd heard from Stephen himself, repeating the old accusation.
None of it can be checked, of course, and the accounts don't agree.
But the museum has made peace with its ghosts.
It now hosts evening paranormal investigations, for visitors who'd like to meet Madame Jumel for themselves.
Look at the hospital buildings around you.
Before the medical center rose here in the 1920s, this hilltop was a ballpark.
From 1903 to 1912, a wooden stadium called Hilltop Park stood on Broadway between 165th and 168th Streets.
It was home to a new American League team, the New York Highlanders, named, it's said, for this high ground.
The Highlanders were not very good, and their park was rough and far from downtown.
In 1913 they moved to the Polo Grounds, beside the Harlem River, as tenants of the National League's Giants, and made official the nickname reporters had been using for years: the Yankees.
There, in 1920, they introduced a new star bought from Boston, Babe Ruth.
The Yankees began to outdraw their landlords, the Giants told them to find a home of their own, and in 1923 they crossed the river to their new stadium in the Bronx.
The Polo Grounds stood about ten blocks south and east of here, at 155th Street, below the cliff called Coogan's Bluff.
There, on October 3rd, 1951, the Giants' Bobby Thomson hit the home run against the Brooklyn Dodgers that won the pennant, the Shot Heard Round the World.
Three years later, Willie Mays made his famous over-the-shoulder catch there in the World Series.
The Giants left for San Francisco after the 1957 season.
The new Mets played their first two seasons at the Polo Grounds, and in 1964 it was torn down for public housing, the Polo Grounds Towers.
New York's baseball story runs right through this neighborhood, from the Yankees' first home to the Giants' last.
You heard that Malcolm X was killed in front of his wife, Betty Shabazz, and their children.
That afternoon, she was in the audience with their four young daughters, and she was pregnant with twins.
When the shooting began, she pushed the girls to the floor and covered them with her body.
Betty Shabazz had grown up in Detroit, trained as a nurse in New York, and met Malcolm through the Nation of Islam's temple in Harlem.
Now, at thirty, she was a widow with four children, and that fall she gave birth to two more girls.
With help from friends, she bought a house in Mount Vernon, just north of the city, and raised six daughters there.
Then she went back to school.
In 1975, she earned a doctorate in education from the University of Massachusetts.
The next year, she joined Medgar Evers College, a public college in Brooklyn, where she worked as an administrator for some twenty years.
She spoke across the country about her husband's legacy, about education, and about the lives of Black women, and she became a respected figure in her own right, not just as a famous widow.
She died in 1997, after a fire in her apartment in Yonkers, set by her twelve-year-old grandson.
When part of the Audubon was saved, the center inside was named for both of them: the Malcolm X and Doctor Betty Shabazz Memorial and Educational Center.
The title before her name is one she earned herself.
As you walk this neighborhood, look at the metal shutters that roll down over storefronts, and at the sides of buildings.
You may spot birds, painted larger than life, in brilliant color.
They belong to the Audubon Mural Project, begun in 2014 by a local gallery owner, Avi Gitler, together with the National Audubon Society.
That year, the society published a study listing hundreds of North American bird species threatened by a warming climate.
The project's goal is to paint every one of them, here, in the neighborhood where John James Audubon spent his last years.
Dozens of artists have taken part, and the birds now perch along Broadway and the side streets of Washington Heights and Harlem.
The setting suits them.
Audubon bought land along the Hudson here in 1841, when he was already famous for The Birds of America.
He called the estate Minnie's Land, after his wife, Lucy, whom the family called Minnie, a Scottish word for mother.
Here, with his sons, he worked on his last great project, a book on the mammals of North America.
But his health and his mind were failing, and he died here in 1851, before it was done.
His sons and a collaborator finished it.
When you've found a painted bird or two, look up.
Red-tailed hawks hunt over the parks of upper Manhattan, and gulls and pigeons wheel over Broadway.
Audubon, who painted pigeons too, would have recognized them.
The bridge you see almost wasn't built like this.

The aqueduct's chief engineer, John Jervis, wanted something cheaper: a low bridge, with the water pipes dipping down across the river and climbing up the other side, the water carried back up by its own pressure.
But the Harlem River was a working waterway.
People who used it, and people who owned land along it, feared that a low bridge would block their boats and their future trade.
They petitioned, and in 1838 the city's aldermen came out against the low bridge.
The state legislature settled the matter, requiring a bridge that left at least a hundred feet of clear space above the water for ships to pass.
So Jervis built high.
It cost more and took years, and it was far grander than the engineers had wanted.
That grandeur is why the bridge still stands, and why it's worth walking across.
The bridge also had to keep up with a thirsty city.
At first, the water crossed in two iron pipes, each three feet across.
By 1850, they weren't enough, and in the early 1860s a third pipe was added, a giant ninety inches wide.
Together, the pipes carried a river of drinking water across this bridge for about a century, until newer tunnels deep underground took over the work.
Look down from the deck at the Harlem River today, with its highway and railroad along the banks.
The ships that worried those petitioners are long gone.
The bridge they demanded is still here.
You heard that the promenade on the bridge was a favorite Sunday outing.
In the later 1800s, the whole valley around it became a playground.
New Yorkers came up by steamboat and by carriage to stroll the bridge, picnic on the cliffs, and eat and drink at the taverns and hotels near each end.
Rowing clubs raced on the river below, and crowds lined the banks to watch.
The bridge itself became one of the sights of New York, reproduced on popular prints, including ones by Currier and Ives, and later on postcards.
Then, in 1898, the city opened the Harlem River Speedway, a broad dirt road along the river's edge, running north from 155th Street, past the foot of this bridge, toward Dyckman Street.
It had one purpose: fast horses.
Wealthy owners drove their trotters at full speed in light two-wheeled carts, racing each other while spectators cheered from the slopes.
At first, cars weren't allowed.
The age of the horse didn't last.
The Speedway was eventually opened to cars, and later rebuilt as part of the Harlem River Drive, the highway you can see and hear along the river today.
But in 2015, when the restored bridge reopened to walkers and cyclists, the old pleasure came back.
On a summer Sunday, you'll find families strolling across between Manhattan and the Bronx, stopping to look down at the water, as they did a century and a half ago.
Look at the granite water tower again, and then at the huge public swimming pool beside it.
The pool sits where a reservoir used to be.
The tower, finished in 1872, solved a problem.
The aqueduct's water flowed by gravity, so it couldn't reach the highest ground of northern Manhattan.
Pumps lifted water from a reservoir here up to a tank near the top of the tower, holding about forty-seven thousand gallons, and from that height it could flow down to the houses on the ridge.
In time, newer reservoirs and tunnels took over, and the old reservoir was no longer needed.
Robert Moses, the city's parks commissioner, saw an opportunity.
In 1934 the Parks Department took over the site, and on July 14th, 1936, Highbridge Pool opened.
It was the fifth of eleven giant public pools the city opened that summer, built with workers paid by the federal Works Progress Administration during the Depression.
Its outline follows the old reservoir, and it was designed to hold almost five thousand swimmers at once.
For neighborhoods of crowded apartments with no air conditioning, the pools were a blessing, and they still are.
The pool and its bathhouse are now a city landmark, like the tower beside them.
On a hot day, listen for the shrieks of kids cannonballing into a basin that once held the neighborhood's drinking water.
You heard that Fort Washington fell in November 1776.
Many historians think it should never have been defended at all.
After the British drove the army out of New York City, Washington doubted the fort could hold.
General Nathanael Greene, commanding across the river at Fort Lee, believed it could, and Washington let him keep almost three thousand men here, under Colonel Robert Magaw.
The British had help from inside.
On November 2nd, Magaw's adjutant, William Demont, slipped out and deserted to the enemy, carrying plans of the defenses.
He's often called the first traitor of the American Revolution.
On the morning of the attack, Washington crossed the river to see for himself, then went back, and watched from the New Jersey side as the British and Hessians closed in from three directions.
By afternoon, the fort was jammed with retreating men, and Magaw surrendered.
The British renamed it Fort Knyphausen, after the Hessian general who led the assault.
Four days later, they crossed the Hudson and took Fort Lee too, and the Americans fled across New Jersey.
Among those retreating was a writer serving on Greene's staff, Thomas Paine, whose bones you may have heard about in Greenwich Village.
A few weeks later, with the cause close to collapse, he published the pamphlet that begins: These are the times that try men's souls.
It's said Washington had it read aloud to his troops.
Within days of its publication, they crossed the Delaware, and the war turned.
You heard that Othmar Ammann was the bridge's chief engineer.
He came to America from Switzerland in 1904, and worked for years under the great bridge builder Gustav Lindenthal, on projects like the Hell Gate railroad bridge.
Then the two fell out over the Hudson.
Lindenthal dreamed of a colossal bridge at 57th Street, carrying trains and cars right into Midtown.
Ammann argued for a simpler, cheaper crossing up here, where high cliffs on both banks gave a bridge its height for free.
Ammann won.
The new Port Authority put him in charge, and the bridge went up in about four years, opening in October 1931, ahead of schedule and under budget.
It hangs from four main cables, each about three feet thick and spun from tens of thousands of steel wires, and its towers rise about six hundred feet above the river.
You heard that the towers were meant to be covered.
The covering was designed by Cass Gilbert, the architect of the Woolworth Building: a skin of stone and concrete, with great arched portals for the roadway.
Imagine two massive stone gateways standing in the river, and you have the bridge that almost was.
By the time the money ran short, many people had decided they liked the steel.
Engineers argued that the bare towers showed exactly how the bridge worked, and that dressing them in stone would be a kind of lie.
Ammann went on to design more of the city's great crossings, among them the Bayonne Bridge, the Bronx-Whitestone and the Throgs Neck, and, at the end of his career, the Verrazzano.
Look up at the crisscrossing steel.
It was meant to be the bridge's hidden skeleton.
It turned out to be its best feature.
Look across the Hudson at the cliffs of Fort Lee, New Jersey.
A little over a century ago, they were the backdrop of the American movie business.
In the early 1900s, before Hollywood, film companies needed cheap land and varied scenery close to the actors, theaters and money of New York.
Fort Lee had all of it, a short ferry ride from Manhattan.
From around 1907, film companies crowded into the town, among them the company of William Fox, the man who built the Audubon Ballroom.
On any given day, the cliffs, woods and taverns of the Palisades might play the Wild West, a medieval castle or a jungle.
The most famous films made around here were the serials, told in weekly episodes.
The Perils of Pauline, in 1914, starred Pearl White as a daring heiress in constant danger.
Episodes ended with her in peril, sometimes hanging from a cliff, and it's often said that's where the word cliffhanger comes from.
The idea is older: in 1873, the novelist Thomas Hardy left a character dangling from a cliff at the end of an installment of a magazine serial.
But the Palisades gave the cliffhanger its most famous face.
Within a decade, the industry moved west, chasing California's sunshine, cheap land, and distance from Thomas Edison's company, which held key patents and sued filmmakers who didn't pay to use them.
By the early 1920s, Fort Lee's film boom was mostly over.
But for a few years, Americans learned to love the movies by watching these cliffs.
You heard that Rockefeller bought the estate of C. K. G. Billings to make this park.
Billings deserves a story of his own.
He was a retired Chicago gas company president, and his great passion was horses, especially fast trotters.
In 1901 he began building an estate on this hilltop, with stables for his horses, and by about 1907 a turreted mansion called Tryon Hall, in the style of a French château, high above the Hudson.
In March 1903, he gave one of the most famous parties of the Gilded Age.
At Louis Sherry's fashionable restaurant on Fifth Avenue, he invited three dozen men from his riding club to a dinner where they ate on horseback.

The ballroom was dressed up as a woodland, the horses were reportedly brought up in the elevators, and the guests sat in the saddle, eating from trays and, it's said, sipping champagne through tubes from bottles in their saddlebags.
A photograph of the evening became an emblem of Gilded Age excess.
In 1917, Billings sold the estate to John D. Rockefeller Junior, for thirty-five thousand dollars an acre.
Rockefeller kept the mansion for a while, but in the mid-1920s it burned in a spectacular fire.
Look along the park's western edge for what's left: an arched stone arcade that once carried the estate's driveway up the cliff, and a small gatehouse cottage.
They're the last traces of a millionaire's castle, in a park now open to everyone.
If you go inside the Cloisters, find the room with the Unicorn Tapestries, and look for the most famous of them, The Unicorn in Captivity.
The white unicorn sits inside a small round fence, chained to a pomegranate tree, on a field thick with flowers.
The scenes before it tell a hunt.
Hunters find the unicorn dipping its horn into a stream to purify the water for the other animals, chase it, trap it and kill it.
Then, in this panel, it's alive again, at peace in its garden.
Whether this panel was even made for the same set as the others is still debated.
Look closely at its flank.
Those red drops aren't blood.
They're juice, dripping from the ripe pomegranates above, a symbol of fertility and marriage.
Many scholars think this tapestry, and perhaps the whole set, celebrated a wedding.
Now look at the plants.

Botanists have identified most of the more than one hundred plants woven into the tapestries, so accurately are they drawn: flowers, herbs and trees, some medicinal, some symbolic, some simply beautiful.
The Cloisters' gardens grow many of the same species.
Then look for two letters, an A and an E, tied together with a knotted cord.
They appear again and again in the tapestries.
Whose initials they were, nobody knows.
The tapestries were woven around 1500, and later belonged to the La Rochefoucauld family in France.

During the French Revolution, they were looted from the family's château, and, as the story goes, spent years covering potatoes or wrapping fruit trees against the frost, before the family got them back in the 1800s.
John D. Rockefeller Junior bought them in 1922 and hung them in his own home in Manhattan, and later gave them to the Cloisters.
You heard that Margaret Corbin took her husband's place at the cannon here, and was badly wounded.
Her story didn't end with the battle, and its strangest chapter came more than two hundred years later.
Corbin was captured with the garrison, then let go.
Her wounds left her unable to use one arm, and in 1779 Congress granted her half a soldier's pay for life.
She lived near West Point, attached to a unit of disabled veterans, where people called her Captain Molly.
She's one of the women whose stories blended into the legend of Molly Pitcher, who carried water to the gunners in battle and then took over a cannon herself.
She died around 1800 and was buried near West Point, in a grave that was soon forgotten.
In 1926, the Daughters of the American Revolution had remains believed to be hers moved to the cemetery at West Point, with full military honors, and put up a monument.
Then, in 2016, contractors working beside the monument disturbed the grave.
The Army studied the bones, and in 2017 announced a surprise: they belonged to a tall, middle-aged man.
Nobody knows who he was, or where Margaret Corbin lies.
A search with ground-penetrating radar found nothing.
The man was reburied, and Captain Molly's monument still stands, honoring a woman whose grave is lost.
Here, at least, the circle at the park's entrance keeps her name on the map.
You heard that there's a reconstructed hut in the garden, like the ones Hessian soldiers lived in.
It exists thanks to two men with a long iron rod.

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, while upper Manhattan was still half countryside, an engineer named Reginald Pelham Bolton and a fellow history lover, William Louis Calver, spent their weekends digging.
