The Dime Savings Bank of Brooklyn, whose domed building stands near the Fulton Mall, reportedly took its name from the idea that a dime was enough to open an account.
Their buildings were part of the pitch.

A savings bank had to convince working families that their money was safe, so it built like a temple or a fortress, with columns, domes, marble halls, and sometimes a tower you could see from anywhere in the borough.
In the late twentieth century, deregulation, the savings and loan crisis and a wave of mergers swept most of these banks away.
Many converted into ordinary banks owned by stockholders, and the Williamsburgh was eventually absorbed into larger banks.
The temples remain, turned into apartments, event spaces and shops, monuments to an age when saving a dime a week was a civic virtue.
You heard that Walter O'Malley wanted a new stadium at this corner, possibly a domed one.
In 1955, he asked Buckminster Fuller, the inventor of the geodesic dome, whom you may have heard about on the East Village tour, to imagine one.
Fuller and his students worked up designs for a huge, light dome over the entire ballpark, so that games would never be rained out and fans would be sheltered from the weather.
It would have been the first domed stadium in the world.
The Houston Astrodome, which usually gets that title, didn't open until 1965.
It never got past models and drawings.
Without the land, there was no stadium, and without the stadium, O'Malley went west.
More than half a century later, a very different arena rose here.
Frank Gehry, the architect of the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, had designed the original plan for the project, but his design was dropped as too expensive.
The Barclays Center that was built instead was designed by SHoP Architects, wrapped in thousands of panels of steel that were rusted on purpose, a nod to Brooklyn's industrial past.
In 2015, a green roof of low, hardy plants was added on top, partly to soften the noise for the neighbors.
Look up at the oculus over the entrance plaza, the great opening in the canopy.
Then imagine, in its place, a dome of shining triangles, with the Dodgers playing underneath.
You heard about Ebbets Field.
It opened in 1913, built by the team's owner, Charles Ebbets, on a site in Flatbush known as Pigtown, a scruffy area of shacks and garbage dumps where pigs once rooted.
It was small, and that was part of its magic.
Fans were close enough to talk to the players, and many did.
Along the right field wall was an advertisement for a clothing store owned by a merchant named Abe Stark: Hit sign, win suit.
Hardly anyone ever won, because the right fielder stood right in front of it.
Stark became so well known that he was later elected Brooklyn borough president.
The fans were part of the show.
Hilda Chester, a woman with a booming voice, rang a cowbell from the bleachers for decades and became the most famous fan in baseball.
A band of amateur musicians called the Dodgers Sym-Phony roamed the stands, playing gleefully off-key, and Gladys Gooding played the organ.
Year after year, the Dodgers reached the World Series, and year after year, they lost to the Yankees.
Fans learned to say, Wait till next year.
Next year finally came in 1955, when they beat the Yankees at last.
Two years later, they were gone.
In 1960, a wrecking ball painted to look like a baseball knocked Ebbets Field down.
Apartment buildings stand there now, called the Ebbets Field Apartments.
And older Brooklynites will still tell you exactly where they were sitting.
The team had many names before it settled on Dodgers.
In the 1880s, it was the Grays, and then the Bridegrooms, after several players married in the same season.
In those years, it played at a ballpark next to the Old Stone House in Park Slope, as you can hear on the Prospect Park tour.
Around 1899, the team became the Superbas, after a popular vaudeville troupe called Hanlon's Superbas, a play on the name of the team's new manager, Ned Hanlon.
From 1914 to 1931, under a beloved, portly manager named Wilbert Robinson, the team was often called the Robins.
Through it all, many people called them the Trolley Dodgers.
Brooklyn in the 1890s was laced with streetcar lines, and pedestrians had to dodge the trolleys to cross the street.
New Yorkers across the river used the name to tease Brooklynites.
The Brooklynites adopted it, and in the early 1930s, Dodgers became the team's official name.
Then there was Dem Bums, the affectionate nickname for a team that always seemed to lose in the end, drawn by the newspaper cartoonist Willard Mullin as a ragged, unshaven tramp with a cigar stub.
When the team moved to Los Angeles, it took the name along, although there were no trolleys left to dodge there, only freeways.
You heard that Junior's has been serving cheesecake since 1950.
Before that, reportedly, the Rosen family ran a sandwich shop on this corner.
When Harry Rosen reopened it as Junior's, he set out to make the best cheesecake in New York.
As the story goes, he worked for months with a baker named Eigel Peterson, trying recipe after recipe.
The result is classic New York cheesecake: tall, dense, rich and creamy, made with cream cheese, eggs, sugar and heavy cream.
Junior's version sits on a thin layer of sponge cake, instead of the graham cracker crust you'll find in many other places.
Cream cheese itself is a New York invention.
In 1872, a dairyman named William Lawrence, in Chester, in upstate New York, began making it.
A few years later, a New York cheese distributor branded it Philadelphia, because Philadelphia was then famous for fine dairy products.
The name stuck, and so did the confusion.

Cheesecake made with cream cheese became a specialty of the delis and restaurants of New York in the early twentieth century, at places like Lindy's on Broadway, and Junior's carried the style into Brooklyn and made it famous across the country.
Today Junior's has branches in Manhattan and ships its cheesecakes nationwide, but this corner is the original.
If you go in, the plain one is the classic.
Purists say you don't need anything else.
Near the corner of Fulton Street and DeKalb Avenue stood the Albee Theatre, a grand vaudeville and movie palace that opened in 1925.
It was named for Edward F. Albee, the vaudeville impresario, whose adopted grandson was the playwright Edward Albee.

In the late 1970s, the theater was torn down and replaced by the Albee Square Mall, an indoor mall that became a hangout for Brooklyn's young Black and Latino shoppers, full of sneaker stores, gold jewelry counters, and stalls selling records and mixtapes.
In 1988, the rapper Biz Markie, the clown prince of hip-hop, recorded a song called Albee Square Mall, celebrating it as the place to hang out, see and be seen, and buy gold.
Fulton Street's gold chains, rings and teeth became part of hip-hop style.
Biggie Smalls, the Notorious B.I.G., one of the greatest rappers of all time, grew up on Saint James Place in nearby Clinton Hill, and came of age a short walk from here.
The mall was demolished in the late 2000s, and the City Point complex, with apartment towers, shops, and an underground food hall, rose in its place.
The old name lives on in the little plaza at the corner, still called Albee Square.
So if you hear old-timers talk about the Albee Square Mall, they're not talking about a building so much as a time and a scene, when this stretch of Fulton Street was one of the capitals of hip-hop.
A few blocks from here, at Hoyt and Schermerhorn Streets, is Hoyt-Schermerhorn station, one of the oddest in the subway.
It has more tracks and platforms than it needs.
Two of its platforms have been out of regular service for decades, left over from a shuttle line to the Court Street station, which closed in 1946 and later became the New York Transit Museum.
Because those empty platforms can be closed off without disturbing riders, film and television crews love them, and the station has appeared in countless productions.
Its long platforms and tiled walls can pass for New York in almost any decade, which is exactly what filmmakers want.
The most famous is The Warriors, the 1979 cult film about a Coney Island gang fighting its way home across a hostile city.
The station reportedly stood in for Union Square in the film's final subway showdown.
In 1987, the director Martin Scorsese filmed Michael Jackson's music video for Bad here, with Jackson and his dancers facing off against a rival gang in the station.
So when you change trains here, look around.
You may be standing on one of the most filmed subway platforms in New York.
You heard that Henry Osborne Havemeyer built one of the most powerful trusts of the Gilded Age.
In 1907, his company was caught cheating the government, right here on the Williamsburg docks.
Havemeyer himself argued that high tariffs, the taxes on imported goods, were what made trusts possible.
In 1899 he told a federal commission that the mother of all trusts was the customs tariff bill.
His refineries paid those taxes too.
Every bag of raw sugar that came off the ships owed a duty according to its weight, and each one was weighed on the company's own dock scales, under the eyes of government weighers.
In November 1907, a Treasury special agent named Richard Parr raided the docks.
According to testimony at the trials that followed, a secret spring had been fitted to the scales, so that bag after bag was recorded as lighter than it really was.
The difference on any one bag was easy to miss.
Multiplied over millions of bags, year after year, it added up to a fortune in unpaid duties.
Havemeyer never had to answer for it.
He died a few weeks after the raid, in December 1907.
The government went after the company and its men.
The company paid back more than two million dollars in duties and penalties.
The dock superintendent, Oliver Spitzer, was convicted, along with four checkers who worked under him, and sentenced to two years in prison.
Then President William Howard Taft pardoned him, so that he could testify against the men above him.
Newspapers reported that Parr himself stood to collect a large share of the money recovered, as a reward.
Some of the profits from this refinery hang today on the walls of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Henry Havemeyer's second wife, Louisine Elder, came from the same business.
Her family name was part of the refinery's old company name, Havemeyers and Elder.
As a young woman in Paris in the 1870s, she met an American painter named Mary Cassatt, and the two became lifelong friends.
Cassatt urged her to buy a pastel by Edgar Degas, a painter few Americans had heard of.
She did, and she kept buying.
After Louisine married Henry, in 1883, they collected together on a grand scale, with Cassatt as their guide, hunting for pictures across Europe.
They bought old masters and modern painters alike: Rembrandt, El Greco, Goya, Courbet, Manet, Monet, Cézanne, and many more works by Degas.
When Louisine died, in 1929, she left nearly two thousand works of art to the Met.
It remains one of the greatest gifts in the museum's history.
She was much more than a collector.
Louisine Havemeyer was a fierce campaigner for women's right to vote.
In 1915 she helped organize an exhibition of old and modern masters, Degas and Cassatt among them, to raise money for the cause.
In 1919, in her sixties, she joined a protest in front of the White House, where suffragists burned an effigy of President Woodrow Wilson.
She was arrested and briefly jailed, and then rode across the country on a train called the Prison Special, with other women who had been jailed for the cause, speaking to crowds along the way.
The next year, the Nineteenth Amendment gave American women the vote.
So if you visit the Met, look for the words H. O. Havemeyer Collection on the labels beside some of its greatest paintings.
They mean sugar from Williamsburg, and the eye of a woman who refused to stay quiet.
You heard that the refinery closed in 2004.
Its last years were marked by one of the longest strikes the city has seen.
By the 1990s, Domino belonged to a British company, Tate and Lyle, and the Brooklyn refinery was old and costly to run.
In June 1999, when their contract ran out, about two hundred eighty workers walked off the job.
Their union was Local 1814 of the International Longshoremen's Association, better known for dockworkers.
The company wanted to cut jobs and weaken the seniority rules that protected workers who had been there for decades.
The union refused.
Week after week, then month after month, the strikers walked the picket line on Kent Avenue, through two winters.
They got little help from the wider labor movement.
The national AFL-CIO turned down calls for a boycott of Domino sugar and for a national strike fund, though New York's Central Labor Council raised money locally.
In February 2001, after twenty months, the remaining strikers voted to go back to work, largely on the company's terms.
Domino was allowed to cut about a hundred ten jobs.
That same year, Tate and Lyle sold Domino to a group led by Florida sugar growers.
They named their new company American Sugar Refining, the old name of Havemeyer's trust.
Three years later, they closed the Brooklyn refinery for good.
As you look at the old building, think of the strikers who stood outside it for twenty months, trying to hold on to some of the last factory jobs on the Williamsburg waterfront.
You heard that the Forman family made Peter Luger the most famous steakhouse in New York.
Here's what happens to a steak before it reaches the table, and after.
It begins with the buying, the job Marsha Forman took on.
The family has kept it ever since, picking out the top grade of beef, called prime, piece by piece.
Then comes the dry aging.
The beef rests, uncovered, in a chilled room for weeks.
Moisture evaporates, so the flavor concentrates, and the meat's own enzymes slowly break down the tough fibers.
The outside dries into a dark crust that has to be trimmed away, so a dry-aged steak loses a good part of its weight before it's ever cooked, one reason it costs so much.
The porterhouse is broiled under fierce heat, sliced in the kitchen, and carried out on a hot platter.
Watch the waiter.
One end of the platter is propped up on an upturned plate, so the butter and juices run down to the other end, and the waiter spoons them back over the meat.

The regulars' order has barely changed in decades: thick-cut bacon to start, sliced tomatoes and onions with the house steak sauce, creamed spinach, German fried potatoes, and, for dessert, anything under a mountain of whipped cream, which the menu calls schlag.
With the check come chocolate coins wrapped in gold foil.
Not everyone is a believer.
In 2019, the New York Times restaurant critic Pete Wells gave Peter Luger zero stars, in a review that became famous in its own right, arguing that the old place no longer lived up to its legend.
The regulars kept coming anyway.
A mile or so southeast of here, on Flushing Avenue, near the border with Bedford-Stuyvesant, stands the old factory of Pfizer, one of the largest drug companies in the world.
Pfizer was born in Williamsburg.
In 1849, two cousins from Germany opened a small chemical business here: Charles Pfizer, who had trained as a chemist, and Charles Erhart, a confectioner, a candy maker.
Their first success needed both of their skills.
Santonin was a medicine for intestinal worms, a common affliction at the time, and it tasted awful.
The cousins blended it with almond toffee flavoring and shaped it into a candy cone, and it sold.
Pfizer grew by mastering chemistry on a large scale.
One of its biggest products was citric acid, which soft drink makers bought by the ton.
It came from lemons, mostly from Italy, until, around the time of World War One, Pfizer's chemists learned to make it by fermentation, letting a mold feed on sugar in big vats.
That skill turned out to matter enormously.
During World War Two, the new antibiotic penicillin could save countless wounded soldiers, but it was hard to grow in quantity.
Pfizer bet on deep-tank fermentation, the method it knew from citric acid, and in 1944 it opened a plant that made penicillin that way, in a converted ice factory in Brooklyn.
By the company's account, most of the penicillin that went ashore with the Allied troops on D-Day was made by Pfizer.
Pfizer moved its headquarters to Manhattan in the early 1960s and closed its last Brooklyn plant in 2008.
The old factory now houses small food companies and other businesses.
As you walk south from here, into the heart of the Hasidic neighborhood, read the street signs.
Together they make a roll call of the men who signed the Declaration of Independence.
Rutledge, Heyward, Lynch and Middleton: those are all four of the signers from South Carolina.
Hooper, Hewes and Penn are the three from North Carolina.
Rodney signed for Delaware, Walton for Georgia, and Clymer, Ross, Taylor and Wilson for Pennsylvania.
Wythe and Harrison were Virginians, and so were two brothers, Richard Henry Lee and Francis Lightfoot Lee, who seem to be remembered in Lee Avenue, the busy main street you heard about.
The numbered streets work differently.
Williamsburg's streets are numbered outward from Grand Street: North 1st, North 2nd and so on in one direction, and South 1st, South 2nd in the other.
That's how the South Side got its name.
The Spanish name you heard, Los Sures, means simply the Souths.
And look across Broadway at the domed building on the corner.
It's the old Williamsburgh Savings Bank of 1875, the bank that kept the h in Williamsburgh, as you may have heard on the Fort Greene tour.
You heard that German immigrants brought lager brewing to Brooklyn.
Lager needs cold, and before refrigeration, cold was one of the hardest things a brewer had to find.
Lager is fermented by a yeast that works slowly at low temperatures and settles to the bottom of the tank, unlike the yeasts of English ales, which work warmer and faster.
Then the beer is stored cold for weeks or months, while it clears and mellows.
The German word lagern means to store.
So the first lager brewers here dug down.
Beneath their breweries they built cellars and vaulted tunnels, sometimes several levels below the street, where the temperature stays cool all year.
Each winter they packed them with ice: blocks cut from frozen lakes and ponds upstate and along the Hudson, shipped down the river, and kept in insulated ice houses.
A big brewery went through thousands of tons of ice a year.
Then, in the 1870s and 1880s, came machines that made cold with compressed ammonia, and brewers were among their first big customers.
Freed from the winter and the cellars, breweries could grow into the great brick plants that once lined these streets.
Some of the old cellars are said to survive, forgotten, beneath later buildings in Williamsburg and Bushwick.
So as you walk, remember that much of Brooklyn's beer was brewed above ground, but aged below it, under your feet.
Brooklyn's brewers didn't just make beer.
They made some of the best-loved advertising in America.
Start with Miss Rheingold.

Every year from 1940 into the 1960s, the Rheingold brewery picked a handful of young women as finalists and asked the public to vote for the next Miss Rheingold, whose face would smile down from billboards, subway cards and bar signs for a year.
Ballot boxes sat in bars and grocery stores.
In its peak years, by the brewery's count, the contest drew tens of millions of votes, and it was said that only the race for president drew more.
The first winner, in 1940, was Jinx Falkenburg, a model and actress who went on to be a pioneer of radio and television talk shows.
Then came Bert and Harry Piel, two cartoon brothers who sold Piels beer on television beginning in 1955.
They were voiced by the comedians Bob Elliott and Ray Goulding, known as Bob and Ray, and viewers adored them.
People said they tuned in for the commercials.
Whether the brothers sold much beer is another question.
And Schaefer had the scoreboard.
At Ebbets Field, the home of the Brooklyn Dodgers, which you may have heard about on the Fort Greene tour, a big Schaefer sign topped the right-field scoreboard.
It did double duty: the h in Schaefer lit up when the official scorer ruled a play a hit, and the e lit up for an error.
Schaefer also sponsored the Dodgers' broadcasts, so a whole generation of Brooklyn fans heard the name between pitches.
You heard that Schaefer and Rheingold, the last big Brooklyn breweries, both closed in 1976.
The end had been coming for a long time.
As the story is usually told, a turning point came in 1949, when a strike shut New York's breweries for weeks.
Beer from Milwaukee and Saint Louis poured in to fill the gap, and many New Yorkers who tried Budweiser, Schlitz or Pabst for the first time never went back.
The local brewers tried to survive by getting bigger and more modern.
Schaefer built a new brewery in Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, which opened in the early 1970s, and soon gave up on Kent Avenue.
The names outlived the breweries, as brands bought and sold by bigger companies, and Rheingold has been revived more than once.
The old Schaefer site on Kent Avenue became apartment towers called Schaefer Landing, with a ferry stop at the water's edge.
By the 1990s, the Williamsburg waterfront was full of empty industrial buildings.
When Steve Hindy and Tom Potter went looking for a home for the Brooklyn Brewery, the one they chose on North 11th Street had been an ironworks, and later a matzo factory.
Brooklyn beer came back in a building that had once baked unleavened bread.
The L train that put artists one stop from Manhattan crosses under the East River through a tunnel that opened in 1924.
The line ran from 14th Street in Manhattan to Williamsburg, and was later pushed all the way to Canarsie, which is why its official name is still the Canarsie Line.
In 2012, its tunnel nearly drowned.
The tunnel is really two tubes, one for each direction, lined with iron and concrete.
Along their sides run low concrete walls, called bench walls, packed with the cables that carry power and signals for the trains.
On the night of October 29th, 2012, Hurricane Sandy pushed a surge of seawater into the subway, and the tunnel filled with millions of gallons of salt water.
Pumps cleared it, and trains were soon running again, but the salt stayed in the concrete, eating at the cables and the steel inside the walls.
Engineers warned that the tunnel had to be rebuilt.
The transit authority decided to close it completely, for fifteen months, starting in April 2019.
For Williamsburg, that was alarming.
Hundreds of thousands of riders a day depended on the L to cross the river.
Businesses braced for the worst, and the city planned extra buses, ferries and a busway across 14th Street in Manhattan.
Some called it the L-pocalypse.
Then, in January 2019, just months before the shutdown, Governor Andrew Cuomo announced a new plan, worked out with engineering experts from Cornell and Columbia universities.
Instead of tearing out the old bench walls, crews would leave them in place, wrap the weak sections in a strong fiber-reinforced plastic, and hang new cables on racks along the tunnel walls.
The work was done one tube at a time, on nights and weekends, and it was finished in April 2020.
The full shutdown never happened.
Next time you ride the L under the river, look out the window: those cables on their racks are what kept the trains running.
A few blocks east of here, at North 8th Street and Havemeyer Street, stands Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the old Italian parish of the Northside.
Every July, for more than a century, the men of the parish have done something astonishing in the street outside: they lift a tower.
The tower is called the giglio, Italian for lily.
It's a slender spire, roughly seventy feet tall and weighing a few tons, covered in papier-mâché saints, angels and flowers, with a platform at the bottom big enough for a brass band and a singer.
More than a hundred men, called lifters, crouch beneath it with the poles on their shoulders.
At a signal from their captain, they raise it off the ground, band and all, and make it dance, turning it, bouncing it, carrying it down the street.
The tradition comes from Nola, a town near Naples, and honors its patron, Saint Paulinus, who was bishop there in the early fifth century.
Here is the legend, as Nola tells it.
Raiders from North Africa carried off many young men of the town as slaves.
A widow begged the bishop to save her son.
With nothing left to pay a ransom, Paulinus offered himself in the young man's place, and was taken to Africa as a slave.
In time, a king there learned who he was and, moved by his sacrifice, set him free, with the other captives of Nola.
When they sailed home, the townspeople met them at the shore carrying lilies.
How much of that happened is anyone's guess.
Pope Gregory the Great was already telling the story less than two centuries later, but historians point out that the raiders it describes seem to have reached Italy only after Paulinus had died.
Over the centuries, the lilies grew into towers.
Immigrants from Nola and nearby towns brought the feast to Williamsburg, along with a boat, also carried on shoulders, in memory of the voyage home.
The streets around the church fill with stands selling zeppole and sausage and peppers.
If you're here in July, follow the brass band.
You heard that the park is named for Patrick McCarren, a state senator and Democratic boss.
Reformers saw him as everything that was wrong with machine politics.
McCarren grew up in Williamsburg and learned a trade as a cooper, a barrel maker, reportedly making barrels for the sugar refineries on the waterfront.
For a time he worked as an inspector of oil.
But his real talent was politics.
He rose through the Democratic clubhouses to the State Assembly and then to the State Senate in Albany, where he served for most of two decades.
By 1903 he was the boss of the Brooklyn Democrats, succeeding Hugh McLaughlin, who had run the party in Brooklyn for decades.
McCarren spent his years at the top fending off Charles Murphy, the boss of Tammany Hall in Manhattan, who wanted Brooklyn's Democrats under his thumb.
By many accounts he was also a heavy gambler.
He made powerful friends, and his critics said some of them were too powerful.

In 1904, Thomas Lawson, a Boston financier who was waging a public war on Standard Oil, charged that McCarren was on the oil company's payroll, at twenty thousand dollars a year, and offered him a hundred thousand dollars if he could disprove it.
The charge was never proven, but McCarren never took up the challenge.
He died in October 1909, at Saint Catherine's Hospital in Williamsburg.
His funeral was said to be the largest Brooklyn had ever seen, and the city renamed what had been Greenpoint Park in his honor.
So the softball games and lazy afternoons here take place in a park named for a barrel maker who became the boss of Brooklyn.
Look along the park's fences, in sidewalk cracks and in the gaps between buildings, for a scrappy tree with long leaves made of many pointed leaflets, arranged in pairs along a stem.
It's probably an ailanthus, called the tree of heaven, and it's the tree in the title of the best-known novel ever written about Williamsburg.
A Tree Grows in Brooklyn, by Betty Smith, published in 1943, follows Francie Nolan, a girl growing up poor in Williamsburg in the years before and during World War One.
Smith knew that world.
She was born in Williamsburg in 1896, to German immigrant parents, and grew up in its tenements.
The novel became a huge bestseller, and in 1945 it became the first feature film directed by Elia Kazan.
In the book, the tree is Francie's emblem.
It grows out of cement and rubbish, in backyards and vacant lots where nothing else will, and keeps reaching for the sky.
The real tree has a story of its own.
The ailanthus is native to China.
It reached America in the late 1700s, and in the 1800s it was planted along city streets, prized because it grew fast and could stand smoke and poor soil.
Then people soured on it.
The male trees' flowers smell rank, and the tree spreads relentlessly, sprouting from its roots and scattering its seeds on the wind.
Today it's considered an invasive species, and parks crews work to remove it.
But it almost never gives up.
Cut it down, and it sprouts again.
In the poorest corners of the old city, it was sometimes the only shade there was.
That's what Betty Smith saw in it, and it's how a weed became one of the most famous trees in American literature.
You heard that Greenpoint was a home of the five black arts.
The list varies a little from one telling to the next, but it usually runs printing, pottery, glass, cast iron and gas, all trades of fire, coal and soot.
Glass was the most glamorous.

In 1860, Christian Dorflinger, a French-born glassmaker, built the Greenpoint Flint Glass Works on Commercial Street, beside the mouth of Newtown Creek, and it turned out some of the finest cut crystal in America.
In 1861, Mary Todd Lincoln ordered a set of glassware for the White House from Dorflinger's works, engraved with a version of the presidential seal.
It was reordered again and again, and stayed in use for decades, until the administration of Benjamin Harrison replaced it, in 1891.
Dorflinger eventually moved to Pennsylvania, but the skills he brought stayed behind, and Greenpoint became a glass town.
By 1883, eighteen of the twenty glass factories in Brooklyn were in Greenpoint.
The works Dorflinger founded carried on under later owners, the last of whom moved across the creek to Queens in 1946.
Pottery came close behind.
The Union Porcelain Works, which you heard about, made true hard porcelain, the kind produced by the great factories of Europe, at a time when few American firms could.
For the Centennial Exhibition of 1876, in Philadelphia, its sculptor, Karl Müller, designed the Century Vase, with bison heads for handles and scenes celebrating American history and invention.
The Brooklyn Museum, on the Prospect Park tour, has one in its collection.
Walk these blocks and you'll notice how many of the old brick factory buildings remain, many of them now studios and workshops, still making things.
Look again at the terra cotta pencils on the old factory.
They're yellow, like most pencils in America, and there's a story behind that color, though it may be more legend than history.
For centuries, the best graphite for pencils came from a single mine at Borrowdale, in the north of England.
In the 1800s, a French prospector named Jean-Pierre Alibert found graphite of similar quality far to the east, in Siberia, near the Chinese frontier.

As the story goes, around 1890 a pencil maker in Austria-Hungary, Koh-i-Noor, launched a luxury pencil made with that Siberian graphite, and painted it yellow, the color of China's emperors, to hint at where its graphite came from, and at royalty.
It sold well, other makers copied the color to signal quality, and yellow became the color of a good pencil.
Eberhard Faber's best seller fits the story neatly.
Its Mongol pencil was yellow, and its name seems to point toward the same faraway East.
It's a good story, and it may even be true, but it's told far more often than it's proven.
Whatever the reason, the color stuck.
So did another feature: most pencils have six sides, so they don't roll off the desk.
You heard about the Polish bakeries and delis along Manhattan Avenue.
The best way to understand them is through the Polish calendar, which is, in large part, a calendar of food.

On the last Thursday before Lent, called Fat Thursday, the bakeries sell rich, round Polish doughnuts, filled with rose jam or custard and glazed or dusted with sugar, and the lines can stretch down the block.
On Holy Saturday, the day before Easter, families carry small baskets lined with white linen to church to be blessed.
Inside are colored eggs, bread, salt, a piece of sausage, horseradish, and often a little lamb made of sugar or butter.
The blessed food is eaten at Easter breakfast.
On Christmas Eve, the great family supper begins when the first star appears in the sky.
Traditionally it has no meat: beet soup with tiny mushroom dumplings, pierogi, herring, and carp, which many families once bought alive and kept in the bathtub until it was time to cook.
Before eating, everyone breaks and shares a thin wafer, often blessed by the parish priest, with good wishes for the year.
An extra place is often set at the table, for an unexpected guest.
The rest of the year, the butchers and delis carry the load.
Look in the windows for long rows of kielbasa, smoked and fresh, and for thin, dry sausages, hard as sticks, made to carry in a pocket.
The Polish population is smaller than it was.
But on a Fat Thursday morning, or the Saturday before Easter, you'd hardly know it.
You heard that the Monitor fought the Virginia to a standoff in March 1862.
It didn't survive the year.
The low hull that made the Monitor such a small target in battle made it a dangerous ship on the open sea.
Its deck sat barely above the waterline, and waves washed right over it.
On December 29th, 1862, the Monitor left Hampton Roads, towed by a steamer, the Rhode Island, bound for North Carolina to join the Union fleet off the Carolina coast.
The next day, off Cape Hatteras, the wind and the seas rose.
Water poured in around the base of the turret and through the hull, faster than the pumps could clear it.
That night the crew signaled for help, and boats from the Rhode Island came alongside in the storm and took off most of the men.
Sixteen did not get off.
In the early hours of December 31st, the Monitor sank.
For more than a century, no one knew exactly where it lay.
In 1973, a team led by scientists from Duke University found the wreck, upside down, more than two hundred feet down, and in 1975 it became the first national marine sanctuary in the United States.
Over the following decades, Navy divers and archaeologists brought up the propeller, the engine and, in 2002, the turret itself.
They went to the Mariners' Museum, in Newport News, Virginia, where conservators have spent years drawing the salt out of the iron.
Inside the turret, divers found the remains of two sailors.
Despite DNA testing, they couldn't be identified, and in 2013 they were buried with full honors at Arlington National Cemetery.
So the ship launched from this shore never came home.
But its turret, at least, made it back to dry land.
The Monitor's designer, John Ericsson, was one of the great engineers of his century, and the ship was his comeback, after a disaster that nearly ruined him in America.
Ericsson was born in Sweden in 1803.

As a young engineer in England, he built a steam locomotive that competed in the famous Rainhill trials of 1829, and he developed a screw propeller for ships, at a time when most steamships were pushed by paddle wheels.
In 1839 he moved to New York.
His first big American project was the Princeton, the Navy's first warship driven by a screw propeller.

In 1844, during a demonstration cruise on the Potomac River, with President John Tyler aboard, a giant gun called the Peacemaker exploded, killing the secretary of state, the secretary of the navy and several others.
The gun had been designed by the ship's captain, Robert Stockton, not by Ericsson.
But Stockton let the blame drift toward Ericsson, who was never properly paid for his work on the ship.
Seventeen years later, when word came that the Confederates were rebuilding the burned hulk of the Merrimack as an ironclad, Ericsson offered the Navy the design you heard about.

To build it fast, the work was split up: the turret was made at the Novelty Iron Works in Manhattan, the engines at the DeLamater Iron Works, and the hull here in Greenpoint, at Thomas Rowland's Continental Iron Works, where it all came together.
Critics mocked it as a cheesebox on a raft.
They stopped laughing at Hampton Roads.
Ericsson spent the rest of his life in New York, working at all hours and inventing constantly, from engines driven by hot air to machines powered by the sun.
He died in Manhattan in 1889, and the next year the Navy carried his body home to Sweden aboard the cruiser Baltimore.
His statue stands in Battery Park.
You heard that millions of gallons of oil leaked into the ground under Greenpoint.
That oil is still part of life here.
It didn't spill all at once.

Over many decades, oil from refineries, storage tanks and pipes seeped down through the soil until it reached the groundwater, where it spread out in a vast underground pool, beneath homes, schools and factories, slowly leaking into Newtown Creek.
The company held most responsible was ExxonMobil, heir to the Standard Oil companies that had refined and stored oil here since Charles Pratt's day.
For years after the leak was discovered, the cleanup crawled.
Recovery wells were drilled to pump the oil up out of the ground, and millions of gallons have been pulled up that way, but the work has stretched over decades.
In the 2000s, residents and environmental groups, and then the state, took ExxonMobil to court.
In 2010, the company agreed to a settlement that called for a more thorough cleanup and put millions of dollars into a fund for the neighborhood's environment.
That fund has paid for projects across Greenpoint, from green roofs and street trees to programs on the creek.
So as you walk these streets, remember that the story of Greenpoint's oil isn't only history.
Some of it is still being pumped out of the ground beneath your feet.
Newtown Creek is named for a town on the far side, in Queens.
The Dutch called the village Middelburgh, and the English renamed it Newtown.
In the 1890s it became Elmhurst, reportedly in part to shed its connection with the smelly creek.
The creek once wound inland for miles through salt marshes, and its branches still carry Dutch names.
Dutch Kills reaches into Long Island City, and English Kills reaches deep into Brooklyn.

Kill is an old Dutch word for a creek or channel, and you hear it all over the region: in the Catskill Mountains, and in the Kill Van Kull and the Arthur Kill, the channels that wrap around Staten Island.
The bridges over the creek honor two Polish heroes of the American Revolution, fitting for the Polish neighborhoods on both banks.
The Pulaski Bridge, near the creek's mouth, is named for Casimir Pulaski, a cavalry commander who died fighting for the Americans in 1779.
Upstream, the Kosciuszko Bridge honors Tadeusz Kosciuszko, the engineer who designed the American defenses at Saratoga and at West Point.
Its new cable-stayed spans replaced a bridge from 1939, which was brought down with explosives in 2017.
Below the creek's dark surface lies a layer of sludge so foul that people who study it call it black mayonnaise.
It's a century and a half of sewage, oil, coal tar and industrial chemicals, settled on the bottom, in places many feet deep.
Why did this creek suffer so much?
Newtown Creek is tidal, but it's a dead end.
Near the mouth, the tides move the water in and out, but in the upper reaches the water barely moves, so whatever pours in tends to settle and stay.
In summer, the oxygen in the water can drop so low that fish struggle to survive.
And the pouring hasn't stopped.
Like much of New York, this part of the city has combined sewers, which carry sewage and rainwater in the same pipes.
When a heavy rain overwhelms them, the overflow, sewage included, goes straight into the creek, through outfall pipes along its banks.

Since the creek became a Superfund site, in 2010, federal scientists have been mapping the contamination and working out who should pay to clean it up: companies whose predecessors lined the creek, and the city itself, whose sewers still overflow into it.
The cleanup will take many years.
And yet, life is coming back.
Look along the shore and the old pilings for cormorants drying their wings, and herons stalking the shallows.
Crabs and small fish live in the water, and here and there, local groups have planted marsh grasses, like the ones that once lined the whole creek.
Why would a city hire celebrated architects to design a sewage plant?
At Newtown Creek, the answer was the neighbors.
The plant opened in 1967, and for decades it was a bad neighbor, outdated and smelly.

When the city set out to rebuild and expand it, in a project that ran from the late 1990s into the 2010s and cost billions of dollars, it hired the firm then called the Polshek Partnership, now Ennead Architects, to make the plant something Greenpoint could live with, and even be proud of.
Instead of hiding the digesters, the designers made them the plant's signature.
Here's what happens inside.
Sewage from about a million people, in parts of Brooklyn, Queens and Manhattan, flows in through big pipes.
Screens strain out the trash, and in settling tanks the heavier solids sink.
In aeration tanks, air is bubbled through the water, and bacteria eat most of the waste that's left.
The cleaned water is disinfected and released into the East River.
The sludge goes to the eggs.
Inside, with no oxygen, kept warm, close to body temperature, other bacteria digest it for weeks, turning much of it into a gas that's mostly methane, the same gas that burns on a kitchen stove.
The plant uses some of that gas for heat.
What's left of the sludge is dried out and trucked away.
So the shining eggs are, in a sense, the city's stomach, and a reminder that what we flush doesn't simply disappear.
The plaza takes its name from the Grand Army of the Republic, the great organization of Union veterans of the Civil War.
It was founded in 1866, the year after the war ended, and it grew into one of the most powerful political forces in the country.
At its peak, around 1890, it had hundreds of thousands of members, with posts in nearly every town in the North.
Its members campaigned for veterans' pensions and for the care of old soldiers, and several of them became president.
The Grand Army also gave the country a holiday.
In 1868, its commander, General John Logan, issued an order setting aside May 30th as a day to decorate the graves of the Union dead with flowers.
It was called Decoration Day.
Over the years it grew to honor Americans who died in all the nation's wars, and it became Memorial Day.
The arch in front of you went up in the Grand Army's heyday, when Brooklyn was full of men who had served in the war.
The plaza itself was renamed for the Grand Army years later, as its members were dying off.
Manhattan has a Grand Army Plaza too, at the southeast corner of Central Park, named for the same veterans.
The last surviving member of the Grand Army, Albert Woolson, who had enlisted as a drummer boy, died in 1956, at the age of one hundred six.
With him, the Grand Army of the Republic came to an end.
Its name lives on here, at one of Brooklyn's busiest crossroads.

The chariot on top of the arch, and the great bronze groups of the Army and the Navy on its sides, are the work of Frederick MacMonnies, whose winged figures on the Washington Square Arch and fountains at the New York Public Library you may have heard about on other tours.
MacMonnies was a Brooklyn boy.
He was born in Brooklyn in 1863.
As a teenager, he went to work in the studio of Augustus Saint-Gaudens, the leading American sculptor of the day, and learned the trade there.
Then he went to Paris, where he spent most of his career.
His first big success at home stands in City Hall Park in Manhattan: a statue of Nathan Hale, the young American spy, his arms bound, about to be hanged.
Then came a scandal.
His Bacchante, a nude, laughing woman dancing with a baby on one arm and a bunch of grapes held high, was given to the new Boston Public Library by its architect, Charles McKim, in 1896.
Proper Boston was horrified by the tipsy, naked figure, and the statue was sent away.
McKim gave it to the Metropolitan Museum of Art instead, where it has been admired ever since.
Late in his career, MacMonnies made one more statue that caused an uproar.
Civic Virtue, unveiled near City Hall in 1922, showed a muscular nude youth standing over two writhing women, the sirens of vice.
Women's groups protested that it showed a man trampling women.
It was moved out to Queens in 1941, and in 2012 it moved again, to Green-Wood Cemetery, here in Brooklyn, where it stands today.
So the triumphal arch at the gate of Brooklyn's great park is crowned by the work of a Brooklyn-born artist who was never afraid of a little scandal.
You heard that the Central Library, across the plaza, was completed in 1941.
It was begun almost thirty years earlier, to a completely different design.
The first plan, by the architect Raymond Almirall, was a grand Beaux-Arts palace, with columns and domes, in the spirit of the arch and the Brooklyn Museum.
Work began before the First World War.
But money ran short, and construction stopped with only part of one wing built, along Flatbush Avenue.
For years, the unfinished hulk sat at the edge of the plaza.
In the 1930s, the library turned to new architects, Alfred Morton Githens and Francis Keally.
They built on what was already there, but threw out the Beaux-Arts design.
In its place they created the building you see: smooth pale stone, almost no ornament, and a facade that curves with the plaza, with nearly all the decoration gathered around the entrance.
The result is one of the city's great buildings of its era, part classical temple, part modern machine.
Look at how the walls rise in plain, flat planes, and how the tall entrance, with its gilded figures, glows against them.
It's as if the architects saved all their ornament for the one place where you walk in.
In the fall of 1999, the Brooklyn Museum found itself at war with the mayor of New York.
The museum was showing Sensation, an exhibition of young British artists from the collection of the advertising executive Charles Saatchi.

One work set off the fight: The Holy Virgin Mary, by Chris Ofili, a painting of a Black Madonna, adorned with a lump of elephant dung and surrounded by tiny collaged pictures cut from pornographic magazines.
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who hadn't seen the show, called it sick and disgusting.
He announced that unless the museum canceled the exhibition, the city would cut off its funding and try to evict it from its building, which the city owns.
The museum refused, and took the city to federal court.
In November 1999, a judge ruled that the city had violated the First Amendment by punishing the museum for the content of an exhibition, and ordered the funding restored.
Ofili, who was raised Catholic, said the dung, a material he used in many of his paintings, was not meant as an insult.
In December, a visitor slipped behind the painting's protective barrier and smeared white paint across it.
It was cleaned and went back on view.
All the controversy did what controversy usually does.
Crowds lined up around the block to see the show.
Every Labor Day, Eastern Parkway, the boulevard in front of the museum, becomes the stage for one of the largest street festivals in North America, the West Indian American Day Carnival.
Caribbean New Yorkers began holding carnival celebrations in Harlem in the 1940s, carrying on the pre-Lenten carnival of Trinidad and other islands.
In the late 1960s, as the Caribbean community grew in Crown Heights and Flatbush, the festival moved to Brooklyn, onto the wide parkway that Olmsted and Vaux designed.
Today the crowds number in the hundreds of thousands, and by some counts more than a million.
Masqueraders dance down the parkway in enormous costumes of feathers and sequins, some so big they ride on wheels, behind trucks stacked with speakers booming soca and calypso.
The air smells of jerk chicken, curry goat and roti from the stands along the route.
Before dawn that morning comes a second, wilder celebration, whose name comes from the French for daybreak.
Revelers covered in paint, powder and mud dance through the streets to steel bands until the sun comes up.
The steel pan, made from an oil drum, was invented in Trinidad in the twentieth century, and it's the national instrument there.
In the days before the parade, some of the best steel bands in New York, many of them with dozens of players, compete in a contest called Panorama, on the grounds behind the museum.
You heard that the Botanic Garden's cherry trees burst into bloom each spring.
The show lasts for weeks, because the garden grows dozens of kinds, and they take turns.
The earliest open in late March.
Next come the Yoshino cherries, with clouds of single, pale pink flowers that fade almost to white, the same kind that ring the Tidal Basin in Washington.
Among the last are the Kanzan cherries, with heavy, ruffled double flowers of deep pink, which bloom along the Cherry Esplanade, usually in late April.
Most of these trees produce little or no fruit worth eating.
They were bred in Japan, over centuries, for their flowers alone.
In Japan, the custom of hanami, flower viewing, goes back more than a thousand years.
People gather under the blossoms to picnic, drink and write poems, and the brief life of the flowers became a symbol of the beauty of passing things.
The exact timing depends on the weather.
A warm March brings the blossoms early, and a cold spring holds them back, so the garden tracks the bloom tree by tree on its website.
Scientists watch those dates closely too.

In Kyoto, records of the blossoms go back more than a thousand years, to court diaries and poems, and in recent decades the trees there have bloomed earlier than at almost any time in that long record, a sign of a warming climate.
As you may have heard on the Central Park North tour, the last ice age scraped its way across Manhattan.
Here in Brooklyn is where it stopped, and the park's hills are what it left behind.
About twenty thousand years ago, a sheet of ice, in places more than a thousand feet thick, covered New England and New York down to about here.
As it crept south, it scraped up rock, sand and soil and pushed them along like a giant bulldozer.
Where the ice reached its limit and began to melt, it dropped that load, building a long, rough ridge of sand, gravel, clay and boulders.
Geologists call it a terminal moraine.
This one, the Harbor Hill Moraine, runs across Staten Island, through Brooklyn and Queens, and out along the spine of Long Island.
You're standing on it.
The park's hills, including its highest point, Lookout Hill, and the ridge the Americans tried to defend in 1776 are all part of the moraine, and so are the hills of Green-Wood Cemetery, nearby.
South of the moraine, rivers of meltwater spread sand and gravel into a broad, flat plain, which is why Flatbush and the rest of southern Brooklyn are so level.
As the ice melted away, the sea rose and flooded the lowlands, shaping the harbor and the bays around Brooklyn.
The ice also left behind boulders carried from far to the north, called erratics.
Keep an eye out for big, lonely rocks around the park.
Olmsted and Vaux put all of it to work.
The Long Meadow rolls over gentler ground, the Ravine cuts into the moraine's steep slopes, and the lake spreads across the flatter land to the south.
Somewhere in the park's woods, behind a fence, is a place few visitors ever see: a cemetery that's older than the park itself.
It's the Friends Cemetery, a burial ground of the Quakers, the Religious Society of Friends, laid out in the 1840s, when this was still farmland.
When the park was created, the cemetery was allowed to stay, and the park grew up around it.
It's still a working cemetery, run by the Quakers, and it's closed to the public, though the park has occasionally offered tours.
In keeping with the Quaker tradition of plainness, the gravestones are small, simple and much alike, with no grand monuments to show who was rich and who was poor.
Its best-known grave belongs to the actor Montgomery Clift, the star of A Place in the Sun and From Here to Eternity.
Along with Marlon Brando and James Dean, Clift helped bring a new, raw and intensely emotional style of acting to the movies, and he was nominated for four Academy Awards.
A car crash in 1956 scarred his face, and his health declined.
He died in 1966, at forty-five.
So as you cross the meadow, remember that the park has a quiet neighbor inside its own borders, one that was here first.
By the 1970s, Prospect Park was in trouble.
The city was nearly bankrupt, and the parks department lost much of its budget and staff.
Buildings were vandalized and closed, the woods were eroding, and many Brooklynites stayed away, afraid of crime.
In 1980, the city appointed Tupper Thomas as the park's first administrator, a new job created so that one person would be responsible for the whole park.
She stayed for more than thirty years.

In 1987, she and a group of supporters founded the Prospect Park Alliance, a private nonprofit that raises money from neighbors, foundations and businesses, and works with the city to care for the park.
The model came from Manhattan, where the Central Park Conservancy had shown, a few years earlier, how private money could help bring a public park back.
The Alliance and the city have since restored much of the park, from the Boathouse to the woods of the Ravine, and today the park counts millions of visits a year.
The arrangement has its critics.
They point out that parks in wealthy neighborhoods can raise far more private money than parks in poor ones, and they worry that this widens the gap between them.
Supporters answer that without the Alliance, this park might never have recovered.
You heard that the British slipped around the American lines through the Jamaica Pass, guided by local loyalists.
The best-known account of that night comes from a boy.

On the evening of August 26th, 1776, some ten thousand British soldiers set off quietly from Flatlands, heading east and then north through the darkness, with General William Howe and General Henry Clinton at their head.
Near the pass stood a tavern called Howard's Half-Way House.
In the small hours of the morning, British officers woke the tavern keeper, William Howard, and his teenage son, and ordered them to guide the army through the hills.
Years later, the son told the story.
General Howe, he said, asked for a glass of liquor at the bar, and then told his father that he had no choice: he must show them the way.
They led the column along a narrow road through the pass.
There, the British found only five young American officers on horseback, keeping watch, and captured them without a shot.
By morning, the British were behind the American lines.
At about nine o'clock, signal guns fired, and the attack came from front and rear at once.
How much of the Howard story is exactly right, no one can say.
The son was a boy at the time, and he told it many years later.
But the night march itself is well documented, and it won the battle.
You heard that the Lefferts family, like many Dutch families in Brooklyn, held people in slavery.
Kings County, as Brooklyn was called, was one of the strongholds of slavery in the North.
In the first federal census, in 1790, roughly a third of the people living in Kings County were enslaved, a larger share than anywhere else in New York State.
On the farms of Flatbush, many, perhaps most, white households held at least one enslaved person.
They did much of the work of these farms: plowing, planting and harvesting, cooking and cleaning, and driving wagons of produce to the ferry for the markets of Manhattan.
Their names survive mostly as first names in wills, account books and census lists.
The war offered some of them a way out.

The British promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped from rebel masters to their lines, and when the British army left New York in 1783, it carried away thousands of Black Loyalists, men, women and children, some of them from Brooklyn, to new lives in Nova Scotia and beyond.
The Lefferts household was among them, and the museum in the house works to tell their stories as fully as the records allow.
As you may have heard on the East Village tour, New York ended slavery slowly, and the last enslaved New Yorkers were freed only in 1827.
Afterward, free Black Brooklynites built communities of their own.
The best known, Weeksville, which you may have heard about on the Central Park North tour, grew up about two miles east of here.
Some of the most American foods have Dutch names, and on a farm like the Lefferts', you might have eaten them all.
The Dutch called a little cake a koekje, and New Yorkers turned it into cookie.
Their cabbage salad, koolsla, became coleslaw.
Wafels became waffles, and crullers, twisted strips of fried dough, take their name from a Dutch word for a curl.
The Dutch also fried balls of sweet dough in hot fat and called them olykoeks, oily cakes, among the ancestors of the American doughnut.
The farms of Flatbush fed the growing city.
They grew wheat, corn and rye, potatoes and cabbages, and their produce went by wagon to the Brooklyn ferries and across the river to Manhattan's markets.
Dutch ways lasted long after English rule began.
Families in Flatbush spoke Dutch at home into the 1800s, kept Dutch Bibles, and worshipped at the Flatbush Reformed Dutch Church, about a mile south of here, whose congregation dates to 1654.
The Dutch left words beyond the kitchen, too.
The stoop of a Brooklyn brownstone comes from stoep, and boss comes from baas, master.
So when you eat a cookie or a spoonful of coleslaw, you're speaking a little Dutch, the language these farmhouses knew.
Prospect Park is one of the best places in New York to watch birds, and the busiest seasons are spring and fall.
The park lies along the Atlantic Flyway, one of the great migration routes of North America.
Each spring, millions of birds fly north along the coast by night, and at dawn, tired and hungry, they drop down wherever they can find trees, water and insects.
In a city of concrete, Prospect Park's woods are an oasis.
In May, the Ravine and the shores of the Lullwater can fill with warblers, tiny songbirds in yellows, oranges and blues, on their way from Central and South America to forests farther north.
More than two hundred kinds of birds have been seen in the park.
In winter, ducks arrive from the north and gather on the lake, and red-tailed hawks hunt over the meadows all year.
Not every bird has been welcome.
In January 2009, a flock of Canada geese knocked out both engines of an airliner leaving LaGuardia Airport, and its pilot glided it down onto the Hudson River, where everyone aboard survived.
Afterward, officials set out to reduce the number of geese near the city's airports.
Early one morning in July 2010, federal wildlife workers rounded up several hundred geese on Prospect Park's lake, and killed them.
Many Brooklynites were outraged.
They held vigils by the lake, and some argued that geese in a park miles from the runways posed little danger.
The debate over how to share the city with its geese still goes on.
Near the Boathouse, look for a strange tree: low, gnarled and weeping, its twisted branches spreading like a great umbrella over a knotted trunk.
It's the Camperdown Elm, planted here in 1872, and it was saved by a poem.

Every Camperdown elm descends from a single odd tree found in Scotland in the early 1800s, on the estate of the Earl of Camperdown, near Dundee: a wych elm whose branches grew down and sideways instead of up.
Gardeners copy it by grafting branches onto the upright trunk of an ordinary elm, which is why the tree looks like an upside-down umbrella.
By the 1960s, like much of the park, the tree was in bad shape: rotting, cracked and neglected.
Then the poet Marianne Moore came to its defense.
She was one of the great poets of her century, with a Pulitzer Prize to her name, and she was known around town for her tricorn hat and black cape.
Moore lived in Brooklyn for decades, in Fort Greene, and she loved the borough, its parks and, famously, the Brooklyn Dodgers.
In 1967 she published a poem called The Camperdown Elm, in The New Yorker, praising the tree's strange beauty and warning that it was dying.
She called it our crowning curio, and said that we must save it.
The poem worked.
Admirers raised money, tree surgeons filled its cavities and braced its limbs, and the elm has been cared for ever since.
It's still here, more than a century and a half after it was planted.
You heard that the Cleft Ridge Span, near the lake, is one of the earliest concrete structures in the country.

In the 1870s, concrete was still a new and experimental building material in America, and this bridge was built with a French version of it, called Béton Coignet, after François Coignet, the industrialist who promoted it.
The builders cast it in molds, like a cake, and the molds gave the blocks their patterns.
Ornament that would have taken a stone carver weeks could be turned out again and again.

The American company that sold the material, the New York and Long Island Coignet Stone Company, built its own headquarters near the Gowanus Canal in 1872 and 1873, out of the same stuff, as a kind of advertisement.
It's one of the oldest concrete buildings in the city.
It still stands, at Third Avenue and Third Street, restored and protected as a landmark beside a supermarket, and you can see it if you walk on toward the canal.
A century and a half later, it's hard to imagine a city without concrete.
This modest bridge, and that little building in Gowanus, are among the places where New York's concrete age began.
You heard that two airliners collided over Staten Island on December 16th, 1960, and that one of them fell here.
Here's how investigators worked out what happened.
It was a gray, snowy morning, and both planes were flying through clouds, guided by radio beacons and by air traffic controllers.
The United jet, a new DC-8 from Chicago, was bound for Idlewild, now Kennedy Airport.
The TWA plane, a propeller-driven Super Constellation from Ohio, was headed for LaGuardia.
Controllers had told the United jet to stop at a point in the sky and circle there until it was cleared to land.
It never stopped.
The jet flew on, miles beyond that limit, into the path of the TWA plane.
In Park Slope, its wreckage set fire to a row of buildings, including the Pillar of Fire Church, and firefighters fought the flames for hours in the snow.
Why?
Early in the flight, the United crew had reported that one of their two navigation radio receivers wasn't working, and the airline later argued that a ground beacon the crew relied on was unreliable.
The government's Civil Aeronautics Board put the blame on the flight itself: it had gone beyond its clearance limit and out of the airspace it had been given.
The investigators had a new tool.
The United jet carried a flight data recorder, a sealed box that logged its speed, altitude and heading.
This crash is remembered as the first in which investigators relied on a recorder like that to work out what happened.
It helped show how far, and how fast, the jet had gone.
Today such recorders are required on airliners.
They're called black boxes, though they're painted bright orange, so they can be found in the wreckage.
You heard that members of the Park Slope Food Coop work shifts in exchange for the right to shop there.
Here's how that works.

Every adult member works a shift of two hours and forty-five minutes, once every four weeks: unloading trucks, stocking shelves, bagging nuts and grains from bulk bins, running a register, or cleaning.
Only members may shop, and there are many thousands of them.
Because the members supply most of the labor, the coop can sell its food for much less than ordinary stores.
The coop takes its rules seriously.
Miss a shift, and you owe make-up shifts, and if you fall far enough behind, you can lose your shopping privileges until you've caught up.
It's also famous for its democracy.
Members debate everything, from plastic bags to boycotts, at monthly general meetings, and in the coop's own newspaper, the Linewaiters' Gazette.
The shelves lean toward organic produce, much of it from farms in the region.
So the next time you see a Park Slope neighbor carrying groceries home, it may be someone who stocked those very shelves.
You heard that the Maryland soldiers charged under Lord Stirling.
He was an American general with a Scottish title that Britain never recognized.
He was born William Alexander, in New York City, in 1726, the son of a Scottish-born lawyer and a successful merchant.
He grew rich in trade, and in supplying British troops in the French and Indian War.
He believed he was the rightful heir to a dormant Scottish title, the Earl of Stirling, and sailed to Britain to claim it.
A Scottish jury agreed, but the House of Lords refused to recognize the claim.
He came home and called himself Lord Stirling anyway, and most Americans went along.
He lived like a lord, too, on a grand estate in Basking Ridge, New Jersey, and ran up enormous debts.
When the Revolution came, he sided with the patriots and became a general.
At the Battle of Brooklyn, he commanded the American right, along the Gowanus road.
When the British flank march trapped his men, he saw that their only escape was across the Gowanus marsh, and he led the Marylanders forward against the British at this house to buy them time.
When the attacks failed, he reportedly refused to surrender to the British, and gave his sword instead to the Hessian commander, General von Heister.
He was exchanged for a British prisoner, went back to war, and served with distinction at Trenton and at Monmouth.
He died in Albany in January 1783, a few months before the peace treaty was signed.
You heard that most of the Maryland Four Hundred were killed or captured here.
Where the dead were buried is still a mystery.
They belonged to the First Maryland Regiment, among the best-drilled troops in the army.
Their colonel, William Smallwood, was away in Manhattan that day, sitting on a court-martial, so Major Mordecai Gist led them into the fight.
After the battle, the fallen were buried hastily, near where they fell.
According to tradition, the Marylanders were laid in six long trenches dug in a farm field, in an area that later became Third Avenue, just a few blocks west of here.
One local historian has spent years combing old records and maps, and by his count, more than two hundred fifty Marylanders may lie there.
Since then, the ground has been farmed, filled, paved and built over, with houses, factories, garages and warehouses.
In 2017, before a lot on 9th Street, between Third and Fourth Avenues, could become a school, the state ordered an archaeological dig.
Archaeologists found a well, a cistern, a privy and part of the brick wall of an old farmhouse, along with nineteenth century trash, but no soldiers.
The searchers haven't given up.
They've called for ground-penetrating radar to look under the pavement nearby, and for care whenever the ground in the area is opened up.
So far, the trenches have not been found.
The Marylanders do have a monument: a column in Prospect Park, at the foot of Lookout Hill, put up in their honor in the 1890s.
So as you walk toward the canal, remember that somewhere under these streets, perhaps beneath your feet, lie some of the first soldiers to die for the newly declared United States.
Gowanus has collected a few good stories over the years.
Start with the name.
It's usually said to come from Gouwane, a Lenape leader who lived along the creek when the Dutch arrived.
Then the oysters.
In colonial times, Gowanus oysters were famous, and they were said to be shipped across the Atlantic as a delicacy.
Some accounts claim they grew as big as dinner plates.
The size may have grown in the telling, but the oysters were real, and celebrated, until pollution and overharvesting wiped out the beds.
The water that the old flushing tunnel pumps into the canal comes from Buttermilk Channel, between Brooklyn and Governors Island, and that name has two stories.
In one, the channel was once so shallow that at low tide, cows could wade across it to graze on the island.
In the other, farm women rowing milk to the Manhattan markets found that the rough water had churned it into buttermilk by the time they landed.
Neither has been proven, and both have been told for a very long time.
And one story from our own time is entirely true.
In April 2007, a young minke whale swam up the Gowanus Canal, one of the most polluted waterways in the country.
Crowds gathered on the bridges, and New Yorkers named it Sludgie.
Rescuers hoped it would find its way back out to sea, but it died before it could get out.

In October 1907, an attempt to corner the stock of a copper company collapsed, and the men behind it turned out to be tied to some of the city's trust companies, the lightly regulated cousins of banks.
Depositors panicked.
On October 22nd, a run on the Knickerbocker Trust, on Fifth Avenue, drained about eight million dollars in three hours, and the bank shut its doors.
Weeks later its former president shot himself.
The United States had no central bank and no lender of last resort.
So the country turned to a seventy year old banker.
J. Pierpont Morgan directed the rescue from his offices here and from his library on Thirty Sixth Street.
He decided which institutions were worth saving and which were not.
He persuaded the Treasury Secretary to deposit government money in New York banks.

When brokers on the Stock Exchange could no longer borrow and the exchange itself was about to close early, he summoned the bank presidents and raised twenty five million dollars to lend on the floor in a matter of minutes.
The climax came on the first weekend of November.

Morgan gathered the heads of the trust companies in his library and, as the story goes, locked the door and pocketed the key, keeping them there until nearly dawn, when they agreed to put up twenty five million dollars to prop up their weakest members.

The same weekend, he arranged for United States Steel, the giant he had created, to buy a struggling company called Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad, whose shares were propping up loans at a teetering brokerage.
President Theodore Roosevelt agreed not to object on antitrust grounds.
It worked.
But Washington drew a lesson: no private citizen should ever again hold that much power over the nation's money.
Investigations followed, then a secret meeting of bankers and a senator on Jekyll Island, Georgia, in 1910, and finally the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.
Morgan died that same year.
The central bank his rescue made necessary sits a few blocks north of here, on Liberty Street.
Three moments on the floor of the exchange behind those columns.
October 24th, 1929, Black Thursday.
Prices are falling off a cliff.

In the early afternoon, Richard Whitney, the exchange's vice president and the floor broker for Morgan's bank, walks to the post where United States Steel trades and loudly bids two hundred five dollars a share for ten thousand shares, well above the last sale.
He moves from post to post placing similar orders on behalf of a pool of the city's biggest bankers.
For a day, the market steadies, and Whitney is a hero.
The next week the crash resumes anyway.
Whitney becomes president of the exchange in 1930.
Then, in 1938, it comes out that he has been stealing, from clients, from the New York Yacht Club, and from the exchange's own fund for the families of deceased members.
He goes to Sing Sing prison.
August 24th, 1967.
A group of young activists led by Abbie Hoffman joins a public tour, reaches the visitors' gallery above the floor, and showers the traders with dollar bills.
Trading stops as brokers scramble for the money, some cheering, some booing.
Soon afterward, the exchange enclosed the gallery behind glass.
December 28th, 1967.
Muriel Siebert, a broker who had been turned down by nine of the first ten men she asked to sponsor her application, buys a seat on the exchange for four hundred forty five thousand dollars.
She becomes the first woman member in its history, which by then was well over a century and a half long.
For years, she said, there was no women's restroom anywhere near the floor, until she pushed the exchange to install one.
The gallery where Hoffman stood was closed to the public after September 2001, and the floor is no longer open to tours.
But the building is still where the opening and closing bells ring every trading day.
The ground you are standing on was once the bed of the Hudson River, and the whole site is, in effect, a bathtub.
To build the original towers, engineers needed a deep basement below the water table, right beside the river.
They used a technique then rarely tried in America: they dug trenches in narrow sections down to bedrock, kept them from collapsing with a heavy clay slurry, then filled them with concrete.
The result was a continuous underground wall around the site, called the slurry wall.
After September 11th, engineers feared the wall would give way, because the basement floors that had braced it from inside were destroyed.
If it had, the river could have flooded the site and the train tunnels beneath it.
The wall held, while crews braced it again from the inside.
A section of it is now on view inside the September 11th museum, below the plaza.
The dig for the new site turned up something stranger.
In the summer of 2010, workers excavating near the southern edge of the site found the hull of a wooden ship, about thirty feet of it, buried more than twenty feet down.
It had been sunk on purpose, as part of the fill used to extend the shoreline in the late 1700s.
Scientists later studied the rings in its timbers and matched them with old trees and historic buildings in Philadelphia, including Independence Hall.
The oak for the ship had been cut around 1773, near Philadelphia.
The workers had found a merchant sloop from the era of the Revolution, used as rubbish to build land.
That's how most of lower Manhattan's western edge was made: ships, piers, and rubbish, sunk and filled and built over.
And the World Trade Center's own excavation, in the 1960s, provided the earth for the next extension: Battery Park City, which you can see to the west.
Underneath the plaza today run PATH trains, subway lines, and the corridors that connect them all to the Oculus.
The site is less a piece of ground than a deep, layered machine.
The engineers here were fascinated by sound: how we hear it, how we speak, and how a machine might do both.
In the 1920s, a physicist named Harvey Fletcher led research here into human hearing, measuring how loud sounds seem at different pitches, and working on hearing tests and hearing aids.
That work led toward stereo.

Fletcher's team worked with the Philadelphia Orchestra and its famous conductor, Leopold Stokowski, and in 1933 they carried a concert over telephone lines from Philadelphia to an audience at Constitution Hall in Washington, through three separate channels and three sets of loudspeakers, so that listeners could hear where each instrument was.
In 1940, they demonstrated stereo recordings at Carnegie Hall.
Another engineer, Homer Dudley, worked on taking speech apart.
Beginning in the late 1920s, he developed the vocoder, which broke a voice into its basic components so that it could be sent more efficiently and rebuilt at the other end.
Then he built a machine that could speak with no human voice at all: the Voder, shown at the 1939 World's Fair in Queens.
A trained operator played it like an organ, with keys and a foot pedal, and astonished crowds heard it say whole sentences.
The vocoder went to war.

During the Second World War, Bell Labs built its principles into a secret system called Sigsaly, which scrambled the telephone conversations of Allied leaders, including Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt, so the enemy couldn't listen in.
After the war, the vocoder found a second life in music, giving robotic voices to electronic and pop records, most famously those of the German band Kraftwerk.
So when you hear a synthesized voice on your phone, or a robot voice in a song, or music that seems to surround you from every side, you're hearing ideas that took shape in this building.

In the 1960s, two young men who had come up through the neighborhood's street gangs, Carlos Chino Garcia and Angelo Gonzalez, helped start an antipoverty group with a name that borrowed from President Johnson's programs: the Real Great Society.
In 1968 the group hosted a lecture by Buckminster Fuller, the inventor famous for the geodesic dome, a shelter built from a lattice of triangles that is light, cheap and astonishingly strong.
Some of the young men in the audience decided to build domes themselves.
In 1970, six of them formed a new group and named it with the first letters of their first names: Chino, Humberto, Angelo, Roy, Anthony and Sal.
That spells Charas.
Fuller's associate, Michael Ben-Eli, came down to teach them solid geometry and spherical trigonometry.
They worked out the math, cut and joined the struts, and raised their first dome on a vacant lot beneath the Manhattan Bridge.
A photographer named Syeus Mottel followed them for months, and his 1973 book, Charas: The Improbable Dome Builders, carried an introduction by Fuller himself.

In 1979 Charas leased an abandoned school, the old Public School 64 on East Ninth Street between Avenues B and C, and turned it into El Bohío, named for the thatched huts of the Puerto Rican countryside.
For two decades it held a theater, studios, classes and meeting rooms for the neighborhood.
Then, in 1998, the city auctioned the building to a developer who had given money to Mayor Giuliani's campaigns, and at the end of 2001 Charas was evicted.
The empty school, its murals painted over, became a symbol of everything the neighborhood felt it had lost, and the fight over its future went on for years.
You heard that publishers hired song pluggers to demonstrate their songs.
The job went far beyond the office piano.
Pluggers sang at the sheet music counters of department stores and five-and-dime stores, and wherever a crowd gathered.
The young George Gershwin left high school at fifteen to plug songs for the publisher Jerome Remick, for fifteen dollars a week, pounding a piano for hours a day.
Publishers also paid popular singers, in cash, gifts or a share of the royalties, to put their songs into their acts, an early form of what radio would later call payola.
The song that showed how much money there was in the business was After the Ball, a sentimental waltz by Charles K. Harris of Milwaukee.
Harris published it himself, a popular singer put it into a hit musical comedy, and it went on to sell millions of copies, an unheard-of number at the time.
After that, everyone wanted a piece of the trade, and publishers crowded onto this street, close to the theaters and the vaudeville booking offices.
For years, though, songwriters were paid only for printed music.
When a restaurant orchestra played their song, they got nothing.
In 1914, the composer Victor Herbert joined other songwriters and publishers to found Ascap, the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, to collect fees for public performance.
Herbert sued Shanley's, a Times Square restaurant whose musicians had performed his song Sweethearts.
The restaurant argued that diners paid for the food, not the music.
In 1917, the Supreme Court sided with Herbert.
Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that if music did not pay, it would be given up.
The fees that restaurants, stores and radio stations pay for the music they play trace back to that decision.
A few blocks from here, on Eighth Avenue at the corner of Carroll Street, stands a grand Romanesque mansion of brownstone and brick, built in 1888 for Thomas Adams Junior.
The money behind it came from chewing gum.
The story begins on Staten Island, with an exiled Mexican general, Antonio López de Santa Anna, the man who had led Mexico's army at the Alamo.
Living there in the late 1860s, Santa Anna had a supply of chicle, the dried sap of the sapodilla tree, which people in Mexico and Central America had chewed for centuries.
He hoped to sell it as a cheap substitute for rubber.
An inventor named Thomas Adams experimented with it for months, trying to turn it into rubber goods, and failed.
Then, as the story goes, Adams remembered that the stuff was meant for chewing.
He boiled the chicle, rolled it into little balls, and sold them in drugstores.
Chewing gum, made until then mostly from spruce resin or paraffin wax, had found its ideal material.
Adams went on to make Black Jack, a licorice-flavored gum, and Tutti-Frutti, sold from vending machines on the platforms of New York's elevated trains.
In 1899, his company joined other gum makers to form the American Chicle Company, whose brands later included Chiclets.
Santa Anna never saw a fortune from it.
He went home to Mexico, and died there, poor, in 1876.
His son, Thomas Adams Jr., helped run the business, and built the mansion on the proceeds.
Its architect was C. P. H. Gilbert, whose houses on Montgomery Place you heard about.
